News.title: What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe
News.content:
A resident who called 999 to report the three white vans in Whelford village said it was "pure luck" that she spotted the vehicles.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme the woman, who wishes to remain anonymous, said she arrived home to find the driveway and road blocked and saw a "large group of hooded and masked men".

"When they saw me they ran ahead of me - some into the field and some towards the neighbouring village of Kempsford. I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place," she added.

The woman told the programme she called the Ministry of Defence police at RAF Fairford but received no answer. She then rang 999 at 01:36 BST and said "within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police".

"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had."

"I am absolutely staggered that it was left to me as a member of the public to see and report this," she said.

"Someone really dropped the ball on this."

Another resident described the moment he said he saw police apprehend the suspects.

Jeff - who did not give his surname - told the BBC he heard "shouting outside his front door", although he could not be sure where it came from.

He said he then looked out of his window and saw "people being held by police outside".

News.title: Police block Protestant Orange Order from controversial parade route
News.content:
The police prevented an early morning attempt by the Orange Order to make a controversial parade down a road which had previously been blocked by protesters.

A group of men tried to march from Drumcree Church down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown in the early hours of Monday but a line of police Land Rovers stood in the way.

They had been unable to make the permitted parade on Sunday morning because protesters had gathered on the Garvaghy Road. The stand-off continued throughout Sunday, with the Orangemen waiting at the church, around a mile from the road, for the go-ahead from police.

Sinn FÃ©in First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined the protest, prompting Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson to accuse her of acting unlawfully.

The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in 30 years after a series of legal challenges.

Since 1998, the Orange Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes.

The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation, while the area where it wants to walk - specifically along the Garvaghy Road - is largely Catholic and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists.

News.title: Watch: BBC team takes cover as Houthi drone spotted on Yemen front-line
News.content:
In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone, the BBC has travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where the Houthi control ends and no man's land begins.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.

From the front-line a drone is heard above, which a soldier accompanying the crew in south-western Yemen said is usually followed by an attack.

Within about 10 minutes, after the crew had driven away, the loud thuds of strikes followed, senior international investigations correspondent Nawal Al-Maghafi reports.

News.title: Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras
News.content:
Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal.

These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones, as well as track criminals.

Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor.

We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved.

Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks.

The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it.

The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition.

News.title: My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die
News.content:
The empty building that used to be the home of Marks & Spencer in Aberdeen is one of the first things you see when you arrive off the train and come into the city centre. The sign has gone, though the shape of the lettering can still be made out; the windows are blacked out and the doors boarded up.

This is my hometown. As a teenager, I spent hours on Union Street, its main thoroughfare, nicknamed the Granite Mile after the local silver-grey stone. It was the place to try on all the latest fashions from the likes of Clockhouse and Chelsea Girl.

The street used to be packed with shoppers from across the north-east of Scotland.

Now, it's pockmarked with empty shops.

"I come to Union Street to take a bus somewhere else... there's nothing to shop for nowâ¦ it's horrendous," complains Marie Sim, a lifelong Aberdeen resident.

It's a similar story across the country: High Streets, once bursting with shops, hit first by the rise of out-of-town retail centres and then by online commerce.

But Aberdeen is in the thick of an ambitious turnaround plan. The port city has essentially declared war on its empty shop problem, taking an unusually hands-on approach to filling vacant units and bringing long-neglected upper floors of buildings into use.

News.title: Felled Sycamore Gap stump has 'encouraging' growth
News.content:
The stump of the iconic Sycamore Gap tree is showing "encouraging" signs with a thick ring of new shoots growing around it, three years on from its illegal felling.

The landmark on Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland was targeted on 28 September 2023 by Daniel Graham and Adam Carruthers, who travelled during a storm from their homes in Cumbria to cut it down.

Their actions sparked widespread outrage and the pair were later jailed for criminal damage to the Victorian-planted tree and Roman wall.

Site owners the National Trust fenced off the stump to see if it would recover, with general manager Andrew Poad saying he is "filled with hope by the way nature is taking its course".

He said: "These flourishing shoots are really encouraging and show the special measures we've taken, including reducing soil compaction around the roots and limiting human disturbance, are paying off."

Poad said the trust was grateful to visitors supporting their efforts to give the tree "the best possible chance to thrive".

He added: "We're monitoring the tree closely and, over time, our rangers will manage it depending on how it develops."

News.title: Angela Scanlon takes over Sara Cox's drivetime slot on Radio 2
News.content:
Angela Scanlon is to take over BBC Radio 2's drivetime show after Sara Cox moved to the breakfast slot.

The Irish personality said it was "properly exciting" to be hosting the station's 16:00-19:00 show every weekday from November.

She said: "Millions of people, all having completely different days, piling into the same conversation for a few hours - what a strange and lovely thing!"

Scanlon, who hosted a Sunday early morning programme on the station from 2018 to 2021, was among a number of people who filled in after Cox vacated the drivetime slot in May, including Joel Dommett, Jason Manford, Ellie Taylor, Alex Jones and Gary Davies.

Scanlon is also known for The One Show, This Morning, Your Home Made Perfect, The Apprentice: Unfinished Business, and for taking part in Strictly Come Dancing in 2023.

News.title: Watch: Madonna and Taylor Swift win big at the MTV VMAs
News.content:
Taylor Swift, Madonna, and LISA were among the big winners at the MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs) on Sunday evening in downtown Los Angeles.

Madonna performed at the awards show for the first time in more than 20 years, and took home a handful of awards including artist of the year.

Meanwhile, Taylor Swift was awarded the first-ever Artist Director Honor and also scooped the night's top award, video of the year.

News.title: More questions than answers after major incident near RAF Fairford
News.content:
But some eyes, too, have turned to Moscow.

Danish intelligence warned last week Russia could in the coming months launch a limited military attack on a Nato country.

Germany has already formally accused Russia of using a drone carrying explosives in an attempted attack on Leipzig in August.

Over the summer, the Russian embassy in London warned the UK against allowing Ukraine to use British drones deep inside Russian territory: "The deeper [the UK's] involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv's terrorist machinery, the higher price it will pay."

That, too, was seen as a direct threat.

There are also possibilities of some kind of Islamist attack, or even an incident of direct action by a group opposed to both the US-Israeli war on Iran or the use of UK bases to launch strikes.

One central question is whether the authorities were prepared for such an attack.

The US handles security within the base; the UK is responsible all threats outside the perimeter. What did the authorities know?

President Trump said the suspects had been under investigation "for a long time".

But there are also suggestions the incident was foiled only because a passing driver reported strange vans to the police.

At the time of the explicit Iranian threat against the UK, a spokesman for the Ministry of Defence said: "Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it's on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself."

So for now, there remain more questions that facts.

Was a hostile foreign state involved, or were proxies acting on its behalf? What was intended and what was the potential risk to local people?

One thing is clear: the threat from conflicts involving the UK will not always stay overseas.

News.title: Healey to promise 'new age of industrialisation' for UK in conference speech
News.content:
John Healey will promise "a new age of industrialisation" for the UK, when he delivers his first Labour conference speech as chancellor on Monday.

Healey will tell delegates "our coal mines are not coming back", but that Labour will remake Britain's industrial past "for the modern age" by backing advanced manufacturing.

He will also announce plans to boost Britain's shipbuilding industry, with new orders for Royal Navy floating docks and a maritime research vessel.

With just a month to go until his first Budget, the chancellor is under pressure to cut spending or raise taxes to tackle the ballooning cost of government borrowing.

But he is not expected to reveal any details about his Budget plans in his speech at Labour's annual conference in Liverpool.

Instead, he will attempt to set out a positive vision for the future of British industry, based around what he will call a "new confidence in Britain".

The former defence secretary will announce that three new floating docks at HM Royal Naval Base Clyde, at Faslane, will be built in the UK, rather than put out to international tender.

Plans for the new docks were first set out in 2023 and are expected to upgrade Faslane's facilities for the next generation of British submarines.

The docks form part of a wider Â£15bn upgrade programme for the Royal Navy's shipyards and are expected to come into service in the early 2030s.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC Breakfast on Monday that the floating docks were an example of investing in defence to build "more jobs and opportunities" in the UK.

It comes as the government is under pressure to reach spending of 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Increasing investment in defence does come with choices and trade-offs - and I would argue very strongly that in the dangerous and turbulent world we find ourselves in, investment in defence is a price worth paying," Streeting added.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said in a speech on Sunday that the government would also commission a new marine research vessel as part of plans for a "new era of reindustrialisation".

The chancellor is expected to announce Â£115m in funding for the ship, which is also set to come into service in the early 2030s.

Ahead of his speech, Healey said: "By backing British shipyards, we are not only boosting national security but also securing resilience in the industries that will drive growth today while building the capabilities the country needs for the future."

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the plans were "reheated announcements" with "no clarity on where the money is coming from".

He added: "Labour are running scared of making the tough choices needed to pay for Britain's defence.

"All they can offer is reannounced docks and more hot air from Healey. Only the Conservatives will cut the welfare bill to fund defence."

Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, national secretary of the GMB union, which has campaigned for the move, said it would be a "massive boost" for the UK's shipbuilding sector.

"For too long juicy contracts have been sent to overseas - often subsidised - yards.

"This policy could reinvigorate UK yards and the communities that depend on them," he added.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who is due to deliver his big conference speech on Tuesday - has previously spoken about his ambition to "reindustrialise" Britain, including in talks last week with US President Donald Trump.

But in a survey to be published on Monday, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) will highlight falling economic activity across key sectors such as retail and services in the three months to September, with manufacturing declining more moderately.

CBI deputy chief economist Alpesh Paleja said rising energy and employment costs combined with weak demand were continuing to put pressure on profit margins.

He added: "Uncertainty ahead of next month's Budget is also holding back activity in some sectors.

"Against the backdrop of renewed fiscal pressures, the Budget must draw a clear red line under any more rises in the cost of hiring, investing and doing business."

The chancellor is also under pressure from some of Labour's trade union backers to do more to tackle the cost of living.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, has called on Healey to "do something for workers and the working class" in his Budget.

She urged him to unfreeze income tax thresholds "to put money back into people's pockets" and take further action on energy bills.

In his conference speech, Healey will also announce plans to bring back a training scheme run by trade unions, to help workers in England gain new skills and adapt as technology, including AI, changes the workplace.

The Union Learning Fund will get Â£15m in taxpayers' money, taken from existing government budgets.

Employees do not need to be union members to benefit, with support options ranging from essential English, maths and digital skills, to training for jobs in growing industries, such as advanced manufacturing.

News.title: Late September warmth before wind and rain return this week
News.content:
A vast area of low pressure in the Atlantic is set to draw warm south to south-easterly winds across the UK early this week, but for some rain will not be far behind.

Tuesday looks as if it will be the warmest day and after that temperatures will generally return closer to the September average.

Much of the UK can also expect a spell of wetter and windier weather from the approaching depression, with the most unsettled conditions likely to affect Scotland, Northern Ireland and western parts of England and Wales.

However, many central, southern and eastern areas of England, which have been affected by drought, may see far less rain.

News.title: Avanti West Coast services to be nationalised from March
News.content:
Avanti West Coast train services will be nationalised from March next year, the government has announced.

"For years, we've heard stories of Avanti underperforming, with passengers left paying the price. Enough is enough," Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said.

The move is part of a government plan to improve rail infrastructure, cut train delays and improve experiences for passengers.

Avanti West Coast's managing director said he was "proud of what we've achieved over the last six years". The company's contract was due to come to an end on 7 March.

In a post on social media, Prime Minister Andy Burnham echoed Alexander's comments.

"For years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti's cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again," he said.

Avanti West Coast runs key routes through northern England and into Scotland, including services between Glasgow and Edinburgh and London Euston. It also runs a service between London and Wales, to Holyhead.

Andy Mellors, managing director at Avanti West Coast, said the company has refurbished its Pendolino fleet and has introduced new Evero trains, to run "more services than ever before".

He added: "Over the coming months, we'll work closely with the government to ensure a seamless transition into public ownership while remaining focused on delivering for our customers and communities."

In May, Avanti West Coast said one-in-seven rail services will be cut on its busiest routes following a government request to reduce spending.

The company - a joint venture between FirstGroup (70%) and Italian state operator Trenitalia (30%) - predicted the move would cause minimum disruption to passengers and not reduce revenues.

Companies such as Avanti West Coast have their finances heavily influenced by the Department for Transport (DfT) due to contracts introduced in March 2020 at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.

All train services operated under DfT contracts are being transferred to public ownership.

Great Western Railway - which is owned by FirstGroup - is to be brought under public ownership in December.

Several rail firms around the country are already publicly owned, including Great Anglia and South Western Railway. Welsh services were nationalised in 2021 and Scotland took trains into public ownership the following year.

News.title: Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England
News.content:
Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election.

The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.

Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this.

Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's and died earlier this month.

While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded.

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work.

"There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush."

Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing.

News.title: Ten NHS staff removed over Noah Woods data breach
News.content:
Ten NHS staff have been removed from duty or suspended following a data breach involving the digital medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods.

Launching an "urgent" investigation, Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said any unauthorised access of patient data was "completely unacceptable".

The trust has apologised "unreservedly" to Noah's family and said disciplinary action would be taken if needed.

A major search for Noah was carried out in the village of Brantham, Suffolk, after the child went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in a nearby pond by police divers.

A spokesperson for the trust said 10 employees had been "removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded".

It comes after Sir Jim Mackey, the chief executive of NHS England, wrote to every trust on Friday, ordering stronger measures to tackle data breaches.

"We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough," said Sir Jim.

"Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient's record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record."

News.title: More than 50 arrested at Palestine Action support rally
News.content:
Merseyside Police said more than 50 people had so far been detained at the Defend Our Juries event and that officers were in the process of making arrests on suspicion of wearing/carrying an article supporting a proscribed organisation.

A force spokesperson said it respected everyone's rights to protest lawfully while also aiming to keep the peace and ensure public safety.

The force said it made "detailed and co-ordinated plans ahead of such events to ensure it can apply this consistently, fairly and proportionately".

The spokesperson said not everyone present at the protest had been committing a criminal offence.

The arrests were criticised by Amnesty International, which called them a "shameful attack on freedom of speech".

One of those detained was human rights barrister Margaret Owen, 94.

A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries said: "We had hoped the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, would do the sensible thing and bin the ban on Palestine Action given the weight of public pressure to do so and the escalating amount of resources required in enforcing it.

"Continuing the charade of the proscription of Palestine Action is illogical, unsustainable and immoral."

News.title: The four 'what next?' scenarios for Premier League after Man City ruling
News.content:
If you were getting the impression that the saga over Manchester City's 115 charges was almost over, think again.

Two years and 10 days since the hearing began, and 1,329 days after City were charged, we now know a verdict has been reached, with the club guilty of the majority of financial rule breaches.

That is not because the Premier League or Manchester City have told us - it is thanks to the Athletic finding out and breaking the story., external

BBC Sport was later told the verdict was sent during the week to club executives, who had to sign a non-disclosure agreement to open the file.

A process can appear to be completely watertight, as this one certainly had been, but when the circle of trust is expanded, the chance of information getting out increases.

Despite this, public silence from the Premier League continues.

City did not address whether they had been found guilty in a statement making it clear - with an appeal expected - that the "process remains ongoing" from their point of view.

It all points to the suggestion that the long-awaited decision of the independent panel was not a case of this process nearing an end, but perhaps instead reaching the end of the beginning.

It appears the chaos and uncertainty is only going to increase now.

City fans, and the rest of football, are left to guess what the punishment might be. And when this all might reach a definitive conclusion.

The charges are so serious that some form of points deduction now appears inevitable, subject to the appeal by City, who have always insisted they have done nothing wrong.

When and how any punishment is applied will be crucial not just for City, but the Premier League as a whole.

And that's before we get to the prospect of clubs suing City for compensation.

Enzo Maresca's side go to Liverpool on 11 October when the Premier League resumes after the international break. They could go six points clear at the top. But is that now rendered meaningless?

Let's look at possible scenarios - none of which are particularly appealing.

UK households should keep small supplies of cash, bottled water and tinned food at home in case of emergency or war, the Defence Secretary has warned.

Wes Streeting said Britain faces a growing threat of being disrupted by fires, floods, and enemy attacks, including cyber warfare.

He called for a "whole society approach" to strengthen national resilience, though he insisted people should remain "alert not alarmed" regarding potential risks.

Speaking to The Sun ahead of the Labour Party conference, he said: "It’s just a simple ask of people.

"Do they have what they need indoors, should they lose access to their online banking for a period? Should they have a power cut?”

open image in gallery British households are being advised to stock up on tinned food. ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

It comes as the government releases a list of supplies for an emergency kit they say everyone should keep at home.

Here we look at the key items you should stock up on on in case disaster strikes.

What should people stockpile?

Wes Streeting has advised the British public there are certain items they should store for emergencies.

He said: "These are basic things, and of course, you know, a lot of people just have that in their cupboard naturally.

"It’s having some cash at home, having a supply of bottled water indoors, having some tinned goods that you can access if your electric goes and you’re not able to cook on the hob or in the microwave.”

Nutritionists and “preppers” on social media also say people should consider intake of carbohydrates and protein, and so suggest items such as oats, rice and pasta be included in any stockpile.

Kidney beans, peanut butter and tinned fish provide high levels of protein.

open image in gallery The government has asked people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water. ( Getty/iStock )

What should I keep in my emergency kit?

The government says people should put together an emergency kit that includes key provisions you and your household would need during a short-term emergency lasting several days, such as a power failure or a disruption to your water supply.

Recommended emergency kit supplies include:

A battery or wind-up torch – torches are safer than candles.

– torches are safer than candles. A portable power bank for charging your mobile phone.

for charging your mobile phone. A battery or wind-up radio to get updates during a power cut – a car radio can be used, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside.

– a car radio can be used, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside. Spare batteries for torches and radio and a backup battery for any medical equipment you rely on.

for torches and radio and a backup battery for any medical equipment you rely on. A first aid kit (or some first aid items) including items such as waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers.

including items such as waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers. Hand sanitiser and wet wipes for hygiene purposes when the water is off.

for hygiene purposes when the water is off. Bottled water – there is no standard figure for this as emergencies can vary in duration and people use different amounts. A minimum of 2.5-3 litres of drinking water per person per day is recommended by the World Health Organisation for survival. 10 litres per person per day will make you more comfortable by also providing for basic cooking and hygiene needs. Additional water might be needed to make up baby formula, for medical devices and for pets.

A minimum of 2.5-3 litres of drinking water per person per day is recommended by the World Health Organisation for survival. 10 litres per person per day will make you more comfortable by also providing for basic cooking and hygiene needs. Additional water might be needed to make up baby formula, for medical devices and for pets. Non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking, such as ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables (and a tin opener). As with water, how much you need will vary based on your own circumstances. Don’t forget food for pets.

that doesn’t need cooking, such as ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables (and a tin opener). As with water, how much you need will vary based on your own circumstances. Don’t forget food for pets. Baby supplies such as nappies and baby formula – ready made or ‘ready-to-feed’ formula is best as you may not be able to boil water or sterilise bottles.

Rather than buying all the items at once, you could just add to your emergency kit when you are able and build it up over time. You should try to store these items together in a single location your home, ideally in a spot that remains simple to locate if the lights are off.

open image in gallery Keep some batteries, a radio, a torch and tinned food in your emergency kit at home. ( Getty Images )

Maintaining a supply of prescription medication to cover several days is also essential. For those who depend on any medical devices or equipment, ensure that printed physical copies of all operating instructions are kept on hand. Furthermore, any available back-up batteries ought to be kept fully charged at all times.

What threats is the government worried about?

Andy Burnham’s government is focusing on national resilience in the wake of threats from Russia.

The government is also concerned following the record-breaking heatwaves the UK has experienced this summer, plunging the country into drought and causing numerous wildfires.

According to the FT, the government is accelerating work on its “war book” – a manual for the defence of the nation against external threats – as well as a social media campaign with advice to help people to deal with the impacts of extreme weather.

It also updated its national risk register last month, with the risk of interference in the UK’s democratic process added to it.

open image in gallery Vladimir Putin’s government warned that British facilities in Ukraine will be considered “legitimate targets” if they are used to support long-range strikes against Russia. ( AFP/Getty )

The national risk register is the government’s assessment of the most significant risks facing the UK.

It is a planning tool designed to help professionals prepare for risks and is not intended to be a prediction of future events.

Vladimir Putin’s government recenty warned that British facilities in Ukraine will be considered “legitimate targets” if they are used to support long-range strikes against Russia.

The Independent also reported that rogue drones are targeting Britain’s military bases almost daily, leaving the UK vulnerable to growing threats from Russia and Iran.

Some 340 security incidents involving drones were reported at or near Ministry of Defence sites in the year to August 2026, data obtained under freedom of information laws show. In 2025, there were a total of 250 incidents recorded – double the 126 recorded the year before.

open image in gallery The Government also plans to advise people on how to deal with the impacts of extreme weather ( Getty )

Why are the heatwaves a concern?

Analysts have warned extreme heat and ongoing droughts are putting Britain at risk of its “worst food security crisis in decades”.

The knock-on impact of five back-to-back heatwaves and prolonged dry conditions could destroy farmers’ harvests, leading to food shortages later this year and increasing reliance on foreign imports, according to analysts from the investment bank Shore Capital.

The National Farmers Union (NFU) warned the situation is “increasingly concerning” and that dairy farmers are already using winter feed because grass has stopped growing.

Flights at Catania airport will remain suspended on Monday for a third consecutive day after volcanic ash from Mount Etna disrupted operations, the Sicilian airport's operator has said.

All flight operations at the airport, which is Italy's fifth-busiest by passenger traffic, are suspended until 21:59 GMT on Monday, according to a revised notice from operator SAC.

Passengers have been advised to check the status of their journeys with their airlines before travelling to Catania airport. The operator added that further updates are set to follow.

Mount Etna, the highest and most active volcano in Europe, regularly interferes with operations at Catania. However, ash releases have been notably intense this summer, disrupting thousands of holidaymakers.

It comes after flights at Catania airport were suspended on 14 September because of volcanic ash.

open image in gallery A view shows volcanic ash and fumes rising during an eruption at Mount Etna, as seen from Milo, Sicily, Italy, September 14, 2026 ( Reuters )

Another closure a month earlier coincided with the Ferragosto holiday, marking the height of the Italian summer season when millions head to coastal and mountain destinations.

The closure lasted for five days, the longest emergency since 2002.

According to airport operator SAC, 36 per cent of nearly 2,000 flights due to arrive in Catania between 6 and 12 August were cancelled, with over 600 flights diverted to the locations Palermo, Trapani, Comiso, and Lamezia Terme.

"Volcanic ash can be a great risk for aircraft," Boris Behncke, a researcher at the National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology’s Etna Observatory, previously said.

"It can be sucked into the motors, and force them to stall. This is why everyone is so very cautious with aircraft when there is a volcanic ash emission."

open image in gallery A picture shows the eruption of the Mount Etna volcano on July 4, 2024 in Sicily ( AFP/Getty )

However, the most recent fatalities linked to an eruption of Europe's most active volcano happened nearly 40 years ago, back in 1987.

According to officials, lightning strikes have resulted in more fatalities on Mount Etna in recent decades than volcanic activity.

An American tourist died in August after being struck by lightning on Mount Etna while hiking in an area closed to visitors due to volcanic activity, Italian firefighters said at the time.

The 29-year-old man from Kansas was rescued by helicopter after being hit and was later declared dead.

Two morgue workers at Lucy Letby's former hospital have won almost £30,000 after complaining they did not have PPE to protect them from 'splashback' from the dead bodies.

John Crayton and Thomas Jones complained that bodies were not properly covered and they were expected to perform beyond the duties the role would usually require.

However when they complained about the hygiene and 'psychological' issues they suffered from the uncovered deceased, a manager became enraged that they went behind his back to anonymously complain.

He revoked the porters' access to the mortuary, which meant they could not do their jobs and even led to rumours about Mr Crayton having done something 'inappropriate'.

The two men went off sick and took the hospital to an employment tribunal where they were awarded a combined sum of £29,561.

Mr Crayton and Mr Jones both worked as porters at Countess of Chester Hospital NHS Foundation Trust in Chester, Cheshire.

They would take deceased patients who had passed away either in the hospital or in the community to the hospital's mortuary.

On January 31, 2024, both men went to Jamie Cunningham, a lead mortuary technician, to discuss concerns they had regarding the hygiene of transporting the bodies.

In the same role at a previous hospital, Mr Crayton had always transported bodies when they were already in body bags and they were not responsible for transporting deceased people from the community to the refrigerators.

open image in gallery Ambulances seen at the Countess of Chester Hospital on January 3, 2023 ( Getty )

He said that while working at the Chester hospital, he had got 'splashback from fluid with no protection for the forearms due to the [hospital's] bare to elbow policy' and inadequate PPE.

They also said that bodies were often not properly covered up and there 'was a risk of psychological damage as a result of signs of a traumatic death and infection', and that they should not be the ones to deal with the valuables of the deceased.

Mr Cunningham 'had some understanding' of the porters' concerns but said that body bag use was discretionary.

In February, the pair took their concerns to Helen Ellis who was the hospital's Freedom To Speak Up Guardian under a policy that allowed staff to freely air their concerns.

They told her about 'the distress caused by exposed bodies the splashback of fluid, inadequate PPE, lack of infection control and the handling of valuables'.

Mr Crayton again complained, saying that: "Policy for transportation of deceased patients was not as robust as that under which he had worked at Wrexham and he was concerned for the safety of staff and the dignity of patients."

The tribunal explained: "It was agreed that Ms Ellis would raise the issues with Cathy Chadwick, the [hospital's] Chief Operating Officer without revealing the identity of those who had raised the concerns, in accordance with the Freedom to Speak Up policy.

"Ms Ellis emailed Ms Chadwick on the same date. In her email, Ms Ellis stated that her understanding of the policies operated in other hospitals for the transportation of a deceased patient/receipt of deceased member of the community was with the use of a body bag.

"Ms Ellis highlighted that it was the ward staff in other hospitals who were responsible for confirming the identity of a deceased patient and dealing with the property on that person."

Ms Ellis set out some of Mr Crayton's issues, including that there was no community death policy and that the patients were wrapped in sheets that became wet when the porters were required to remove the bodies.

Other issues included that they were required to check the identity of the deceased and that the ward staff, whilst responsible for infection control, 'were merely dealing with a tick box and that the community deaths were inadequately covered'.

Ms Chadwick reached out to Mr Cunningham so they could discuss the procedures, and he 'accepted that there were issues with the way the [hospital] dealt with the deceased'.

However when Mr Cunningham learned of the porters' identities - which was in violation of the hospital's policy on anonymous complaints - he became 'upset' that they had violated the chain of command and revoked Mr Crayton's access to the mortuary on February 16.

He claimed it was because he was suspicious that their complaints about DNA transference on the uncovered bodies meant they had 'something to hide', but when he was told to restore Mr Crayton's access four hours later he admitted he had been 'hot headed'.

Mr Crayton told colleagues he could not help them that day because he did not have access to the mortuary.

Him and Mr Jones both went off sick afterwards, and it became clear from colleagues' texts that they believed Mr Crayton had done 'something inappropriate' in the mortuary and that was why his access had been revoked.

They took their case to an employment tribunal in Manchester, alleging they had suffered detriments in the workplace after making protected disclosures.

Employment Judge Jennifer Ainscough agreed with the men, concluding: "Mr Cunningham was unhappy about Ms Chadwick’s email... Mr Cunningham was upset.

"[Mr Crayton's] role, as we know from the job description, involved mortuary duties. He was, for a number of hours, unable to fulfil his job description had he been required to do so.

"Mr Cunningham said in the grievance that he acted in haste and was hot headed and he was aware he should not have removed the access.

"The explanation given is that Mr Cunningham was concerned about [Mr Crayton's] comments that there could be DNA contamination. Ms Chadwick’s email to Mr Cunningham makes no reference to DNA contamination concerns.

"This was something raised by [Mr Crayton] on 31 January 2024 in conversation with Mr Cunningham.

"His decision to remove [Mr Crayton's] access was materially influenced by the disclosures made on 31 January 2024 and 8 February 2024."

The hospital has been ordered to pay Mr Crayton £2,121 net in compensation for wage loss and £15,000 in compensation for injury to feelings.

It must also pay Mr Jones £1,439 net in compensation for wage loss and £11,000 in compensation for injury to feelings.

News.content:

Wes Streeting has said the farmer who phoned police about suspicious activity near RAF Fairford has only “a partial picture” of the situation.

The woman made the call during the early hours of Sunday morning after spotting a “large group of hooded and masked men” making their way from three large vans.

Five men were arrested on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offences, with counter-terror police understood to be investigating whether Iran is linked to the suspected bomb plot at the military base, which is used by US bombers.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, the woman said she noticed something “highly unusual was taking place” and attempted to contact the Ministry of Defence police but received no response.

She contacted 999 at 1.36am as she was aware that RAF Fairford had been operating at a high security level at the time.

open image in gallery The woman contacted the police after spotting a group of masked men near three white vans ( Sky News )

The defence secretary told Sky News: “Thank you to that member of the public.

“She has done exactly what we would hope that someone in that extraordinary situation would do.

“I’m really grateful to her – I think she acted, by her own admission, quickly and thoughtfully, and she did the right thing.

“With respect, though, she does only have a partial picture.”

Asked whether the the incident “may have been driven by a hostile foreign state”, Mr Streeting told the broadcaster he did not “want to speculate at this stage of the investigation”.

The woman who raised the alarm has claimed that police had “dropped the ball” and said she was “absolutely staggered” that it had been left to her to report the incident to officers.

“The airbase were operating a roadblock close to the entrance to the base, but not on any of the other roads.

open image in gallery Police stand at the entrance at a base set up at the Fairford Youth Football Club near RAF Fairford base ( AFP/Getty )

“But we assumed someone would be monitoring the roads around the base perimeter and taking regular patrols in the village.

“Clearly, this was not happening, and I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had,” she said.

“Even more surprising that, following my call at 1.36am, the police were aware of the presence of the three vans, but didn’t evacuate the village until 6am.

“No one from the police has been in touch to ask me anything about it.

“I think they were hyper-focused and vigilant about the base itself, and had absolutely no regard for our village.”

She added: “I’m just really keen to highlight that it appears someone really dropped the ball on this.

“Also, I am finding it strange that at the press conference, the police are saying they responded to a call at 12.45 about three suspicious vans travelling towards the base.

“If this is the case, why did they not know they were in Whelford when I called almost an hour later?”

Speaking on Times Radio on Monday morning, Mr Streeting said the investigation into a suspected terror plot against the Gloucestershire airbase “continues today”.

open image in gallery Counter-terror police have arrested five men on suspicion of explosive and terror offences (Ben Birchall/PA) ( PA Wire )

He added: “We are grateful for the vigilance of the members of the public.

“But I also want to state personally my enormous thanks to our police, our counter-terrorism police, emergency services and the security services for their hard work to defend our base at RAF Fairford. I also want to thank the members of the public who’ve beared (sic) with us.

“We’ve had a number of people evacuated from their homes in the early hours of yesterday morning, there’s a cordon that remains in place and there has been disruption to their lives – and I want to thank them for their forbearance.”

Suspects detained under the Terrorism Act 2000 can be held for up to 14 days without charge, compared to the 24-hour limit for standard arrests without an extension application.

Aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot spending hours inspecting three white vans, two of which had open rear doors. Large black barrels appeared to be scattered around.

A 400-metre cordon was erected and 85 evacuated households were unable to return home overnight. Cotswold District Council was seeking accommodation for some.

The Army’s ordnance disposal unit was still examining the vehicles in the cordon by the evening, temporary chief constable Maggie Blyth, from Bedfordshire Constabulary, told a press conference.

Agencies “believe the matter to be contained”, she later added.

Prime minister Andy Burnham said the incident was “deeply concerning” and the Government would “always take every step necessary” to protect people.

News.title: Taylor Swift becomes most-awarded artist in MTV history
News.content:
Taylor Swift broke records at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs) on Sunday, becoming the most-awarded artist in VMA history.

The pop star, 36, was previously tied with Beyoncé for the title, with 30 VMAs each. However, Swift took home three awards at the ceremony, bringing her career total to an unmatched 33.

The Fate of Ophelia, ⁠Swift’s first single from her record-breaking The Life of a Showgirl album, claimed the top trophy – Video of the Year – and she dedicated the honour to the late country music legend Dolly Parton.

During her speech, Swift praised Parton as “the ultimate showgirl” who told stories that were “so vivid and so rich”.

“I think that we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time,” she said.

Parton, an award-winning country singer, died in August at the age of 80.

Swift also received the inaugural Artist Director Honors, a new award meant to recognise artists “whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling”.

The 36-year-old has written and directed 18 videos of her roughly 60 videos during her career. The ‌most recent, for ‌her new single Patient Zero, debuted during ⁠the ceremony.

News.title: Five reasons why Australia’s win over Boks was an all-time classic
News.content:
If the Wallabies play like this in their own backyard at their own World Cup next year, boy we are in for a treat. After years in the doldrums, this five-try victory over South Africa was the latest reminder of their transformation under the stewardship of Les Kiss.

Their gritty performance in Perth – the city where Australia will open rugby’s showpiece in 12 months’ time – was caveated by the fact they were facing a second-string Boks side. But there can be no denying they are on an upward trajectory, even if their discipline dramatically deserted them late on.

In a helter-skelter denouement, Australia played the majority of the final 10 minutes of the match with 11 men on the pitch as South Africa threatened to mount a late comeback. Tom Wright’s eye-catching intercept try looked to have secured a match-winning moment, but it was scratched off after Hunter Paisami joined Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan and Joseph Sua’ali’i in the bin.

Ox Nche’s 80th-minute score made it a four-point game with time left for the restart, but Australia had enough fight to secure a dramatic victory largely built on execution and patience.

Five tries by the hour mark, including a Len Ikitau first-half double, ultimately gave South Africa a mountain to climb. The Wallabies’ field coverage and industriousness in defence was far superior to that of the four-time world champions, while Max Jorgensen and Sua’ali’i were pillars of excellence out wide.

After clinching a 3-1 win over New Zealand in their historic “Greatest Rivalry” series, Rassie Erasmus had the luxury of resting several of his A-listers for this one-off Test in Western Australia. The changes ultimately had an adverse effect, with the visitors faulty at the set-piece and lacking their usual snarl and bite. They found themselves playing catch-up in a chaotic game that Australia, despite their discipline creaking in the dying moments, deserved to win.

Here, Telegraph Sport explores five reasons why this was one of the craziest Test matches in recent memory.

Wallabies outmuscle Boks over 60 emphatic minutes

The Wallabies front up impressively to earn a seven-point lead at the break after a quickfire Len Ikitau double cancels out tries from Johan Grobbelaar and Edwill van der Merwe, before Ben Donaldson finishes a sublime attacking set from the hosts.

News.title: England show ODI depth in thrashing of Sri Lanka
News.content:
England’s international summer comes to an end at the Oval with a series decider against Sri Lanka. After England won the first game in Durham, Sri Lanka bounced back to take a 16-run win at Headingley on Thursday to set up this winner-takes-all match today. Sri Lanka put up a much better fight in the second one-day international than they have throughout the rest of their white-ball tour. The tourists posted 321 for six, with their captain Kusal Mendis leading the way with 121 off 100 balls, his seventh ODI century.

England’s reply got off to the best possible start, with both openers Tom Banton and Ben Duckett hitting fifties. It appeared to be going well for England, with Jos Buttler and Will Jacks also registering half centuries, but Buttler’s hamstring injury in addition to the regular loss of wickets meant Sri Lanka were able to claim victory to take us to a series decider in London today.

“I am so happy winning and getting the hundred,” Mendis said. “The overall performance was very good. We started really well and the middle order batted really well. Nothing special, basic cricket and I was very happy with 320, we wanted more than 300 on this pitch. [Dunith] Wellalage bowled really well, the whole team, after the powerplay. The guys gave 100 per cent. Today [Thursday] is finished and now we have to focus on the next game and do the basics right.”

When Buttler retired hurt in the 38th over of England’s run chase, the hosts were 254 for four and were in a great position to chase the total down and claim a series victory. From the 37th over onwards, England were only able to score one four and one six.

“It was an outstanding game,” England captain Harry Brook said. “You can look back and dwell on some many different areas but that is not what this team does, we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the Oval. We put up a really good fight with the ball. To restrict them to 320 and have the chance to chase that down was a hell of an effort.

“The lads got the chase off to a flyer. You could not really ask for much more. We probably stalled in that middle period and lost a few too many wickets, but the fight we showed was great. We have got a great opportunity now to try and win this series, and a great opportunity for 12 months’ time. In pressure situations, like the one that awaits us at the Oval, it will be great to see where we are as a team.”

Buttler has been ruled out of this match due to a hamstring injury and has been replaced in the squad by Dan Lawrence, who had been playing for Surrey in the final round of the County Championship.

Play from the Oval will get under way at 10.30am.

News.title: Saracens storm Leicester to launch new Venter era in style
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Gallagher Prem meeting as Leicester Tigers host Saracens at Welford Road.

Last season, Leicester reached the play-off semi-finals in Geoff Parling’s first full season at the club, before losing to arch-rivals Northampton Saints, who went on to win their third title in the competition.

In a new era for Leicester as they plot a route back to the very top, Aaron Wainwright and Mako Vunipola make their Prem debuts.

Leicester head coach Geoff Parling is brimming with excitement ahead of this tasty match and has talked about his side’s preparation for the new season.

“Firstly we are looking to evolve our game, we’re not looking to rip it up and completely restart,” he said. This team is built on being competitive and winning, we’ve got to be in the mix every year. For me it’s all about being consistently near the top and then getting in those big games and having the ability to perform in them.”

“I’m well aware that there’s lots of elements from the season and different circumstances but the main thing is that the league is designed to have a top four that go into the play-offs so the top four is the aim.”

Saracens finished one place below Leicester in the previous campaign and missed out on the play-offs after a 32-12 final round loss to Exeter Chiefs.

Boss Joe Shaw has handed debuts to Tomos Williams and Alfie Barbeary, and he’s raring to go ahead of this fixture.

“We’ve had a great pre-season, but we’re itching to get stuck into the league campaign now,” he said. “We have a really competitive squad who are driving standards and good habits across the pitch. We are confident in the squad we have put together and are excited to see what they can achieve this campaign.”

Kick-off is at 15:00.

News.title: England throw it away with defending unworthy of a top nation
News.content:
Tuchel does not plan to address the issue with his players ahead of the remaining Nations League games against Czech Republic and Croatia.

Asked if the City verdict had been a cause of discussion ahead of the Spain game, Tuchel replied: “Not for me, but I can imagine maybe for the Man City players. I won’t comment on it as it’s an ongoing case.

“I didn’t make it a topic. It was not a topic for me. I’m just thinking about Spain and the team and meetings. The players have more time than me. So I can imagine they talk about it. It’s good they do. I don’t think it was a distraction for them.”

Kane added: “There was a discussion, but when we’re with England, we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week.”

Tuchel also refused to point the finger of blame at Guéhi, O’Reilly or Kane, who missed a penalty, for England’s defeat despite admitting his team got off to the worst possible start by conceding a goal after two minutes.

“We will focus on the positives, but also highlight the stuff we can do better,” Tuchel said. “Not even speaking about individual mistakes because this is normal. It just happens. It should not happen, and for sure not in this amount. But there is no sense in showing the individual mistakes or telling them ‘please don’t make mistakes’. That is normal, but we can do things better. We can defend the third goal better. But we will focus on the positives. There is a lot to take away from the game.

“We wanted to be the team desperately to beat them [Spain] and we think we had them. We still think we had them at half-time. That was the way the team showed up after half-time. So we will focus on that, but the reality is we lost and the reality is we need to prove it again.”

News.title: Red Roses triumph over New Zealand in chaotic late scenes – how it unfolded
News.content:
Just when it looked like the Red Roses’ lustre was beginning to fade, up stepped Zoe Harrison.

In one of the most dramatic finishes to an England match in recent memory, the fly-half gobbled up Amy Du Plessis’s pass to glide over the whitewash and secure a pulsating win over New Zealand.

Ever the epitome of calmness, Harrison was undeterred by the fact she had just missed what would have been a match-winning penalty from 42 metres out with the score locked at 19-19.

But after their arm-wrestle with Canada last weekend in Exeter, which finished 26-26, there was simply no way the Red Roses were going to settle for a draw for a second week running.

A year to the day since they were crowned world champions in their own back yard, England’s status as the most dominant side in the women’s game was all but confirmed by this never-say-die victory over the Black Ferns.

News.title: Russell holds his nerve to see off Verstappen and win Azerbaijan GP
News.content:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend went the way many believed the 2026 season would play out. George Russell strolled to victory from pole, though with a little late jeopardy, whilst Kimi Antonelli’s crash in qualifying meant he had to fight his way through the field to finish fifth. That, after all, was the order of things last season.

Yet the past few days in Baku are an inversion of the season’s storyline. It is Antonelli who has been the faster driver, heading for a maiden world title at the second time of asking. Russell has been the troubled one. This was only the Briton’s third victory of the season and his first since Austria in late June. Antonelli has racked up eight wins and, before this weekend in Baku, a well-deserved 81-point lead over Russell.

Russell’s dominant and impressive run from pole to the chequered flag on Saturday is both a reminder of what he is capable of and also what might have been, had he been able to find this type of form earlier and more often. The reality, though, is that he needs to replicate this for the rest of the season to even be in with a sniff, barring a catastrophic meltdown from Antonelli. Still, Russell looked elated to have ended his barren run.

The finish was a little more tense than Russell deserved, having established a healthy lead in the first half of the race. Two late safety cars eradicated his advantage and helped put Max Verstappen’s Red Bull on his gearbox. In the end, he triumphed by just under 0.2sec and, as Antonelli finished fifth – with some help from two safety-car inducing crashes – he made up 15 points on his Mercedes team-mate. Isack Hadjar completed the podium for Red Bull after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.

News.title: Scotland’s Pocognoli era starts with encouraging signs but familiar issues in front of goal
News.content:
Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

Sports.title: I preferred my life before fame – I’ve lost my peace and tranquillity, says World Cup hero Vozinha
Sports.content:

VOZINHA claims that he preferred life before he became a World Cup viral sensation.

The veteran goalkeeper, 40, shot to stardom as Cape Verde earned a 0-0 draw with eventual winners Spain in the group stage.



His social media following shot from 56,000 to over one million during the match.

The stopper, then a free agent after leaving Portuguese second tier side Chaves, subsequently landed a big move to Chilean giants Colo-Colo.



Previously little known, Vozinha was mobbed as he arrived to sign for his new club.

On his newfound fame, Vozinha told The Observer: “I’ve lost my peace and tranquillity.

“I no longer have any privacy, or at least much less than I used to.

“Now I go out, I go to a restaurant, and there’s always someone who wants to take a photo with me or asks me for an autograph.



“Or, worse, someone is filming me. That’s what has changed most in my life, and I don’t think there’s anything I can do about it.”

Vozinha, who has previously played in Moldova, Cyprus and Slovakia, is not particularly comfortable with his status – having now reached a staggering 28.4 million Instagram followers.

He added: “A lot of people want to be famous and have a public profile, but they only see the positive side of that reality.

“To be honest, if I were offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I’d choose the one I had before.”



Vozinha has so far played three matches for Colo-Colo, and has had to sit on the bench for a couple of games.

Last week he played for Cape Verde for the first time since bowing out of the World Cup to Argentina, earning his 93rd cap in a 3-1 defeat to Mali in Afcon qualifying.

Sports.title: Roberto Mancini breaks silence on Man City guilty verdict as former boss bluntly snaps: ‘Not my problem’

ROBERTO MANCINI has broken his silence on Manchester City’s gargantuan breaches of Premier League’s financial rules.

It was revealed on Friday that the Etihad club had been found guilty of all but ONE of its alleged 115 breaches.



Among the club’s violations was their failure to properly disclose former manager Mancini‘s salary between 2009-10 and 2012-13.

The leaked emails which sparked the investigation into the club alleged that City paid the Italian two salaries – £1.45million a year for managing the Citizens and an additional £1.75million annually for four days of consultancy work for Al Jazira.



Al Jazira, of course, is also the portfolio of City owner, Sheikh Mansour.

Despite the threat of serious sanctions against his former club, newly reappointed Italy boss Mancini isn’t concerned.

He said: “I don’t think Manchester City were found guilty, on the contrary.

“It’s not a problem that concerns me, but it’s not a new thing.

“Manchester City are not guilty and the double contract is not my problem, but theirs if anything.”

City have maintained their innocence since being charged by the Prem back in February 2023.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

They are expected to appeal any sanctions, which are expected to be SEVERE, imposed on them.

In a statement last weekend, chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said: “I have been part of this Club for 18 years. I have had the privilege to stand with you in the Etihad, at Wembley, and in Istanbul.

“This Club matters to me, and you have shown and told me – time and time again – how much Manchester City matters to you. This is why I am writing to you today.



“Following Friday’s media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I.

“Here’s what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the Club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.

“There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position.

“But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment.

“Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies.



“I ask you to please carefully read the statement, which we gave on Friday, and the statement we issued in February 2023.

“Every word matters and holds true.

“While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed.

“We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed.

“There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our Club. We will not give them that opportunity.



“We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break.

Sports.title: Gary Neville names Man Utd’s two WORST transfers since Sir Alex Ferguson left featuring £150m of failed talent
Sports.content:
Next

GARY NEVILLE has named Angel Di Maria and Antony as Manchester United’s two worst signings of the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era.

The Red Devils have failed to come close to replicating Ferguson’s success during the 13 years since his departure, despite forking out eye-watering sums on players.



During a game of padel with The Athletic’s David Ornstein, Neville was asked to name United‘s worst transfer of this period.

The former Old Trafford hero said: “Di Maria was a bad one and I was so excited about him, by the way.



“I thought that was an amazing signing. Can get from box to box, he’s quick, quality and then obviously he just didn’t adapt, didn’t settle. All those reasons. That was a bad one.”

United paid a then-British record £59.7million to sign Di Maria from Real Madrid in 2014.



The Argentine went on to play just 32 times for the Red Devils over one season, scoring four goals and laying on 11 assists.

Di Maria left for Paris Saint-Germain in 2015 – going on to win five league titles and nine domestic trophies with the French giants.



The winger’s wife Jorgelina subsequently blasted life in England, telling Los Angeles de la Manana: “It was horrible! All of it was horrible, we went to the house and we were like… ‘See you later guys, we’re out of here’.

“When we left, I said to him, ‘Go to any country – except England’. Anyway, one year later and there we were in England and it was horrible, a s***hole.”

BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

In addition to Di Maria, Neville also took aim at Brazilian flop Antony, who signed for United in an £85.5m deal from Ajax in 2022.

The former full-back, 51, said: “When you’re looking at massive outlays, Antony. This is not a criticism of the boy, it’s reflective of United that he paid that money for him after panicking,’ he said.



“I would say Antony and Di Maria. I’d have to say Antony.”

The 16-cap Brazil international played 96 times for the Red Devils, scoring 12 goals and laying on five assists.

Antony was loaned to Real Betis in 2025 and subsequently made the move permanent.

Ornstein brought up Marouane Fellaini, the first signing of the post-Ferguson era.

But Neville defended the towering Belgian, saying: “Fellaini I’ve no problem with.



“He shouldn’t have signed for the club, but he’s not the worst signing. He gave his all and he was £25m-£30m, it’s not the biggest outlay.”

Sports.content:
Bernardo Silva gives blunt response to Martin Odegaard fury after Arsenal star injured

Martin Odegaard was left furious after being on the end of a nasty challenge by Bernardo Silva during Norway's defeat to Portugal on Sunday

View 2 Images Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard was furious with Bernardo Silva (Image: TV2)

Bernardo Silva simply said, 'It's football, my friend,' after leaving Arsenal skipper Martin Odegaard furious when his challenge left the midfielder with an ankle issue. Odegaard hobbled out of the stadium after being on the end of a vicious challenge from the Real Madrid ace, in Norway's defeat to Portugal.

‌



The former Manchester City star's challenge ensured that Odegaard required some treatment following the full-time whistle. Silva waited until Odegaard had released the ball in one exchange of play before lashing out at the back of his leg.

‌



Odegaard was incensed and visibly confronted his former Premier League rival, making his anger known the next time the pair found themselves close together on the pitch. The 27-year-old was left with no choice but to limp off the field when the final whistle blew.

‌



After receiving treatment, Odegaard paused to speak to Norwegian broadcaster TV2, giving a damning verdict on Silva's challenge.

"It doesn't belong on a football field," he said. "It's a shame that people do that."

"It's a head fog from him," he added. "Just kicks me down long after I've played the ball away. I don't understand what he's doing."

Odegaard declined to repeat what he had shouted at his opponent. "I don't think we should do that on TV," he added.

‌

Despite the discomfort he was feeling, Odegaard remains hopeful that the knock will not rule him out of action. "I hope not," he said. "But I got a knock on my ankle there, so it probably won't be good tonight."

The incident sparked outrage amongst Norwegian broadcasters as well. "Look at Bernardo Silva. It's completely unnecessary, it's ugly," commentator Simen Stamso Moller said.

‌



Mikel Arteta will be hoping he hasn't got another injury concern to deal with after Germany forward Kai Havertz was forced to pull out of international duty.

Odegaard's frustrations were made worse by Norway's defeat. Joao Felix got the opener in Oslo before Manchester City star striker Erling Haaland equalised in the 51st minute.

Goncalo Ramos swiftly responded to put the visitors back in front just three minutes later. Cristiano Ronaldo remained an unused substitute.

Sports.title: Real Madrid make Erling Haaland transfer decision after Man City learn 'likely' punishment
Sports.content:
Real Madrid make Erling Haaland transfer decision after Man City learn 'likely' punishment

Real Madrid are long-term admirers of Erling Haaland, whose future at Manchester City could now be uncertain after the guilty verdict on their Premier League charges

View 2 Images Real Madrid are long-term admirers of Erling Haaland (Image: Getty Images)

Real Madrid are unlikely to pursue a move for Erling Haaland even if Manchester City are punished, according to reports in Spain. The Norwegian hot-shot faces an uncertain future in the wake of the verdict that City were found guilty of 114 of their charges during the legal dispute with the Premier League.

‌



Spanish outlet Sport are suggesting that even if City are penalised for wrongdoing they're deemed to have committed, it won't prompt movement from Los Blancos. It has been said that figures in the Spanish capital have not planned to make a move for Haaland due to the lengthy contract he has signed, which was penned without exit clauses.

‌



The logistics of a move to Madrid have also been disputed, despite an impressive relationship with Jude Bellingham from their time at Borussia Dortmund.

‌



It has been said that Haaland wouldn't fit into the Madrid mould, which consists of Kylian Mbappe and Vinicius Jr. Yan Diomande's big-money move to Madrid could also provide a stumbling block to a move in the event of significant demotion for City.

FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



But a move to Barcelona hasn't been taken off the table as the Catalan giants have been deemed a better fit for the Premier League great.

City are expected to lodge an appeal against the verdict from the legal battle with the Premier League. It leaves supporters in a perilous position as they face an agonising wait to see what degree the sanctions are handed out.

The possibilities appear endless with a number of punishments available ranging from fines, points deductions, expulsion from the top-flight or stripping of the titles they won between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

‌



Roberto Mancini, who was City boss during the period in question, disregarded the verdict and reaffirmed that the North West club are not guilty of wrongdoing.

View 2 Images Haaland could consider leaving City next summer (Image: Carl Recine/Getty Images)

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire believes the sanctions for Nottingham Forest and Everton have set a precedent following their respective points deductions for financial breaches.

‌



He told TalkTV: "There is no doubt a points deduction would be the most likely outcome in the view of many.

"We have seen points deductions before for Nottingham Forest and Everton for breach of the financial limit rules. So that is feasible.

"There is a separate issue of whether clubs who have missed out on titles, could they put in for financial compensation for not getting into Europe and loss of prize money."
