Sports.title: Liverpool news: Jurgen Klopp makes unfortunate claim as Alexander Isak suffers 'real blow'
Sports.content:
Liverpool news: Jurgen Klopp makes unfortunate claim as Alexander Isak suffers 'real blow'

There are still two weeks left to wait for Liverpool fans to see their Reds back in action against Manchester City

View 3 Images Alexander Isak has suffered a 'real blow' (Image: Jonathan Nackstrand / AFP via Getty Images)

Fans will have to wait another two weeks for Liverpool to return to action against Manchester City. Andoni Iraola will be busy preparing his tactical plan after an up-and-down start to the 2026/27 Premier League season.

‌



The Reds sit in sixth place on nine points after three draws and two wins. Iraola has urged his team to be as ruthless as possible in order to return to a good run of form.

‌



Speaking after a winning return to Bournemouth, the 44-year-old admitted that the coming weeks will be extremely demanding for his team, but improvements have been made. He said: "I think overall we've improved, definitely since the first games.

‌



"Some of the things we still need to improve, more things. I am happy it is the third clean sheet in a row in the league. But we still have to get ready because the schedule that we have now, it's very difficult.

"I think we are playing against top-four teams and then in between Champions [League] and then in between Chelsea in the Carabao [Cup] and everything in two, three days. So we have to get ready because this next month, after this break, it's going be very demanding for us."

Here, Mirror Football has the latest headlines coming out of Anfield.

‌



Jurgen Klopp's unfortunate claim

Jurgen Klopp claims that Florian Wirtz joined Liverpool at an "unfortunate time" for the club as he continues to defend the struggling star. Criticism has followed the Germany international since his £125million move from Bayer Leverkusen, with Jamie Carragher worried that Wirtz isn't actually in poor form.

Despite this, Klopp has backed Wirtz to eventually succeed at Anfield. He called the star up to the national team squad early due to Kai Havertz and Jamal Musiala sustaining injuries.

View 3 Images Klopp has backed Florian Wirtz (Image: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty Images)

‌



Discussing the 23-year-old, Klopp explained: "When you look at the overall context, Flo joined Liverpool at a very unfortunate time. It's about the passing of Diogo Jota. He joined a team with the players whose priority was not football at that time, which is very understandable.

"He learned a lot from his first year. Now is a new season under a new coach, he started all games, I think. He's physically doing very well. The team is starting to find itself again. Attacking players always need a functioning team around them.

"Everyone who loves football can still see what an outstanding player Flo Wirtz is. His footballing ability is beyond any doubt. He is on a good path, but people are never satisfied with how quickly things happen. We have to make sure that Flo feels comfortable with us and can fit into what we want from him. With us, hopefully, he can simply be Flo."

‌



Alexander Isak blow

View 3 Images Alexander Isak's toe was bloodied after the challenge (Image: Mike Hewitt/Getty Images)

Alexander Isak has returned to Anfield after suffering a "real blow" of an injury while on international duty with Sweden. The striker injured his toe against Romania after being stamped on, but still completed 90 minutes.

His foot was visibly bloodied in a picture shared by Sportbladet, but Isak has played down fears that it is a serious issue. He said: "It was a real blow. You can see it. It was a real punch. Those of you who have played may know that it takes a few minutes before it releases, but it was okay."

Article continues below

Sweden boss Graham Potter was planning to play Isak in all four games, but he will now miss the clashes against Poland and Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the return leg against Romania.

Sports.title: Man Utd chief Sir Jim Ratcliffe to settle £180m dispute after 'months of heated arguments'
Sports.content:
Man Utd chief Sir Jim Ratcliffe to settle £180m dispute after 'months of heated arguments'

Manchester United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe reportedly wants to resolve a £180million legal dispute involving Ineos after what are said to have been 18 months of heated arguments

View 2 Images Sir Jim Ratcliffe is said to be in talks over settling with Sir Ben Ainslie (Image: PA)

Sir Ben Ainslie and Sir Jim Ratcliffe reportedly want to settle their legal row out of court rather than wait over 12 months for the next available trial date. Ineos sued the four-time Olympic champion sailor's Athena Racing team in March over their use of a racing yacht they claim to have spent £180million on.

‌



Ainslie and Ratcliffe stopped working together last January. They teamed up for two America's Cups in Auckland in 2021 and in Barcelona in 2024.

‌



Manchester United's minority shareholder previously committed to a third. However, that all changed last year after the pair fell out.

‌



Eric Cantona teams up with Gary Lineker as Man Utd chief Sir Jim Ratcliffe slammed again READ MORE :

Man Utd announce record revenues but debt rises as Old Trafford grass goes on sale for £125! READ MORE :

More than a year after proceedings commenced, Ainslie told The Telegraph in Naples this weekend: "A lot of water has flowed under the bridge over the last 18 months.

"We had a mutual desire to win the America's Cup, and I'm confident we'll be able to find a way to resolve this before it goes to court."

As initially reported by The Telegraph, the earliest available slots for hearings and trials at the Commercial Court that are anticipated to run longer than a week are from 15 November 2027. That would be four months after next year's America's Cup concludes.

‌



Ainslie's defence against the High Court proceedings initiated by Ratcliffe alleges that he demanded "all of [the team's] assets and intellectual property" be transferred to him in exchange for his continued backing. The filing claims Ineos Sport chairman Rob Nevin "stated to Sir Ben: 'This is what Jim wants.

View 2 Images Sir Ben Ainslie and Sir Jim Ratcliffe teamed up in 2018 (Image: Lloyd Images, Getty Images)

"We have a phrase at Ineos: 'scorched earth'. It means that if you don't give Jim what he wants, he will burn your house down' (or words to that effect)."

‌



Chief executive Jean-Claude Blanc is also alleged to have confronted Ainslie alongside chairman Nevin. Their legal representatives did not dispute that.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Ineos stated in submitted court documents: "It is admitted that Mr Nevin indicated that Sir Jim would not back down (and had only ever done so in a dispute concerning the People's Republic of China) and in that context referred to 'scorched earth'.

Article continues below

"But it is denied that these comments would reasonably have been understood by Sir Ben as a 'threat' of anything other than the claimant enforcing its legal rights to the fullest extent possible.

"Mr Nevin's words were intended to be, and would reasonably have been understood to be, used in a figurative rather than a literal sense."

Sports.title: Ireland star Jack Moylan in pointed celebration after scoring vs Israel in Nations League
Sports.content:
Ireland star Jack Moylan in pointed celebration after scoring vs Israel in Nations League

Republic of Ireland winger Jack Moylan scored Ireland's third goal against Israel on Sunday night, removing his black armband and kissing it in a pointed tribute to those who have died in the Israel-Palestine conflict

View 2 Images Jack Moylan lifted his black armband in the air after scoring for the Republic of Ireland against Israel

Republic of Ireland forward Jack Moylan made a pointed gesture by removing his black armband and kissing it in celebration after netting against Israel on Sunday evening.

‌



The winger made it 3-0 with with Ireland's third goal, following earlier strikes from Troy Parrott and Adam Idah, with all three goals coming within a breathless 12-minute spell before the half-hour mark.

‌



Having slotted home his effort, Moylan sprinted towards the corner flag, where he removed the black armband - worn by him and his teammates in tribute to all those who have lost their lives in the Israel/Palestine conflict - before planting a kiss on the Ireland badge.

‌



Despite the celebrations remaining largely subdued, Ireland presented a united front on Sunday evening, coming together in the aftermath of a turbulent few days that had left the squad split over whether to go ahead with the fixture.

Ireland players snub Israel handshakes and take action during national anthem before match READ MORE :

Ireland forced into unusual decision after squad split over controversial Israel match READ MORE :

Pre-match, Ireland players snubbed shaking hands with their Israeli opponents during the Nations League clash at the Nagyerdei Stadion. Hallgrimsson's men also bowed their heads during Israel's national anthem.

Gavin Bazunu removed himself from the squad, citing atrocities in the region of Palestine, where more than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed since the October 7th Hamas attack on Israel.

‌



Speaking ahead of the game, Ireland manager Hallgrimsson acknowledged that it had been a testing few days for the entire squad.

View 2 Images Ireland's Jack Moylan celebrates after scoring his sides third goal of the match (Image: Mandatory Credit ©INPHO/Ryan Byrne)

"It's been tough on everyone. But I mostly feel for the players that just want to play football and are somewhere in between...In between decisions and and other things, so I just feel for the players that came here to play football and represent their country."

‌



Speaking about Ireland's decision to go ahead with playing the match, Football Association of Ireland chief, David Courell said: "The squad were in Pristina yesterday. An extensive conversation took place where ultimately the consensus from the group was to travel to Hungary.

"That was something that we all entered into this window with our intention to fulfil these fixtures and that was the consensus that the group finished on at the end of that two-hour meeting yesterday. This morning a player (now confirmed to be Bazunu) expressed their discomfort with fulfilling this fixture to the head coach and indicated their intent to withdraw from the squad.

"As you can understand, this new variable required time and deliberation for the rest of the squad to consider. What proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly amongst the players themselves but also at times with the coaching staff and at times with the executive."

Sports.title: Rio de Janeiro's seven-second miracle - NFL Sunday Review
Sports.content:
The lead

Seven seconds of chaos. Seven seconds to win it all. Seven seconds to send Brazil samba dancing into the night. Seven seconds to crown one of the greatest international games in NFL history. If not the greatest international game in NFL history.

Ricky Martin, baile funk, Lamar Jackson magic, Tyler Loop heroics, Dallas Cowboys disbelief and a last-gasp thriller staged within a cauldron of sporting iconicity. Obrigado, Brazil. Obrigado.

The beach-collared beauty of Rio de Janeiro dazzled on its debut as an NFL host city, its famed magnetism as a hub for otherworldly fun and theatre translating to football as the Baltimore Ravens claimed a 34-31 win over the Dallas Cowboys at the Maracana Stadium.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Baltimore Ravens at the Dallas Cowboys from Week 3 of the NFL season

On a stage graced by Pele and Zico and Romario and Ronaldo and Ronaldinho, it was all too fitting that the very first regular-season game to be played at Rio's sporting home would be decided by a boot. The boot, in this instance, of Tyler Loop.

The Cowboys had just levelled the game at 31-31 on Brandon Aubrey's 23-yard field goal with seven seconds to play, overtime on the horizon as Brazil strapped in for an extended night. Lamar Jackson had other plans, connecting with Zay Flowers for 27 yards to set Baltimore up at the Cowboys 38 on the first play of the ensuing drive. One second left.

Out came Loop, nine months on since he missed the 44-yard field goal that would have gifted the Pittsburgh Steelers the AFC North division title and accompanying playoff berth. Rio redemption would prove sweet as the 25-year-old held his nerve to split the posts from 56 yards and spark a Ravens frenzy.

Loop sprinted off in joyous celebration with a full-speed Jackson and his entire team in tow, spiralling his finger to request some space amid the madness before launching into an imitation of Cristiano Ronaldo's 'SIU', mirrored by the Maracana crowd. Unbridled carnage and the NFL's dream advert for international representation.

The build-up had been marred ever so slightly by question marks over the turf at the Maracana. By the end of Sunday night all had been forgotten as the Ravens showcased their dig deep credentials in the face of a rampant Cowboys offense.

Twitter Twitter , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. You can use the buttons below to amend your preferences to enable Twitter cookies or to allow those cookies just once. You can change your settings at any time via the This content is provided by, which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. You can change your settings at any time via the Privacy Options Unfortunately we have been unable to verify if you have consented to Twitter cookies. To view this content you can use the button below to allow Twitter cookies for this session only. Enable Cookies Allow Cookies Once

The fourth quarter had depicted the complete Super Bowl contender that Dallas might hope to become this season during a sequence that began with their widely-criticised run defense stuffing Derrick Henry on fourth-and-goal at the one-yard line. Dak Prescott rewarded the turnover by igniting the following drive with a 49-yard strike to CeeDee Lamb, before KaVontae Turpin finished off the possession with a nine-yard touchdown run for a 28-24 lead with 9.42 to play.

After the teams exchanged punts Jackson orchestrated an 11-play 64-yard march culminating in his two-yard touchdown pass to Matthew Hibner with 1.30 left, prompting a steely pursed-lip look of determination from Prescott, enough to suggest this wasn't over. And it wasn't.

But instead of six, the Cowboys settled for three on the next possession as four plays inside the Ravens 10-yard line camp up empty, bringing out Aubrey for the field goal most believed had teed up overtime. Between Lamar and Loop, how wrong 'most' were.

Sunday's matchup marked the third to be played in Brazil following regular-season games at Corinthians Arena in Sao Paulo over the last two years. Rio meanwhile represented one of three new host cities alongside Melbourne, Australia and Paris, France this season as the NFL shows no signs of slowing in its international aspirations. It would have its sceptics, as international games tend to, but Rio and the league will wake up Monday morning having combined to produce one of football's most dramatic globe-trotting moments.

Next week, it is the turn of London once more as the UK welcomes three more games across October. Beat that.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Joe Burrow throws to Tee Higgins for a 28-yard touchdown against the Pittsburgh Steelers

What we learned

The Cincinnati Bengals defense isn't good enough, yet. The first two weeks of the season displayed encouraging signs that Cincinnati might have finally mended the defense that has harmed their Super Bowl aspirations in recent seasons, Dexter Lawrence in particular appearing to add a new dimension to the interior of their defensive line. That narrative took a hit on Sunday as they suffered a 30-27 defeat to the Pittsburgh Steelers and Aaron Rodgers' much-maligned offense. Steelers running back Jaylen Warren in particular forced 10 missed tackles on the way to a career-high 176 yards from scrimmage, including 69 of 127 rushing yards before contact. That doesn't equate to a Championship-calibre team, no matter how incredible a trio of Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins is.

"Cook, he gets angry, and Cook starts cooking, the food was pretty good," Buffalo Bills offensive tackle Dion Dawkins told Sky Sports. He was referring to Bills running back James Cook, who had just underlined why he is perhaps still the most underrated and underappreciated player in the NFL by starring for Buffalo in their 24-16 win over the Chargers. Cook has been a defining piece to Joe Brady's offense ever since his early days as the Bills coordinator, his increased prominence proving the key difference from the Bills attack under Ken Dorsey. On a day when Josh Allen was far from his cleanest and most dominant, it was Cook who punished Chargers mistakes with 24 carries for 154 yards and a touchdown. Greg Rousseau meanwhile resumed his emphatic start to the season by recording two sacks for the third successive game, retaining his place as the league leader in that department. Between them came some further evidence of the Bills having ways to win beyond the heroics of their star quarterback.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Mike Evans throws a lateral pass to wide receiver Deebo Samuels for a 82-yard touchdown

The flip side to Buffalo's win was another edition of the Chargers finding new ways to hurt themselves, Jim Harbaugh's side wasting five turnovers in another dismal day for Mike McDaniel and Justin Herbert's offense. For a time their defense had Allen and Joe Brady's offense under wraps, but saw three first-half takeaways become just 10 points before a late collapse opened the door for Buffalo to take control. One of the staple moments came on Herbert's dreadful interception to CJ Gardner-Johnson, an ill-advised decision to, as Tom Brady lamented, "throw him a meatball sub" over the middle of the field negating back-to-back sacks including a fumble recovery. In very Chargers fashion they would then give up an automatic first down with the Bills staring at a second-and-26, paving the way for Allen's one-yard touchdown for a 17-13 lead with seven minutes to play. To make matters worse, Quentin Johnston reverted to serial dropper tendencies as he mis-held a Herbert bullet on third-and-10 on the next drive before the Chargers turned it over on downs.

Overreaction or reality?

Brock Purdy is the early - very very early - MVP frontrunner. The 49ers quarterback continued his near-faultless start to the season by throwing for 297 yards and four more touchdowns in San Francisco's 36-30 win over the Arizona Cardinals, two of his scoring strikes finding the hands of George Kittle. There is an argument he is playing the best football of any quarterback in football, his confidence epitomised by his touch-perfect touchdown pass to Mike Evans. He is clean, clinical and navigating an unbeaten team rediscovering some of its pizzazz on offense under Kyle Shanahan; as much tends to happen when the injury bug stays away, which still isn't quite the case after Evans and Trent Williams both picked up issues.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Genesis Smith picked Josh Allen with a catch on his chest during Chargers' game at Bills

Winners & Losers

Winners:

Mason Graham: The departure of Myles Garrett has opened the door for a fresh face at centre stage for the Cleveland Browns defense - step forward, Mason Graham. The second-year defensive tackle came up with two more sacks in Cleveland's 21-18 win over the Carolina Panthers, including a crucial stop on third-and-10 with the Panthers driving with 1.34 to play. In doing so he lifted his tally to four sacks through three games this season, his impact also underlining the pocket-squeezing influence of Jared Verse since arriving as part of the Garrett trade.

Patrick Mahomes: The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback underlined his place in greatness as he tied seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady for the most wins (115) by a quarterback in his first 150 career starts, including the playoffs. He looks as close to a prime Mahomes as the NFL has seen in at least two years, among his highlights in Kansas City's 24-10 win over Miami being a beautifully-timed strike to Noah Gray. The return to a heavy play-action scheme, boosted by the presence of Kenneth Walker III, has reignited both Mahomes and his passing attack. His Chiefs are now 3-0 and looking like contenders once more.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ndamukong Suh was teasing a comeback to the NFL to Josh Allen and Bridget Condon and it sounded kind of real...

Losers:

Mike Vrabel: The New England Patriots are in the middle of a miserable Super Bowl hangover. What was a championship-calibre defense is being torn apart and what was an MVP-contending quarterback in Drake Maye is struggling to maintain the heights of last season. Maye threw two more interceptions and lost a fumble to increase his turnover tally to seven in three games, having surrendered 11 in 17 regular-season games last season.

Brian Daboll/Cam Ward: Cam Ward threw his first interception in 209 pass attempts on Sunday, which would have been a forgivable blemish had it not been an end zone pick with 24 seconds left in the game. Jevon Holland would be the man to come up with a gift-wrapped throw by Ward as the New York Giants held on for a 12-7 victory, at which point cameras would quickly turn to Titans offensive coordinator and former Giants head coach Brian Daboll. Ward isn't Tennessee's only problem, but he is a problem and is struggling to look like a starting NFL quarterback.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Atlanta Falcons at Green Bay Packers from Week 3 of the NFL season

Player of the Weekend - Jahmyr Gibbs, RB, Detroit Lions

Nothing typified Jahmyr Gibbs better than his shake-and-bake third-quarter touchdown run on Sunday, the Detroit Lions running back scurrying right before putting one defender on skates with a shimmy move to explode in the opposite direction on his way to the end zone. It was one of the latest reminders that he remains the heartbeat of Dan Campbell's Lions offense, contributing to three total touchdowns and 164 yards from scrimmage as Detroit held off a New York Jets fightback in a 31-24 victory. Only Jim Brown and Marshall Faulk have recorded more games with at least two rushing touchdowns and one receiving touchdown.

(Second best) Game of the Weekend

Sorry, the Ravens and Cowboys win the title of Game of the Weekend. Marcus Mariota delivered one of the surprise stories of the weekend as the backup veteran quarterback led the Washington Commanders to a 33-31 win over the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks while standing in for the injured Jayden Daniels. It would be Mariota who iced the game with a nine-yard scramble on third-and-seven to quash any Seahawks fightback. Sam Darnold returned for the Seattle for the first time since his injury early in the Week One win over the Patriots, but featured amid a mistake-ridden Seahawks performance that saw him intercepted on a crucial fourth-quarter pick-six by Kain Medrano. Mariota finished 19 of 31 for 183 yards and three touchdowns, seven of his passes going for over 10 yards as Washington clinched their first win of the season.

Sports.title: Why Man City charges case could still drag on for years
Sports.content:
Manchester City have been embroiled in legal disputes with UEFA and the Premier League for 12 years and they are so determined to clear their name, and the 115 charges case is so big, that it could still be years before the saga is concluded.

According to reports last week, an independent tribunal has reached decisions in the case and Sky Sports News understands that the process is moving to the appeal stage.

In 2014 City paid a £49m fine for breaking UEFA's financial fair play rules and in 2020 they were given a two-year European competition ban and fined €30m for breaking the rules again. The ban was overturned at the Court of Arbitration for Sport where City were cleared of disguising owner funding as sponsorship income.

That victory may give City fans hope that they can win again when their Premier League appeal is heard by a new three-person panel.

If the appeal goes against them, they will not be able to go to CAS but there is the strong possibility that City's owners would turn to the High Court to clear their name.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Miguel Delaney, Riath Al-Samarrai and Jack Rosser joined Sunday Supplement to discuss the latest in the Manchester City charges case

In 2014 City chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak said he would spend £30 million on the best 50 lawyers in the world and sue UEFA for the next 10 years rather than lose the FFP case. In his open letter to City fans on Saturday he sounded just as determined as he was 12 years ago: "The Premier League process still has a long way to run and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began".

Al-Mubarak means what he says and there is so much at stake that City will do whatever it takes to clear their name. In the meantime, the most high-profile sports lawyers are keeping their thoughts to themselves until the full judgment is released. Friday's leak, which led to reports that City had lost on 114 of the 115 charges, may well end up being used as evidence in City's legal fight to prove that, in their opinion, the whole process has not been fair and impartial.

At the heart of all the legal challenges City have faced is the question of how they became so big and successful so quickly. City's owners have been accused of putting too much money into the club and disguising it as sponsorship income. City have always insisted they have irrefutable evidence to prove that they did not break the rules.

City will face serious sanctions if they fail to clear their name and the case will continue to cast a shadow over Enzo Maresca and his players until it is finally resolved.

City's reputation, and that of their owners, depends on this and the final judgement will also have implications for relations between Abu Dhabi and the United Kingdom. The two countries have close ties and common trade and diplomatic interests but the strength of that relationship will be tested if City are found definitively to have broken the rules.

City's legal dispute with the Premier League would never have existed if it had not been for documents obtained illegally by convicted Portuguese hacker Rui Pinto. From City's perspective, these leaked internal documents are "out-of-context materials purportedly hacked or stolen" which have been used in an "organised and clear attempt to damage the club's reputation".

Sports.title: Will Littler defend World Grand Prix title? Humphries, Price, Smith in the mix
Sports.content:
Will Luke Littler successfully defend his World Grand Prix title? Can Luke Humphries, Gerwyn Price, James Wade or Ross Smith trouble the world No 1 in the unique double-in, double-out format?

Littler will be hoping the home crowd at Leicester's Mattioli Arena is more welcoming after the two-time world champion was booed and whistled at during the World Series of Darts Finals exit in Amsterdam earlier this month.

The 19-year-old headed into the tournament chasing a historic clean sweep after winning the first six major titles of the season but suffered a crushing 10-4 defeat to Jonny Clayton in the last eight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Paul Nicholson backed Littler's reduced schedule for the rest of the season

Stephen Bunting backed Littler, saying he has "changed" darts since bursting onto the scene a few years ago.

"It's really hard, isn't it? Obviously, Luke is the best player in the world. For whatever reason, the crowd got on his back, they didn't want him to do the [clean sweep]," said Bunting.

"He was probably on edge, anyway, going into [the tournament]. Maybe in Germany, in Belgium, I've had it a few times where the crowd has whistled out.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mark Webster and Michael Bridge discuss Littler's concerns over crowd whistling at the World Series of Darts in Amsterdam

"If you let the crowd know they're getting to you, it can be 10 times worse. It's a hard one to say, but I don't like the whistling. I'd rather have someone shouting abuse at me than whistling.

"It's a horrible noise to hear when you're trying to concentrate. But I understand it'll keep happening, no matter how much we talk about it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stephen Bunting says Littler has 'changed' darts since bursting onto the scene a few years ago

"Punishments need to be brought in, maybe. Until that happens, it'll keep happening."

Littler takes on Luke Woodhouse in the first round and if he wins he will go on to play either Nathan Aspinall or Kevin Doets in round two.

Humphries under pressure?

Image: Humphries has been back on the practice board in preparation for the World Grand Prix

Luke Humphries lost the World Grand Prix final two years ago but 'Cool Hand Luke' must at least match that run this time, otherwise he will surrender second place in the world rankings to Gian van Veen.

The former world champion opens his campaign against Dave Chisnall, with a potential second-round showdown against Chris Dobey or Jermaine Wattimena.

Humphries, who suffered a shock defeat to Mike De Decker in the 2024 final, only returned to competitive action at the end of August for the first time since his shock round-one exit to Cameron Menzies in the World Matchplay on July 20 and went on to win Players Championship 28 before defeat to Littler in the final of the Czech Open.

Humphries said: "I'm going to get back on the practice board at home as much as I can now and I'm going to dedicate the rest of the year to trying to be my best and trying to push Luke - and not just Luke, but everyone else because I want to stay at No 2.

"Whether that happens or not, I'm going to fight for it because I'm going to try my best."

Sports.title: 'Frustrating' - Vasseur responds after Horner's 'dream' Ferrari job comments
Sports.content:
Frederic Vasseur admits Ferrari are not able to work in "perfect serenity" amid persistent speculation about his future, which was heightened after comments from Christian Horner about Formula 1's "dream" job.

Vasseur, who joined Ferrari as team principal from Sauber in 2023, has an overseen their return to race-winning ways this year after a poor 2025 but their world championship challenge to Mercedes has faded in recent months amid a five-race run without a podium finish.

In an interview with The Times published last week, former Red Bull team principal Horner said Ferrari were the only team he would consider returning to the pit-wall for without the ownership stake that he has been prioritising for any comeback to the sport.

Asked after Sunday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, in which his drivers finished fourth and sixth, whether the external noise around him and the team recently was affecting them, Vasseur conceded it was frustrating.

"We are not working in perfect serenity," said Vasseur.

"For me, first, but for everybody in the team, for the media, for the 50 per cent of the questions about this. I think it's a bit of a frustrating situation.

"We are fighting for P2 in the championship. At the end of the day, we are all speaking a lot about this, and even for the guys in the garage to discuss about this, it's not the best discussion that we can have.

"But it is what it is, it's not in my hands."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Christian Horner spoke to Craig Slater when he returned to the paddock at this year's British Grand Prix.

Referencing his former Red Bull counterpart, Vasseur added: "Mr Horner is looking for a job. Everybody knows, everywhere.

"What can I do? I just try to do my best to push the team, to ask the team to be motivated, focus on what is better today, and not to spend time with gossips.

"In each interview, it will be 25 times a day."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Vasseur signed a multi-year contract extension last year and said there was no doubt about his commitment to the role as he bids to lead F1's most-famous team back to world title-winning ways for the first time since 2008.

"For sure. The sport is my life, it's my business," said the 58-year-old Vasseur. "I'm trying to do my best. For sure, I'm there to do my job. I have the best job in the world.

"It is like it is. We still have seven races to go and we will push to the last corner."

Lewis Hamilton credited the presence of Vasseur, who he worked with in junior series, as a central reason for him joining Ferrari from Mercedes in 2025. The seven-time world champion replied "yes" when asked by Sky Sports F1 after the Baku race whether the team remained on a good path forward with Vasseur at the helm.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton reflects on his Azerbaijan Grand Prix, which saw him finish sixth.

Villeneuve: Horner someone you must have under consideration

Even before he was sacked by Red Bull in July 2025, Horner had been intermittently linked with Ferrari over the years owing to the success which saw the Briton lead their rivals to eight drivers' and six constructors' world titles.

Sky Sports F1 pundit Jacques Villeneuve believes Horner's availability has to be a consideration for a team.

"Christian Horner is someone you have to take seriously and under consideration because he built up the winning Red Bull team," the 1997 world champion told Sky Sports News in Baku.

"He has a lot of very good and positive baggage, full of successes so you have to take that into consideration.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Craig Slater takes a look back at Christian Horner's 20-year run as Red Bull CEO and team principal.

"I wouldn't say it's scary for who is in place, but you need to be on your toes."

Vasseur became Ferrari's fifth team principal in nine years when he was hired from the start of the 2023 season, with the current campaign his fourth in charge.

Villeneuve added: "Ferrari is not an easy place to be. We have seen so many changes - two or three years, next one, because the results don't come.

"So you are always on an ejectable seat and you have to be careful."

Sports.title: Broncos score in final minute to beat Rams in thrilling comeback
Sports.content:
Bo Nix crossed for a touchdown from close range with 47 seconds left in the fourth quarter as the Denver Broncos came from 16-0 down at half-time to beat the Los Angeles Rams 30-26.

Quarterback Nix's keeper from inches outside the goal line capped a wild final five minutes that included a 66-yard pick-6 by Denver and a quick touchdown response by Los Angeles.

After Nix put the Broncos (2-1) in front by reaching over the scrum with both hands gripping the football, Matthew Stafford, whose 17 comebacks in the last 2 minutes are the most by any active quarterback, drove the Rams to the Denver 14, where he spiked the ball with 2 seconds left.

A false start moved the ball back to the 19, the Rams (1-2) sent out five receivers but safety Talanoa Hufanga secured his second interception of the night - this one in the end zone - to seal the win for the home side.

Image: Talanoa Hufanga had two interceptions on the night including a game-winner

The Rams dominated Denver before halftime, outgaining the Broncos by more than 200 yards in the first half while piling up 17 first downs to five, outrushing them 87 yards to 21 and besting them 186 yards to 46 through the air.

But it was only 16-0 at halftime because the Rams kept stalling and settling for field goals after Stafford hit tight end Tyler Higbee with a 5-yard touchdown throw on the Rams' second possession.

The Broncos went three-and-out to start the second half but finally revved up their sputtering offense and cut their deficit in half on Nix's 5-yard strike to Bryant and 2-point conversion pass to Jaylen Waddle on a throw between the hands of Wallace midway through the third quarter.

Image: Pat Bryant (13) and Courtland Sutton (14) celebrate a first down

The Broncos tied it on another touchdown and 2-pointer. Nate Adkins caught an 8-yard throw from Nix, who found Bryant again to tie the game heading into the final period.

Talanoa Hufanga's 66-yard pick-6 with 4:49 left in the game gave Denver its first lead at 23-19. Hufanga jumped in front of running back Kyren Williams, cradled Stafford's pass and weaved his way down the field and into the end zone.

Just four plays later, however, Stafford hit Konata Mumpfield from 48 yards out when cornerback Riley Moss fell down, restoring the Rams' lead at 26-23.

Image: Broncos linebacker Que Robinson (51) celebrates a tackle against the Rams

Nix drove Denver 65 yards in 10 plays with the aid of three defensive penalties and, with the ball nearly touching the goal line, leapt over the pile for the go-ahead TD. Nix had completions of 39 and 21 yards on that drive, finishing the evening with 17 completions for 186 yards and two touchdowns to accompany a first-half interception.

Stafford, on the other hand, finished 30 for 55 for 390 yards. He threw 32 passes in the first half, the most of his career. With Puka Nacua out again with a hip injury, Davante Adams had seven receptions for 137 yards, giving him 15 catches for 332 yards over his last two games, the best such stretch of his career.

Sports.title: KP promises to challenge McCullum as England push to be 'world's best'
Sports.content:
Kevin Pietersen has promised to challenge England white-ball head coach Brendon McCullum in his new role as a specialist mentor to the team, saying it's precisely why he was brought in.

Since retiring as a player in 2018, Pietersen has, at times, been an outspoken critic of the England setup, including when accusing the white-ball team of inadequate preparation on a tour of India last January after McCullum had just taken over.

Pietersen's work with England began with a 3-0 T20 series whitewash of Sri Lanka, before the hosts then also clinched a 2-1 ODI series success over the same side on Sunday. His role with the team will continue through to the 2027 50-over World Cup in just over a year's time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of England against Sri Lanka in their third ODI at The Oval

"Brendon, when he first called me, I thought I was in trouble because I'd said something, but he said this exact point: 'I'd like you to come in and challenge me,'" Pietersen told Sky Sports Cricket ahead of England's series-clinching 223-run win over Sri Lanka at The Oval.

"He's since said to me: 'I absolutely love the fact that you are inside the rooms and you are picking on things that can make the players better.'

"And at the end of the day, if we can't do that as a coach, try and challenge players to be the best versions of themselves, I think we're letting them down because these guys are too good."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at Kevin Pietersen's incredible insight for England's batters, including the importance of 'rotation of strike'

Pietersen added on his coaching approach: "No stone unturned. There are a few things I don't like. There are many things that I do like, and I think if we can get that balance right, I think that these guys are going to be very, very good.

"That messaging and that constant drive to be the best version of themselves is something that we're drilling down on.

"It's been a brilliant period to understand what actually is happening inside that dressing room. There's a crazy amount of talent up there."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England white-ball coach Brendon McCullum spoke on Kevin Pietersen becoming a mentor for the side and discussed if previous criticism of the team will affect their relationship

McCullum was similarly bullish about his hopes for the 50-over side, specifically with a World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia in a year's time.

The T20 team have won 22 of their past 25 completed T20 internationals since the start of last summer, assuming the No 1 spot in the world rankings as a result, and McCullum wants similar for the ODI team, currently sixth in the standings.

"I've also found that with a little bit of extra time, I've been able to drill down on some aspects of where you want to take this team and how you want to shape it," McCullum, who was removed as England Test coach earlier this summer, told Sky Sports Cricket.

"At the time, I was very comfortable doing it all [Test and white-ball jobs]. Change happens and my focus now is on how to make this side the best white-ball team in the world.

"We're not there yet. We've got a lot of growth within us and a lot of improvement to make, but there's a determination within the dressing room to be the best team in the world.

"I want us to become the strongest, fastest and most robust cricket teams in the world, one that can play at a high-octane speed.

"The performance we saw today [against Sri Lanka] was brilliant. You go to a World Cup, you got to do it time and time and time again over a long period of time. So that'll be a focus for us over the next little while.

Pietersen: Brook finds game 'too easy' at times

McCullum and Pietersen also both singled out white-ball captain Harry Brook, specifically, for praise.

Brook, despite being vice-captain, was overlooked for the Test captaincy in favour of Joe Root when Ben Stokes retired, but continues to impress in the white-ball role.

"I think he's an outstanding tactician, he's growing as a leader and maturing as a person - and doing it at rapid speed," McCullum said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Brendon McCullum talks about Harry Brook as a captain for England, singling him out for praise

"Tactically he's outstanding; he's very much the leader of the side. The boys respect him immensely, and not just for his cricket brain but the way he creates the right environment.

"It's like a group of mates playing together, which is which is plain to see when when you watch them play out in the middle."

With the bat against Sri Lanka, Brook notched two half-centuries in the ODI series to go with a 42-ball hundred - England's joint-second-fastest - in the opening T20I.

That innings saw Brook hailed as an "absolute freak" by Ben Stokes, who took to social media to say that, in his opinion, the Yorkshireman's ability outstrips that of Pietersen.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Harry Brook shares his thoughts on Kevin Pietersen's impact on England's white-ball side

But as well as being capable of achieving the incredible, both Brook and Pietersen have had their share of percieved 'brain fade' moments.

Addressing that similarity, Pietersen said: "Looking back at my career, the brain fade moments happen because sometimes you see the game differently. And that's what the fan and the spectator needs to understand... Harry Brook is a player that sees the game differently.

"There are times when Harry Brook stands at the wicket and he goes, 'This is too easy.'

"The one thing that I'm working really hard with Brooky, and will continue to work hard on, is just being better at assessing game situations.

"I will never in my life try and take the flair and that genius out of him."

Sports.title: Kohli passes 15,000 ODI runs as hundred helps India beat West Indies
Sports.content:
Virat Kohli celebrated his return to the international arena by hitting his 55th ODI hundred as India beat West Indies by eight wickets in the series opener on Sunday.

India's star batter - who now only plays this format in international cricket - smashed an unbeaten 139 off 88 balls, including 10 fours and nine sixes, as India successfully chased down 296 in just 41.4 overs.

In doing so, the 37-year-old also became only the second batter after Sachin Tendulkar (18,426) to pass 15,000 runs in ODIs.

"My focus has never been on milestones. Just looking back at the start of my journey, it makes me feel very grateful," Kohli said. "I enjoy each and every minute that I am out there playing for India, and I am able to do the job for my team. As a cricketer, this is all I could dream of."

Skipper Shubman Gill also notched a century, scoring 110 off 108 deliveries as India registered an easy win - clinched with a Kohli six - to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.

Earlier, West Indies had posted 295-7 from their 50 overs after being put into bat. Opener Justin Greaves (101 off 108) scored his maiden ODI ton, sharing in an impressive 135-run opening partnership with John Campbell (62 off 60) inside the first 20 overs.

Wrist spinner Kuldeep Yadav (4-40) ultimately accounted for both as he wreaked havoc in the middle overs to see West Indies reduced to 198-5 by the 36th.

Amir Jangoo's unbeaten 58 off 43 balls helped revive the innings, but their target of 296 ultimately proved an under-par one on a batter-friendly pitch.

It was a quick-fire chase for India as openers Gill and Rohit Sharma added 74 off 72 balls, Sharma scoring 32 off 35 before he fell to Alzarri Joseph (1-81) in the 12th over.

Kohli came to the crease and promptly eased his way to fifty in only 40 balls, hitting the 15,000-milestone on the way - the fastest to do it at 303 innings, compared to Tendulkar's 377.

He and Gill put on 151 off 132 balls for the second wicket before the captain departed against the run of play to Roston Chase (1-64) in the 34th over.

But Kohli cruised to a 74-ball hundred, before finishing the game in style with 8.2 overs to spare. Kohli's nine sixes were his most in an ODI innings.

Guwahati and Chandigarh will host the second and third ODIs on Wednesday and Saturday, followed by a five-match T20 series starting on October 6.

Sports.title: Arsène Wenger and Arsenal: 30 years on from appointment that changed English football
Sports.content:
As feedback goes, even a character as relentlessly optimistic as David Dein might have considered the reaction to his bold managerial appointment suboptimal. Thirty years ago, Arsenal were in a state of chaotic flux, having sacked Bruce Rioch, with the interims Stewart Houston and Pat Rice in charge. There had been talk of Johan Cruyff arriving and Dein wanted to fill the information vacuum. Summoning the team, he reassured them a new manager would soon be appointed and that he was a world-class addition.

“His name is Arsène Wenger,” Dein, the club’s vice-chair, beamed. A brief pause ensued before a player’s voice called out: “Who the fuck is he?” His exclamation echoed conventional wisdom. “Arsene Who?” famously read The London Evening Standard’s billboards prior to Wenger being confirmed as manager on 30 September 1996.

Ultimately Dein’s decision was arguably the most seismic managerial appointment in modern English football history, not only providing proof that a foreign manager could succeed in this country but also ushering in an irreversible era of multiculturalism, giving birth to the globalised Premier League we know today. Wenger described the Arsenal dressing room he inherited as “culturally English” and set about making his first signings, the characteristically unknown Frenchmen in Patrick Vieira and Rémi Garde; when he departed the job in 2018, every Premier League dressing room was a veritable United Nations.

He was the trailblazer, preceding Gérard Houllier and Rafael Benítez at Liverpool and, ironically given their mutual animosity, José Mourinho at Chelsea, all beneficiaries of his success. On the flip side, there would never have been Tottenham’s ill-advised experiments with Christian Gross and Jacques Santini were it not for Wenger.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal’s squad for the 1996-97 season. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

Undoubtedly he was the right man at the right time: Chelsea were already embracing the continental drift, having appointed Ruud Gullit, and Wenger’s arrival chimed with contemporary geopolitics. Tony Blair was about to become prime minister and a wave of European Union migration was coming; Polish plumbers and French footballers alike. Equally, Sky TV’s money was making England the best-paid country for footballers.

The first non-British or non-Irish manager in the top flight had been Dr Jozef Venglos, appointed by Aston Villa in 1990, ticking all the boxes of English football’s old prejudices: foreign, academic, whimsical, tactical. Gratifyingly for sceptics, he was an utter failure. Wenger seemed to fit the Venglos mould. Nicknamed Le Professeur (because he wore glasses and spoke five languages), his captain, Tony Adams, thought him a “geography teacher”, while Ian Wright noted his clumsiness and dubbed him Clouseau, taking delight in pranking him about a bomb scare. “There is bum?” replied a bemused Wenger, oblivious to the hilarity among Wright’s teammates.

View image in fullscreen Arsène Wenger’s arrival brought many changes for the Arsenal squad. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

“Arsène Wenger’s been in Japan, he doesn’t know anything about the English game,” said Sir Alex Ferguson, laying the foundations for a decade-long feud that would become, in Ferguson’s words, “toxic”. Yet even the bastions of the English game acknowledge the magnitude of Wenger’s contribution. “Wenger changed the whole course of [English] football,” says Neil Warnock, not a natural soulmate. “He made people who’d been in the game a long time [realise] that you had to change with the times because of all the nutrition coming, the fitness guys who were coming, and that if you didn’t move with the times, you got trodden on.”

Wenger’s aesthetic playing style was encapsulated upon securing his first Premier League title in 1998, with a pastiche of Total Football that culminated in Steve Bould drifting out of the back four to chip a pass on to the advancing Tony Adams, who finished perfectly in a 4-0 win over Everton. “Would you believe it?!” said a stunned Martin Tyler in commentary, reflecting the views of the nation. “That sums it all up.” Derided as a donkey, Adams had become a thoroughbred.

View image in fullscreen Arsène Wenger with Tony Adams after Arsenal had turned on the style against Everton to clinch the title. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Action Images

Wenger’s genius was in maintaining an English core to his early side, grafting on Vieira, Emmanuel Petit, Marc Overmars and allowing Dennis Bergkamp to flourish. “There were rumours that he was advised to get rid of the back four,” said Nigel Winterburn, part of that legendary quartet. “But I think he made his own decisions when he saw the players playing and training, and saw the desire they had.” Later Thierry Henry, Robert Pires and Freddie Ljungberg would arrive to reach the even greater heights of the Invincibles.

Dr Yann Rougier joined as a sports scientist and Ferguson, in charge of a dominant Manchester United team, was instinctively suspicious of the new methods challenging his success. When the England manager Glenn Hoddle, a Wenger protege at Monaco, used Rougier at the 1998 World Cup and United players came back singing the praises of his nutritional approach, Ferguson was infuriated, demanding FA investigations. Yet most of the interventions nowadays would be regarded as standard, such as using creatine to supplement diets.

Chocolate was famously banned at Arsenal but Winterburn revealed the manager’s strictures were not always adhered to. “We’d wait for Arsène to walk [away], then most of the players would pile into the little kiosk and buy chocolate and eat Mars bars under the table.” What became known as the “Evian broccoli” diet was introduced just as Adams had announced himself an alcoholic, lager being the habitual post-match refreshment of British football. Adams attributed his late-career transformation to Wenger’s nutrition and his teetotalism. Eschewing alcohol is unremarkable among elite England players now.

View image in fullscreen A 2-1 win over Leicester at Highbury in May 2004 saw them finish the season with a record of P38 W26 D12 L0, which led them to acquire the nickname ‘The Invincibles’. Photograph: Sean Dempsey/PA

Hoddle had also been transformed by Wenger’s holistic approach to exercise. “We were in the dark ages [in England] by comparison,” he said. “I had never had a massage or done a warm-down at Tottenham. I became more supple and I was soon fitter than ever.” Wenger employed a French osteopath, Philippe Boixel, and used the English psychologist David Elliott. Arsenal were the first club to sign up with ProZone, using stats to analyse performance. There aren’t many innovations in modern English football not pioneered by him and, in that respect, his influence is greater than even Ferguson’s, even if his success never measured up to the Scot’s achievements. By the end, Wenger’s French revolution had become common practice; he was a victim of his own success, his competitive edge dulled.

Only when the prizefighters had laid down their gloves was Ferguson able to articulate his appreciation. “Arsène is, without doubt, one of the greatest Premier League managers and I am proud to have been a rival, a colleague and a friend to such a great man,” he said when Wenger left Arsenal. Wenger might raise a quizzical Gallic eyebrow at the “friend” description. But 30 years on, few dispute the scale of Wenger’s transformation of the English game.

Sports.title: Data shows England made inroads against Spain but they must be more clinical | Andrew Beasley
Sports.content:
England dominated Spain to an extent very few teams have in recent years. Sadly for them, not in terms of goals. Nor possession. But ownership of the ball is less important than where on the pitch it occurs. Thomas Tuchel’s side had 36 touches in the visitors’ penalty area, a ridiculously high total when put in context of Spain’s last decade.

They allowed just 9.5 touches per 90 minutes at the 2026 World Cup. The combined efforts of Belgium, France and Argentina registered 38 touches in the Spain box in the final three rounds of the tournament. Since available records began (at the start of Euro 2016), the most box touches a side has had against Spain was the 45 Germany had in the quarter-final of Euro 2024. However, that game went to extra time. France had 42 in normal time in the ridiculous Nations League semi-final they lost 5-4 last year, then come England, second best in regular time from a sample of 133 matches.

Given they were so active in the penalty area, they should have created more. Germany generated 2.15 non-penalty expected goals in the above example, France 1.95 and England just 0.95. The latter averaged 5.1 box touches for each shot they had in the penalty area, or 5.8 without Harry Kane’s spot kick. Tottenham have been criticised for being inefficient in this regard this season and their average of 3.6 – the highest in the Premier League – is well below England’s level against Spain.

England struggled to create high-value chances even when in the box because the Spanish compressed the space so well, leaving very few passing lanes or lines of sight to goal. Bukayo Saka’s performance provides an excellent case study. His total of 10 touches in the box was two more than Argentina managed in the 120 minutes of the World Cup final.

Saka had one shot from within the penalty area, which he curled wide of the far post midway through the second half. He was tackled twice when trying to make things happen, and was unable to control the ball when receiving it a couple of times. The key lies in his box touches where he was attempting to find a teammate – four of the five passes Saka made from within the penalty area went outside it, away from goal.

View image in fullscreen Morgan Gibbs-White was the only England substitute to complete a pass in the Spain penalty area. Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty Images

Anthony Gordon was second for box touches for England, with five. One of his two passes there was a cutback Unai Simón gathered, the other went backwards to the edge of the box. But at least that one was successful; Jude Bellingham’s one pass in the area went astray, while Kane did not attempt any. Morgan Gibbs-White completed one pass in the Spain box in the 95th minute, the sum total from the five substitutes.

As both of their assists and one of their goals came from outside the box, England proved inefficiency within the penalty area need not be decisive. The problem was Spain showed how lethal they could be inside the 18-yard box even with limited possession there.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Their Wembley total of 15 box touches was less than half of their per 90 average at the World Cup (32.5). But ignore the volume, feel the quality. Spain had five shots worth at least 0.26 expected goals inside the box whereas England only had one effort (plus the penalty) that cleared that benchmark. Tuchel’s men frequently hit a defensive wall once they were in the penalty area, unlike Spain, who sliced through the home side’s backline with relative ease.

The highest-value chances the visitors created were set up with a pass into the box or a through ball. Two of the latter laid on Opta-defined big chances at 1-0, both of which were missed by Ferran Torres. Could England have recovered from two goals down? It feels doubtful.

To have 36 box touches against the team that World Football Elo Ratings considers to be the greatest international side of all time is an achievement that should not be readily dismissed. But despite Gordon claiming afterwards there isn’t a gap between England and Spain, there is. Tuchel must figure out how to make his side as resolute as the world champions at the back and as rapier-like in attack.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland put controversy aside to earn impressive win over Israel
Sports.content:
Football and politics are inseparable in the modern world, no matter how many people wish they were not. But whether the beautiful game can ease the ills of our age is another matter. After a week in which the issue of Irish support for the people of Gaza had turned this fixture into a battle of conscience, the outcome of this underwhelming match ultimately felt inconsequential.

In the end the result was indeed a walkover, just not because of a boycott. On Saturday night the question had been whether Heimir Hallgrimsson’s side would take to the field in Hungary at all. If they did, would their heads be in the game? It turned out that a week of internal angst had been enough to produce collective resolve among the Irish squad, or at least those selected to play. Strong and assertive from the off, their forwards each scored in the first half to settle the contest, with plenty of symbolic action to assure those back home of their feelings.

“It’s probably been the toughest days of my coaching career,” Hallgrimsson said after the match. “But it’s not about me. It’s about the players and they’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them. They represented themselves on the pitch with dignity but also with the power of proud Irishmen. They’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them and hopefully they will have the support of the Irish people.”

In a way the atmosphere in Debrecen was reminiscent of a match played during Covid. Every word uttered in the ground was audible and the nigh-on empty stands carried their own oppressive weight. As the nominal home side, Israel had been allowed a small delegation of fans, about 150, who were doing their best to be excitable. Meanwhile, two blocks away were the Irish contingent, around a dozen people who had got into the ground despite the Football Association of Ireland’s decision not to bring an away allocation. They were all stood hands in pockets in a stairway.

This odd, almost haunted mood was heightened further by Ireland’s mannered approach to the pre-match rituals. Irish staff faced away from the pitch when their national anthem was played. Ireland’s players, all wearing black armbands, stared at the ground during Israel’s. There was no exchanging of pennants and no shaking of hands, with both squads hurried away from the centre circle into their own huddles.

The game had come close to being abandoned on Saturday, when the goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu made himself unavailable for selection, his decision prompting emotional exchanges among players and management. Hallgrimsson therefore picked a team with defender Jimmy Dunne nominally a third goalkeeper and also dropped the key forward Finn Azaz to the bench in one of five changes to the team that lost meekly to Kosovo. Azaz’s mother has Israeli citizenship and the Southampton forward was reported to have made an impassioned contribution to Saturday’s discussion. “Today we thought others would fit this game better than him,” Halgrimsson said.

View image in fullscreen The Republic of Ireland team bow their heads during the Israeli national anthem. Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty Images

After all the soul-searching, Ireland decided the contest in only 11 first-half minutes. Troy Parrott opened the scoring in the 14th minute, turning home a low shot through the body of Daniel Peretz after impressive work on the right by wingback James Abankwah. Two minutes later the lead was doubled when, running on the shoulder of the last defender, Adam Idah collected a smart through ball from Jack Moylan and wrapped a calm finish inside Peretz’s left-hand post.

In the 25th minute Moylan got a goal of his own, his fourth in as many caps to continue a stellar start to his international career, driving 25 yards into the box before shooting low into the net. Moylan wheeled away to the corner flag, took off his black armband and kissed it.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Israel raised their levels momentarily in the second half, with the substitute Dor Peretz drawing one excellent save from Caoimhín Kelleher. But ultimately the game deteriorated into just a series of scuffles, cheered on deliriously by the Israeli support who appeared to be chanting for the IDF as the final whistle blew.

Their manager, Ran Ben-Shimon, was asked by Israeli media after the match if he would resign following the defeat, to which he answered no. “We didn’t handle the pressure well that is obvious, we failed mentally, we failed tactically,” Ben-Shimon said. “But in a few days there is another game we will have to find the energy to rise again.”

Sports.title: Nations League: Greece stun Klopp’s Germany, Netherlands sink Serbia but Gakpo hurt
Sports.content:
Greece stunned Germany 1-0 in Augsburg to go top of their Nations League group and spoil Jürgen Klopp’s debut in the home dugout.

Dimitrios Kourbelis scored the only goal in the 74th minute, earning Greece their first-ever victory in 11 matches against Germany. Ivan Jovanovic’s side now lead ⁠Group A2 with six points ⁠from two matches; Klopp’s side are third with one point from two games after a 1-1 draw against the Netherlands on Thursday.

The hosts were in control for most of the game and had close to 80% possession in the first half alone. Germany were ultimately punished ⁠for sloppy defending, especially in the second half, which gave the visitors space to attack.

Felix Nmecha fired wide in the 54th minute, moments after the Greece keeper Konstantinos Tzolakis ‌had palmed a Joshua Kimmich free-kick over the bar. The Greeks then almost scored in the 66th after Kimmich lost possession in his own half, but the substitute Fotis Ioannidis fired just wide of the post.

View image in fullscreen It was a frustrating first home game in charge of the Germany side for Jürgen Klopp. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters

They did better eight minutes later, with Kourbelis’s deflected low drive earning their second victory in a row after their last-gasp 2-1 win over Serbia on Thursday. Greece will now host the Dutch on Thursday, while Germany are at home to Serbia.

Klopp shrugged off the defeat after the final whistle. “Personally, I’m completely unbothered by it,” he told ARD. “I’ve lost far more matches in my life than I would have liked … but as long as you draw the right conclusions, a loss is ultimately just a piece of information – no different from a win.”

“We absolutely need these kinds of matches – they are exactly the games we wanted to have,” Klopp added, while Kimmich said his new coach “has been very clear about what he wants – as players, we need to implement it”.

Earlier, the Netherlands earned a 2-1 victory in Serbia thanks to Mexx ‌Meerdink’s double on his second appearance for his country. It was their first win under their new coach, Xavi Hernández, following Thursday’s draw with Germany.

Meerdink, who plays for the Eredivisie leaders, AZ, opened the scoring with a confidently taken penalty in the 30th minute. Luka Jovic equalised for the hosts but Meerdink struck again in the 69th minute to earn three points.

“It’s a boyhood dream,” Meerdink said. “Everything is happening so quickly. You just don’t realise what can happen in the space of a week. It’s also great that we managed to win here. I did feel a little pressure, but you play that out of your system. And then to score two ​is fantastic.”

Cody Gakpo is an injury concern after going off in the 17th minute and will undergo a scan on Monday. “It’s his ankle, that’s all I know,” Xavi said on the Liverpool winger’s injury. “Tomorrow we will know, but hopefully it’s not too important.”

View image in fullscreen Mexx Meerdink scores his second goal in the Netherlands’ 2-1 victory in Belgrade. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters

João Félix scored for the second ​consecutive Portugal match as the defending champions edged past Norway 2-1 in Oslo to top Group A4 with two wins from two games. Erling Haaland cancelled out João Félix’s 17th-minute opener in the 54th minute, but Gonçalo ​Ramos’s chip three minutes later secured victory for Jorge Jesus’s side in Oslo.

Bruno Fernandes was left out of the Portugal squad on Sunday, with Jesus revealing beforehand that the Manchester United captain had “played through the pain” in Thursday’s 1-0 win over Wales.

“He played with an injury he brought from Manchester United,” the Portugal head coach said. “He wasn’t his usual self … [but] he really wanted to play against Wales.”

Portugal stay in Scandinavia for their next game, away to Denmark on Thursday. Norway visit Cardiff to take on Wales, who earlier lost 2-0 to the Danes in Copenhagen.

Sports.title: Tony Pulis says he and Stoke were ‘cheated’ in 2011 FA Cup final after Manchester City verdict
Sports.content:
Tony Pulis has said his Stoke City team were “cheated” out of the 2011 FA Cup after Manchester City were found guilty on virtually all counts of breaching Premier League financial rules.

Pulis’s Stoke lost the 2011 Cup final 1-0 after Yaya Touré’s goal. Yet following Friday’s news that City are guilty on all but one of the more than 100 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, Pulis feels serious discontent. City are expected to appeal and they deny any wrongdoing.

“When do we get our FA Cup?” the 68-year-old wrote in his BBC Sport column. “That is what all Stoke fans have been asking me since the news broke on Friday. I thought exactly the same.

“I don’t expect Manchester City to offer back the 2011 FA Cup and the winners’ medals their players received. I don’t seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either. A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely.

“But I still feel cheated. We won’t ever get that day back and the chance to celebrate around Stoke-on-Trent with the cup and medals we so honestly fought for. After breaking the rules, Manchester City got to do that instead. While the process is far from over because City are expected to appeal, I have to say this verdict and the whole situation has left a very sour taste in my mouth.”

Pulis pointed to City’s outlay on Touré, who was signed from Barcelona for £24m and earned about £180,000-a-week. He said: “Yaya Touré, who scored the winning goal, was reportedly earning 10 times what we were paying any of our players and, on his own, had cost more than our entire starting 11 when they had signed him from Barcelona in 2010.”

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Yaya Touré (left) scores during the 2011 FA Cup final. Photograph: Andrew Yates/AFP/Getty Images

Pulis underlined how his emotion has been changed by the verdict. “My disappointment was buried in the fact we had played a team full of superstars, and faced an elite coach in Roberto Mancini, and had just fallen short. Today, I feel very differently, as I am sure people connected with the other clubs affected by City’s successes in the same period, between 2009 and 2018 [will feel].

“We lost, but to a team that have been found guilty of breaking the financial rules set out by the Premier League. In doing so, they did not just beat Stoke in an FA Cup final, they collected a stack of titles and went on to completely dominate English football for more than a decade. So, with those rules having been broken, what will the punishment be?”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Tony Pulis of Stoke City reacts in defeat. Photograph: Laurence Griffiths/The FA/Getty Images

Pulis believes action may be widespread. “I know all Stoke supporters will be demanding that City pass the trophy over and every club that has been affected by their actions will be considering their legal options,” he said.

On Saturday, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, reiterated the club’s position. “There is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity,” said City’s chair.

On Friday a City spokesperson had said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023. The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

Sports.title: Chelsea turn up heat on Arsenal as Alyssa Thompson strike settles WSL derby
Sports.content:
Arsenal’s title chances were dealt a significant blow after a narrow defeat at the hands of Chelsea. Alyssa Thompson’s first-half finish was the difference on a competitive afternoon at Stamford Bridge but one that ultimately left Renée Slegers with more questions than answers about how to save their season.

“Worried? No,” Slegers said. “Confidence is something that fluctuates. They know who they are and they know what they can bring. What’s important is that there’s always phases in the season and there’s different things you need to work on or focus on.

“It’s important that we keep any pressure and any complexity away from the players because we believe in them. It’s just really important that we keep that simplicity and clear minds for the players.”

There is no game quite as eagerly anticipated in the Women’s Super League as the meeting between Chelsea and Arsenal. While other derbies and duels are in their early development, the London derby is the one year after year that brings the pressure, the drama and, of course, the eyeballs. While both sides clearly respect each other off the pitch, there is a distinct sense that once they cross the white line there is true competitive animosity there, one that lifts the levels of everyone in the vicinity.

This edition was no different with expectation and apprehension buzzing around Stamford Bridge before kick-off and no shortage of new narratives. This was the first time Katie McCabe, 11 years a Gunner, would face her old team having moved in the summer. Would she help Chelsea to inflict more pain on Arsenal’s stuttering start, or could Slegers’s side put a pin in the pressure balloon and breathe new life into their search for a first title in eight years?

Both teams came into this encounter having not yet hit form. Arsenal have created opportunities but have looked predictable in their buildup and lacked a finishing touch. In contrast, Chelsea have looked energetic and full of ideas but, excluding their win against Manchester United, have also struggled with ruthlessness in front of goal.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea’s Katie McCabe took on her former Arsenal teammates for the first time since her summer move. Photograph: Harriet Lander/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Sonia Bompastor was handed a significant boost before kick-off with the news that both Keira Walsh and Lauren James were available to start. Lexi Potter was given the nod alongside Walsh in midfield, a sign of how much trust the head coach has in the 20-year-old, while Melvine Malard was fit enough to begin up front.

Slegers, meanwhile, rang the changes from Arsenal’s hard-fought victory against HB Køge during the week. Two who remained were Kyra Cooney-Cross and the goalkeeper Anneke Borbe, who kept out Misa Rodríguez.

The visitors came out full of energy and looking to make an early statement. They dominated early on with 44.2% of the action happening in Chelsea’s defensive third in the first quarter and Arsenal looking to reap the rewards of their high press.

Their biggest threat early on came from Lisa Baum. The 19-year-old has been one of the more positive aspects of their season to date and was given space down the right by Chelsea.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

For all of their control, however, it was much of the same old story for Slegers’s side, haunted by their inability to take their chances. Of the eight shots they created, they failed to register one on target and hit the woodwork twice through Kim Little and Mariona Caldentey.

With every rattle of a post that reverberated around Stamford Bridge, Arsenal’s early confidence dwindled and Bompastor’s side started to find more joy. In direct contrast to their opponents, the Blues took their chance when it came when Malard pounced on Steph Catley as she played out from the back. Borbe made a good save to deny Walsh initially but the rebound fell perfectly for Thompson to hammer home.

It was the ideal time to score and Chelsea went in ahead at the break with the momentum of the game having shifted significantly. They went on to create big opportunities of their own with Malard dragging a shot narrowly wide on two occasions.

While Arsenal were able to create opportunities, the hosts looked comfortable in the circumstances and defended resolutely to see out the game and take home a valuable three points.

Sports.title: Liverpool sink Everton and end derby drought after Olsson and Kapocs strike
Sports.content:
At last, their wait is over. Liverpool’s players could gather in front of the Kop for a celebratory team photograph after the final whistle and rejoice in a new feeling, after beating Everton at Anfield in a Women’s Super League fixture for the first time and finally ending their long run of derby pain.

After six wins from six visits to Anfield for Everton in the WSL era and even quips from their former manager Brian Sørensen in previous campaigns about making Anfield their “training pitch” during their persistent run of victories in this showpiece fixture, Beata Olsson’s early header and Cornelia Kapocs’s late finish were enough to give them a deserved 2-0 victory.

“It’s nice to break that duck, definitely,” the Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, said. “We just downplayed the game, if that makes sense, because it becomes something that’s so big that players start to worry. We want players to go out and feel natural, like they’re playing like they were when they were growing up.

“It is nice because it’s a stat that can just grow and grow. I felt we were hard done by [at Anfield] last season – if you look at their xG in that game, they scored four goals but they were absolute worldies, whereas today we’ve scored two [but] we probably could have had six.”

Taylor was not wrong; the hosts were undeniably the better side and should have scored more goals. Indeed, they would have done had it not been for the heroics of the Everton midfielder Ruby Mace.

When Olsson got in front of her marker, Hannah Blundell, to meet Natalia Ramos’s right-sided corner and angle her header perfectly, diagonally across goal and into the far corner inside the first four minutes you could have been forgiven for thinking Liverpool were set for an easy afternoon such was the simplicity of the goal. Instead, what followed was something of a slog at times with Liverpool trying to break down an Everton backline that initially proved difficult to open up.

After the break, another set piece almost did the job for Liverpool but Vivien Endemann’s volley smacked against the crossbar. By now the pressure was almost relentless and, with just over 20 minutes remaining, Ramos looked certain to score, with time to shoot less than 10 yards out. But the effort was blocked by Mace, who threw her body in front of the ball to keep her side in the contest.

Five minutes later, Mace again came to Everton’s rescue and hooked Kapocs’s effort off the line. The Liverpool forward’s attempted header had come off the top of her shoulder and bounced goalwards, but Mace intervened just in time.

View image in fullscreen Cornelia Kapocs fires in Liverpool’s second goal against Everton. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

Eventually, Kapocs found room inside the area to turn and fire home in the closing stages, much to the relief of Liverpool’s supporters. The result continued the side’s encouraging start to the campaign as they moved on to seven points from their opening four games, their only defeat having come away against the defending champions, Manchester City.
