Sports.title: Alpine condemn online abuse again: “It has become a regular occurrence” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Alpine has issued another condemnation of social media abuse following the reaction to the crash triggered by Franco Colapinto yesterday.

Further abusive comments targeted various people involved in yesterday’s crash. Lando Norris , who sharply criticised Colapinto’s driving, was among those who received abusive messages.

“As a team, we feel it’s necessary to speak out once more about the hate and abuse online following the Azerbaijan Grand Prix,” said Alpine in a statement. “Not only aimed at one of our own drivers, but also members of the Formula One community, including media, and to our racing counterparts who we respect, admire, and revel competing against in the pinnacle of motorsport. Mistakes happen when racing at the limit and no matter the result or outcome, nobody should be subject to hateful or abusive comments.

“Condemning abuse on social media is not aimed at any one fan base or the supporters of one team or driver, this is universal and should be called out and recognised to all fans of the sport. As we have said in previous instances, we strongly condemn the reaction of some fans online and stand in solidarity with Formula One, the FIA, and other teams in wanting to stamp it out. It has become a regular occurrence in recent races and cannot be condoned.

“We know as a proud participant and stakeholder in the sport, we hold a responsibility to speak out and also help support in finding a solution. We will continue to work closely with the championship promoter and rights-holder, and the governing body to discuss ways in which to tackle online abuse and encourage healthy sporting rivalry, which Formula One is renowned for and what makes it so special.”

Alpine’s statement comes just three days after the FIA condemned the abuse aimed at Alpine’s other driver, Pierre Gasly, who was attacked by supporters of Colapinto for briefly delaying his team mate during the Spanish Grand Prix.

The FIA also defended its stewards last month following further abuse by supporters of Colapinto over the two penalties he received in the Dutch Grand Prix.

Sports.title: Final laps of Azerbaijan GP “exceptionally fun” because tyres didn’t degrade – Russell | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell said the final stint of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix was an exciting challenge because the tyres performed so well.

Formula 1’s high-degradation tyres ordinarily do not allow drivers to push flat-out continuously. However Pirelli’s selection for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix proved unusually durable.

Russell spent the final laps of the race being pursued by Max Verstappen. Both drivers were running the soft tyre but found they didn’t have to manage it as much as usual and could drive closer to the limit.

“Max and I spoke about this,” said Russell, “the final stint, I think, is the most fun I’ve had in a race for as long as I can remember because the tyre felt great.

“We were pushing flat-out every single lap. It was like qualifying, one after another. You needed to be so alert around this circuit because the walls are so close, especially through the castle. You’re threading the needle.”

Verstappen was seldom more than a second behind Russell following the final Safety Car restart but never got close enough to attempt a pass.

“Those final 10 laps felt really, really fun. It almost felt like the stories I hear of the drivers in the early-mid-2000s, when every lap was like a qualifying lap. The heart rate is higher, you’re pushing the limit every single lap, there’s no management.”

While F1 has faced criticism this year as its power unit regulations force drivers to conserve energy, Russell pointed out that tyre management often continues to prevent them from pushing flat-out.

“We’ve had a lot of conversations this year about [power unit] energy management, but the tyre management is still there and it has been there for years and years,” he said. “But just with how the temperatures and the circuit fell out today, with the tyres there was no management, and that was exceptionally fun.”

Verstappen also enjoyed the final laps of the race.

“The last stint was fun,” he said. “I kissed a few walls as well, just to leave my mark here in Baku.

“It’s always very challenging around here, qualifying and in the race now at the end as well, just pushing flat-out. It comes with risk, being close to certain walls on the inside, the outside. But it’s cool.”

Sports.title: Hadjar says Red Bull made clear performance gain with car during his absence | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar said he immediately felt an improvement in performance from Red Bull’s car when he returned from injury this weekend.

He finished on the podium in his first race having sat out the last three rounds with a wrist injury. Hadjar said he immediately felt confident in the car around the Baku City Circuit

“Baku is a very specific track, specific Tarmac. But to me, the way the car was behaving in terms of through-corner balance this weekend, from lap one in FP1, I was like, ‘Okay, this is looking pretty good.’

“Then the second half of the car, we’re lacking compared to Mercedes, definitely. But in terms of handling on the brakes, the car was, to me, compared to Budapest, it definitely did a step. So I’m really pleased with that.”

Hadjar finished on the podium earlier in the season in Monaco but called yesterday’s result “an actual first proper podium on pure pace.”

“The Monaco podium, of course it was a podium, but it was not on pure pace, not because I qualified in the top three or whatever,” he said. “I felt like this is my first time with the team that I actually get to do a very clean weekend and actually, like, fight my way into that podium.

!So actually, for me, it feels like a real first and it gives me good confidence heading into the next races.”

Sports.title: Marshals incorrectly showed Safety Car boards to drivers during Azerbaijan GP | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Marshals incorrectly warned drivers the Safety Car had been deployed during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The stewards confirmed marshals showed Safety Car boards to drivers following the first restart during Saturday’s race.

Several drivers crashed at the first corner following the restart. In the aftermath marshals at some corners showed Safety Car warning boards to drivers even though race control had not sent it back out.

“At the relevant time, marshal posts in this area were displaying physical ‘SC’ boards together with waved yellow flags,” the stewards noted in a document. “However, the stewards established that, at that time, the Safety Car had not in fact been deployed by race control.”

The stewards made the admission while explaining why Gabriel Bortoleto was given a 10-second time penalty for overtaking under yellow flags. They acknowledged Bortoleto was confused by the incorrect signal.

“[Bortoleto] explained that he initially reacted to the SC boards and yellow flags. However, he did not see any corresponding electronic indication and did not receive a Safety Car indication on his steering wheel. He was also informed by his team that the Safety Car had not been deployed. Bortoleto therefore became uncertain as to the actual status of the race and, not wishing to lose position unnecessarily, subsequently overtook [Perez].

“The stewards accept that the conflicting information contributed significantly to the situation. In particular, as the Safety Car had not been deployed, Bortoleto cannot be considered to have overtaken another car under Safety Car conditions.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

However the stewards ruled Bortoleto’s confusion about the Safety Car situation did not justify him breaking the rules by overtaking under yellow flags.

“Bortoleto confirmed that he had seen the yellow flags but explained that, because they were displayed together with the SC boards, he understood them to be part of the same Safety Car indication and therefore considered that they were no longer relevant once he had been informed that the Safety Car had not been deployed.

“The stewards do not accept this interpretation. A waved yellow flag is an instruction in its own right and must be respected irrespective of any accompanying signal. A driver cannot disregard a yellow flag based on his own assessment as to why it has been displayed or whether it should have been displayed. The 2026 FIA practice likewise treats yellow flag indications as requiring compliance even where surrounding circumstances are unusual.

“Accordingly, notwithstanding the understandable confusion concerning the SC boards, Bortoleto had seen the waved yellow flags and nevertheless overtook Perez while the yellow flag condition remained in effect. The stewards therefore determine that Bortoleto overtook another car under yellow flag conditions.

“The stewards acknowledge that the erroneous SC indications and the conflicting information contributed to the circumstances of the incident. However, these circumstances do not remove the obligation to respect a waved yellow flag and the stewards therefore apply the standard penalty for overtaking under a single yellow flag.”

Sports.title: Stewards explain decision not to penalise Lindblad for colliding with Lawson | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix stewards have explained why they chose not to penalise Arvid Lindblad for his collision with his team mate.

Lindblad knocked Liam Lawson into a spin when he hit the other Racing Bulls car following the first Safety Car restart. The stewards decided the collision was caused by the incident unfolding in front of them involving the two Alpine drivers and Lando Norris.

“Following the restart, [Lindblad] and [Lawson] approached turn one, with Lindblad in a three-car situation.

“Ahead of them, a collision occurred involving [Colapinto, Gasly and Norris]. That incident, together with Colapinto locking his brakes, triggered a braking reaction among the cars immediately ahead of Lindblad. At the same time, Lindblad was positioned between cars on either side.

“During the corner, Lindblad made contact with Lawson. Having reviewed the positioning and movement of the cars involved, the stewards determined that the contact was primarily the result of the restricted space available to Lindblad and the chain reaction caused by the incident ahead, rather than any action or error for which Lindblad could be considered wholly or predominantly to blame.

“The stewards therefore considered this to be a typical first-corner incident following a restart, with no driver predominantly to blame.”

Sports.title: Jaime Munguia Faces Bektemir Melikuziev’s Fight or Vacate Demand
Sports.content:
Bektemir Melikuziev wants Jaime Munguia to defend his WBA super middleweight title or give it up. Reports that Munguia’s camp is considering vacating have given that demand an edge: if the champion leaves without a major fight lined up, fans will have reason to ask why he would not face the challenger he was ordered to fight.

“Now it’s simple for Munguia. Fight me, or give up the title. I earned my opportunity. I waited long enough. Now it’s time to fight. There are no more excuses, and no other opponents. I am his mandatory challenger. I earned this position in the ring. When I was already the mandatory, I was asked to step aside, and I agreed to work with the promoters because I was promised that I would be next,” said Melikuziev to The Ring.

Melikuziev earned his mandatory position by beating Darius Fulghum last year. The WBA has now given both camps until October 21 to reach a deal and may call a purse bid if they cannot.

The promotional connection makes the choice more striking. Golden Boy has worked with both fighters and knows Melikuziev’s southpaw stance, pressure, and body attack. Those are genuine risks for Munguia, who can leave openings while pressing forward. None of that proves his team fears the matchup. It does make a decision to surrender the belt harder to explain as an inability to assess the challenger.

Rick Glaser has reported that Munguia’s camp is examining whether to vacate. Munguia has announced no such decision. A purse bid, if one is called, would add uncertainty over who stages the fight, though its outcome cannot be assumed.

Munguia won the belt from Armando Resendiz in May. Since losing to Canelo Alvarez, his run has included a win over Erik Bazinyan, a knockout loss to Bruno Surace, victory in their rematch, and the Resendiz title win.

If he gives up the belt now, a substantial next fight would at least explain the trade. Without one, vacating would look like he wanted the standing of a champion but balked when Bek’s promised opportunity came due. Melikuziev could still pursue a vacant title, but he would lose the chance to take it directly from Munguia.

Sports.title: Floyd Schofield Risks Ring Rust Against Lucas Bahdi
Sports.content:
Floyd Schofield is eager to punish Lucas Bahdi for his pre-fight trash talk. That could be a dangerous way to approach their October 10 lightweight title fight. Schofield has not fought in more than 15 months, and Bahdi has already knocked out one unbeaten prospect who appeared to be in control.

Schofield’s last fight ended in 78 seconds when he stopped Tevin Farmer in June 2025. It was an impressive finish, but it offered no evidence of how his timing or stamina will look after a long layoff. Bahdi presents a different problem from a quick return opponent: he can change a fight with one punch. Schofield made clear that their comments have stayed with him.

“I’m going to beat some ass October 10th. I will be victorious, and I just can’t wait to get in that ring. I got something for all the trash talking that Lucas was doing, him and his team,” said Schofield to MillCity Boxing.

Schofield also said he respects Bahdi as a fighter and a father. Once the fight starts, though, that anger could affect his decisions. If he rushes in looking to make Bahdi pay immediately, he gives a dangerous counterpuncher the exchanges he wants.

Bahdi produced his breakthrough by knocking out Ashton Sylve in 2024 while trailing on the scorecards. He later went twelve rounds to beat Roger Gutierrez, showing he does not need an early knockout to win. Bahdi has had a layoff of his own since that August 2025 victory, so neither man comes in with recent fight activity on his side.

The vacant WBA belt has not generated much buzz by itself. Gervonta Davis is champion in recess, and the Schofield–Bahdi winner will become the active lightweight champion.

Davis may choose other opponents rather than fight the winner, leaving Schofield or Bahdi to carry the belt forward. For Schofield, the more immediate task is staying disciplined if Bahdi survives the opening rounds and starts firing back.

Sports.title: Takuma Inoue Wants More Belts After Nasukawa Win
Sports.content:
Takuma Inoue wants to collect bantamweight belts after beating Tenshin Nasukawa for a second time on September 27. The demand is clear. The harder question is whether he can take one from a champion whose boxing experience matches his own.

“I’m not satisfied with just this one belt. I want to collect more,” said Takuma.

The Ring shared Inoue’s comment after his unanimous decision victory in Tokyo. His WBC title remains secure, and he is now 23-2. But two decision wins over Nasukawa tell us more about Inoue’s ability to handle a talented boxing convert than his chances against the division’s other champions.

Nasukawa’s stoppage of Juan Francisco Estrada earned him another opportunity. It did not erase the difference in professional boxing experience between him and Inoue. Takuma could control their exchanges without proving he can discourage a seasoned bantamweight who keeps pressing after the first counter lands.

The opponent who makes this title chase especially interesting is Seiya Tsutsumi. He already beat Inoue by unanimous decision to take the WBA belt in 2024. Tsutsumi is currently listed by the WBA as champion in recess, while Antonio Vargas holds its world title, so a rematch would require the sanctioning body’s title situation to be resolved. Still, Tsutsumi has done what Nasukawa could not: impose himself on Inoue over twelve rounds.

IBF champion Jose Salas Reyes and WBO champion Christian Medina offer other routes to a second belt. Medina stopped former WBO titleholder Yoshiki Takei, making him a more meaningful test of whether Inoue’s careful, low-output approach can hold up against a champion who brings a genuine finishing threat. Ryosuke Nishida has moved to super bantamweight, and Takei no longer holds the WBO belt; neither should be presented as a current bantamweight unification opponent.

Takuma does not need to fight like his explosive older brother Naoya to be a good champion. He does need to show that his style works against someone beyond Nasukawa. If he wants more belts, Medina or Salas Reyes would give him the chance to prove it.

Sports.title: Teofimo Lopez Pushes Ryan Garcia Fight to May
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia asked Teofimo Lopez to fight in December. Lopez’s answer was May 2027. The two welterweight champions agree that they want a unification fight, but Lopez says a meeting with Garcia’s promoter has already put a later date in view.

Garcia challenged Teofimo on X after asking why other fighters did not want to face him. Teofimo replied that he and Golden Boy Boxing had met for lunch two days after Garcia’s win over Conor Benn.

“We’ve said that a showdown in May 2027 is ideal for the welterweight world championship unification fight,” said Teofimo in response.

That is an expression of preference, not an announced deal. Garcia, the WBC champion, wants to return sooner. Lopez holds the WBA title he won from Rolando Romero in August. If Garcia takes a December fight of his own, the two could still meet in May, provided both retain their belts.

Lopez has a more immediate problem. The WBA has ordered him to face Jack Catterall, with their negotiation period ending October 22. If they fail to agree, the organization may order a purse bid. Lopez cannot simply pencil in a May unification and assume his title will still be available for it.

That order gives Catterall a place in the discussion that neither champion can dismiss through social media. Lopez could fight him, seek an agreement that lets him face Garcia first, or give up the WBA belt. The last option would remove the unification label Lopez used in his reply.

Garcia’s December challenge puts pressure on Lopez to explain what happens between now and May. Lopez’s response puts the same question back on Garcia: if May is already the preferred window, is Ryan asking for the unification early, or asking Lopez to abandon the plan?

Until the Catterall order and the date are settled, their public exchange is a negotiation over timing, with two titles at stake.

Ryan Garcia Pushes Teofimo Lopez Toward December Decision

Garcia has challenged Teofimo to fight in December, turning a possible 2027 welterweight unification into an immediate question for the WBA champion. The timing puts Teofimo in a bind: he has already been ordered to negotiate with Jack Catterall, and Garcia is asking him to make room for a different fight.

“Literally no one really wants the smoke in boxing what’s actually going on??? Yall really scared??? Teo does December sound good to go???” posted Ryan on X with his direct challenge of Teofimo.

Ryan holds the WBC welterweight title, and Lopez won the WBA belt from Rolando Romero in August. Their fight would be a unification, but Lopez has an obligation to Jack Catterall, who earned his shot by beating Shakhram Giyasov. Lopez and Catterall have until October 22 to reach an agreement.

That order gives Catterall a real say in Garcia’s December plan. He has indicated that he wants the Lopez fight rather than a payment to step aside. If Lopez cannot obtain an exception or reach an arrangement with Catterall, he may have to defend the title first or give it up to pursue Garcia. A fight without Lopez’s belt would still be valuable, but it would lose its unification claim and some of Lopez’s bargaining power.

Ryan also gains something by making the challenge publicly. He can show fans that he asked for the biggest available December opponent. If Lopez declines, Garcia can return to his proposed fight with Isaac “Pitbull” Cruz while arguing that he tried to make the unification first. That is a negotiating advantage, though a post alone cannot establish why any eventual fight fails to happen.

December would be a quick turnaround for both men. Garcia fought only two rounds against Benn; Lopez went twelve with Romero and was cut and shaken during their August bout. That makes Garcia’s proposed timing understandable from his side, but it does not establish that Lopez would be drained or unprepared.

A major fight would still need a contract, a date, a venue, and a broadcast agreement in the coming weeks. Ryan has put Lopez on the clock in public. Catterall and the WBA have already put him on one in writing. Lopez’s response to the mandatory order will say more about the prospects for December than either champion’s next callout.

Sports.title: Tim Bradley Questions Russell’s Plan to Delay Shakur Fight
Sports.content:
Gary Antuanne Russell wants a fight with Shakur Stevenson to grow, but Tim Bradley says the WBA champion is gambling with an opportunity already in front of him. According to Bradley, Russell has been offered $2 million to face Shakur in a 140-pound unification. Russell’s talk of making the fight later left Bradley asking what more he expects to gain by waiting.

Dan Rafael reported that Zuffa Boxing contacted PBC with an offer for Russell, and Shakur then called him out publicly. The reported offer did not disclose a purse, so the $2 million figure remains Bradley’s claim. Russell has indicated he would rather make the fight down the line.

“When $500,000 is your biggest paycheck, okay? And you got an opportunity to make $2 million to fight one of the best fighters on planet Earth, right? You can dethrone him. And this is for the 140 lb crown. And you turn it down. You talking about duck,” said Bradley on his channel about Antuanne Russell.

Bradley’s frustration is understandable, even if the full terms of the offer are unknown. A fight does not become more valuable simply because two champions wait. Russell needs either a bigger audience or a stronger negotiating position to make the delay pay off. Holding the WBA belt gives him leverage today; another defense does not guarantee more of it.

His fight with Andy Hiraoka is a reminder of the risk. Russell retained his title, but it was a difficult night rather than the sort of performance that made a Shakur fight feel too small to stage now. Every bout he takes while waiting creates another chance to lose the belt or emerge with less momentum.

Shakur has reasons of his own to want the fight immediately. Adding Russell’s WBA title would strengthen his position at 140 pounds while he considers more lucrative names and a possible move to welterweight. He is unlikely to reserve his schedule indefinitely for Russell. That gives Russell a reason to examine the offer seriously, though it does not oblige him to accept terms he considers inadequate.

Bradley recently challenged Shakur over the prospect of fighting Manny Pacquiao. Now that Shakur is calling for an active champion in his division, Bradley is asking Russell to meet that challenge.

Russell can argue for better money or a better date. But if his plan is simply to let the matchup “marinate,” he needs to explain what will make it bigger. Right now, he has a belt, a reported offer, and a chance to beat Shakur. None is guaranteed to be there later.

Sports.title: Ben Whittaker’s Step Up Faces Wallace Test
Sports.content:
Ben Whittaker’s fight with Conor Wallace on October 3 is being sold as a step up, but his path to the IBF eliminator deserves a closer look. He struggled with domestic-level Liam Cameron before winning their rematch, then faced lesser opposition after signing with Matchroom. At 29, Whittaker is now one win from a mandatory position without having beaten an established contender. Wallace is supposed to validate that leap.

In terms of ranking and stakes, Wallace is a step up. Whittaker’s recent opponents have rarely forced him to show what happens when his speed and theatrics fail to take control immediately. His two-round stoppage of Richard Rivera in June looked spectacular, but Rivera was 35, and the fight ended before Whittaker had to make a difficult adjustment. It was a useful American showcase, not an answer to questions about his stamina, defense or composure over twelve rounds.

Matchroom has chosen the available IBF route instead of putting Whittaker in with an established light heavyweight such as Anthony Yarde or Joshua Buatsi. A promoter is entitled to seek the fastest route to a title shot. But an eliminator label cannot give Whittaker the experience those fights might have provided. He can reach mandatory status while still learning how to handle the kind of resistance a champion will bring.

Wallace (17-1, 12 KOs) should not be treated as a guaranteed win. He is ranked above Whittaker in the IBF rankings and earned a split-decision victory over Jerome Pampellone. He is also an Australian-based southpaw who has yet to fight professionally outside Australia. His record establishes him as a legitimate ranked opponent, though it offers limited evidence of how he would fare against the best fighters at 175 pounds.

His best chance is to make Whittaker work at a pace the favorite does not choose. Whittaker likes space to move, set traps, and perform for the crowd. If Wallace can close that space, touch the body, and keep coming after Whittaker lands, the bout could become an examination of discipline rather than reflexes. Dropping his hands against an opponent who is still pressing forward in the later rounds would be a different gamble from doing it during a brief showcase.

Birmingham brings its own challenge for Wallace. He cannot afford to surrender the early rounds while getting accustomed to Whittaker’s movement and the atmosphere. That does not mean the judges would deny him a close win. It means that a slow start on the road could leave him needing to take risks against the faster boxer as the rounds run out.

There is a longer-term problem for Whittaker even if he wins clearly. Becoming Bivol’s mandatory challenger does not guarantee that the champion will be available next. Bivol has other potential obligations and recently completed an IBF mandatory defense. Whittaker could gain the position, wait for his turn, and still need the hard fights his title route allowed him to bypass.

That is what makes the Wallace fight more revealing than the poster suggests. Another early knockout would strengthen Whittaker’s appeal, but it would leave familiar questions unanswered. If Wallace forces him through difficult rounds, Whittaker has an opportunity to show that the fast track has produced a boxer capable of handling more than opponents selected for his highlight reel.

Sports.title: Dana White Doubts Ryan Garcia Brings Crawford Back
Sports.content:
Dana White is unsure whether Ryan Garcia is the opponent who could bring Terence Crawford out of retirement. His answer to a question about the rumored fight pointed toward another possibility without naming anyone.

“I don’t know if that’s the fight Crawford would come back for. There’s a lot of options out there obviously for Ryan, the question is what is the fight that Crawford would come back for. I think there’s a fight out there that Crawford would come back for. I don’t know if Ryan is it,” White told reporters.

White smiled as he said he thought such a fight existed. Canelo Alvarez is the obvious candidate, but White did not say he meant Canelo. He offered no indication that Crawford has agreed to return or that negotiations are underway.

The only figure with the commercial weight to justify the physical tax is Canelo, and that road is blocked. Canelo first has to survive Christian Mbilli on October 31. Mbilli throws hundreds of punches, presses forward without taking a backward step, and represents an exhausting stylistic nightmare for an aging champion. If Canelo drops that fight or looks faded, the market for a Crawford rematch disappears instantly.

If Canelo gets through Mbilli, there are much more violent, commercial pairings available for him than running back a bout he already lost. Staging Canelo against aggressive punchers generates real drama. Crawford’s win over Canelo was a safety-first clinic that drew sharp criticism from casual viewers for being a tactical one. It did not create a viral explosion the way mega spectacles do. Spending massive money to stage a repeat of a fight Crawford already won makes zero business sense.

Crawford himself confirmed that Turki never placed an actual rematch offer on the table after their bout. Turki threw out a playful social media post about Crawford trying to become a four-division undisputed champion, but playful online talk is not a nine-figure contract. The reality is that Riyadh Season moved straight along.

Sports.title: Dillian Whyte Calls Out Johnny Fisher, But Who Pays?
Sports.content:
Dillian Whyte saw an opening after Johnny Fisher labored to a majority decision over Michael Pirotton on Saturday. Fisher looked exhausted after his Zuffa Boxing debut and went to a hospital for precautionary checks before being cleared. Whyte promptly called for the fight. The harder question is whether Zuffa should pay to make it.

“I’d fight Johnny Fisher, and I’d knock him out,” Whyte told Sky Sports.

Fisher’s struggles make that an easy challenge to issue. Pirotton lasted ten rounds and forced Fisher to work well beyond his early bursts of power. Whyte would expect to press him inside, attack the body, and test whether his stamina holds up.

Whyte represents real danger for Fisher despite looking faded in recent outings. Fisher often leaves his chin unprotected when he throws that looping right hand, inviting Whyte to land his trademark left hook. That single punch is Whyte’s main world-class asset, and he still has it in his arsenal.

That makes his asking price the deciding factor. Whyte would likely want a large purse for a domestic fight with Fisher. Zuffa would be paying for a familiar name coming off a defeat, while taking the chance that Fisher loses to a fighter with limited value as a long-term investment.

At a modest price, the matchup might be worth considering. At a large one, Zuffa has a better use for Fisher’s next fight: a younger opponent, preferably one ranked in the top 15, who can test his stamina and defense while moving him toward the division’s contenders. Fisher needs that kind of progress after Pirotton. Whyte needs a comeback payday. Zuffa does not have to treat those needs as the same thing.

Whyte got accustomed to massive paydays with Matchroom, pay-per-view guarantees against Tyson Fury, and made millions over the years. He might accept the B-side label against Fisher, but Zuffa would still have to meet his price. That price, rather than his pride alone, is what could kill the fight.

Ghana News.title: Refugees in South Africa face mounting tensions as September 30 deadline looms
Ghana News.content:
An impending September 30 deadline issued by an anti-immigration movement has ignited profound anxiety across migrant communities in South Africa. The group, known as March and March, has spearheaded protests throughout the year demanding that undocumented foreign nationals leave the country.

Organisers warn of further demonstrations if their demands remain unmet. For many refugees, however, official paperwork provides little solace. The hostility unfolding on the streets rarely begins with a request for identification documents. Instead, foreign nationals find themselves caught in a climate of escalating fear as the nation approaches local government elections.

Pavement Lives and Desperate Conditions

For months, hundreds of asylum seekers and refugees occupied the pavement outside the Durban Refugee Reception Centre on Che Guevara Road. Fleeing violence in nations such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Uganda, Mozambique, and Tanzania, they sought sanctuary near the Department of Home Affairs. Instead, the street became their home. Men, women, and children spent roughly four months exposed to the elements, relying entirely on volunteers and civil society organisations for necessities. Conditions quickly deteriorated into a desperate struggle for survival. Migrants reported irregular access to food and necessary medication, alongside tragedy when a man suffering from tuberculosis died at the encampment.

"It has been very tough," Bahebwa said. "Never before have I experienced something like this."

The camp offered no immunity from the hostility its residents hoped to escape. On September 3, members of March and March confronted the refugees living outside the centre. Violence erupted, prompting police intervention that left at least four people injured. Subsequent protests saw police officers form physical human barriers between opposing groups. March and March frames its mobilization as a campaign against crime, deteriorating community conditions, and insufficient government enforcement of immigration laws. Leaders repeatedly reject accusations of xenophobia, insisting their sole target is undocumented migration. Yet refugees report that documented status offers no protection. Earlier this year, six refugee salon workers near Warwick Street Market were beaten with sticks, sending two to the hospital. Allegations of police inaction compounded their isolation.

"Police said we can't open cases because we are foreigners. We had nowhere to go," Bahebwa alleged.

Relocation Realities and Historical Echoes

In mid-September, authorities cleared the makeshift Durban camp, presenting residents with stark choices. They could return to neighborhoods they previously fled or accept temporary placement at the Lindela facility in Gauteng. Located hundreds of kilometres away, Lindela is a government-run immigration detention center historically utilized for repatriation. While some feared detention, others felt they could no longer endure life on the pavement. On September 15, authorities transported 274 individuals by bus to Lindela, while roughly 150 others remained in Durban to seek alternative shelter.

Leaving the street failed to resolve underlying safety concerns. Kafuti Muyumba, a Congolese small business owner and community representative, noted that returning to previous neighborhoods remains terrifying.

People are afraid, he said. "Even the police allow March and March violence. They came with sticks and say we are attacking them."

Muyumba noted that many refugees lost their livelihoods during months of upheaval. He linked current tensions to painful historical precedents, recalling deadly xenophobic outbreaks in 2008 and 2015 that displaced thousands. Distrust of local law enforcement runs deep among community members who feel abandoned by authorities.

"We don't trust the police. They are not being fair with us. Some of them are also saying we must go," he said.

While police maintain that normal policing approaches remain unchanged and protesters must obey the law, refugees argue that returning to their countries of origin is impossible. For Congolese refugees, ongoing conflict at home eliminates repatriation as a viable option.

"There is still war there," Muyumba said.

State Enforcement and Looming Anxieties

In response to sustained public pressure, the South African government intensified immigration enforcement operations. Between June 14 and August 20, authorities processed 86,596 foreign nationals for deportation and repatriation through the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration. Malawians constituted the largest group, followed by Zimbabweans and Mozambicans. Government figures indicate that 90 percent of those repatriated entered illegally, with 95 percent crossing outside official border ports. Officials stress these actions reflect broader efforts to strengthen border management while repeatedly warning private citizens against taking law enforcement into their own hands. The state maintains that common citizens possess no legal authority to deport anyone, rendering the September 30 deadline legally void.

Despite lacking legal force, deadlines carry psychological weight and generate widespread panic. Bishop Raphael Bahebwa, who has lived in South Africa for 26 years after arriving as a refugee from the DRC, now lives in hiding. Having witnessed anti-foreigner sentiment flare repeatedly over more than a quarter of a century, he believes the current political climate surrounding local government elections makes this year distinct.

"I am in hiding now because they say they are going to kill me for speaking about the rights of foreigners," he noted.

As the September 30 deadline arrives, migrants face deep uncertainty. Some reside hundreds of kilometres away in detention facilities, while others navigate precarious housing in communities they once fled. For Bahebwa and countless others, the core anxiety remains unchanged.

"They are scapegoating us as foreigners," he said. "It is not going to end on September 30. It has to do with the elections."

Balancing structural pressures against fundamental human rights principles, independent observers note that navigating this complex social friction requires sustained institutional accountability and active community dialogue to protect vulnerable populations from political exploitation.

Ghana News.title: At least 12 dead, dozens missing after vessel capsizes in DR Congo
Ghana News.content:
At least 12 people are dead, and dozens remain missing after another maritime disaster struck the Democratic Republic of Congo. A vessel carrying fish traders capsized in Lake Kivu late Saturday night near Idjwi Island in South Kivu province.

Local authorities confirmed the boat was carrying more than 50 passengers and cargo. The voyage started in Bwina on Idjwi Island and was heading toward Boza. Félix Habiragi, chief of the nearby village of Kisheke, noted that about 15 people were rescued from the water. The precise cause of the accident remains unclear.

Videos circulating from the scene show villagers and passengers pulling bodies from the lake. The human toll has devastated local communities. Christian Amini Ndahira, a resident of Idjwi, lost a close friend in the accident. He shared his grief, stating, "We had even spoken in the evening, before he boarded that boat. It's so sad for me and for his family."

This incident follows another major maritime disaster in the country earlier in the week. At least 41 people died and 49 others were rescued when a vessel capsized on Lake Tanganyika near the village of Mapera. That boat was reportedly carrying roughly 100 people and cargo.

Water transport serves as a lifeline for more than 100 million people across the Congo, where roads are sparse. However, safety standards are frequently ignored. Vessels routinely operate heavily overloaded with goods and passengers. Many travelers board without access to life jackets.

Civil society members point to a persistent gap between policy and enforcement. Dorcelle Bagazane, a civil society activist in Idjwi, highlighted the ongoing enforcement challenges. She explained, "The authorities had, in particular, begun requiring passengers to wear life jackets. Today, however, many people continue to travel without them."

While national agencies face mounting pressure to overhaul inland waterway regulations, local governance experts emphasize that sustained public safety campaigns must accompany punitive enforcement measures to protect vulnerable commuters relying on informal river and lake networks. Ghana News.title: Two dead, 14 rescued after accident on Kpetoe-Sarakope road
Ghana News.content:
Two people have died after a road crash involving a Hyundai H100 bus and a Ford tractor on the Kpetoe-Sarakope stretch of the Accra-Aflao Highway.

The accident occurred on Saturday, September 26, 2026, when the two vehicles, which were travelling from Kpetoe towards Aflao, were involved in a collision.

The Hyundai H100 was carrying 12 passengers, while the Ford tractor had two occupants.

Firefighters from the Kpetoe Fire Station rescued all 14 occupants and handed them over to personnel from the National Ambulance Service and the Ghana Police Service.

They were subsequently conveyed to the Ho Teaching Hospital for medical attention, where one male and one female were later confirmed dead.

The Ghana National Fire Service has urged motorists to exercise caution on the road, avoid improper overtaking and strictly adhere to road safety regulations to help prevent crashes and loss of life.

Ghana News.title: Our mental health is restored – How Medical Trust Fund is giving doctors hope again
Ghana News.content:
For neurosurgeon Dr Hadi Mohammed Abdallah, the impact of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) is being felt far beyond the operating theatre.

One year into the Fund’s existence, Dr Abdallah says its support for patients with complex neurological conditions has not only saved lives and restored quality of life but has also given doctors something many had quietly been losing: hope.

As a neurosurgeon at the Korle Bu Teaching Hospital, Dr Abdallah has been involved in treating more than 10 patients supported by the Fund.

Among the most significant cases, he said, were six patients who underwent brain aneurysm surgery with GMTF support.

According to him, this marked the first time six such cases had been sponsored and carried out in a public hospital.

Dr Abdallah explained that a brain aneurysm can be like a ticking time bomb. Although treatment is available in Ghana, the cost of coiling ranges from US$15,000 to US$20,000, putting the procedure out of reach for many patients.

For those unable to raise the money, the diagnosis comes with a heavy psychological burden.

“They were living with the mental torture that they were a walking time bomb,” Dr Abdallah said, describing the fear that another blood vessel could rupture in the brain at any time.

GMTF, he said, has changed that reality for several patients.

In one emergency case, the Fund stepped in and settled the patient’s treatment costs, allowing care to proceed without lengthy delays.

For Dr Abdallah, the intervention was more than financial assistance.

“We saved this patient.”

The Fund has also supported patients with brain tumours, including pituitary tumours that can progressively destroy a patient’s vision and, if untreated, become fatal.

Dr Abdallah said that without financial support, some patients could wait months or even years while trying to raise money for surgery.

By then, some could lose their sight, while others could face the risk of dying as their tumours continued to grow.

GMTF’s intervention, he said, therefore goes beyond paying hospital bills.

It can mean giving patients back their sight, their lives and, in some cases, a second chance.

But Dr Abdallah believes the Fund is also addressing another less-discussed problem: the psychological burden on healthcare professionals.

Doctors, he explained, are often confronted with the painful reality of diagnosing a patient early and knowing that timely treatment could make a difference, only to see that patient return much later in a worse condition because the family could not afford the required surgery.

“That can be depressing,” he said.

When families exhaust their resources, doctors and other hospital staff sometimes step in, contributing from their own pockets or organising collections among colleagues to keep patients alive.

The emotional toll, Dr Abdallah said, does not end at the hospital.

Doctors may go home reflecting on patients who could have had better outcomes if they had received treatment earlier.

When such situations occur repeatedly, the psychological burden can begin to affect healthcare professionals themselves.

That is why the emergence of GMTF represents a different kind of relief for doctors.

“The fact that I don’t have to dip my hands into my pocket to do round collection to save a patient, I think it is great,” he said.

For Dr Abdallah, the Fund is restoring confidence among healthcare workers that patients can receive the treatment they need without doctors having to personally carry the financial burden.

“It gives us a lot of hope,” he said.

He expressed optimism that as the Fund grows, more complex surgeries can be performed and treatment outcomes can increasingly match those seen in developed healthcare systems.

For the patients supported by GMTF, the interventions may represent a new beginning.

For the doctors caring for them, Dr Abdallah says, the impact is equally profound: relief from an invisible burden and renewed confidence that they do not have to fight alone to save a life.

And in his words:

“Our mental health is restored, courtesy of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund.”

Ghana News.title: 2027 budget to provide for grain silos – Agric Minister
Ghana News.content:
Adequate allocations will be made in next year’s budget for the construction of silos for the storage of grains, the Minister of Food and Agriculture, Eric Opoku, has disclosed.

He said the country produced 4.6 million tonnes of maize last year against an estimated national demand of 3.6 million tonnes, creating a surplus of about one million tonnes.

He, therefore, urged the Ghana Food Buffer Stock Company (NAFCO) to play a critical role in putting up many silos to store the growing level of cereal production in the country.

Mr Opoku disclosed at the first Annual General Meeting of NAFCO in Accra on September 24.

The AGM, which was held on the theme "Strengthening Food Security through Strategic Partnership,” provided an opportunity for the company to present its annual reports and financial statements for the financial years from December 31, 2010, through December 31 last year and account to shareholders on the stewardship of the board and management.

NAFCO’s reserve

He said strengthening NAFCO’s capacity to mop up excess production would help create a reliable market for farmers while ensuring that increased domestic production did not translate into losses for producers.

The minister said NAFCO currently had 20,443 tonnes of grains in storage, describing the stock as a step towards rebuilding the country’s strategic food reserves.

He said his ministry had worked with the board and management to strengthen NAFCO’s operations and rebuild its reserves after years of financial and operational constraints.

Mr Opoku also disclosed that the government had directed NAFCO to release 50,000 bags of grains to settle the country’s outstanding obligation to the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).

He recounted that in 2018, the country borrowed grains from ECOWAS to support the School Feeding Programme.

“Today, by the grace of God and with the prudent management of the company, we have been able to procure enough, more than enough, for us to pay back what we borrowed,” he said.

The minister further directed NAFCO to ensure that suppliers contracted to support public feeding programmes purchased food directly from Ghanaian farmers rather than relying on imported produce.

Mr Opoku said purchasing imported food for programmes such as Free SHS undermined local production because the expenditure created jobs outside the country while reducing demand for locally produced food.

The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of NAFCO, George Abradu-Otoo, said NAFCO had recorded profits in some previous years, including 2018, 2019, 2020, 2022, and 2023, but the latest performance surpassed all previous results.

“The 2025 net profit before tax of GH¢91.7 million not only erased a GH¢19.4 million loss posted the previous year, but it is the highest profit made by the company,” he said.

Mr Abradu-Otoo said the company’s gross profit margin also increased significantly from 1.61 percent in 2024 to 13.96 percent in 2025.

He attributed the improvement to stronger cost discipline and revenue growth.

He said NAFCO’s return on operating assets also rose from negative 63.80 per cent to positive 26.29 per cent, reflecting improved deployment and management of the company’s assets.

“Crowning these achievements, NAFCO paid GH¢20.3 million in taxes to the state in 2025, the highest annual tax contribution in its 16-year history,” he said.

Despite the improved financial performance, the CEO said the company continued to face operational risks, particularly in the area of working-capital management.

Ghana News.title: Damongo Communique: Democracy Not For Sale
Ghana News.content:
Issued by the Democracy Not for Sale Project (Impact Makers Foundation, in partnership with Joy News/Multimedia Group) Savannah Regional Coordinating Council, Damongo — Friday, September 25, 2026

Preamble

On Friday, September 25, 2026, the Democracy Not for Sale project convened its Joy News-hosted third regional dialogue at the Savannah Regional Coordinating Council in Damongo, the fifth regional dialogue held under the project overall, alongside two further editions separately hosted by Adom. The forum brought together the security services, academia, traditional authority, civic education, and local government, alongside a large and highly engaged public audience, to examine the growing influence of money in Ghana’s democratic processes. It was organised by the Impact Makers Foundation in partnership with Joy News and the Multimedia Group.

The dialogue was grounded in field survey data gathered by a research team across the Damongo area, drawing on more than 90 interactions and 55 structured respondent interviews, well above the region’s calculated ideal sample of 36, derived from the project’s national target of 1,600 respondents across 10 regions at a 95% confidence level and a margin of error of ±2.45%. This communiqué sets out, in full, the findings presented and the recommendations that emerged from the dialogue.

Survey Findings

Respondents were 60% female and 40% male, the first female-majority sample recorded under the project, with the most evenly spread age profile recorded to date: 32.5% were aged 26–35, 25% were 18–25, 22.5% were 36–50, and 20% were 51 and above.

Awareness of Vote Buying

Damongo recorded the first fully saturated awareness result under the Democracy Not for Sale project: every single respondent had either personally witnessed or credibly heard of vote buying, with 0% reporting no awareness at all, a first, as every other region surveyed to date has recorded at least a small share with no awareness. 52.5% of respondents said they had personally witnessed a candidate offering money or gifts for votes, and 47.5% had heard credible reports.

Awareness of candidates offering money or gifts for votes

By occupational group, students recorded the highest personal-witness rate of any group in any region surveyed under the project: 83.3%, with the remaining 16.7% having heard reliable reports. Professionals reported 58.3% personal witness and 41.7% reliable reports; the informal sector reported 40.9% and 59.1% respectively. No occupational group reported any respondents with zero awareness.

Witnessed versus heard reports of vote buying, by occupational category

Money’s Perceived Influence — A Reversed Age Pattern

Damongo produced the inverse of the age pattern seen in other regions. 80% of 18–25 year-olds rated money’s influence on election outcomes as high (6–10) — the highest of any age group — followed by 76.9% among 26–35 year-olds, then declining to 55.6% among 36–50 year-olds and 50% among those 51 and above. Elsewhere under the project, older respondents have generally been the most convinced that money determines outcomes; in Damongo, it is the youngest who are most convinced.

Perceived influence of money on election outcomes, by age group

Willingness to Vote on Ideas Over Money

82.6% of respondents said they would vote for a candidate with fewer resources but better ideas over a wealthier opponent. This was most uniform among younger respondents: 100% of both 18–25 and 26–35 year-olds said yes, against 88.9% of 36–50 year-olds and 87.5% of those 51 and above. Damongo’s youngest respondents thus hold two views at once: the strongest belief that money currently decides elections, and, together with 26–35 year-olds, the strongest and most unanimous stated preference for voting on ideas instead.

Willingness to vote for a candidate with less money but better ideas.

Sources of Political Financing

68% of respondents identified government resources in the research team’s framing, taxes citizens themselves pay as the primary hidden financier of political campaigns, ahead of businessmen (18%) and criminal proceeds (5%, explained on air as a money-laundering channel for illicit actors). 20% said they did not know the source but would accept the money regardless. No respondents cited politicians’ personal savings.

Perceived “hidden” financiers of political campaigns in Ghana

Confidence in Existing Laws

Across every age group, the dominant view was that laws exist but are not enforced, rather than that the laws themselves are weak: 70% among 18–25 year-olds, 84.6% among 26–35 year-olds, 66.7% among 36–50 year-olds, and 87.5% among those 51 and above.

Confidence in the strength and enforcement of current laws, by age group

Preferred Remedies — A Different Ranking

Unlike every other region surveyed, where strict jail time for vote-buyers and vote-sellers has led the ranking of preferred remedies, Damongo respondents ranked mindset change first (28%), followed by improving standard of living (25%) and public education (20%). Strict jail time was cited by only 10% tied with the 10% who said the practice cannot be stopped at all, with a further 5% calling for an overhaul of political party financing.

Perceived most effective way to stop “democracy for sale.”

Taken together, Damongo marks several firsts for the project: full awareness saturation, a female-majority sample, a reversed age pattern on money’s perceived influence, and a public whose preferred remedy is cultural and attitudinal change rather than legal punishment.

The Dialogue

The panel comprised Superintendent Francis Ekoh (District Commander, Damongo, Ghana Police Service); ASP Michael Adjei (Regional Operations Director, Savannah Region, Ghana Police Service); ASP Emmanuel Frimpong (District Crime Officer, Ghana Police Service); Professor Adams Sulemana Achanso (Associate Professor, Department of Development Management and Policy Studies, University for Development Studies, and a three-time parliamentary aspirant); Alijata Haruna (Queen Mother of Damongo Traditional Area); and Issaka Zetor (NCCE Director, Savannah Region). The Savannah Regional Minister, Salisu Be-Awuribe, and Victor Wonder Kutor, a leading NDC party official, also addressed the forum.

A Region That No Longer Sees Vote Buying as Misconduct

The dominant theme of the evening was that many respondents who described receiving money, cloth, sewing machines, or hair dryers from politicians did not classify it as vote buying at all. A widow interviewed at the market described cloth and a sewing machine for her daughter as ordinary help; a woman who travels from Techiman to vote in Damongo described cash, cloth, and a hair dryer as gestures of thanks. Multiple audience members said they had never demanded money from a politician, while separately acknowledging they would accept it if offered.

Professor Achanso, drawing on three of his own parliamentary campaigns, linked this to a long-standing cultural practice of gift-giving tied to courtship and social obligation and to a genuine public ambiguity about where legitimate constituency support ends and vote buying begins, an ambiguity he said leaves citizens unable to recognise the practice even as it happens to them.

Law, Evidence, and the Case No One Reports

Regional Minister Salisu Be-Awuribe cited Section 33 of PNDC Law 284 (as amended), which criminalises inducing a vote through money or gifts regardless of amount, but acknowledged the law’s practical application remains genuinely contested: politicians, police, and the public alike struggle to distinguish inducement from customary courtesy or gratitude.

ASP Michael Adjei and ASP Emmanuel Frimpong said neither had received a single formal vote-buying complaint in the district despite widespread public acknowledgement that the practice is common, explaining that police cannot investigate what is never reported, and that prosecution requires evidence sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, difficult when giver and receiver share an interest in silence. ASP Michael Adjei urged citizens to preserve and report mobile money transfer records from politicians as a concrete, traceable starting point for investigation. An audience member pressed the panel on why no prosecutions have followed widely publicised cases, including a reported GHS 700-per-delegate primary payment and a reported distribution of television sets to delegates by a parliamentary aspirant, surfacing a tension between the panel’s insistence that the law is adequate on paper and the audience’s experience that it is essentially unenforced.

Poverty and the Demand Side

An assembly member representing Canteen electoral area cited 2021 census data showing poverty near 50% and youth unemployment near 30% in parts of the region, both above the national average, arguing the debate must confront these economic realities rather than assign blame solely to givers or receivers. Two audience members said plainly, through a translator, that they would accept money regardless of its source, since declining it while unemployed made little practical sense. A tutor at Damongo College of Education said rural voters in particular feel entitled to accept money immediately, since they do not expect to see a winning candidate’s development promises delivered for another four years.

Youth Disillusionment and a Change of Heart

A young first-time-eligible voter said on air that he did not intend to vote at all, citing both the prevalence of vote buying and his frustration that police cannot act without formal evidence. Panelists argued that abstaining does not remove money’s influence from politics but cedes the decision entirely to those willing to participate on existing terms, and urged him to vote and organise others around advocacy instead. By the end of the exchange, he said he had reconsidered and would register to vote. Separately, a young teacher and regional youth parliament representative asked where exactly the line falls between legitimate campaign support and vote buying, given that a viable campaign is financially out of reach for most young people; Queen Mother Alijata Haruna’s answer was to judge politicians on delivery against their manifesto promises rather than on gifts given at campaign time.

Financing, Transparency, and the Delegate System

Victor Wonder Kutor argued vote buying should not be understood only as cash, comparing it to unpaid academic support in student politics, and contrasted Ghana’s opaque political financing with jurisdictions where campaign donors and amounts are public record, while declining, when asked directly, to unambiguously label two high-profile examples put to him as vote buying. Several panelists welcomed the Supreme Court’s recent ruling opening party primaries to all registered party members rather than a smaller delegate college, reasoning that a much larger electorate raises the practical cost of directly influencing primary outcomes with cash.

Recommendations from Panelists

Encourage citizens to preserve and report mobile money transfers and other traceable payments from politicians, giving police a concrete evidentiary starting point even without witness testimony.

Publish clearer, publicly communicated guidance distinguishing legitimate constituency support and customary gift-giving from criminal vote buying, given how many respondents received money or goods without recognising it as vote buying at all.

Expand civic education, delivered through schools, community outreach, and media, on the specific content and consequences of PNDC Law 284.

Hold politicians accountable principally against delivery of their manifesto commitments, rather than treating election-time gifts as a substitute for that accountability.

Address the region's underlying economic conditions poverty and youth unemployment above the national average recognising that moral appeals alone are unlikely to change behaviour among voters who see little else to gain from the political process.

Introduce greater formal transparency in political campaign financing, including public disclosure of donors and amounts, and a clearer regulatory line between legitimate lobbying and corruption.

Reduce the financial barriers that keep women from contesting elective office in the region.

Conclusion

The Damongo dialogue surfaced a region whose relationship with vote buying is now nearly universal in its familiarity but genuinely ambiguous in how it is understood a place where citizens overwhelmingly recognise money's role in politics, yet increasingly describe individual transactions as gifts rather than corruption. That ambiguity, more than any gap in the law, appears to be the region's central challenge: respondents themselves point to mindset change, not legal punishment, as the most effective remedy available. Closing the gap between what the law prohibits and what citizens recognise as prohibited will require the concrete steps identified in this dialogue: traceable evidence from mobile money records, clearer public guidance on where gifts end and inducement begins, sustained civic education, and accountability measured against delivery rather than largesse. The Democracy Not for Sale project will continue its engagement across Ghana's remaining regions, building an evidence base to inform national dialogue and policy reform toward strengthening the integrity of the country's democratic processes

Ghana News.title: Yusif Sulemana pushes community benefits, national systems in Global Forest Finance Debate
Ghana News.content:
Ghana’s Deputy Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Yusif Sulemana (PhD), has urged the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) to design its financing model around predictable funding, community benefits and strong national systems.

Addressing the TFFF Roundtable in New York, Dr Sulemana said countries need clear eligibility criteria and payment rules that allow them to plan forest protection programmes beyond short-term project cycles.

The Bole-Bamboi MP said Ghana’s experience under REDD+ provides useful lessons for building a financing framework that can work over the long term.

He stressed the importance of ensuring that communities receive transparent and meaningful benefits from forest protection, arguing that people should be able to see a clear connection between conserving forests and improving their livelihoods.

He also called for the TFFF to build on existing national monitoring, safeguards and benefit-sharing arrangements rather than creating parallel structures that could increase costs.

Dr Sulemana further renewed Ghana’s July request for representation on the TFFF Interim Board, saying Ghana’s practical experience could contribute to discussions on the realities facing tropical forest countries in Africa.

He expressed appreciation to Norway and Brazil for their leadership and said the central issue for Ghana is how international forest finance can provide reliable support for keeping forests standing.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
