World.title: As Congress debates college sports, athletes-turned-senators have a seat at the table
World.content:
As Congress debates college sports, athletes-turned-senators have a seat at the table

toggle caption Doug Benc/Getty Images

WASHINGTON — With a major college sports reform bill on the brink of a milestone in Congress, some former athletes have a special place in the debate: the handful of U.S. Senators who played college sports themselves.

Supporters of the Protect College Sports Act, which is poised to pass the Senate on Monday, say the bill is needed to fix what they call an era of chaos in Division I athletics, characterized by ballooning pay for athletes, unlimited transfers between schools, constant lawsuits over eligibility rules and runaway athletic department budgets.

At least half a dozen sitting senators were NCAA Division I athletes, and a handful of others played in Division II or in sports governed by other organizations. As the debate over the bill has unfolded over the past year, their experiences have informed their approach to the legislation.

Sponsor Message

No one in the Senate spent as many years in college sports as Tommy Tuberville, the football coach turned Alabama senator (who is stepping down after this term as he runs for governor in this fall's election in the state).

Tuberville played football at the Division II school Southern State, then went on to be a head coach at Ole Miss, Auburn, Texas Tech and Cincinnati. Tuberville retired in 2016, soon after a federal lawsuit filed by former UCLA basketball player Ed O'Bannon over the use of his name and likeness in a video game began to chip away at the NCAA's longstanding tradition of amateurism.

A decade later, name-image-likeness payments, known as NIL, have transformed college sports, as high-level athletes — especially in the revenue-generating sports of football and basketball — now regularly sign deals worth thousands, or even millions, of dollars per season.

Pay for athletes is here to stay, Tuberville, a conservative Republican, said during a speech on the Senate floor in June.

"For years, everyone around college sports made money — schools, conferences, television networks, sponsors, coaches — while the athletes were told they could not make any money," he said. "That needed to change, and it did."

But other changes, many of them brought about by the flood of litigation that followed O'Bannon, have been harmful, he argued — especially the erosion of NCAA rules about who is eligible to play college sports and the freedom of athletes to transfer between schools without penalty, as thousands of Division I athletes now do each year.

Sponsor Message

Tuberville initially opposed the Protect College Sports Act because he saw it as government overreach into college sports.

But a primary purpose of the Protect College Sports Act is to grant the NCAA a limited antitrust exemption in order to restore the five-year eligibility rule and the one-time free transfer for athletes (subsequent transfers would require an athlete to sit out from competition for a year, with some exceptions).

So, this month, Tuberville switched his vote to yes.

"When I was coaching, you used to be able to develop a young person over a four- or five-year period and send them out into the real world as a man or woman with a degree, an education. And that's what it's about," Tuberville said in June. "Now you're lucky to keep a player one season."

Though Tuberville may be the Senate's most recognizable name to sports fans, he is far from the only senator with a background in Division I college athletics. Jim Justice of West Virginia played golf at Marshall. Ron Wyden of Oregon went to U.C. Santa Barbara on a basketball scholarship. Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania co-captained the wrestling team at West Point.

And several senators played college football — including Cory Booker, the Democrat from New Jersey, who played tight end at Stanford. He qualified for the academic powerhouse, he jokes, not because of his 4.0 GPA and 1600 SAT but rather his 1,600 reception yards and 4.0 yards per carry.

toggle caption Win McNamee/Getty Images

Booker was on the team from 1987 to 1990, when college football's big money era was just getting started. The modern lucrative television contracts were new then, and the sport was still a few years away from its first million-dollar coach.

Still, Booker said, he soon began to wonder how fair the whole arrangement was, especially for teammates who had come from a lower socioeconomic status than his middle-class family. "I just saw the economic bargain that they were getting — coming hundreds, if not thousands of miles away from family, not having the resources in any way proportionate to what they were doing for the university and for TV contracts and for well-paid coaches," he said.

Sponsor Message

After he graduated, Booker said, his discomfort grew as he saw friends at other schools have to pay out of pocket to finish their degrees after their playing careers ended. Teammates who had been injured playing football were still feeling the effects years later, but paying for their own medical care, as schools had no obligations to cover those costs.

Meanwhile, college athletic department budgets have ballooned.

Earlier this month, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, the lead Democrat on the bill, released a report that cited enormous increases in spending from 2005 to 2023: a 200% bump in travel costs, 250% in gameday expenses, more than 300% in recruiting, and the whopper — a 370% boom in pay for coaches.

"That's what frustrates me — we have a bill that's going to protect the wealth and the gravy train for a lot of folks but puts burdens on college athletes," said Booker. "It doesn't even put burdens on the coaches."

Booker has consistently voted against the bill in procedural votes so far. And he has proposed a handful of amendments, including one that would limit coaches' annual salaries to $5 million. According to databases maintained by USA Today, nearly 50 college football coaches earn more than that each year, as do more than a dozen basketball coaches.

The bill has plenty of other provisions. It significantly increases the amount schools are allowed to pay players directly in revenue sharing, from about $21 million this season — an amount established by a landmark legal settlement last year — to $49 million. It attempts to crack down on above-market-value NIL deals and caps agent pay. It gives conferences the option to pool their media rights. It has measures designed to protect roster spots for women's sports and Olympic sports, which generally do not earn revenue for schools.

The bill also aims to prevent the formation of "super conferences" by capping the membership of big-revenue conferences to 19 schools and disincentivizing schools from jumping from one power conference to another, a controversial provision that prompted "no" votes from Florida's two senators on behalf of schools like Florida State and Miami who hope to keep their realignment options open.

Sponsor Message

The negotiations over the bill have been ongoing for well over a year.

toggle caption Pool/via Getty Images

Sen. Eric Schmitt, a Republican from Missouri, is determined to get it passed. Schmitt was a two-sport athlete — football and baseball — at Truman State University, an NCAA Division II school. Juggling both sports and school simultaneously informed his approach to legislating, he says.

"There were moments when I was competing and you'd have to run the extra wind sprint, or you'd be running after a practice or after a game, and you just don't really want to do that. But when you push yourself physically and mentally, you get stronger," he said in an interview with NPR. "There are times in a negotiation or in a legislative process where things are difficult or challenging. So I have taken the position on how I handle things professionally that I'm just not going to quit."

Schmitt is a co-sponsor of the bill. Like his fellow conservative Tuberville, he was initially opposed to the idea of the federal government being so involved in college sports. But over time, he became convinced that Congress had a role to play, and he got to work convincing others, too.

Those negotiations have led to a remarkably bipartisan bill. Now, after more than a year of negotiations, the bill appears poised to pass the Senate with 70 votes (or more) with a mix of Republicans and Democrats.

"You don't get too many opportunities the way things are set up now in the U.S. Senate, where you can truly legislate something, [where] you can navigate in a bipartisan way, talk to people on issues that aren't clearly partisan," he said. "There's no red jersey, blue jersey. It's just how you're making the case."

The final Senate vote is scheduled for 5:30pm Eastern time on Monday. Its approval would be the most significant development yet in the effort to legislate reform to college sports, an effort supported by President Trump. But the bill faces an uncertain future in the House, which is on recess until after the November midterms.

World.title: Ohio governor's race: Ramaswamy and Acton clash in rare Democratic pickup opportunity
World.content:
Ohio governor's race: Ramaswamy and Acton clash in rare Democratic pickup opportunity

The Ohio governor's race pits former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy against Democrat Amy Acton, a former state health advisor. Democrats see a chance to win a state that usually votes Republican.

Transcript

AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:

The race for Ohio's governor pits biotech entrepreneur and former Republican presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy against Democrat Amy Acton, the state's former health director. Ohio usually votes Republican, but this race is competitive. Sarah Donaldson with Ohio Public Media's Statehouse News Bureau reports.

SARAH DONALDSON, BYLINE: Hours before this kickoff in Columbus, fans of the Ohio State Buckeyes have taken over asphalt lots and garages for tailgate parties. The Ohio State Women's Glee Club is making its rounds, serenading fans grilling and eating.

UNIDENTIFIED WOMEN'S GLEE CLUB: (Vocalizing).

DONALDSON: Tailgaters in a sea of scarlet and gray who talk with me know who they'll cast a ballot for or against.

JIM COY: There's just no way in the world I would vote for Amy Acton.

DONALDSON: That's Jim Coy (ph). He's an electrician from a small city in north-central Ohio. The three-time Trump voter didn't like Democratic nominee Amy Acton when she advised the governor on shutdowns as the state's health director in 2020.

COY: I believe she's hurt this state massively during COVID.

DONALDSON: Gretchen Conturo (ph), a healthcare worker and Democrat, says she's voting for Acton.

GRETCHEN CONTURO: I want somebody who's not going to be polarizing. I'm afraid Ramaswamy is going to be very polarizing.

DONALDSON: Neither Acton or Ramaswamy have been elected before. It's something Acton mentions often, like at this August law enforcement union endorsement.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

AMY ACTON: As a doctor and not much of a politician - becoming one every day - but a lifelong public servant at the age of 60, I'm telling you, I will do everything to fight for the people who keep us safe and well.

DONALDSON: Both candidates want more data center restrictions, property tax relief, a gas tax break. Ramaswamy, who President Trump endorsed, has made eliminating the state's income tax gradually a cornerstone.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

VIVEK RAMASWAMY: So I think when we take our income tax rate down to zero, we're actually going to see more economic expansion. We're going to see more sales tax revenue because more people are spending right here in Ohio.

DONALDSON: Both candidates also talk about 2020 a lot. Paul Sracic, an Ohio resident and senior fellow at the Washington D.C.-based Hudson Institute, says COVID is salient because of Acton's work under Republican Governor Mike DeWine.

PAUL SRACIC: And she was kind of - fairly or not - the face of those restrictions early on in COVID because she stood next to Governor DeWine, who has defended her.

DONALDSON: As for Ramaswamy...

SRACIC: Can Vivek Ramaswamy capture those Republican votes, particularly the sort of working-class votes? He's an odd candidate to appeal to those voters. He said things, for example, about, you know, H-1B visas and importing workers.

DONALDSON: Political groups for each candidate have launched attack ads. Republicans have rehashed a 2019 police report of a domestic disturbance at Acton's home, where she admitted she had been drinking. She's described the incident as, quote, "a normal marital fight." But the Ohio GOP created AI-generated images of Acton's car with a fake drunk-mom license plate. She calls the accusations of substance abuse lies, hate and vitriol.

And Democratic-backed ads slam Ramaswamy over investments in drugs for Alzheimer's, labeling him a, quote, "conman and swindler." He's called the ads outright defamatory lies.

Christopher Devine, University of Dayton political science associate professor, says Acton's prospects could depend on the national mood.

CHRISTOPHER DEVINE: Certainly, the biggest factor in her win - if it happens - would be a strong Democratic environment, or you might say a weak Republican environment.

DONALDSON: Ramaswamy, the son of Indian immigrants, would be the first person of Indian descent elected governor of the state. Acton would be the first woman elected governor here. Early voting starts October 6.

For NPR News, I'm Sarah Donaldson in Columbus, Ohio.

(SOUNDBITE OF ALABAMA SHAKES SONG, "SOUND & COLOR")

World.title: Trump's tariffs are unpopular in Maine. A Republican senator may pay the price
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs could bring manufacturing back to places it has fled, the town of Millinocket, Maine, ought to be a likely candidate.

Millinocket was for decades a thriving paper mill town, until Great Northern Paper ceased operations in 2008. Its fenced-off property sits abandoned, and although there's a growing outdoor recreation sector in the town of 4,100, its economy has struggled ever since.

Then came a plan, backed in part by Norwegian investors, for a $300 million US aquaculture venture repurposing the giant lagoons on the old mill site, to be called Great Northern Salmon.

"It was a marriage made in heaven," said Gail Fanjoy, the president of the local chamber of commerce. "Out of the gate, they were going to employ 50 people. That's a home run."

The project was about 80 per cent toward completion when the company announced last month it was pausing indefinitely, resting blame squarely on the uncertainty caused by the Trump administration's tariffs. Much of its salmon farming equipment was to be imported from Canada.

"That was a huge, huge, huge blow," Fanjoy told CBC News. "The Norwegian investors just said, 'We're done, we just can't deal with this.'"

One of the abandoned buildings on the former site of Great Northern Paper in Millinocket, Maine. A new $300 million US aquaculture venture repurposing the lagoons on the site, to be called Great Northern Salmon, was put on hold last month over what its backers described as the volatility caused by the Trump administration's tariffs. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Fanjoy, a lifelong resident of Millinocket, says nothing will make her believe Trump's claim that his trade policy will revive manufacturing in places like this.

"It's a fallacy," she said. "Paper companies all up and down the Penobscot River and the state of Maine closed, went bankrupt, and a tariff is not going to bring them back."

Cross-border trade matters to Maine

Maine does $6 billion US in annual two-way commerce with Canada — a significant amount in a state that's less populous than Manitoba.

The trade war is playing out amid a tight race for U.S. Senate in Maine, an election that will help determine which party controls Congress for the second half of Trump's term.

Maine's incumbent Sen. Susan Collins is something of a political phenomenon. The Republican has held her seat for the past 30 years in a place that hasn't voted statewide for a GOP presidential candidate since 1988.

If the Democrats are to win a majority in the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, Maine is a seat they'll almost certainly need to flip.

Tim Woodcock is a lawyer in Bangor, Maine, who has known Collins since the late 1970s and is supporting her re-election campaign. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

One big question in the race is if Maine voters will punish Collins as a proxy for their antipathy to Trump, whether over the trade war or other issues.

Tim Woodcock, a Bangor lawyer and a staunch backer of Collins, says many businesses have been adversely affected by tariffs, including those on Canadian products.

"These two economies are deeply intertwined," Woodcock told CBC News. "Anybody who is either trying to conduct a business in Maine or is dependent on a business in Maine would be very concerned about all the uncertainty that these tariffs have imposed."

'Canada's our friend'

CBC News spoke with Collins on the weekend as she walked in a parade in Carmel, a town of about 2,900.

Asked how concerned she is that Trump's tariffs will hurt her re-election chances, the 72-year-old senator parried the question.

"I'm much more concerned about the impact on the people of Maine in general. Many of our products, whether it's blueberries or potatoes or timber or lobster, are harvested here but processed in Canada," Collins said.

"Canada's our friend, our neighbour, our biggest trading partner," she added. "I urge the administration to get back to the table and both sides should engage in negotiations."

In 2020, Collins was the only Republican Senate candidate in the country to win in a state that voted for Joe Biden. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Among the townspeople lining the parade route was Chris Morang, who shook hands with Collins.

"I love her. She's always voted for helping the people in Maine. She's kept a lot of the hospitals going. She helped the lobster industry a lot," Morang told CBC News.

Although Collins has opposed Trump's trade war, Morang sides with the president.

"I think Canada has taken advantage of the United States a lot," he said. "They had unfair tariffs on us for many, many years, especially on lobster and lumber. I think at this point we're just getting what we deserve."

Collins has often tried to distance herself from Trump and his tariffs.

She was one of only seven Republican senators who voted to convict Trump in his impeachment trial for his role in the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the U.S. Capitol. Last week, she supported a resolution calling for an end to the war with Iran.

Carmel resident Chris Morang sides with Trump on tariffs, saying he believes that Canada has taken advantage of the U.S. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Collins claimed victory this month when the White House lifted tariffs on two imports that Maine relies on from Canada: cement and road salt.

Her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, says tariffs are crushing Maine and he's dismissive of Collins' approach.

'Concerned letters' to Trump

"Everything costs more for people, and you can tell it's a big deal because Susan Collins was writing concerned letters to Donald Trump," Jackson told CBC News.

"She got us rock salt back, but we can't eat that."

Both Collins and Jackson grew up in northern Maine, each within a half hour's drive of the Canadian border. But that's where the similarities end.

Collins comes from a prosperous family who owned a lumber yard, and now has a net worth as high as $9.6 million US, according to a Democratic Party analysis of her Congressional financial disclosures.

Troy Jackson, the Democratic Party candidate for U.S. Senate in Maine, greets a supporter following a town hall event in Bethel, Maine. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Jackson was a logger and union activist who jumped into local politics after participating in a border blockade protesting companies bringing lower-paid Canadian loggers into Maine in the late 1990s. If he wins, he'll become the only sitting U.S. senator without a four-year college degree.

During a weekend town hall in the small coastal city of Belfast, Jackson wore a ball cap while talking proudly of his roots in northern Maine and his two decades in local politics.

Jackson replaced Graham Platner

"I speak funny, I know that. I didn't go to the right schools and all that. But what I think people have come to understand is that I am 100 per cent dug in on getting shit done," Jackson said to whoops and cheers from the audience.

Jackson only became the Democrat candidate in July after the original nominee Graham Platner stepped down when a former partner accused him of sexual assault.

John Luft, who came to the town hall from the nearby coastal town of Lincolnville, says Jackson is different from the typical political candidate.

"He actually speaks to what Mainers need right now. He actually gets it," Luft said.

The audience at Jackson's town hall in Belfast, Maine, cheered when he told them, 'I am 100 per cent dug in on getting shit done.' (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Luft calls the trade war with Canada atrocious.

"I see no reason for this at all," he said. "Canada and United States have been friends forever and that's the way it should be."

Canadian companies have major investments in Maine, notably New Brunswick's Irving family empire with interests in logging, forest products and petroleum.

Despite what polling suggests is widespread opposition to Trump's tariffs among Maine voters, it's only one of the issues at play in the election contest between Jackson and Collins.

Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine Farmington, says while both candidates have staked out positions against the trade war, Collins can pitch Mainers on her influence in Washington as a veteran senator and her record of defying Trump.

"In some ways, how this (trade war) has played out may favour her more than Jackson," Melcher told CBC News.

At the same time, Collins is seeking a sixth term from an electorate that Melcher describes as weary of the status quo.

"Certainly Troy Jackson is different, more blue collar, has a different approach to things," he said. "The perception of the economy and the national Republicans, I think, isn't helpful to [Collins] either."

Woodcock, the lawyer in Bangor, remains optimistic about Collins' re-election chances given what he calls the long tradition of independent judgment shown by Maine voters.

"They have tended to support, I'd say, the candidates who are willing to reach across the aisle, who are prepared to put the merits of an issue ahead of party," said Woodcock.

In her last election in 2020, Collins defied the anti-Trump wave. Despite polls that suggested she was poised to lose, she defeated her Democrat challenger by nine percentage points. She was the only Republican Senate candidate in the country to win in a state that voted for Joe Biden.

World.title: 'Thrown under the bus': Former defence chief's memoir lays bare his battles with the Trudeau government
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's former top military commander considered resigning "several times" during his tenure in battles with the former Trudeau government over the sexual misconduct scandal, and the lack of commitment towards defence spending.

Retired general Wayne Eyre's new memoir, Into the Breach: A Soldier's Journey, also peels back the curtain on the internal debate that took place over how to end the convoy occupation of downtown Ottawa in early 2022.

The prologue to the book, titled The Accidental CDS, is a tongue-in-cheek reference to his unusual, unexpected rise to the position of chief of the defence staff.

Eyre was promoted from being army commander to the top job after now-retired admiral Art MacDonald stepped aside in February 2021 because of allegations of inappropriate behaviour. Those allegations never resulted in charges and MacDonald didn't return to the defence chief's job.

Eyre was left to navigate the wider sexual misconduct scandal and a flurry of allegations which engulfed several high-ranking military leaders — an experience he described as "soul crushing."

He candidly writes about how, in the first few months, he often questioned whether he was up to the task.

Eyre's memoir recounts a highly charged incident in June 2021 where he said he felt thrown "under the bus" by former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland.

At the time, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Freeland both publicly questioned Eyre's decision to allow the now-former commander of the navy, Vice-Admiral Craig Baines, to remain in his post after he took part in a golf game with former chief of the defence staff Jonathan Vance, who had been under military police investigation following allegations of inappropriate behaviour.

In Eyre's view, Freeland's criticism amounted to forcing the prime minister to choose between his deputy and his senior military adviser.

"If there's no trust between the nation's senior military leader and the nation's senior elected leader, one of them has to go, and it's not going to be the elected leader," Eyre said in an interview with CBC News.

Support from Trudeau kept him from resigning

The incident culminated, Eyre said, when he was on the phone with the prime minister to discuss the decision to retain Baines. He was just about to resign when Trudeau stopped him by saying he still had confidence in him.

After his initial criticism, the prime minister made a further statement of support for his defence chief — remarks Eyre had not seen when the phone call was placed. The crisis was defused, but the tension remained.

WATCH | Eyre thought about resigning 'several times' during tenure: Former military commander Eyre says he thought about resigning 'several times' | Duration closed caption 4:01 Retired general Wayne Eyre speaks to CBC senior reporter Murray Brewster about a description in his memoir of a moment when he considered resigning as chief of defence staff after being thrown 'under the bus' by the former deputy prime minister, Chrystia Freeland.

Eyre served another three years after the incident.

Resignation crossed his mind "several times" as internal battles unfolded over defence funding and the deteriorating state of readiness in the military.

Ultimately, he decided to stay because quitting would have precipitated a further crisis in an already wounded institution.

"You've got to be very careful as a military leader about resigning. You can fall on your sword, but generally it hurts and you can only do it once," he said.

"Resigning is an inherently political act, which could further fray political-military relations, [and] would cause a momentary blip in the media cycle. But at the same time, [it would] cause significant turmoil in the institution."

Throughout his tenure there was a series of rolling crises including the various waves of the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 11, 2022.

At the time, the Trudeau government faced public criticism about its reluctance to approve lethal aid for the embattled Eastern European country. It was a struggle, Eyre acknowledged.

"What we experienced at that time was a collision of ideology with reality," he told CBC.

"The ideology being, we are Canada, we don't supply weapons to a conflict zone. The reality was, OK, this is coming, Ukraine is a friend, this [is] one way we can help."

'Lethargy to approve a new defence policy'

Eyre's book is littered with further examples related to Canada's mission to train Ukraine troops and the transfer of M-777 artillery, underlining his frustration with the government's seeming "inability to make decisions at the speed of war."

He did note there were times when Canada later outstripped its allies in the swift delivery of war supplies and equipment, such as Leopard tanks.

The overall sense of frustration came into sharp focus during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's September 2023 visit to Canada, which included a series of speeches in Toronto.

"Both the PM and Deputy PM Freeland gave bellicose, impassioned speeches about being strong and supporting Ukraine," Eyre wrote, noting the contradiction between the political rhetoric and the fiscal reality that faced the Canadian military at the time.

"I, like the handful of CAF senior leaders present, had a hard time reconciling these otherwise great speeches with both the billion-dollar budget cut that they had just inflicted on us and their lethargy to approve a new defence policy."

The deeper the war in Ukraine became, the more concerned Eyre became about the state of Canada's readiness.

WATCH | Eyre urges Canada to support Ukraine's defence: ‘Urgency is required,’ says outgoing chief of defence staff Gen. Wayne Eyre on Russia-Ukraine war | Duration 2:48 In his final words as Canada’s chief of defence staff, Gen. Wayne Eyre said ‘evil walks this earth' and urged Canada to continue to support Ukraine's defence.

He described how, in June 2022, during the run-up to the unveiling of Canada's new policy commitment to NORAD — the by national aerospace command — no one seemed to know where $38 billion in funding was going to come from, or where it would be allocated.

"Most galling was the 'smoke and mirrors' funding approach, with billions already allocated for other military equipment taken away and reallocated, with most investments only coming years into the future," Eyre wrote.

"With confusion persisting several days later, I drew some government ire when I frankly told a journalist that the source of funds 'wasn’t clear to me.'"

Military 'compartmentalized' Ottawa convoy involvement

The memoir also sheds light on a passing reference that appeared in the public hearings related to the invocation of the Emergencies Act to end the convoy protest.

Former deputy defence minister Bill Matthews testified that the military prepared operational plans as a precaution, but they were dismissed due to significant concerns that deploying troops would escalate tensions and mirror the 1990 Oka Crisis.

Throughout the convoy protest crisis, Eyre was firmly opposed to the notion that the military had any sort of role whatsoever. He attempted to correct the public perception by saying there's a difference between planning and scenario spinning.

"We looked at various scenarios, and it wasn't planning because a plan entails assigning troops to task and warning at all levels and the like," Eyre told CBC News.

"No, it was more thinking about various scenarios, and what questions would we have to ask, what measures would have to be taken. But given the sensitivity at the time, it was very compartmentalized."

Most of the discussion, he said, revolved around the use of military tow-trucks to remove protest vehicles.

In his memoir, Eyre wrote: "At the time one of my staff commented, 'If you accomplish nothing else as CDS, keeping the CAF out of this mess is a singular achievement.'"

Canada 'on the right path,' Eyre says

During his final months as defence chief and in his departure speech, Eyre warned about how dangerous the world had become and how Canada needed to prepare.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government reversed many Trudeau-era policies and has begun substantially investing in defence — taking the country to the NATO standard of two per cent of the gross domestic product.

Several European political leaders, as well as security and intelligence agencies have warned that the West is likely to face a major conflict with Russia and possibly even China by the end of the decade.

Asked by CBC whether he thought the country was ready for what may be coming in the next few years, Eyre said no.

"But we're on the right path, and we are getting there."

World.title: Incoming Air Canada CEO's current airline engaged in 'anti-labour' behaviour, says Canadian union head
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The union representing Air Canada pilots says it is concerned about what it calls a "retaliatory and anti-labour" action by Scandinavian Airlines — which is currently run by Air Canada's next CEO.

Anko van der Werff will soon leave his role as president and CEO of Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) to take on the same position at Air Canada by the end of January.

Last month, Scandinavian Airlines Captain Mattias Åman Thiel — who also is the chair of the SAS section of the Swedish Pilots' Association — was fired.

The airline confirmed the dismissal to Radio-Canada but did not provide the reason why it took that measure.

The union, as well as the International Federation of Air Line Pilots' Associations — representing over 160,000 pilots worldwide — has called for Thiel's reinstatement.

The president of ALPA Canada, which represents pilots at major and regional Canadian airlines, called the dismissal "unwarranted" in a letter to van der Werff obtained by Radio-Canada.

"How you choose to respond will, without a doubt, be a clear indication on how you intend to engage with ALPA Canada pilots as you assume the leadership role at Canada's largest airline," wrote ALPA Canada president Tim Perry.

He echoed the other unions' demand to "immediately reinstate" Thiel in the letter, which was copied to Air Canada board of directors chair Vagn Sørensen.

Reached by Radio-Canada, an Air Canada spokesperson said the airline doesn't comment on "a situation involving another carrier."

Van der Werff did not respond to Radio-Canada's interview request, whereas SAS defends its decision.

SAS spokesperson Alexandra Lindgren Kaoukji said the airline does not comment on "individual employment matters." But she said the airline "strongly values the Scandinavian labour model and the important and constructive co-operation we have with our colleagues and their representatives."

"We cannot and will not make exceptions or treat colleagues differently based on their position, seniority or personal relationships," said Kaoukji in an email.

Dismissal challenged

The chair of the Swedish Airline Pilots Association (SWEALPA), Tristan Okkonen, worked closely with Thiel as part of his union duties.

"We are still in shock," he told Radio-Canada in an interview.

He says, according to the employer, Thiel was dismissed because he travelled abroad when he should have been working for the union. Those allegations were also reported by foreign media at the end of August.

An Air Canada Airbus A220-300 aircraft is seen in Richmond, B.C., in July. The company will soon have a new CEO. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

In court documents obtained by Radio-Canada, Thiel's union argues he was working remotely at the time. The pilots' union is asking the Swedish Labour Court to reinstate him and order SAS to pay damages.

Okkonen said Thiel's firing comes a few months after difficult salary negotiations between pilots and their employer. He said last spring, many pilots refused to work overtime in an act of protest — but said that action was not ordered by the pilots' union.

The Canadian pilots' union head says he fears the situation bodes poorly for the future Air Canada CEO's relationship with his employees.

"A healthy relationship requires trust," Perry told Radio-Canada in an interview.

He said he plans to mobilize members to support the captain in his demands.

World.title: Can I get AI face? Plastic surgeons say AI-generated inspiration is more than meets the eye
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

AI might be finding its way into surgeons' waiting rooms. Patients are taking in AI-generated images of the results they are hoping for from plastic surgeries. So, what could this mean for the medical community?

Dr. Ian MacArthur is accustomed to dealing with new trends in cosmetic surgery, but he's starting to see more patients coming into his Ottawa clinic with expectations that aren't entirely realistic.

Some clients, he says, bring in "fairly stylized" images generated with artificial intelligence, seeking results that may not even be "physically possible."

The experiences he's had so far motivated him to share a few cautionary thoughts on his Instagram page.

But it's a trend that plastic surgeons are dealing with more often.

The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS) recently warned about the rise of "AI face" — flawless, AI-enhanced images of patients' own faces that they believe can be recreated surgically.

The concern, says the organization's president, is that AI could also lead some people to put their desire for an unachievable look ahead of their own safety and well-being.

"The less realistic the image, the more dangerous that becomes if someone says, 'Yes, I can do it,'" Dr. Nora Nugent told CBC News.

More than meets the AI

BAAPS surveyed about half its roughly 350 members about how often they're seeing instances of AI face during consultations, Nugent said, with about 15 per cent of them responding that it's happening more often.

It's not that people are asking for anything unusual, she says. It's that the chatbot may have made other enhancements that it doesn't immediately disclose, such as a sharpened jawline or smoothed-out skin.

CBC News uploaded a photo of a journalist's face to three commonly used generative AI platforms — the free versions of OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google Gemini's Nano Banana and Anthropic's Claude — and prompted them to show the outcome of a rhytidectomy (a facelift).

Claude would not complete the task, responding that it wouldn't generate "realistic manipulated images of actual people."

Nano Banana did complete the task. When prompted, the chatbot explained that in addition to simulating the rhytidectomy, it also reduced loose neck skin and applied dermatological treatments like laser resurfacing or a chemical peel. (It also appeared to shave off facial hair).

It would not, however, create a medical before-and-after image comparison, encouraging consulting with a certified plastic surgeon for a realistic assessment.

ChatGPT did not hesitate to produce a visualization, as well as a side-by-side comparison. Like Nano Banana, it actually simulated multiple procedures — including what appeared to be an eyelid lift, brow lift and neck lift. ChatGPT said it smoothed out the forehead.

The chatbot did not immediately recommend consulting with a surgeon but later said the outcomes depend on one's anatomy, goals and doctor.

Pixels, not human tissue

Nugent says it's important for anyone seeking cosmetic surgery to know that AI can't account for an individual's anatomy.

"[AI] works in pixels, not human tissue," she said.

"Some tissue intrinsically is stronger, has more collagen, maybe thicker skin, and will hold a lift better," she said, adding that there are limits to "what's structurally safe to do" with a person's face.

"If you make a nose too small and too narrow, that person won't be able to breathe properly through their nose," she said. "If you take too much skin from an eyelid, someone can't close their eyes properly and that creates a medical problem."

On top of that, a patient's age, weight and lifestyle are also factors in the outcome.

WATCH | Real doctors appearing in AI deepfakes peddling unreal medical advice: AI deepfakes of prominent Canadian doctors are coming for your money | Duration closed caption 1:56 Health officials are warning Canadians about hyper-realistic AI deepfake videos of prominent doctors selling products or pushing bad advice. Victims are urged to contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, but doctors warn the videos are hard to take down.

Nugent says people can likely recognize the "more extreme changes" as unrealistic.

"But it's the mild to middle changes that they might think are realistic," she said.

Karen Rowa, a psychiatry and behavioural neurosciences professor at Hamilton's McMaster University, says it could also worsen problems for those who struggle with their appearance or have body dysmorphic disorder.

AI chatbots tend to "please the person they're talking to," she says. Asking them to fix something a person doesn't like about their face or body may "reinforce a problem that may not actually exist."

An unachievable risk

Dr. Michael Weinberg says he hasn't consulted any patients who have used generative AI tools to simulate their cosmetic surgery outcomes, but he's not entirely against the idea.

Weinberg, a plastic surgery division lead at Ontario's Trillium Health Partners, says AI may help a patient visualize their own goals in advance of an appointment. A surgeon can then help them determine what's possible and what's not.

He says plastic surgeons have already been using digital 3D simulation tools in their consultations for some time — for procedures like breast augmentations or eyelid lifts.

"If it's used wisely and judiciously with realistic results, then it is great because it can show you what you can look like," he said.

What he worries about is doctors who overpromise on what can be achieved — whether it's due to inexperience, pressure from the patient or unscrupulous business practices.

"There's a lot of bad plastic surgeons," he said, and a patient's desire to meet AI-generated expectations may lead them to seek less reliable options if they're told that their goals aren't achievable by a more responsible doctor.

He says "tourist plastic surgery" is another issue, with some people travelling abroad for aesthetic procedures.

That comes with a big risk, Weinberg says, of returning with the "absolute worst complications" that can require additional surgeries and months of care.

LISTEN | Just how dangerous is AI — and what we should do about it: Front Burner 33:35 Why are AI leaders calling for a slow down?

But Ottawa surgeon MacArthur says most patients are reasonable and aren't looking to go to any extremes. He says those who turn to AI tools may be doing so because they want to better communicate their wishes.

As long as he's clear with them about what is achievable, he says, they're generally understanding. But he does think some people have unrealistic expectations, and that AI could "be like gasoline on the fire."

World.title: As Canada deepens ties with Europe, could it leave U.S. banks and dollars behind?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians know how it feels to be hit by U.S. tariffs. But Canada hasn't been subjected to Washington's more aggressive tactics such as trade sanctions and asset freezes.

Or rather, most Canadians haven't.

Judge Kimberly Prost, a Canadian jurist who serves on the International Criminal Court, is the exception. She found her credit cards cancelled, her Google accounts closed and was effectively " de-banked " after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the court "an instrument for lawfare against the United States and our close ally Israel."

Prost is a living example of the dangers of digital and financial interdependence with the United States — and a warning of what would happen if such controls were turned against this whole country.

WATCH | More about the trade war: Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That | Duration closed caption 9:14 How can Canada win a trade war with the U.S. when leverage isn't equal? Andrew Chang explains how Canada is retaliating against massive tariffs levied by a neighbour 13 times its economic size. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Until now, Trump's main tool of coercion for most countries has been tariffs, said Fen Osler Hampson, chancellor of Carleton University and co-chair of the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations.

Trump has responded to court defeats by bringing the same tariffs back under new legal justifications . But he is running out of pretexts.

"There's concern that he may shift to using various forms of financial pressure," he said.

"What may happen is that, as the tariff lever becomes harder to pull, the president decides to pressure key trading partners — including Canada — by for example issuing executive orders barring U.S. financial institutions from processing Canadian transactions, or attaching conditions on access to dollar clearing. And those financial tools sit squarely within presidential authority."

Dollar clearing is the process of ensuring that real funds have been received from one party before releasing to the other.

The most drastic tool a U.S. president could use might amount to a "kill switch" on a large part of Canadian commerce, says Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute think-tank.

"If Visa or Mastercard were to be compelled by the Trump administration to turn off our access or geographically restrict service so that the province of Ontario just can't process transactions anymore, it would effectively halt a huge part of our economy," Bednar said.

"It would be unfathomable, but it's not impossible. And that's what happens when you grow too reliant and allow fragility like that to be introduced."

'This amazing weapon'

Karl Schamotta is chief market strategist at Corpay, one of the world's largest corporate payments companies. He says the U.S. has always sat at the centre of the world's transactions, but started to realize the power it had when it effectively iced North Korea out of the U.S. financial system.

Schamotta said a small number of banks in New York validate most international U.S. dollar transactions — creating the opportunity for vast "secondary sanctions" against any financial institution connected to those banks.

"Not only did they have control of banks within the U.S., but they had secondary control over any bank that touches those banks," he said.

"[The U.S.] realized, wait a second, we have this amazing weapon that we can use … so that escalated fairly rapidly over the years."

Incoming Canadian system has its limits

Canada is expected to launch its new payment system, called Real-Time Rail, later this year. But Bednar says it was conceived at a time when the priority was greater efficiency, not sovereignty, and offers little protection from outside threats.

Visa and Mastercard are central to the U.S. government's ability to shut down other countries' economies, handling about $32 trillion US of transactions annually — 90 per cent of all card transactions outside China.

In Britain, where Visa and Mastercard control about 95 per cent of card transactions , banks are co-operating with the government to create DeliveryCo , a system that can handle payments if the credit card companies ever hit the kill switch.

One country that has succeeded remarkably in freeing itself from Visa and Mastercard is Brazil, with a government system called Pix, originally set up by Brazil's central bank in 2020 to allow people without bank accounts to transfer money and make payments.

LISTEN | Trump is reshaping U.S. alliances. The world is taking notice: Two Blocks from the White House 28:09 Does Donald Trump want to have allies?

"Pix has been phenomenally successful, beyond anyone's expectations," said Schamotta. "There was no expectation that we would see it essentially go viral and displace basically everything else in the Brazilian system."

But the Trump administration accused Brazil of reducing market opportunities for Visa and Mastercard, and cited it as one justification for 25 per cent tariffs.

"They are targeting and bullying another jurisdiction, and saying that your pursuit of a form of digital sovereignty is unacceptable to us," said Bednar. "This is all the more reason to keep building up sovereign systems like this."

American banks and American dollars

But Pix, like Canada's Interac system, only avoids the U.S. banking system for domestic transactions, said Schamotta.

Still, he said some countries are setting up "swap lines" that go around the U.S.

Cryptocurrencies — including some that are pegged to currencies such as the U.S. dollar — are also gradually replacing dollars in international transfers.

The biggest non-U.S. system is China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which works with a digital currency interchange developed by China and other partners called mBridge. When the U.A.E. and Saudi Arabia sell oil to China, the payments clear without touching U.S. banks.

Canada and Europe similarly have the technical ability to design a way for their parallel systems to "talk to each other in a smooth fashion, and clear between one another in a smooth fashion without much difficulty," said Schamotta.

A new lane on an existing highway

Just as Canada seeks to protect its trade with Europe, it should also seek to do the same with other like-minded partners, Bednar said.

"It would be smart for Canada and the middle power alliance to be building up this payment infrastructure … in a way that can maintain that neutrality we expect, instead of a superiority and control that can be weaponized," she said.

The goal, says Hampson, is not to stop dealing with U.S. banks entirely, but rather "adding a lane to a highway."

And if the U.S. were to block or toll international transactions as a form of leverage, he said, the rest of the world will be looking for such a lane.

Coercion is a double-edged sword

In an interview with Bloomberg days before heading to Europe last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney referred to financial transactions as an example of "those interconnections, that integration [that] can be used as leverage against you."

And speaking to the European Parliament, he listed payments as one of several areas where Canada and the EU can "secure our strategic autonomy through deep co-operation."

Hampson says countries are increasingly seeing their ties to the U.S. as vulnerabilities, rather than advantages.

"Once you start weaponizing the bonds of economic or financial interdependence, it cuts both ways. Just as you know, tariffs impose a real cost on American consumers … the same is true when it comes to government intervention in financial markets, which depend heavily on trust, on stability."

Continued U.S. control of the world financial system depends on the U.S. not abusing its position, he said. Such abuse, he said, would "run the risk of losing it."

With most international credit and currency reserves being held in U.S. dollars, Schamotta said breaking free of that dominance is unlikely to happen fast.

But in the meantime, Bednar says Canada can do a lot to reduce its vulnerabilities to reckless behaviour from the U.S.

"We used to smoke cigarettes in the hospital, and that used to be a norm of our society that we didn't question. We moved away from that for very good reasons," Bednar said.

"Right now, when it comes to digital sovereignty and our own payment sovereignty, I would say we're smoking cigars in the hospital, and we can't do that anymore."

World.title: Speed over species? What experts are saying about Ottawa's new major projects bill
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The new Building Canada Strong Act contains a list of measures that Prime Minister Mark Carney says will get projects moving faster in the face of major threats to Canada's economy from U.S. President Donald Trump.

But experts warn Bill C-39 could also dismantle environmental safeguards that protect Canadians and prevent wildlife from extinction, despite the federal government claiming otherwise.

"It greatly saddens me that in standing up to bullying from the United States, we are willing to put some of the things that make Canada so special on the table," said Gretchen Fitzgerald, executive director of the Sierra Club Canada Foundation.

When he tabled Bill C-39, government House leader Steven MacKinnon called it one of the most important economic pieces of legislation in a generation, adding that its purpose is to make project decisions in one year.

Tucked inside are a dizzying array of more than 300 clauses that amend more than a dozen separate pieces of federal legislation, including laws to protect species at risk, water quality and fisheries. Not to mention proposed changes to the Labour Code, which have upset unions.

CBC News combed through the bill's more than 200 pages and spoke with environmental and resource development experts about its impact.

Here's a detailed look at what's inside.

Shovels before science?

Typically before construction can begin on projects like mines, railways and ports, the environment and climate change minister needs to sign off on an impact assessment review — a thorough evaluation of a proposed project's potential environmental, social, economic and health effects.

Under the new bill, Ottawa could grant permits for preliminary construction before the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada completes its work — if the environment minister considers it "enabling activities" and in the "public interest."

It would still maintain the right to stop a project if an impact assessment determines it should not go forward.

The federal government insists the environment won't be harmed.

"We are not rolling back our environmental regulations," said Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin.

But critics say the proposed legislation will claw back environmental protections, and that its vague wording asks the public to place too much trust in the government's interpretation of the bill.

"I want to see evidence that our government understands what the national interest is because I think it's in our national interest not to poison our lakes and rivers," said Megan Leslie, president and CEO of World Wildlife Fund Canada.

"I think it's in our national interest to have safe communities when it comes to floods and fires.… It's in our national interest not to have species go extinct."

WATCH | Ottawa defends Building Canada Strong Act: Ottawa moves to extend its powers to push through major projects | Duration closed caption 8:50 Tucked into the Liberal government's new omnibus bill is a change that would extend Ottawa's powers to exempt major projects from certain environmental protections. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Corey Hogan says this move 'provides more certainty' to those looking to invest in Canada.

Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said the proposed legislation responds to the needs of industries to build faster.

"Overall, it's very positive," she said.

Exner-Pirot also said early construction will be done in narrow exceptions, such as minor work before winter.

"Canada's construction season is very constrained," Exner-Pirot said. "And so if you can get something done … you can save months and millions or tens of millions of dollars on the project."

Henry VIII powers

The bill also makes permanent controversial sweeping powers in the Building Canada Act, Bill C-5, which the government passed last year promising they would be temporary.

Under C-5, Ottawa can exempt certain projects deemed in the national interest from a wide set of environmental regulations and acts of Parliament. Academics and critics accuse the government of inserting Henry VIII clauses, a reference to the autocratic King Henry VIII of England.

Alberta's West Coast pipeline and the Robert Banks Terminal 2 port expansion in B.C.'s lower mainland are on track to obtain this treatment.

These powers were supposed to last five years. But C-39 removes that sunset clause.

Exner-Pirot said people shouldn't be worried.

"Any Parliament can revoke laws that were made in the previous Parliament," she said. "If the people think it's being abused, then there will be an incentive for future governments to change that."

Preapproval of projects over large regions

This new bill also expands the "project of national interest" concept to create entire regions of national interest.

For this to happen, the government would need to conduct an environmental assessment of the region under consideration. One is currently underway in the Ring of Fire, a mineral-rich and ecologically sensitive area of northern Ontario.

Following such a study, cabinet would then be able to designate the entire area a region of national interest, giving Ottawa broad authority to approve future activities. But federal officials told reporters the activities must adhere to specific types and criteria which Ottawa will outline when granting the designation.

For example, Ottawa could say that mining for critical minerals in the Ring of Fire is permitted along with any roads, bridges and high-voltage power lines, but a natural gas pipeline may not be allowed to go through the same area.

Environmentalists worry the government is putting speed and shareholders over survival of sensitive wildlife species and habitat.

"It's essentially the Building Canada Act on steroids," said Julia Levin, associate director of Environmental Defence Canada, calling the regions "sacrifice zones where projects could get rubber stamped."

Bill C-39 could devastate endangered orcas, experts warn. (Elaine Thompson/The Associated Press)

But regions of national interest could also offer a path to advance renewable energy projects.

A regional assessment has been completed for wind development offshore of Nova Scotia. The 300,000-square-kilometre study area could unlock significant sustainable power generation for the province and the country.

"In some ways, for those who wanted to see clean energy projects and electrification and decarbonization fast-tracked, that's more possible than ever under this act," said David Wright, an environmental and energy law professor at the University of Calgary.

But Wright said even clean energy projects come with risks to people and the environment.

"That could come at the expense of the rights and interests of Indigenous Peoples, ecosystems, species at risk and private landowners," he said.

Easier to drain lakes, dump in waterways

Bill C-39 keeps intact protections for species at risk, but experts say it also has loopholes.

Proponents already have the ability to dump stones, gravel, rubbish and other material in rivers. They can even drain lakes. But as it stands, they have to get the approval of the federal cabinet.

"What this power allows the minister to do is exempt those water bodies so that there's no more oversight," said Anna Johnston, a staff lawyer with West Coast Environmental Law.

This could be a problem, she and others note, in places like northern Alberta where oilsands companies use considerable amounts of water.

WATCH | Prime Minister Mark Carney rallies his MPs to fast-track projects: Carney: 'High standards do not mean decisions have to be slow' | Duration closed caption 1:02 In his opening remarks to the Liberal caucus meeting on Friday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said new projects will be approved or denied with speed with the passage of his Building Canada Strong Act that will be tabled this fall. 'Predictability is a competitive advantage,' Carney said.

The proposed legislation would also amend the Species at Risk Act (SARA).

A provision known as the "jeopardy test" was kept intact after academics wrote an open letter and environmentalists launched a media campaign opposing its removal. But the ministers of fisheries and environment would still be able to consider "technical, economic and practical" considerations when permitting construction in sensitive areas.

Environmentalists say this waters down the key protection measure, which prohibits any project from going forward if it could drive a wildlife species extinct.

"That's really backwards thinking," said Lisa Gue, a national policy manager with the David Suzuki Foundation. "Unravelling these standards actually leaves our country vulnerable to missteps that could cause long-term damage and harm to communities.… It looks like nature is going to be steamrolled."

Fish habitat potentially at risk

Similarly, the bill proposes changes to the Fisheries Act, which could allow projects to harm fish and fish habitat if it's not economic or practical to protect them.

Ottawa is proposing to make up for the possible damage through an expanded fish habitat bank regime that proponents could pay into for restoration, but the bill doesn't say how that would work.

Margot Venton, a lawyer and director of the nature program at Ecojustice Canada, is worried about ecosystem collapse, which could lead to fishery closures, like that of the cod industry in Newfoundland during the early 1990s.

"We don't have an economy over the long term if we destroy the ecosystem," Venton said.

After reviewing the proposed legislation, Sally Otto, a professor in the department of zoology at the University of British Columbia, said the government is willing to draw Canada's environmental deficit down deeply into the red to balance the country's finances.

"I'm all for building Canada strong, but we also need to build Canada safe," Otto said. "Safe for the environment, safe for humans, safe for nature."

World.title: Ukraine uses drones to make airdrops of aid to occupied city of Oleshky on brink of starvation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian officials say they dropped four tonnes of food at 100 different locations in the Russian-occupied community of Oleshky, where there are fears that food has become so scarce that residents are resorting to foraging for weeds.

The operation, which involved several Ukrainian military units, was carried out in waves, with drones dropping boxes filled with food and cooking oil throughout the community, according to regional authorities.

Oleshky lies just three kilometres south of the Dnipro River, which forms the front line between Ukrainian forces — who control the city of Kherson and surrounding areas — and Russian forces occupying Ukrainian communities on the left bank of the river.

Before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Oleshky had a population of about 20,000. Today, Ukrainian officials estimate that about 6,000 people remain in the city and surrounding area, including approximately 200 children.

"This [aid] will give people the opportunity to live there for up to a month," Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, said in an interview with CBC News. But he warned that the solution could be short-lived.

A screengrab of a promotional video shows the contents of aid packages dropped over the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky on Saturday. (Kherson Regional Military Administration)

Residents under 'full blockade' by Russian troops

Tolokonnikov said video from drones, which were launched on Saturday, confirmed that some residents had received the food, but Russian troops forcibly seized supplies from civilians in some cases, he said.

The Ukrainian military has carried out several other aid drops since April, but they were on a much smaller scale, he said.

In recent days, Ukrainian officials have warned that many residents of Oleshky are on the brink of starvation. Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha said residents were under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, which he said were refusing to allow humanitarian aid into the city.

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia to allow humanitarian assistance into the city and open an evacuation corridor for residents who want to leave.

Russia, which seized Oleshky on the first day of its full-scale invasion more than four and a half years ago, has acknowledged that the city is facing critical shortages of food and medicine, but the Kremlin has said Russian forces are working to address the problems.

Oleshky has no functioning stores, and the nearest place where residents can obtain supplies is about 20 kilometres away, in the rural community of Radensk.

A man holds a placard reading 'Mass Starvation in Occupied Oleshky. Americans! Make Russia Agree to a Humanitarian Corridor' as he protests outside Kyiv's city hall on Sept. 20. Ukrainian officials want Oleshky to be evacuated. (Sergei Supinsky/AFP/Getty Images)

Bartering for food

Ukrainian officials say travelling out of Oleshky is extremely dangerous, and they've accused Russia of laying landmines around the area.

It is difficult to independently verify reports from inside the community as people living under Russian occupation fear reprisals for speaking publicly, and mobile connections can be unreliable.

CBC News has not been able to connect with any residents still inside the city but spoke by phone with a woman whose 70-year-old mother-in-law managed to leave Oleshky on Tuesday after walking for six hours.

A screengrab of drone footage shared by a Ukrainian marine brigade shows homes in Oleshky in ruins in August. (34th Separate Marine Brigade 'Borysfen')

"Over the last six months, their circumstances had deteriorated significantly," the woman said. "People have been constantly searching for food. What they could obtain was sometimes just two potatoes and two pieces of garlic."

The woman, who last spoke with her mother-in-law in early September, did not want her name published because the 70-year-old still lives in territory occupied by Russia.

She said she was told people have been bartering with their neighbours for supplies, exchanging things such as vegetables for eggs.

Desperate messages

Tetiana Hasanenko, the Ukrainian head of the Oleshky military administration who is working in exile, shared messages with CBC News that could not be independently verified that she received from local residents.

In one message, a resident described how some people have resorted to finding plants to eat.

"[People] are exchanging information about how to cook, basically, grass and weeds that grow in the gardens. Because there are no basic food products,” Hasanenko said in an interview via Zoom from the southern Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv.

She said the area is constantly being shelled and that residents are losing limbs — and, in some cases, dying without adequate access to medical care.

Ukrainian officials said the aid drop carried out on Saturday had been planned for several weeks. Before the drones carrying the boxes of food were launched, officials said Ukrainian forces tried to clear the neighbourhoods of Russian positions and drones.

Tolokonnikov, of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, said the Ukrainian military had carried out several other aid drops since April, but they were on a much smaller scale.

A soldier prepares one of the 100 boxes of food that were dropped by drones into Oleshky on Saturday. (34th Separate Marine Brigade 'Borysfen' and 11th National Guard Brigade 'Bolharych')

Spotlighting Oleshky

The plight of Oleshky's population has been garnering attention in Ukraine but less so internationally. In recent days, Ukrainians have been urging the international community to take notice by posting on social media and, in some cases, holding signs at sporting events.

Cory Woods, a Canadian who previously worked in humanitarian efforts in Ukraine before becoming a drone-interceptor pilot, said he has been disappointed that the situation has not received more attention globally.

"There's a lot going on with talk of negotiations and peace negotiations for the war at large. All of that needs to be put on hold, and our focus needs to be on Oleshky and helping these people," he said.

"At the very least, get food, water and, at best, get them out of there."

World.title: Loved ones pay tribute to victims of helicopter crash outside of Montreal
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One day after a helicopter crash in Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville, Que., that killed four people, tributes are pouring in for the victims.

In a moving social media post, Océane Perreault recounted how on Sept. 26, a part of her life "flew off to heaven."

Perreault lost her life partner Gabriel Jasmin in the crash, as well as her mother Chantal Raymond and her brother Loucas Perreault .

Perreault said the helicopter ride was meant to celebrate her mother's birthday but instead turned into a tragedy.



"I have no words to describe the pain, the shock, and the emptiness I feel. Three people I love more than anything are gone far too soon — right before my eyes," she wrote in French.

WATCH | Crash killed pilot and 3 members of the same family: Helicopter crash near Montreal kills 4 | Duration closed caption 2:03 Police are investigating a helicopter crash that killed all four occupants in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville, Que. It’s believed the private aircraft ran into issues shortly after taking off.





She called Jasmin the love of her life and "the best dad in the world." She described her mother as "her rock, her comfort, her home," while her brother, she said, was her "partner-in-crime."

Perreault said the tragedy was a reminder to cherish the people in your life.

"Hold your loved ones a little tighter. Tell them you love them. Call the people you miss," she wrote. "Cherish the little moments, the fits of laughter, the ordinary days. And above all, stop worrying about the small stuff. Because, in the end, the people we love are what matter most."

Jasmin was a radio host and advertising producer at Énergie Sherbrooke radio.

Énergie 106.1 took to social media to express their condolences to Jasmin's loved ones, including his wife and daughter and his team at Bell Media.

"Our thoughts are with all those affected by his passing," the post reads.

Suzanne Jutras is seen in an undated photo, posted to Facebook by members of the agricultural community. They extended their condolences to Jutras' family, noting that her partner was a field crop farmer and former dairy farmer in the area. (Syndicat UPA du Haut-Richelieu/Facebook)

Suzanne Jutras was 'our favourite pilot'

The other victim of the helicopter crash was identified by organizers of a Quebec cultural festival as pilot Suzanne Jutras.

The helicopter crashed in a corn field near near Rang des Écossais, just off Highway 10, around 2:30 p.m. on Saturday.

Initially, the Sûreté du Québec said they believed the aircraft had experienced difficulties shortly after takeoff leading to the crash. In an update Sunday, however, SQ spokesperson Valérie Beauchamp said the crash happened when the aircraft was returning.

Jutras, a commercial pilot, was based in Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville, according to a Linkedin profile in her name.

She regularly offered helicopter tours, including last weekend at les Félixeries, a cultural and community festival in Saint-Félix-de-Kingsey, near Drummondville.

Festival organizers confirmed to CBC News that Jutras was the pilot killed in Saturday's crash.

In a post on social media, les Félixeries paid tribute to Jutras, calling her their "favourite pilot of the past three years."

"We extend our deepest sympathies to her partner, family, friends, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing her through her passion," the French-language post said.

Jutras had plenty of experience, said one of her friends, a fellow pilot who spoke to Radio-Canada off camera.

The region's agricultural community also expressed their support to Jutras' family, noting that her partner was a field crop farmer and former dairy farmer in the area.

The SQ did not confirm the identities of the victims, referring any inquiries to the Quebec coroner's office.

The office did not respond in time for publication.

The SQ says it had concluded its investigation and the matter is now in the hands of the Transportation Safety Board of Canada.

Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said on Saturday that he would appoint a minister's observer to monitor the response alongside the TSB.
