Burstone Group has entered into binding agreements with Nedbank Property Partners (NPP) to launch a South African funds-management platform seeded with 14 of its retail, industrial and logistics properties, the Johannesburg-listed company said in a stock exchange announcement on 25 September 2026. Burstone will keep 50% of the platform and act as fund and asset manager.

Dollar figures in this article use the 25 September 2026 closing rate of about R16.28 to the US dollar.

What the Burstone Nedbank property platform holds

The seed portfolio comprises five retail properties and nine industrial and logistics properties. The malls are Dihlabeng Mall and Fleurdal Mall in the Free State, The Neighbourhood Square in Gauteng, Kriel Mall in Mpumalanga and Zevenwacht Mall in the Western Cape.

The industrial assets are five warehouse properties in Gauteng and four in the Riverhorse area of KwaZulu-Natal. Burstone describes the malls as dominant rural and peri-urban shopping centres and the warehouses as backed by strong tenants on long leases.

The seed assets carry a book value of R5.429 billion (about US$333 million) as at 31 March 2026, and Burstone’s announcement describes the portfolio’s gross asset value as “approximately R5.4 billion” (about US$332 million). The price agreed with NPP is lower.

The price and the terms

The platform has been priced at a gross asset value of R5.155 billion (about US$317 million), a 5.0% discount to book value. That implies a blended asset yield of 8.4%, based on 12-month rolling net operating income of R435 million (about US$26.7 million).

NPP will pay about R677 million (about US$41.6 million) in cash for its 50% equity interest. The platform will start with debt equal to 70% of its asset value, which is why half of the equity costs far less than half of the property value.

The deal is subject to Competition Commission approval and other conditions. Payment is staggered: part on closing, once at least 70% of the properties by value have transferred, and the rest as each remaining property is registered. The price carries a 5% escalation on properties still untransferred three months after competition approval.

Why Burstone is selling half

Burstone says the transaction releases R4.5 billion (about US$276 million) for redeployment into local and international growth. Part of that capital will cover the group’s first-loss obligations on its European logistics platform with Blackstone.

The group expects its loan-to-value ratio to fall from 39.6% at 31 March 2026 to between 17.5% and 19.5%, and its look-through ratio from 48.6% to between 40.5% and 42.5%. Burstone says the deal will be earnings accretive and leaves its guidance of 4% to 6% growth in distributable income per share unchanged.

Fee income becomes a bigger part of the business. Burstone says fee revenue rises to 19.3% of total earnings, from 15.5% for the year to 31 March 2026, and third-party assets under management rise by 10.9% to R26.8 billion (about US$1.65 billion).

What Nedbank gets

NPP is the real estate equity and mezzanine financing business within Nedbank Corporate and Investment Bank. Its stake gives the bank exposure to income-producing malls and warehouses without running them.

Burstone and NPP will hold joint control. The platform is set up as a permanent capital vehicle with no fixed exit date, and it can admit new investors or dilute existing ones without a new structure.

The deal comes as Nedbank also expands in East Africa, where the Central Bank of Kenya has cleared it to buy up to 66% of NCBA Group.

What to watch next

The first milestone is Competition Commission approval. Burstone expects the transaction to take effect no later than 1 December 2026.

The second is a further investor. Burstone says it is in talks with a significant institutional investor for a second close, but it has not named the investor or the terms.

After the deal, Burstone’s directly held South African assets fall from R13.9 billion (about US$854 million) to R8.5 billion (about US$522 million), on its own figures. Whether more of that book moves into similar vehicles will show how far the group shifts from owning property to managing it, a theme that runs through Africa: The New Scramble.

World.title: Nigeria’s AG Mortgage Bank Lifts Assets 48% as Profit More Than Doubles
World.content:
Nigeria · BANKING

Key Facts — Nigeria Africa’s most populous country has a thin mortgage market, and much of its home lending runs through small specialist lenders known as primary mortgage banks.

— The lender AG Mortgage Bank Plc is one of them. In June it raised N3.97 billion (about US$3.0 million) in commercial paper at yields of 22.5 percent to 24 percent, a measure of how costly funding is.

— What happened At its annual general meeting on September 25, 2026, the bank reported that total assets rose 48 percent in 2025 to N33.04 billion (about US$24.9 million), and profit after tax jumped 130 percent to N1.06 billion (about US$0.8 million).

— The lending Loans and advances grew 44 percent to N22.71 billion (about US$17.1 million), far faster than customer deposits, which rose 14 percent to N9.48 billion (about US$7.1 million).

— Why it matters to you The gap was bridged partly by a N7.83 billion (about US$5.9 million) facility from MREIF, the federal government’s mortgage refinancing fund, a sign that state money is now doing much of the work in Nigerian home lending.

— Still open Whether the bank can keep growing its loan book without its funding costs or bad loans rising, and how much of its 2026 growth will again depend on government refinancing.

Nigeria’s AG Mortgage Bank grew its assets by nearly half in 2025 and more than doubled its profit, but the numbers show the lender is leaning on government refinancing money rather than its own depositors to fund new home loans.

AG Mortgage Bank assets grew 48 percent to N33.04 billion (about US$24.9 million) in 2025, up from N22.37 billion (about US$16.9 million) in 2024. The Nigerian primary mortgage bank presented its results for the year to December 2025 to shareholders at its annual general meeting, held virtually on September 25, 2026. Dollar conversions in this article use the closing rate of Friday, September 25, 2026, of about N1,327 per US dollar.

What the AG Mortgage Bank assets numbers show

The balance-sheet expansion was driven by lending. Loans and advances rose 44 percent to N22.71 billion (about US$17.1 million), from N15.82 billion (about US$11.9 million) a year earlier.

Earnings grew even faster than the balance sheet. Gross earnings rose 42 percent to N4.93 billion (about US$3.7 million), profit before tax climbed 89 percent to N1.38 billion (about US$1.0 million), and profit after tax rose 130 percent to N1.06 billion (about US$0.8 million) from N458.7 million (about US$346,000).

Shareholders’ funds increased 17 percent to N7.16 billion (about US$5.4 million). Total liabilities grew much faster, up 59 percent to N25.88 billion (about US$19.5 million), so the expansion was financed mostly with borrowed money rather than new capital.

Where the money came from

Customer deposits grew only 14 percent to N9.48 billion (about US$7.1 million), well behind the loan book. The bank named its other sources: a N7.83 billion (about US$5.9 million) facility under MREIF, and continued access to Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria funding for National Housing Fund loans.

MREIF is a real estate investment fund set up by the Ministry of Finance Incorporated (MOFI), the federal government’s investment arm. It channels money through approved lenders so that homebuyers can borrow at 9.75 percent a year for up to 20 years, far below market rates. AG Mortgage Bank has described itself as the first primary mortgage institution accredited under the scheme and the first to receive a disbursement.

Market funding is far more expensive. The bank’s N3.97 billion (about US$3.0 million) commercial paper issue in June was priced at implied yields of 22.5 percent to 24 percent, and was fully subscribed, BusinessDay reported.

What management says

Chairman Abel Amadi said the results came despite “persistent inflation, elevated interest rates and exchange-rate volatility.” He added that “the quality and sustainability of the Bank’s growth are as important as the growth itself.”

Managing Director Ngozi Anyogu called the loan-book growth “particularly important,” saying it showed the bank’s widening capacity to put funding into mortgages. The bank ties its strategy to a plan it calls Project Momentum 2030.

Why a small mortgage bank matters in Nigeria

Nigeria has a large housing shortage and very little long-term home lending. Most households cannot get a conventional 20-year loan, because banks fund themselves short term and interest rates are high.

That is why government schemes such as MREIF and the National Housing Fund matter so much. They supply the long-dated, cheaper money that small lenders cannot raise from depositors, and lenders such as AG Mortgage Bank pass it on to homebuyers.

AG Mortgage Bank is small: its total assets of about US$24.9 million are a fraction of a single large Nigerian commercial bank. Its results are a useful read on whether state-backed housing finance is actually reaching borrowers.

Who gains and who carries the risk

Shareholders gain from a profit that more than doubled and a larger capital base. Homebuyers gain if concessional funding keeps flowing through lenders like this one.

The risk sits in the funding mix. With liabilities growing more than three times as fast as equity, the bank depends on continued access to government refinancing and on investors rolling over its commercial paper.

For readers following frontier markets, the pattern is familiar from other emerging economies: mortgage growth arrives when the state supplies cheap long-term money, and slows when it does not. Nigeria has also courted overseas buyers, with a diaspora mortgage programme launched in London in August.

What to watch next

The first test is whether deposit growth picks up, which would reduce the bank’s reliance on MREIF and expensive commercial paper. The second is loan quality, as borrowers carry high rates and inflation.

Any change to MREIF’s size, pricing or accreditation rules would feed directly into lenders such as AG Mortgage Bank. So would decisions by the Central Bank of Nigeria on capital and liquidity rules for primary mortgage banks.

World.title: Nigeria’s Pension Funds Pledge US$182 Million to Infrastructure
World.content:
Nigeria · PENSIONS

Key Facts — Nigeria Africa’s most populous country has large gaps in roads, power and other infrastructure, and a growing pool of mandatory pension savings that sits mostly in government securities.

— The background The National Pension Commission, PenCom, regulates that pool. Working with FSD Africa, a UK-funded financial-sector development agency, the industry has set up a Pension Industry Infrastructure Consortium to invest part of it in infrastructure.

— What happened On September 24, 2026, PenCom Director-General Omolola Oloworaran said pension funds have committed N241 billion (about US$181.6 million) to the plan, and expect that to reach almost N300 billion (about US$226 million).

— The catch No money has been invested. A framework with FSD Africa, a memorandum of understanding and a fund manager are still needed, projects have not been chosen, and participation by pension fund administrators is voluntary.

— Why it matters to you If it works, Nigerian retirement savings become a steady local source of long-term infrastructure money, which could create co-investment openings for foreign investors and development lenders.

— Still open Which projects and asset classes get the money, who manages it, and whether the first tranche is actually deployed by the target of the second quarter of 2027.

Nigeria’s pension funds have pledged N241 billion (about US$181.6 million) to a new infrastructure consortium, but no money has moved yet, no projects have been picked and the first deployment is not due before the second quarter of 2027.

Nigeria’s pension funds have committed N241 billion (about US$181.6 million) to a pension infrastructure investment plan, and expect the total to reach almost N300 billion (about US$226 million) once an outstanding commitment from an undisclosed participant arrives. Omolola Oloworaran, Director-General of the National Pension Commission (PenCom), gave the figures at a press briefing in Lagos on Thursday, September 24, 2026, after the fourth meeting of the Pension Industry Leadership Council. Dollar conversions in this article use the closing rate of Friday, September 25, 2026, of about N1,327 per US dollar.

How the pension infrastructure investment plan works

The money is being pooled through the Pension Industry Infrastructure Consortium, set up by the pension industry together with FSD Africa. FSD Africa is a specialist development agency funded by the UK government that works on deepening African financial markets.

“We haven’t invested any money just yet. This is just a commitment in terms of what the industry will do,” Oloworaran said. Before any investment, the industry still has to conclude a framework with FSD Africa, sign a memorandum of understanding and appoint a fund manager.

The first tranche is expected to be deployed by the second quarter of 2027. Oloworaran said development partners could add money alongside the pension commitments.

What has not been decided

Specific projects and asset classes have not been selected, and discussions on allocation are continuing. Oloworaran called the N241 billion (about US$181.6 million) only the first phase of a wider effort to mobilise pension capital for infrastructure.

Participation by Pension Fund Administrators, the private firms that manage Nigerians’ retirement accounts, is voluntary. Each administrator is expected to decide in the best interest of its contributors, so the final amount could end up above or below the current commitments.

Why Nigeria is turning to pension money

Nigeria’s pension assets are overwhelmingly invested in government paper. PenCom data show total pension assets of N29.52 trillion (about US$22.2 billion) at the end of March 2026, with 58.07 percent in federal government securities. Infrastructure funds held just N224.23 billion (about US$168.9 million), less than 1 percent of the total.

That makes the new commitment significant in relative terms: at N241 billion (about US$181.6 million), it is already larger than everything the industry held in infrastructure funds in March.

Oloworaran argued that infrastructure suits pension funds because of its long life and its potential to protect savers against inflation. For the government, the attraction is local, long-term money for roads, power and other projects without adding to public borrowing.

The consortium is not the only vehicle chasing this money. In August, Africa Finance Corporation launched a Nigeria infrastructure fund aimed at the same pension, insurance and asset-management investors.

The risks for savers

Infrastructure assets are long-dated and hard to sell. That makes governance, transparent project selection and a credible fund manager essential if pension contributors are to be protected.

As regulator, PenCom will need to balance its push for national development against its duty to protect retirement savings. The fund-manager appointment and the first project choices will be the first real test of that balance.

The regional read-through

Nigeria is following a path other emerging economies have tried: using domestic pension savings to build infrastructure instead of relying only on foreign borrowing. Mexico is pursuing a similar plan for its pension funds.

FSD Africa’s role gives the plan an international partner. It fits the wider contest over who finances the continent’s hard assets, covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

Watch for the signing of the memorandum of understanding and the appointment of a fund manager, both of which must come before any money moves. Then watch for the first named projects.

PenCom is also working on a Pensions 2030 transformation agenda, expected to be finalised around December or January. The industry’s 2026 Annual Pension Week is scheduled for October 26 to 30.

World.title: Zambia Convicts Copper Miner Over Concentrates Declared as Cement
World.content:
Zambia · MINING

Key Facts — Zambia The southern African country depends on copper: copper and cobalt made up 74.3% of export earnings in January 2026, according to the Zambia Statistics Agency, so export duties on the metal matter for public revenue.

— The company Avocado Mining Limited runs a copper processing plant in Kalulushi, Copperbelt Province. Environmental regulator ZEMA has shut the plant over sulphur dioxide pollution and in September 2026 approved a trial run after abatement equipment was installed.

— What happened On 22 September 2026 the company pleaded guilty to 10 counts of attempted smuggling before the Economic and Financial Crimes Court Division of the Kitwe Subordinate Court and was convicted, the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) said on 27 September.

— The cargo In July 2025 it tried to export 13 consignments of copper concentrates, valued for duty purposes at more than K23.9 million (about US$1.27 million), declared as Portland cement on 13 bills of entry. The export duty involved was K4 million (about US$212,000).

— The penalty The court fined the company K100,000 (about US$5,300), payable by 30 September 2026. Separately, it has paid K5.4 million (about US$286,000) in assessed duty and penalties and K1.5 million (about US$79,500) in prosecution costs.

— Why it matters For exporters, clearing agents and investors in Zambian mining, misdeclared cargo now leads to criminal conviction on top of back duties, and the ZRA says it will keep prosecuting.

— Still open Whether the fine is paid by the 30 September deadline, and whether the ZRA brings similar cases against other exporters. ZEMA’s environmental oversight of the plant is a separate matter.

A Zambian court has convicted Avocado Mining Limited after the Copperbelt copper processor pleaded guilty to trying to export copper concentrates declared as Portland cement, the Zambia Revenue Authority said.

The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) has secured the conviction of Avocado Mining Limited, a copper processor based in Kalulushi, for trying to smuggle copper concentrates out of the country as Portland cement. The company pleaded guilty on 22 September 2026 before the Economic and Financial Crimes Court Division of the Kitwe Subordinate Court, the ZRA said in a statement issued in Lusaka on 27 September.

The Lusaka newspaper News Diggers reported that the ZRA and the company had signed a plea agreement in the case. Dollar figures in this article use the 25 September 2026 closing rate of about K18.87 to the US dollar.

What the Avocado Mining smuggling case involved

The case dates to July 2025, when Avocado Mining tried to export 13 consignments of copper concentrates. On 13 bills of entry, the company declared the cargo as Portland cement, according to the ZRA.

The consignments were valued for duty purposes at more than K23.9 million (about US$1.27 million), and the export duty involved amounted to K4 million (about US$212,000). The court convicted the company under Section 149(a), read with Section 155, of the Customs and Excise Act, Chapter 322 of the Laws of Zambia.

The court imposed a K100,000 (about US$5,300) fine, payable by 30 September 2026. The ZRA said Avocado Mining has also paid K5.4 million (about US$286,000) in assessed duty and penalties and reimbursed the State K1.5 million (about US$79,500) in prosecution expenses, and that those payments are separate from the fine.

Why copper misdeclaration matters in Zambia

Copper is the backbone of Zambia’s economy. Traditional exports, copper and cobalt, accounted for 74.3% of total export earnings in January 2026, according to the Zambia Statistics Agency. Declaring copper concentrates as cement takes that cargo outside the duty net.

“Smuggling and deliberate misdeclaration undermine revenue collection and disadvantage compliant businesses,” ZRA Manager for Corporate Communications Oliver Nzala said in the statement. He said the authority would keep using intelligence-led operations, risk-based inspections and post-clearance audits to detect customs offences.

“Where offences are established, ZRA will pursue appropriate enforcement action, including prosecution,” Nzala said.

The company behind the Avocado Mining smuggling plea

Avocado Mining is already known to regulators in Kalulushi, a town in Zambia’s Copperbelt Province. The Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) cited the plant in October 2024 for environmental breaches, including sulphur dioxide emissions without approval, and issued a cease-and-desist order in November 2024, News Diggers reported.

Mines Minister Paul Kabuswe told Parliament in November 2024 that the government had suspended the plant’s operations. ZEMA shut the plant again in November 2025, and in September 2026 approved a trial run after the company installed pollution abatement equipment, according to News Diggers, which has described the firm as Chinese-owned.

The guilty plea in the customs case does not settle ZEMA’s oversight of the plant’s emissions. The two matters run through different regulators.

The wider customs enforcement push

The same ZRA statement reported a second case: on 18 September officers seized two Toyota Land Cruisers at the Kafue checkpoint after finding they had been misclassified. Only K192,000 (about US$10,200) had been paid against a tax bill of more than K2.3 million (about US$122,000).

The Avocado Mining case was heard by the Economic and Financial Crimes Court Division in Kitwe, the country’s main Copperbelt city. The ZRA pursued the matter as a criminal prosecution, not only as an administrative duty claim.

For companies in Zambia’s mining supply chain, the case is a reminder that export documentation must match the actual cargo. The cost of getting it wrong now includes a criminal conviction, not just back duties.

What the conviction means for mining investors

The conviction resolves the criminal charges against Avocado Mining in this case, and the duty, penalties and prosecution costs have already been paid. The K100,000 (about US$5,300) fine itself is still due by 30 September.

The fine is small next to the K5.4 million (about US$286,000) in duty and penalties already paid. The larger cost for the company is a criminal record in a sector where export licences and regulatory goodwill matter.

For international investors, the case shows the ZRA taking customs fraud in the mineral trade to court. That supports governance, and it raises compliance stakes for smaller processors as well as large miners.

What to watch next in Zambia’s copper enforcement

The immediate deadline is 30 September 2026, when the fine falls due. After that, attention turns to whether the ZRA brings similar cases against other exporters.

Zambia’s copper earnings are central to the national budget, and the ZRA has said it will keep using the courts where offences are established.

For readers following the contest over critical minerals, Zambia’s copper is a strategic asset. Tighter customs enforcement is part of a wider effort to capture more value from it, a theme explored in Africa: The New Scramble.

How much was the fine in the Avocado Mining smuggling case? The court imposed a K100,000 (about US$5,300) fine payable by 30 September 2026. Separately, the company has paid K5.4 million (about US$286,000) in assessed duty and penalties and K1.5 million (about US$79,500) in prosecution costs. What was Avocado Mining accused of smuggling? In July 2025 the company tried to export 13 consignments of copper concentrates, valued at more than K23.9 million (about US$1.27 million) for duty purposes, declared as Portland cement on 13 bills of entry.

World.title: First Cargo for Dangote Refinery Docks at Kenya’s Lamu Port
World.content:
Kenya · ENERGY

Key Facts — The country Kenya, East Africa’s main trade gateway, relies on imported fuel. Its only refinery, at Mombasa, closed in 2013, and it has no commercial oil output yet.

— The project Nigerian industrialist Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote , Africa’s richest man, chose Lamu on Kenya’s north coast in July for a second 700,000-barrel-a-day refinery, after his plant near Lagos.

— The price tag Dangote has put the cost at US$15 billion to US$16 billion, Reuters reported. Kenyan officials and media cite Sh2.2 trillion (about US$17.1 billion).

— What happened On Saturday, 26 September, the MV Da Yang Bai He docked at the new Lamu Port with 2,930 tonnes of construction materials and heavy machinery from China, the first cargo for the project.

— What comes next A groundbreaking is scheduled for Wednesday, 30 September. President William Ruto and Dangote are expected, and the Daily Nation reports 14 other heads of state are invited.

— Why it matters to you The refinery is meant to supply eight countries in a region that imports nearly all its refined fuel, so it could shift pump prices, freight and trade flows across East Africa.

— Still open Where the crude comes from, how the build is financed, and whether Kenya takes up a 10% stake. Dangote aims to finish by 2030.

The first cargo for the Dangote refinery in Kenya docked at Lamu Port on 26 September, four days before a groundbreaking that is meant to turn a years-old corridor plan into East Africa’s biggest industrial build.

A China-sourced ship carrying construction equipment for Aliko Dangote’s planned East African refinery docked at Lamu Port on Saturday, 26 September 2026. It is the first physical delivery for a 700,000-barrel-a-day project that Kenya hopes will make Lamu an energy hub for the region.

What arrived at Lamu

The MV Da Yang Bai He berthed at Berth 3 of Lamu Port in Kililana, Lamu West, carrying 2,930 tonnes of construction materials and heavy machinery, the Daily Nation reported. The Star and Capital FM carried the same tonnage.

“The vessel comes from China. This is the first caller vessel,” said Captain William Ruto, managing director of the Kenya Ports Authority, who shares a name with the president. He said the docking showed the port could handle very large ships.

Lamu used to receive three to four ships, he said, and he expects traffic to climb once the refinery project starts. The authority is also planning a dry port at Moyale on the Ethiopian border.

A US$15 billion-plus bet on East African refining

Dangote picked Lamu in July, as The Rio Times reported. The plant would match the capacity of his refinery at Lekki near Lagos, which turned Nigeria from a fuel importer into an exporter.

Dangote has said the Kenyan plant will cost US$15 billion to US$16 billion, according to Reuters. Kenyan officials and local media put the project at Sh2.2 trillion, about US$17.1 billion. Shilling figures are converted at Friday’s closing rate of 128.54 per US dollar.

The company plans to fund it through internal cash flow, bonds and a share sale, and hopes to finish by 2030, Reuters reported. Kenya says it has been offered a 10% stake worth about US$500 million, as part of a 30% block offered with Ethiopia and Rwanda, as The Rio Times reported in August. No stake deal has been announced.

The groundbreaking on 30 September

The ceremony is scheduled for Wednesday, 30 September, at Lamu. President William Ruto and Dangote are expected to attend, and the Daily Nation reports that 14 other heads of state are due.

A groundbreaking starts construction; it does not settle crude supply or financing. Reuters had reported earlier in September that the ceremony would be held at the end of the month, which Kenyan outlets have since dated to 30 September.

The crude supply question

Kenya has proven oil reserves in Turkana but no commercial output yet, although small-scale production is expected later this year, Reuters reported. The country’s only refinery closed in 2013.

Dangote hopes to source 600,000 barrels a day from within East Africa, including South Sudan, Uganda and Kenya. But Uganda’s planned export pipeline runs to Tanzania, and South Sudan’s crude goes out through Sudan.

That could leave the plant “dependent on a volatile international seaborne market,” Nigerian oil and gas lawyer Maximillian Ezeude told Reuters. Dangote vice-president Devakumar Edwin played down the hurdles.

LAPSSET and Kenya’s hub ambitions

Lamu Port anchors the Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia Transport corridor, known as LAPSSET, Kenya’s plan to link landlocked neighbours to the sea. The port has long been underused.

The refinery is designed to supply Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, South Sudan, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. If it runs as planned, it would bring a steady flow of crude tankers in and product cargoes out of Lamu.

Kenya’s hub pitch competes with Tanzanian ports and with Djibouti, where Ethiopia has started a fuel pipeline built with Dangote Group. These are part of the wider contest traced in Africa: The New Scramble.

Who gains and who carries the risk

Kenya gets a flagship project that tests whether LAPSSET can pay off, and Lamu gets construction jobs and port business. Local residents have demanded a share of jobs and contracts, the Daily Nation has reported.

East African fuel buyers could eventually get shorter supply chains than today’s long seaborne imports. The main risk sits with Dangote, his lenders and any governments that take equity, if crude supply or financing falls short.

What to watch

Watch who actually attends on 30 September and whether any crude supply deal, stake agreement or engineering contract is signed there. After that, the next signs are the arrival of major refinery components at Lamu and the terms of any bond or share sale for the Kenyan plant.

Then walk about fifteen minutes to the Museu do Amanhã on Praça Mauá, open 10am to 6pm with last entry at 5pm (it closes on Wednesdays, not Mondays). Admission is R$40 (about US$7.70), half price R$20 (about US$3.90). The museum’s science-meets-sustainability building, designed by Santiago Calatrava, is worth the visit alone. Give yourself ninety minutes inside. Reach Centro on Metrô Line 1 to Uruguaiana station; single journey costs R$7.90 (about US$1.50). From there, the VLT light rail also connects to Praça Mauá. By lunchtime you are well-placed for a casual meal around Praça XV or the renovated Porto Maravilha district, neither of which needs a booking.

OUTDOORS — JARDIM BOTÂNICO A green morning in the gardens Jardim Botânico opens today from 8am to 5pm on Rua Jardim Botânico. Entry is R$40 (about US$7.70) for residents of Brazil and R$80 (about US$15.40) for foreign visitors. Go early, ideally before 10am, to enjoy the palm avenues and orchid house while it is still cool. The gardens are vast, so bring water. It pairs well with a later coffee stop in the leafy Jardim Botânico neighbourhood, not far from Lagoa.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — CENTRO AND LAGOA Laptop-friendly corners for a quiet Monday In Centro, the cafés around Rua do Lavradio are handy for a strong espresso and a laptop hour. It is a historic street lined with antique shops. If you head south to Jardim Botânico, the bakeries and cafés along Rua Pacheco Leão and Rua Lopes Quintas suit a slower working lunch. Both areas are quieter on a Monday — good for video calls in the afternoon.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — SANTA TERESA Cobbles, studios and a slower pace If you prefer a bohemian contrast, take the yellow tram or an inexpensive ride-share up to Santa Teresa. The neighbourhood’s studios and small museums open at varying hours, so check before knocking. Parque Glória Maria, the former Parque das Ruínas, offers a free panoramic terrace over Centro; check its opening days before going. The surrounding streets reward wandering with views. End with a coffee at a small roastery on Rua Almirante Alexandrino. It feels a world away from the beach flatness.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Low-key Monday, mostly local Monday is not Rio’s strongest night, but Lapa’s bars and samba clubs begin to stir after 9pm. The arches area fills with a mixed local and tourist crowd. For something calmer, Botafogo’s Rua Nelson Mandela area has wine bars and casual pizza places that are busy on a Monday. Choose a spot near a Metrô station for an easy ride home. Botafogo has its own station, and Lapa is a short walk from Cinelândia and Glória on Line 1.

ALSO ON TODAY Museu do Amanhã — Praça Mauá — 10am to 6pm, last entry 5pm; open on Mondays, closed on Wednesdays. Parque Lage — Jardim Botânico — 8am to 5pm, free; the café in the mansion courtyard is a good pause. Real Gabinete Português de Leitura — Centro — 10am to 5pm, free; a stunning 19th-century library off Rua Luís de Camões. CCBB evening slot — Centro — open until 8pm; ideal for a late-afternoon visit (closed on Tuesdays). VLT light rail — Centro — links the CCBB area with Praça Mauá and the port district. Porto Maravilha waterfront walk — Centro — free; best before sunset if you want a view of Guanabara Bay.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô Lines 1, 2 and 4 run normally today; a single journey costs R$7.90 (about US$1.50). The VLT light rail also operates through Centro, useful for the port museums.

Expect ride-share surge pricing in the evening rush, especially from Centro to Zona Sul. The winding roads of Santa Teresa are steep and narrow — ask drivers to go slowly.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Try Confeitaria Colombo on Rua Gonçalves Dias in Centro for an old-school Brazilian experience — expect roughly R$50 to R$80 (about US$9.70 to US$15.40) a head. For something quicker near CCBB, the lunch counters around Rua da Candelária and Praça XV serve set menus.

Dinner: In Botafogo, the bistros and pizzerias around Rua Nelson Mandela and Rua Voluntários da Pátria cover most budgets. In Lapa, the bars around the Arcos serve Brazilian comfort food until late.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Keep a compact umbrella handy for later in the week, when rain returns on Thursday. Wear shoes that grip on stone and mosaic pavements.

Most museums and cafés take cards and Pix, so no need for large cash. Booking is rarely required for culture on a Monday, but restaurants near Lapa fill after 9pm.

Stay alert on quiet Centro streets after dark, especially between Uruguaiana and Praça Mauá when the museum crowd thins. Walk on the main lit roads and use a ride-share after 8pm.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Digital nomads tend to gather informally in the cafés of Botafogo and Jardim Botânico — look for laptops and Brazilian Portuguese phrasebooks. Monday afternoons are usually quiet.

Newcomers plug in through neighbourhood WhatsApp groups and the coworking spaces of Botafogo and Centro. Many offer day passes and community events for new members.

08

Game Day

THE WEEK AHEAD

The CBF has just set dates and kick-off times for Brasileirão rounds 31 to 34, including the Vasco–Flamengo derby on Thursday, October 29, at 8pm Brasília time. Check the fixture list before planning an evening out.

If you want to watch matches later in the week, Bar Urca draws a crowd onto the sea wall across the road. In Botafogo, the bars along Rua Voluntários da Pátria put big games on screen.

Brasileirão kick-offs usually fall between 4pm and 9:30pm Brasília time. Confirm times on the CBF website or official club channels.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

The settled Friday session showed a divided mood across Latin America, with some bourses retreating and a couple finishing higher. The board carries every level and change — read it as a cautious regional picture.

Brazilian investors are watching the final trading days of the month for direction from global yields and the US dollar. The board shows those moves without needing repetition here.

For an expat professional, the useful signal is not one index but the pattern: defensive positioning, modest moves, and little conviction either way. That suggests waiting for clearer local catalysts before making allocation calls.

Key Facts What happened — Eight gunmen with assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela at about 9:30 p.m. local time (SAST) on Saturday, killing 17. Around 1 a.m. Sunday, gunmen killed 10 people in Lwandle, near Cape Town.

Around 1 a.m. Sunday, gunmen killed 10 people in Lwandle, near Cape Town. The pattern — South Africa has recorded at least 196 deaths in mass shootings since January 2026, according to a running count by the Daily Maverick newspaper. The country of about 62 million records roughly 60 murders a day.

— South Africa has recorded at least 196 deaths in mass shootings since January 2026, according to a running count by the Daily Maverick newspaper. The country of about 62 million records roughly 60 murders a day. What it means for foreign residents — All three attacks took place in townships, away from the areas where most expats live and work. Police say the violence is usually tied to gangs and organized crime, not random targets.

Two mass shootings in one night have left 27 people dead in South Africa, in a week that has pushed the country’s gun violence to a level that is drawing attention even in a nation accustomed to high crime.

The first attack came on Saturday, September 26, at about 9:30 p.m. South African Standard Time. Eight gunmen armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols stormed a bar in Wedela, a township southwest of Johannesburg. They shot patrons outside, then continued inside. Seventeen people were killed — 13 men and four women — and at least 15 were wounded. Police said the attackers searched some patrons, took their mobile phones, set two vehicles alight and fled in two unidentified cars.

Hours later, around 1 a.m. on Sunday, gunmen killed 10 people at a venue in Lwandle, a township near Cape Town. Five victims died at the scene and five more on the way to hospital. Eleven people were wounded. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects.

A week of three attacks

The two shootings followed an attack on Tuesday, September 23, in KwaMakhutha, south of the coastal city of Durban. Three gunmen fired on a house party there, killing 11 people, including a pregnant woman. Police said several people at the house were known to authorities as part of criminal investigations. The three attacks together killed 38 people in five days.

The Guardian reported that police suspect the Johannesburg-area attack may be linked to a turf war between illegal gold miners, known locally as zama-zamas. Police statements so far list the motive in both weekend attacks as unknown, and no suspect has been arrested in any of the three cases.

The longer picture

Mass shootings are not new in South Africa, but they are becoming more frequent. The Daily Maverick counts at least 196 people killed in such attacks since January 2026. In June, 12 people died when gunmen stormed an informal settlement in Johannesburg, an attack blamed on rivalry between zama-zama groups.

The state has answered past waves of violence with the army. Soldiers moved into Johannesburg crime hotspots in March 2026 to support police. Earlier deployments included the Cape Flats in 2019, the unrest after former president Jacob Zuma’s jailing in 2021, and a wave of truck burnings in 2023. President Cyril Ramaphosa has called crime one of the biggest threats facing the country. Police investigations into all three of this week’s attacks are under way.

What it means for expats and visitors

The three attacks happened in Wedela, Lwandle and KwaMakhutha — townships that lie outside the neighborhoods where most foreign residents live, work and socialize. Police and criminologists describe this kind of violence in South Africa as mostly targeted: tied to gangs, illegal mining networks and disputes between informal businesses, rather than directed at strangers or foreigners.

Practical guidance stays the same as before these events: follow the advice of local authorities, use registered transport at night, and stay informed through official channels. No foreign embassy had changed its travel guidance for South Africa at the time of publication.

What We Could Not Confirm The motive for either weekend attack. Police say both are unknown; the reported gold-mining link is a suspicion, not a finding.

Whether the three attacks of the past week are connected to each other.

Whether the government plans a new army deployment or other emergency measures in response.

Gunmen killed 17 people at a bar in Wedela township near Johannesburg on Saturday night, and 10 more at a venue in Lwandle near Cape Town around 1 a.m. Sunday. At least 26 people were wounded.

How many people have died in the recent attacks?

Have police made any arrests?
