World.title: Why the EU must stand firm on its Common Fisheries Policy
World.content:
The CFP is widely recognized as one of the world’s most ambitious and comprehensive fisheries management frameworks. Following years of overfishing and declining profitability, its reform in 2013 placed sustainability at the heart of fisheries decision-making. Progress has been neither uniform nor easy, but the overall direction has been clear: healthier fish stocks, improved management and a stronger foundation for the long-term viability of the sector.

According to the European Joint Research Centre, in 2003 only 27 percent of fish stocks in the North Atlantic were fished at levels below the maximum sustainable yield. By 2021 that figure stood at 74 percent, demonstrating the positive result of the CFP.

Progress has been neither uniform nor easy, but the overall direction has been clear: healthier fish stocks, improved management and a stronger foundation for the long-term viability of the sector.

The policy has not just contributed to positive outcomes in European waters. Its legally binding commitments to end overfishing, restore fish stocks to sustainable levels, tackle overcapacity and destructive fishing practices, and promote access for small-scale fishers to marine resources also apply to EU fleets operating outside EU waters. Moreover, the policy is fully aligned with SDG14, which is dedicated to the conservation and sustainable use of the ocean’s resources. This is no coincidence, for it reflects a deliberate effort to ensure fisheries management serves both people and nature around the globe over the long term.

Influence far beyond EU waters

The CFP’s significance extends well beyond the EU’s maritime borders. As one of the world’s largest seafood markets and fishing powers, the EU exerts considerable influence over global fisheries governance. Through its Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements with non-EU countries, participation in regional fisheries management organizations and market requirements for imported seafood, the EU has helped promote higher standards on sustainability, transparency and labor rights.

Oceana / Ángeles Sáez

At a time of geopolitical uncertainty, biodiversity loss and mounting pressure on marine resources, the EU’s leadership in ocean governance is more important than ever. International partners look to the EU as a credible advocate for science-based management that can deliver environmental, social and economic benefits simultaneously. Thus any move to weaken the EU’s own commitments would send a troubling signal globally.

World.title: Europe’s divided conservatives launch 2029 plan to beat far right
World.content:
“The main polarization across the continent in many national elections, and certainly in the European election 2029 … will be the anti-European populists against the EPP parties,” said EPP vice-chair and Romanian prime minister nominee Siegfried Mureșan.

Anything beyond the “battle” between EPP and the far right “will be of secondary importance,” echoed the conservative group’s spokesperson Pedro López de Pablo. “Because they are not in government, they can promise the earth. Faced with that kind of rhetoric, we need to think of which alternatives we can offer to the people.”

Siegfried Mureșan participates in a meeting in Brussels on June 26, 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

With the European Parliament not yet halfway through its current term, the task force marks an unusually early start to the EPP’s 2029 election preparations — and underscores the urgency party leaders feel as far-right parties gain ground across the bloc.

Led by Spanish MEP Esteban González Pons, the task force will help draft the party’s final electoral program. Talks are due to start at an October retreat in Sicily and continue through next spring’s EPP congress in Rome.

EPP lawmakers are already wrestling with the choice ahead.

“This is the political history, the historical dilemma EPP needs to decide — it needs to be clear and it needs be truthful for the voters, are we center right or are we another right-wing party?” said Finnish EPP lawmaker Sirpa Pietikäinen.

World.title: EU is drawing up membership action plans for most promising candidates
World.content:
The roadmaps will make clearer exactly what’s expected of each candidate country, one of the officials said, as well as create obligations for current members, which need to give their blessing for the process to go ahead. The plans also set rough dates for when groups of reforms, known as negotiating “clusters,” will be formally completed — major milestones on the path to membership.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged targeted support for the candidate countries “that have made most progress” during her State of the Union speech earlier in September.

However, other candidate countries at an earlier stage in the process, like Kosovo, North Macedonia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina would not be offered the roadmaps at this stage, the officials confirmed. Nor would Georgia, Turkey or Serbia, which have seen their applications grind to a halt over concerns about democratic and judicial backsliding.

A spokesperson for the Commission confirmed that the new roadmaps “will provide a pathway toward the conclusion of the accession negotiations. They will set out a clear priority list: timelines and deliverables to help the most advanced candidates complete the necessary reforms.”

‘Geopolitical imperative’

EU leaders are increasingly looking to other pro-trade democracies, particularly in their neighborhood, amid tensions with partners like the U.S., hostile practices from China and threats from Russia. Officials are concerned that joining the EU takes too long, exposing would-be new members to disillusionment or pressure from rivals not to pursue membership.

The move comes as the EU’s “pre-enlargement” policies undergo a separate overhaul. Candidate countries need to be offered a better path toward “gradual integration” into the bloc, officials believe, one that would use economic benefits and access to joint projects to reward them for progress. That policy review, led by von der Leyen’s close adviser Alexandre Adam, is to be presented to top officials Oct. 6; it is designed to keep them on the path toward the EU while their applications unfold.

World.title: Independent wins Kraków election first round ahead of Tusk-backed candidate
World.content:
For Gibała, Sunday’s result gives him another shot at winning an office he came within a few thousand votes of securing in 2024, when he lost to Miszalski.

Miszalski subsequently faced mounting local opposition, including over Kraków’s clean-transport zone, before being recalled. Opposition parties, including Law and Justice (PiS) and parties on the far right, presented that result as evidence of weakening support for Tusk’s government ahead of the fall 2027 general election. A similar referendum may be held in the capital Warsaw, targeting Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, also from Tusk’s party.

Earlier statements from parties opposed to Tusk’s coalition indicated some could back Gibała against Piątkowska in the second round.

Turnout Sunday was 43.5%.

This article has been updated.

World.title: Britain to keep tariffs on Chinese EVs ‘under review,’ UK business chief says
World.content:
EU capitals are currently considering whether U.K. auto exports should qualify for preferential treatment under the Buy European program, as Brussels moves to protect its member economies from U.S. tariffs, China’s manufacturing might and an influx of cheap EVs subsidized by Beijing.

European Union lawmakers and officials are preparing new legislation to deny overseas manufacturers access to subsidies, tax incentives and public procurement deals. The bloc slapped double-digit tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024.

But Reynolds said the U.K. government’s calculation on whether to impose tariffs differed from that of the EU.

“We are an export-orientated sector. So clearly, you shouldn’t do anything that risks your export markets, and you always have to take heed of retaliatory action if you put tariffs in place,” he said Sunday, calling the U.K.’s position on Chinese EVs “finely balanced.”

Cutting the U.K. out of Brussels’ new industrial program “wouldn’t be to the benefit of Europe,” Reynolds added.

The Made in Europe push is supposed to be “about greater resilience, greater autonomy for European industry in the face of very significant pressures from both the U.S. and China,” Reynolds added. “Now, if that is the objective, it stands to reason that the U.K., that’s the second-biggest economy in Europe, should be a part of that.”

World.title: Trump’s threat to ban diesel exports a ‘significant concern’ for UK
World.content:
The U.K. receives around one-sixth of its diesel from the U.S. and would be one of the countries most exposed to an export ban. However, Reynolds cautioned that it is important to “make a distinction between the statements and what is actually being proposed by the U.S.”

Donald Trump has said he is in favor of proposals to bar American diesel exports against a backdrop of high prices for American drivers and farmers, and with midterm elections looming. A 90-day ban has been considered, along with more limited voluntary export restrictions.

“Clearly something like that … would be a significant concern to the U.K,” Reynolds said when asked about the prospect of a full ban. “Our resilience comes from a diverse supply in a whole range of areas and fuel is no different to that.”

Reynolds is the latest senior European politician to voice concern over potential diesel export restrictions. On Thursday French President Emmanuel Macron said he had urged Trump against it, warning it would be a bad idea “not just for the rest of the world, but for the U.S. economy as well.”

World.title: At least 62 killed after heavy rain and flooding in northern India, officials say
World.content:
At least 62 people have been killed after days of heavy rain and flooding in northern India’s Uttar Pradesh state, officials said on Monday.

 

The state government said 46 people were injured and more than 1,000 houses were damaged after three days of heavy rainfall caused flooding in several districts.

Schools were closed in parts of the state on Monday, including the capital Lucknow, while rescue teams moved people from flooded areas to safer locations.

Residents were advised to avoid unnecessary travel through waterlogged areas and stay away from fast-flowing rivers, streams and drains.

Rainfall was expected to ease from Monday as a weather system over the Bay of Bengal weakened, said Atul Kumar Singh, a senior scientist at the Regional Meteorological Centre in Lucknow.

Light rain could continue in eastern and western parts of the state through Tuesday, he said.

Residents of a low-lying neighbourhood watch as floodwaters submerge their area following heavy rains in Kanpur, 22 September, 2026 AP Photo

Flooding also affected the eastern state of Odisha, where more than 75,000 people were evacuated to safer areas, officials said.

In neighbouring Nepal, 21 people died in weather-related incidents between Thursday and Sunday, the country's disaster management agency said.

Five people remained missing and five others were injured, while floods and landslides damaged 194 houses.

Nepal is recovering from devastating August floods that killed more than 1,400 people and left nearly 6,000 missing.

World.title: Serbia's President Aleksandar Vučić resigns to run for prime minister in snap elections
World.content:
Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vučić resigned on Sunday to pursue a bid to become prime minister in upcoming snap parliamentary elections that will test his rule in the Balkan country, which was rattled by nearly two years of protests.

 

Vučić’s second presidential term would otherwise end in May next year. He is banned by the Serbian Constitution from seeking a third term and said he was resigning to lead his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party in the 25 October vote.

The governing populists face a major challenge at the ballot box from a youth-backed movement that led protests triggered by the 1 November 2024 train station canopy collapse in the northern city of Novi Said that killed 16 people.

University students demanded accountability for the tragedy. Their struggle for justice and against corruption has grown into a strong movement that will attempt to oust Vučić’s government after 14 years in power.

Vučić himself has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years.

“I am resigning the duty of the President of the Republic,” Vučić said, reading the text of his resignation.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić signing his resignation in Belgrade, 27 September, 2026 Serbian presidential press office via AP/Serbian presidential press office via AP

Tensions rising ahead of high-stakes election

The ballot in October will be held against a backdrop of high political tensions as Vučić’s populists seek to remain in office despite widespread popular discontent.

His decision to run for prime minister is seen as a carefully planned manoeuvre to retain a top positio, and to boost his party’s chances against the student movement.

Before signing his resignation, Vučić briefly addressed his supporters outside the presidency building in Belgrade.

He said “tonight is a very special occasion for me, my last evening in this beautiful building.”

“But I look to the future with joy, new victories await us,” he told the crowd as they chanted his name. “Let’s beat them (opponents) more convincingly than ever before.”

People welcome a group of university students at the end of their cycling tour of Serbia ahead of a snap election next month, 26 September, 2026 AP Photo

Vučić in recent weeks has toured the country tirelessly, opening new roads, offering assistance money and cheaper medicines and visiting voters in their homes. More recently, Vučić was filmed driving in his brother’s car to some of the events.

The prime minister in Serbia is formally more powerful than the president. But Vučić still took a dominant role during his two five-year terms, sometimes presiding over government sessions and routinely announcing all important decisions and plans.

The Independent Bureau for Social Research (BIRODI) has filed a complaint alleging that Vučić has abused a public institution as president to promote his party, which he has dismissed.

There has been no response from the anti-corruption authorities that are under government control.

Presidential vote to be held later

After Vučić’s resignation, the acting president will be close ally and former prime minister, Ana Brnabić, who is the outgoing speaker of Serbia’s 250-member Parliament.

Vučić said the first round of the early presidential election must be held by the end of this year because of a 90-day deadline.

Vučić and his party have been accused of rampant corruption, organised crime links and a clampdown on democratic freedoms, including the critical media.

People fill the streets near the train station before observing 16 minutes of silence for the victims of the Novi Sad disaster, 1 November, 2025 AP Photo

The SNS party has gradually taken control over all state institutions since coming to power in 2012, while denying abuse of office and repeatedly pledging to fight graft.

The student-backed election list includes little-known experts, professors, teachers, athletes and other individuals from all walks of life.

Groups of students have been touring the country on bicycles as part of their campaign calling for the rule of law and an end to corruption.

Analysts say the student group and Vučić are polling close, heralding a tight race and a referendum-like atmosphere.

Also running are Vučić’s allies, the Socialist Party, a pro-EU opposition alliance and several smaller groups.

Vučić said that as of Monday, he will be “everywhere in Serbia to listen to the people.” While praising his government's achievements, Vučić contended that “I have made mistakes but I have worked diligently like hardly anyone in this position.”

Vučić also said he had pardoned 49 people before leaving the office, including 23 who have been prosecuted for alleged offences during the protests. They include a group of anti-government activists who fled Serbia after being accused of anti-state activities.

Authorities have pushed hard against protesters with police violence and detentions as Vučić, without offering evidence, accused his opponents and critical media of intending to “destroy the state” under unspecified foreign influence.

He told Serbia’s state-run RTS Television earlier on Sunday that foreign powers and unidentified people in the country plan to stir unrest on election night.

Serbia’s efforts to join the European Union have stalled under Vučić because of democratic backsliding and a refusal to join sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.

World.title: The top 10 countries for tourism have just been named – and six are in Europe
World.content:
The 2026 edition of the World Economic Forum’s Travel & Tourism Development Index (TTDI) has just been published, with Europe dominating the top 10.

 

The index looks at factors and policies that enable sustainable and resilient development in the travel and tourism space, under broad pillars like air transport structure, price competitiveness and safety and security.

Within these pillars, things like hotel prices, visa requirements, efficiency of public transport, number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites and how tourism is distributed geographically are assessed.

While Japan took the top spot overall, Spain came in third, followed by France (fourth), Germany (sixth), the UK (seventh), Switzerland (ninth) and Italy (10th).

“The latest Travel & Tourism Development Index shows that the enabling conditions for travel and tourism are at their strongest since the pandemic, with 92% of economies improving since 2024,” Ramya Krishnaswamy, head of experience economy and cities at World Economic Forum, said.

“The next chapter is not simply about attracting more visitors, but it is going to be about creating greater value by investing in people, infrastructure and stronger public-private collaboration so tourism delivers lasting benefits for communities, businesses and destinations.”

The top 10 countries for travel and tourism

Japan USA Spain Australia France Germany UK China Switzerland Italy

Looking more closely at Japan, the report notes that the country has extended its visitor base and encouraged travel beyond major tourism centres, thereby reducing concentration risk while still welcoming record numbers of travellers.

WEF also shared the fastest improvers, with the strongest overall being Albania, with a score increasing by 7% over the past two years.

The report notes that the country has “benefitted from offering visitors a more affordable alternative to neighbouring destinations while still providing a compelling tourism experience”.

Its score went up thanks to improvements in air transport infrastructure and tourist services.

The fastest improvers on the index

World.title: How successful is Europe at closing the gender gap between men and women?
World.content:
It is widely known that a gap remains between men and women in the world, not only when it comes to equal pay, but also to access to the labour market, education and health. This difference in opportunities is referred to as the gender gap.

 

Europe has regained its position as the global leader in closing this divide, according to new data from the World Economic Forum (WEF), which has measured this gap since 2006.

The continent closed 75.7% of its overall gender gap this year. This leaves a 24.3% gap to achieve equal representation. It narrowly overtook North America, which ranked first last year.

Since 2006, Europe's gender parity has improved by 7 percentage points. It is not expected to reach full parity — meaning there is no difference in the opportunities for men and women, or a zero percent gender gap — in 70 years.

The report looked at education, health, economic participation and politics. Europe is the champion in the latter category with a score of 37%. It is closely followed by Latin America and the Caribbean (34.2%). Other regions trail behind by ten percentage points or more.

Europe's performance per subindex

Europe continues to maintain near parity in the categories of Educational Attainment (99.5%) and Health and Survival (96.9%). Still, it is in third and fourth place in these indexes compared to other regions.

When it comes to Economic Participation and Opportunity, it ranks in fifth position (69.5%), almost eight percentage points below the table's leader, North America (77.1%).

Uneven growth

Of all regions in the world, Europe accounts for the most countries in the top ten. "Since the index was launched in 2006, Europe has occupied 69% of all top 10," the WEF report noted. "Continuing the trend established in prior editions, this year’s top performers include seven European economies."

These countries are Iceland, Finland, Norway and Sweden (which have featured in every top ten for the past two decades), as well as the United Kingdom, Germany and Ireland.

Only Iceland has closed more than 90% of the gender gap (93%).

"Iceland has demonstrated a consistently positive trajectory towards gender parity over the past two decades, remaining in the global top 10 throughout the period and holding the top position since the 2009 edition," the WEF report read.

It scores particularly well when it comes to Political Empowerment (95.4%). This is driven by the country's intentional public policies promoting gender balance and its history of female representation in top positions of power: Iceland was the first country in the world to democratically elect a woman, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, as president in 1980.

Despite Europe's top position, a deep divide remains within the continent. The countries topping the region’s ranking are mainly located in Northern Europe, while many of the states trailing behind are located in the East.

The bottom three performers, Türkiye (0.649%), Romania (0.698%) and Hungary (0.707%), stand more than 20 percentage points below Iceland.

In Romania, this low score is largely due to its low score in the Political Empowerment category (0.145%), placing it in 104th place for this category. This is driven by a lack of mandatory quotas and closed internal party systems.

This category is also the driving factor for Hungary's low score (0.132% in Political Empowerment). It has no women in ministerial positions, giving it a score of 0% in this particular category of this subindex.

The European Union wants to close the broader gender gap through a range of policies and measures, ranging from EU Pay Transparency Rules requiring companies to share information on salaries in a bid to bring down the pay gap, to rules on parental leave and flexible working hours to help divide care and work duties.

World.title: UK counter-terrorism police probe Iran link to suspected bomb plot at RAF base
World.content:
Counter-terrorism police in the UK are investigating whether there is a link to Iran after police found explosives on three vans near an RAF base in Gloucestershire on Sunday.

 

Speaking to the BBC on Monday morning, the Defence Secretary Wes Streeting cautioned that it would be "irresponsible to speculate."

"As soon as we can keep the public informed, we will. I would just ask people for a bit of forbearance to give the police and security services the time and space to do their job," he said.

Since March, RAF Fairford has been used by the US military to launch air strikes on Iran as the war in the Middle East rumbles on.

In July, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it was aware that the base was being used by US bombers and warned the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces.”

Armed officers detained a group of five men on Sunday after a call to emergency services about three "suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the air base," London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement.

US President Donald Trump told reporters they had been "looking to do big damage" at the base in southwest England.

"We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding the US and UK had been working together on the incident.

A local resident who said it was known locally that the base was on lockdown due to a "terror threat" alerted emergency services after seeing three vans blocking the road and a large group of men wearing hoods and balaclavas.

She told the PA news agency she found it "astonishing" it had been effectively down to a "plucky amateur" spotting unusual activity to raise the alarm.

Some 85 households in the nearby village of Whelford were advised to evacuate and army bomb disposal experts called in to examine three large white vans stopped on a rural road.

Incident 'contained'

"Counter Terrorism Policing can now confirm they are leading an investigation into an incident which took place overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire," the Met statement added.

Broadcast aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot moving around the vans, two of which had their rear doors open.

Police believed the incident had been "contained" and a 400 metre cordon had been put in place.

Armed officers could be seen guarding the entrance to the base.

Police officers guard a road leading to RAF Fairford, 28 September, 2026 AP Photo

In March, then prime minister Keir Starmer granted permission for "defensive" US action against Iranian missile sites from two UK bases including Fairford.

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being kept updated on the incident, a government spokesperson said.

Burnham, who was in the northwestern city of Liverpool along with other senior ministers for his Labour Party's annual conference, thanked the police, armed forces and residents who had been asked to leave their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out."

Attacks by proxies

Fairford is the UK base of the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US air force administrative support wing, which said in a statement that no US air force personnel had been involved in the incident.

"The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," it said.

"We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities," it added.

US B1 bombers seen at RAF Fairford, 27 September, 2026 AP Photo

The incident comes amid concerns about the actions of hostile foreign states.

Interior Minister Shabana Mahmood has accused Iran and Russia of using proxies to carry out criminal activities on their behalf on UK territory.

Earlier this month, reports said British military sites had been targeted by drones more than 300 times over the past year.

World.title: MTV VMA 2026: Taylor Swift makes history again as female artist take top honours
World.content:
Taylor Swift has broken yet another record by becoming the most-awarded artist in MTV VMA history.

 

The mega popstar picked up the inaugural Artist Director Honors on Sunday night in recognition of artists "whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling."

“I got to start making music videos and being a part of music videos 20 years ago,” Swift said in her speech, adding that she's been involved in making roughly 60 music videos, 18 of which she wrote and directed.

Swift also debuted the music video she directed for her latest song 'Patient Zero' which stars actors Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson.

Swift, who was previously tied with Beyoncé for titles with 30 VMAs each, also went home with the top prize of the night - video of the year - for 'The Fate of Ophelia' from her album 'The Life of a Showgirl.'

Taylor Swift and actor Dakota Johnson pick up the MTV VMA Artist Director Honor at the MTV Video Music Awards, 27 Sep, 2026 AP Photo/Chris Pizzello

Madonna wins big

The other major winner of the night was Madonna who kicked off the proceedings by performing her single 'Bring Your Love' alongside Sabrina Carpenter. The pair won the award for best collaboration for the song.

If her aim was to bring the dance floor to the award show stage, Madonna did exactly that in her opening number — and then some, when Charli xcx emerged from a club bathroom to perform their reworked version of 'Danceteria.' Around them? A trove of dancers and various famous friends, including actor Debi Mazar, Sombr and Julia Garner.

Madonna also won the coveted artist of the year award and completed her hat-trick with the best dance honour.

“First of all, I would like to thank my fingers because I can always count on them,” she said on collecting the artist of the year trophy.

Dolly dedication

Picking up the award, Swift heaped praise on the late, great country singer Dolly Parton whom she described as the "ultimate showgirl."

Parton, whose soaring vibrato vocals, emotive songwriting and sparkling costumes defined her rise from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to the height of stardom and acclaim, died in Nashville of cancer last month. She was 80.

“I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time," Swift said.

Other stars also paid tribute to Parton with a string of performances and covers of her most well known tracks. Kacey Musgraves sang 'I Will Always Love You' while Raye delivered a medley of her throwback soul, including 'I Will Overcome' and 'Where Is My Husband!'

British singer RAYE, centre sings 'Where is my husband!' at the MTV Video Music Awards, Sun 27 September, Los Angeles . AP Photo/Chris Pizzello

US Urban country star Shaboozey performs during the MTV Video Music Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. AP Photo/Chris Pizzello

Bruno Mars slowed things down with 'Dance With Me.' Shaboozey launched into his saloon single 'Cowgirl,' before being joined by Gunna for some hybrid country-rap with their crossover track, 'High Noon.'

Night of Nirvana

One of the most coveted prizes, the Video Vanguard Award, went to legendary grunge band, Nirvana.

The honour was presented to surviving members Krist Novoselic, Dave Grohl and Pat Smear. Frontman Kurt Cobain died in 1994.

“They were completely original and always fearless at a time when the status quo kind of got to the point of being formulaic,” Public Enemy rapper Chuck D said when presenting the award.

“Kurt was one of one,” Novoselic said in their acceptance speech, adding that the band never imagined its sound and aesthetic would resonate with so many people. He said the music continues to endure because people are still hungry for “something real, something uncompromising” and a message that “it’s just OK to come as you are.”

World.title: Death toll in South Africa bar shooting rises to 18, police say
World.content:
The death toll from a mass shooting at a South African tavern has risen to 18 after one person died in hospital, police said on Monday, announcing at least two of the dead were Lesotho nationals.

 

The shooting west of Johannesburg late on Saturday was part of a bloody weekend in the crime-weary country, with 10 people killed in another mass shooting in Cape Town on Sunday.

Eight gunmen armed with assault rifles stormed the bar in the semi-rural township of Wedela, around 80 kilometres from central Johannesburg, killing 13 men and four women, police said.

"One more victim has died in hospital, bringing the total number of deceased to 18," they said.

"Only four of the deceased have been identified, two South Africans and two Lesotho nationals."

Forensic officers and the army at the scene of a mass shooting at a bar in Wedela township, 27 September, 2026 AP Photo

The motive for the attack was not clear but the area is reportedly gripped by rivalry between gangs involved in illicit mining for gold.

Thousands of unregistered miners operate in abandoned mining shafts in South Africa, many coming from across southern Africa, including the kingdom of Lesotho which is within South Africa.

The sector has been linked to organised crime, assassinations and other illegal activities.

In a separate shooting at the weekend, gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more at an entertainment venue in a township outside Cape Town early on Sunday.

South Africa is awash with legal and illegal firearms, and shootings are common, often fuelled by gang rivalry, extortion and competition between informal businesses.

The country of around 62 million people has one of the world's highest murder rates, with about 60 people killed each day.

World.title: Adieu, dear listeners!
World.content:
This week is the final Sound Kitchen program, and it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listeners Corner’s” with Paul Myers, plus a special musical choice from me to you. Just click the “Play” button above to join the feast!

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October, and today’s show is our last meal together. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 7 February: I asked you a question about the 68th annual Grammy Awards that took place on 1 February. You were to re-read our article “French DJ wins Grammy for Lady Gaga remix” and send in the answer to this question: Which six artists were given “Lifetime Achievement” awards?

The answer is, to quote our article: “On Saturday evening, Nigeria's Fela Kuti was posthumously awarded a lifetime achievement award, becoming the first African artist to receive the distinction.

The king of Afrobeat was one of several artists to receive the award, including Cher, Whitney Houston, Carlos Santana, Paul Simon and Chaka Khan.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question, suggested by RFI Listeners Club member Alan Holder from the English Isle of Wight. Alan’s question was: “What would be your ideal gift from your best friend or spouse? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Mohamed Elsayed Abd Elraheim from Elsharkya, Egypt. Mohamed Elsayed is also this week’s bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club members Hans Verner Lollike from Hedehusene, Denmark; Helmut Matt from Herbolzheim, Germany; Kashif Khalil from Faisalabad, Pakistan, and last but not least, gentle Debashis Gope from West Bengal, India.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 14 February: That week, I asked you a question about the Benin Bronzes, the trove of Nigerian sculptures and artifacts that were looted by colonial powers.

One of the most well-known organizations working for the return of these works is in Nigeria: it’s the National Commission for Museums and Monuments – the NCMM- which requested the return of bronzes from Britain that were looted from the Kingdom of Benin during the British Benin Expedition of 1897. Some of the sculptures date to the fourteenth century, but the bulk of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

And that week, the NCMM had a win, as my good colleague Melissa Chemam noted in her article: “Cambridge University museum set to return Benin bronzes to Nigeria”.

You were to re-read Melissa’s article and give the details of the artefacts to be returned. What did Melissa name in her article about the Benin Kingdom artworks that went home to Nigeria?

The answer is, to quote Melissa: “Among the returned bronzes that will travel in the coming months are wood and ivory sculptures, as well as commemorative heads of King Oba and Queen Mother Lyoba Idia.

The term ‘Benin bronzes’ refers to objects crafted from brass and ivory as well as bronze, which were seized during the colonial-era military expedition.”

The bonus question you answered that week was: “What do you know after all these years? What have you found are important life truths?

The winners are: Faithful RFI Listeners Club member Jayanta Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Jayanta is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club member Nasyr Muhammad from Katsina State in Nigeria, as well as RFI English listeners M. Ganesan from Goa, India, and three listeners from Bangladesh: Rafiq ul Islam from Naogaon, as well as Abdul Mannan and Mahfuza Akhter, both from Chapainawabganj.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Minor Swing” by Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grapelli, performed by the composers with Le Quintette Hot Club de France; "Water No Get Enemy" by Fela Kuti, performed by Fela Kuti and Africa ’70; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer; “L'hymne à l'amour” by Edith Piaf and Marguerite Monnot, sung by Edith Piaf, and “I Wish You Love” by Charles Trenet and Léo Chauliac, performed by Laufey with the Iceland Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hugh Brant.

With much affection from The Sound Kitchen team – Erwan Rome, Paul Myers, and yours truly, Susan Owensby - fare thee well!

World.title: India: LPU suspends classes after violent protests over alleged campus rape
World.content:
Skip next section Lovely Professional University protest: Classes suspended after violence during protests over suspected assault

Punjab's Lovely Professional University (LPU) has suspended classes starting Monday and postponed mid-term examinations after a protest over an alleged rape turned violent on Sunday with protesters clashing with the police and vandalism being reported.

The private university located in the city of Phagwara witnessed massive student unrest after claims spread on social media that a female university student was allegedly raped within the campus premises by an outsider and had later died by suicide.

The protests grew to be violent when the protesters clashed with the police, pelted stones at the security personnel, smashed windows and set fire to some objects within the university complex, reports said.

Some students later claimed in social media posts that the vandals were not students, but outsiders.

Heavy police deployment

The university has suspended regular classes for 10 days, news agency ANI cited a statement from LPU as saying.

The statement said students could travel to their hometowns during the suspension of classes and advised those who stay back to remain in their hostels or places of accommodation and avoid any unnecessary movement. The statement also called on students to avoid involvement in the unrest.

Over 2,000 police personnel were deployed to ensure security on the campus, reports quoted the Additional Director General of Police Fayaz Farooqui as saying.

The protesters also blocked the national highway between Jalandhar and Phagwara highway early Sunday, leading to traffic disruptions.

On Monday, police said that the situation had been brought under control and traffic movement on the highway had been restored.

Claims of rape remain unverified

Meanwhile, the police are yet to confirm whether a student was raped within LPU's campus. They have launched an investigation to examine the facts of the incident.

Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann has taken note of the situation and has directed the Director General of Police to visit the campus, reports said on Monday.

Meanwhile, the Punjab State Women Commision is seeking a detailed report on the alleged rape, ANi reported.

What has LPU said?

The LPU has denied that the alleged rape took place, calling the claims "false, baseless and fabricated rumors".

The university on Sunday posted a video with three female students who it said reside in the girls' hostel room where the alleged incident is claimed to have taken place.

The video purportedly shows the girls denying that there had been a rape, with one of them asking the police to stop visiting the room repeatedly.

However, media reports on Monday said that the same girls later appear in a separate purported video, claiming that they were instructed on what to say in the statement. They then allegedly claim that their clips were "trimmed" and used without their consent.

World.title: Venezuelans demand opposition leader Machado's return
World.content:
Hundreds of people held rallies in Venezuela demanding the safe return of Maria Corina Machado, and fair elections.

Supporters of Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado held a rally on Sunday demanding her safe return and for fair presidential elections in Venezuela.

Her supporters joined the rally wearing sky-blue shirts which is the color of Machado's Vente Venezuela party and rode motorcycles through the streets in Caracas.

Similar rallies were held in several state capitals including Valencia, Maracaibo and Merida.

"This is not a matter of parties or politics," said Flavio Valentini, a Vente Venezuela activist in Caracas who grabbed a megaphone and addressed the crowd.

Machado's supporters rode motocycles through streets as they demanded a free and fair election in Venezuela Image: Juan Carlos Hernandez/REUTERS

"This is a movement for the people and by the people."

The demonstrators demanded a clear timeline for presidential elections in 2027 and chanted slogans including "Freedom, freedom!"

Machado's return from exile

For the past nine months, Machado has been living in exile. Last year in December, Machado left for Oslo to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Since then she has tried returning to Venezuela multiple times.

Machado, who is currently in Panama, has so far made seven unsuccessful attempts to return, according to media reports.

Activists allege the Venezuelan government keeps blocking her return, however, Venezuelan authorities deny the claim.

Venezuelans want elections — but when will they get them? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Courts had barred Machado from running in elections under the government of President Nicolás Maduro. But her stand-in candidate is widely believed to have won the election.

Maduro refuted the election results. After his disputed victory, his government led a crackdown against dissidents who protested the official results, forcing Machado and dozens of opposition leaders to flee.

The US captured Maduro in January. But Machado has been unable to return to Venezuela since then.

Currently, the country is being led by acting President Delcy Rodríguez, who has worked closely with Washington.

"We hope this transition process leads us to presidential elections and consolidates a free, democratic country that will be the main ally of the United States," said Anthony Romero, a leader for Vente Venezuela in the nation's capital.

World.title: Germany news: Berlin's Left files complaint against Dobrindt
World.content:
Skip next section NRW leader calls for 'new chapter' in German-Turkey ties

The delegation accompanying Wüst includes a high-profile business group Image: Rolf Vennenbernd/dpa/picture alliance

Hendrik Wüst, the conservative leader of the state of North-Rhine Westphalia (NRW), has kicked off a three-day trip to Turkey to mark the 65th anniversary of the 1961 agreement allowing "guest workers" from Turkey to work in West Germany.

Wüst, whom many see as a potential successor to beleaguered Chancellor Friedrich Merz, called for a "new chapter" in relations with Turkey as he began his visit, accompanied by a large delegation.

Wüst noted that one-third of the some 3 million people of Turkish origin or ancestry in Germany live in its most-populous state of NRW, saying: "They are naturally part of our state."

On Monday, Wüst is due to visit a plant in the Turkish capital, Ankara, that belongs to the company Henkel, which is based in Düsseldorf, the capital of NRW.

He then plans to visit the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, the founder of modern Turkey, while a meeting with Turkish business figures is scheduled for the evening.

On Tuesday, Wüst will hold political talks in the capital before traveling on to Turkey's largest city, Istanbul, where a business conference is on the agenda.

Tuesday will also see the presentation of a prize for tolerance and reconciliation between cultures to former Germany football captain Ilkay Gundogan.

The 51-year-old Wüst is the first premier of the state to make an official visit to Turkey.

World.title: What would Francis of Assisi make of his fame today?
World.content:
The Catholic saint renounced wealth and fame to become a mendicant friar. Yet over history, his teachings and life have inspired popes, Dante, and even Mussolini.

One could safely say that Francis of Assisi's life — and afterlife — is defined by paradox.

He embraced poverty, yet lies entombed today in a grand basilica with frescoes by renowned medieval artists in his native Assisi in central Italy.

He advocated meekness, yet hundreds of thousands venerated his remains when they went on public display earlier this year to commemorate 800 years since his death on October 3, 1226.

Thousands came to venerate the saint's remains earlier this year, amid wide media coverage Image: Emanuela Bianconi/IPA/ZUMA/picture alliance

So, why has this Catholic saint inspired papal encyclicals, ecological activism, global pet‑blessing rituals — and even the propaganda of former Italian fascist leader Benito Mussolini?

And what might Francis make of this fame that he'd shunned while alive?

From riches to rags

Born in Assisi — a hill town in central Italy — in 1181 or 1182, he was first named Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone. But his father, a cloth merchant with trade links to France, renamed him Francesco.

Early Franciscan hagiographers — medieval writers who recorded his life and shaped how later generations understood him — describe him as a lively, sociable young man who enjoyed singing, parties and the privileges of wealth.

The magnificent interior of the Basilica of St Francis of Assisi Image: Sepp Spiegl/IMAGO

However, he didn't want to join his father's trade; he dreamed of becoming a knight.

In 1202, Francis joined Assisi's forces in a battle against neighboring Perugia. He was captured, spent a year in prison, and returned home shaken and ill. This, and a series of subsequent events, precipitated a slow shift in his outlook.

One took place at the small, ruined Church of San Damiano outside Assisi, where Francis believed he heard Jesus Christ calling on him to "rebuild my church." Taking it literally, he began repairing local chapels. And when he ran out of money, he sold cloth from his father's shop, which enraged the latter and led to a dramatic episode in Assisi's town square.

Norberto Proietti's 'The Return of St Francis' captures the saint returning as a dejected knight after his imprisonment in Perugia Image: Gabriele Thielmann/imageBROKER/IMAGO

Before the bishop and gathered townspeople, Francis stripped off his fine clothes, renouncing his father, his inheritance and all material comforts. He committed himself to a life of poverty, humility, care for the poor and sick, and a deep kinship with nature.

A relatable saint

As a wandering preacher, he drew followers and eventually founded the Order of Friars Minor, known today as the Franciscans.

Widely considered the first saint to have miraculously received the stigmata — physical wounds resembling those on the crucified body of Jesus Christ — Francis was canonized by Pope Gregory IX on July 16, 1228. This unusually swift recognition amplified his fame beyond Assisi.

In the following centuries, Francis became one of the most frequently depicted saints in Western art, inspiring works from Dante's "Divine Comedy" to films, children's books, and even a 1980 Marvel comic.

Cover of the 1980 Marvel comic on Francis' life Image: Marvel Comics Group

"Most saints are seen as unapproachable or unrelatable, but Francis' story of lifelong conversion and the desire to be in a positive relationship with others, God and the rest of creation speaks to people across time and cultures," theologian and former Franciscan friar Daniel P. Horan tells DW.

According to cultural historian Amanda Minervini, this broad appeal is also what made Francis so adaptable across eras: "In Francis, there seems to be something for everyone: the pacifist, the ascetic, the mason, the environmentalist, the minimalist, the lover of animals also loved by animals, the diplomat, the mystic, the radical, the performer, and even the model of a different kind of masculinity," they tell DW.

Painting depicting Francis receiving the stigmata — the wounds of the crucified Jesus Christ Image: Heritage Images/IMAGO

Pacifist mascot of a fascist regime

His image has been reconstructed throughout history, points out Minervini, who has explored in their research one particularly jarring example: Francis' political appropriation by Benito Mussolini's fascist regime.

In their recent book, "St. Francis and Mussolini: Fascist Appropriations of a Beloved Italian Saint" (2026), they explain how fascist rhetoric manipulated Francis' stigmata, reframing them as symbols of heroic suffering and sacrifice. "The wounds of the saint were thus invoked to glorify sacrifice and inspire Italian youth to go to war."

Noting how Mussolini chose to be rebaptized in 1927 to strengthen his alliance with the Vatican, they add, "St. Francis offered a particularly useful means of conferring religious legitimacy upon political power."

Italian leader Benito Mussolini (left), who in fact inspired Germany's Adolf Hitler, appropriated Francis' teachings to legitimize fascist ideals Image: United Archives International/IMAGO

Minervini's research shows that Francis' pacifism — "likely because he had known what war meant" — was deliberately played down. Their book reproduces a confidential note addressed to military chaplains in 1929, which expressed concern that they might preach ideals of peace to the troops.

"This document provides clear evidence that peace was an aspect of Francesco's legacy that fascist groups sought to suppress rather than promote."

Furthermore, after Italy — a former Axis power along with Nazi Germany — switched sides and joined the Allies during World War II, the latter were often willing to condone or overlook Italy's crimes rather than investigate its fascist past.

"In this climate, many fascists remained in place, and the politically compromised image of Francis was quietly set aside," explains Minervini.

Painting depicting St Francis having an audience with Sultan Malik al-Kamil Image: IMAGO/Heritage Images

Medieval peace envoy

Francis has however remained associated with peace-making.

In 1219, during the Fifth Crusade, he traveled with the crusading army to Damietta, a port city in northern Egypt, and obtained permission to cross into the Muslim camp and meet personally with the sultan, Malik al-Kamil. His aim was to convert the sultan and bring an end to the bloody conflict.

Describing his action as "an extraordinarily audacious thing to do," Minervini says the encounter did not produce the conversion or political breakthrough Francis may have hoped for, but his return unscathed ensured that early sources took notice of him.

Daniel Horan adds that despite Christians viewing Muslims as the enemy back then, St Francis "would not go along with that dehumanizing perspective" and instead celebrated "the shared humanity and brotherhood he recognized in the Sultan."

2019 picture of the saint's namesake, Pope Francis, meeting Swedish climate activist, Greta Thunberg (holding poster), at St Peter's Square Image: picture alliance / abaca

From mendicant friar to climate icon

But he is most widely known as an animal lover and an early figure of environmental consciousness.

"He was ahead of his time both theologically and in terms of modern natural sciences, recognizing the complexity of the cosmos and the fact that human beings are also creatures in relationship with the world around us," says Daniel Horan, author of "Francis of Assisi and the Future of Faith" (2012).

In 1979, Pope John Paul II declared Francis the patron saint of ecology, while the Argentinian Jorge Mario Bergoglio chose the saint as his papal namesake when he became Pope Francis in 2013.

Copies of Pope Francis' encyclical 'Laudato Si'' or 'Praise be to you' based on St Francis' 'Canticle of the Creatures' Image: imago/ZUMA Press

This pope would later publish "Laudato Si'" in 2015 — based on the saint's 1225 hymn "Canticle of the Creatures," in which he addresses natural elements as "Brother Sun," "Sister Moon" and "Sister Mother Earth."

The pope's encyclical connected environmental destruction directly to human suffering, besides critiquing consumerism and the "throwaway culture," and urging humanity to undergo an "ecological conversion."

"I also believe that in a time of deep polarization and economic inequality that St Francis models another way of being in the world, one that prioritizes relationship and community over individual gain and power," says Horan.

St Francis' annual feast day on October 4 is also when pets are blessed, as seen here in a church in Mumbai Image: picture alliance / Sipa USA

But what might Francis make of his fame today?

"It's always tricky to try and guess what St. Francis, who died 800 years ago this October, would think about anything today. Our world is so unlike his own. But we do know that in his own time he was very uncomfortable with the positive reception he and his brother friars were receiving across Europe," says Horan.

Minervini suggests that he might have been more comfortable with representations of himself as a pacifist saint.

"I suspect he would be profoundly troubled, perhaps even furious, as it is known he could get upset, by the condition of our late-capitalist, technocratic world and by the ways in which we continue to understand ourselves as separate from, and superior to, the other creatures."

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

World.title: Ukraine, South Korea relations sour over North Korean POWs
World.content:
South Korea has accused Ukraine of breaching a confidentiality agreement over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war — and of denying the deal's existence. Seoul has demanded an apology.

South Korea has demanded an official apology from Ukraine after accusing Kyiv of breaching — and then reportedly denying the existence of — a confidentiality agreement regarding the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul.

Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer in an address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, adding that the soldiers were "not easy to capture alive."

Hours later, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung wrote on social media: "I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing."

On Sunday, the South Korean consternation was made official when Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, demanded "an official explanation and apology."

"The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine's unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement," Seong said in a statement.

"It is in itself a very serious matter that … seriously undermines trust between the two governments and gravely damages friendly relations between the two countries."

Seong said Seoul was "considering additional measures that may be necessary regarding this matter," but did not specify what they might be.

Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine: When were the North Korean soldiers captured?

The North Korean soldiers were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025 — two of around 14,000 North Korean troops deployed to the area to help halt and push back a surprise Ukrainian incursion.

Ukrainian intelligence estimates that around 3,000 North Korean troops were killed and another 1,500 injured, with the rest still stationed on Russian territory. To date, no North Korean troops are believed to have operated on Ukrainian territory itself.

Ukrainian troops reported that North Korean soldiers who were surrounded or injured on the battlefield preferred to die by suicide than surrender — and only two were captured.

Under President Lee, who has attempted to improve relations with the North, South Korea has appeared hesitant to take custody of the pair. But, under Article 3 of the South Korean constitution, North Koreans are still considered citizens of the South and are permitted to live in the South.

South Korea is an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which has so far only provided non-lethal aid. But Kyiv has been pressing Seoul to provide advanced air defense systems.

Last month, President Zelenskyy claimed that up to 50,000 more North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia.

World.title: Israel strips Dutch diplomats of status in West Bank
World.content:
The move by the Israeli Foreign Ministry is a response to Dutch sanctions targeting goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The Dutch Foreign Ministry is yet to comment.

The Israeli government said on Sunday that it was revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats representing The Netherlands at the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, the administrative capital of the Palestinian Territories.

Israeli ​Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the move was a response to Dutch sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

"Israel will not ignore measures intended to harm it," Saar wrote on social media.

He ordered Dutch diplomats operating in Ramallah to ​return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documentation within seven days.

"After this period, the diplomatic privileges and immunities granted to them by the State of Israel will expire," he added.

Israeli settlement trade ban widens across Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Monday, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen called the move an "unnecessary decision," and that his government's suspension of imports from the West Bank was "not directed against Israel."

Dutch ban on settlement goods: what does it entail?

Dutch authorities announced earlier this month that they would begin enforcing a ban on settlement goods.

The ban, which applies to personal baggage as well as commercial shipments, came into force on September 22 and, in recent days, Dutch and Israeli media have reported that passengers arriving at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport from Israel had their luggage searched for banned goods.

Earlier in September, Israel also ordered the closure of ⁠the British Consulate ⁠in East Jerusalem, the United Kingdom's representative to the Palestinian Authority, after London announced similar sanctions banning the import of goods from illegal settlements.

"Any country that acts in a hostile and unilateral manner against Israel will lose influence and relevance in the region," said Saar.

France and Canada have also announced a ban on goods from settlements, but Israel has not yet taken any action against ​those two countries.

In August, Israel also banned Dutch diplomats from a Israeli-based, US-led coordination center for Gaza over what the foreign minister described as "anti-Israel measures."

World.title: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announces resignation
World.content:
Aleksandar Vucic will now be running to be prime minister in the upcoming snap parliamentary elections slated for next month.

Serbia's long-time President Aleksandar Vucic announced on Sunday that he would resign from his post in order to run for prime minister in the upcoming October snap elections.

From the presidential palace in Belgrade, Vucic spoke to supporters: "I am resigning as president."

"Tomorrow morning I will hand over my duties to the parliament speaker," he added "This is the last evening for me in this building," Vucic declared.

"I served you faithfully. I served all of you, and our homeland Serbia, honourably and honestly throughout my presidential term," Vucic told supporters. "The fight is only beginning," he added.

Dominating Serbian politics

Vucic is banned by the Serbian Constitution from seeking a third term. He was serving his second term and would have left office in May of 2027.

The 56-year-old, who has ties to Serbian nationalism and had once served as minister under the administration of Slobodan Milosevic, has dominated Serbian politics for more over a decade.

Vucic supporters praise him for his stability, stated commitment to development projects in Serbia and his patriotism, in a country long overshadowed by war in the 1990s and subsequent international isolation.

Opponents, however, have decried what they see as increasingly authoritarian tendencies and leading a government accused of endemic corruption.

Abroad, Vucic has had to juggle the competing interests of his country's European Union aspirations and its close ties to Russia.

Opposition had sought snap elections

Earlier in September, Vucic called for snap elections for October. He cited "major turbulence on the domestic political scene," as the reason.

Vucic was referring to the political movement and major setback for his government that was triggered by a tragedy in Serbia's second-largest city of Novi Sad. In November 2024, an awning of a newly reconstructed railway station in Novi Sad collapsed, killing 16 people.

The disaster triggered nationwide ⁠protests by students and the opposition. They ​demanded accountability for those responsible for the disaster, transparency in public procurement, an end to systemic corruption, and an early parliamentary vote.

Vucic's government repeatedly denied accusations, but still, several officials, including two ministers, were arrested or resigned after the incident. The upcoming snap election will test Vucic's popularity and political survival.

World.title: Yemen: Houthis report deadly Saudi strikes on Taiz market
World.content:
The Houthi-run health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," vowing to retaliate. The Houthis' account of the attack cannot be independently verified.

Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday accused the Saudi Arabian Air Force of having struck a shopping area around the central market of Taiz. The Iran-aligned Houthis said at least seven people had been killed and dozens injured.

What do we know so far?

The group's Al-Masirah TV channel showed footage of large plumes of smoke and a destroyed warehouse stacked with food in cardboard boxes. Al-Masirah TV also reported that children were among those wounded, citing the Houthis' health ministry.

Taiz is currently under the control of Yemeni government forces, but it has long been besieged by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in the country's civil war. Taiz is located in southwestern Yemen.

The escalation in fighting comes after a fragile truce between Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels broke down months ago and new regional tensions sparked by the Iran war.

The Houthi health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," saying it was directly and deliberately targeting civilian sites in Taiz.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit the market, adding that blood was "unjustly and aggressively spilled" in a statement posted online.

The group has vowed to retaliate.

The claims made by the Houthis cannot be independently verified.

In response to the Houthi report, troops loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen confirmed that their air force had struck a Houthi depot and vehicles in the area.

France sends troops as Houthi attacks threaten Saudi oil To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Saudi-backed coalition ramps up attacks after new Houthi offensive

The civil war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government. They went on to take control of vast swaths of the country's north.

Saudi Arabia joined forces against the Houthis the following year, leading an international coalition against them. But so far, Yemen's government forces have not been able to effectively repel the latest Houthi offensive.

Fighting has spiked in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. The rebels have also launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports to coincide with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Renewed clashes are is under way in several parts of the country, with at least 125,000 people displaced by it.

The Yemeni government has meanwhile called for a general mobilization, urging Yemenis to join the army and security forces.

Yemen is one of the poorest in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.
