World.title: Poland issues guidance on responding to air attacks and warns of Russia threat
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Polish government has launched an information campaign on how to respond in the event of an air strike. It has also announced that 85,000 shelters are to be marked with clear signs across Poland and an evacuation plan is being developed. The moves come amid growing concerns over Russia strikes in Ukraine near the Polish border. The prime minister and foreign minister have warned that Russia could be planning “something big” this year, without specifying what that might involve. 🟡 KOMUNIKAT | MSWiA publikuje instrukcję reagowania podczas zagrożenia atakiem z powietrza. 📄 Ministerstwo Spraw Wewnętrznych i Administracji udostępnia nową instrukcję postępowania na wypadek ataku z powietrza. To rozwinięcie treści zawartych w „Poradniku Bezpieczeństwa”,… pic.twitter.com/aw3h07mdeF — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 25, 2026 On Friday, Poland’s interior ministry published information on how to respond to the threat of an air attack, expanding on a safety handbook sent to all 17 million households in the country earlier this year. The new guidelines explain where to seek cover during an air raid, how to prepare homes and what to do if an attack occurs while people are at home, at work, outdoors or in a car. They advise people to seek a shelter point, take a prepared evacuation backpack and any necessary medication, and use only stairs. If reaching a shelter would require spending a long time outdoors, people are advised to remain inside and move to a central room without windows. Separately, the ministry has prepared guidelines for schools after some were criticised last week for evacuating children outside school buildings during alarms in the eastern province of Lublin. W całej Polsce mają pojawić się obowiązkowe oznaczenia Punktów Schronienia. Specjalna aplikacja pokaże ich lokalizacje, a nowe oznakowanie ma ułatwić mieszkańcom znalezienie bezpiecznego miejsca w sytuacji zagrożenia. Materiał 🎥 Michał Niewodowski pic.twitter.com/HVoo3ypETT — 19.30 TVP (@1930_tvp) September 21, 2026 To make shelter points easier to identify, the interior ministry has prepared a draft regulation requiring local authorities and managers of designated sites to mark them clearly by the end of the year with a blue triangle on an orange background, as well as a green sign saying “Punkt schronienia” (“Shelter point”). The locations can also be found using a mobile application launched last year. According to the ministry’s own data, Poland currently has about 85,000 shelter points, which could host 23.7 million people, or 64% of the country’s population. A national plan is also being developed to coordinate potential evacuation as a result of war, a threat of war or a natural disaster. The plan is intended to establish evacuation routes and reception areas in advance, including how many people may need to be moved and where they could be accommodated. “When a threat arises, we warn the Polish people and defend our security. It is only natural that we prepare for worst-case scenarios, while deeply believing that they will never come to pass,” interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told the Rzeczpospolita newspaper. “Evacuation plans are being prepared…These plans rely heavily on the strength of the entire crisis response system. The more we strengthen that system, the more precise the plans will be,” Kierwiński added. Poland has launched a mobile application and website that allows people to find their nearest shelter in times of war or other emergencies https://t.co/YE3rsltCj5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The evacuation plans have become the subject of false claims circulating on social media. These posts allege that the government is preparing to forcibly displace Poles and ultimately eliminate the Polish nation, with some linking the alleged plan to an agreement between Berlin and Kyiv, reports the Onet news service. They claim that evacuees would never be allowed to return, allegations the government quickly moved to debunk. 📢 STOP FAKE NEWS! W sieci krążą fałszywe informacje, jakoby przygotowywany Krajowy Plan Ewakuacji miał oznaczać masowe wysiedlenie mieszkańców Polski ‼️To nieprawda‼️ 🔎 FAKT: Krajowy Plan Ewakuacji określa procedury na wypadek wojny, zagrożenia wojną lub klęski żywiołowej.… pic.twitter.com/YNEqXF3StJ — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 18, 2026 The measures are part of a broader effort to strengthen Poland’s civil protection system. Last week, Kierwiński said Poland plans to triple the current number of warning sirens in Lublin province to more than 1,000 by the end of 2026. This follows a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border. The recent escalation comes after several incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response. Those warnings were echoed yesterday by Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, who said that multiple sources suggested that “Russia is planning something big this year.” “I think Putin needs a pretext for mobilisation, so they might carry out a false-flag attack to tell the Russians, ‘We are under attack, and that is why we must mobilise,’” he added. World.title: Zelensky condemns knife attack by Ukrainian at Polish abbey that left priest dead and others injured
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has expressed his horror at an “evil” knife attack carried out today by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland, which left one priest dead and others seriously injured. The incident has caused shock in Poland, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledging that the perpetrator, who is in police custody, will face the “full severity of Polish law”. W Opactwie Sióstr Benedyktynek w Jarosławiu obywatel Ukrainy dopuścił się straszliwej zbrodni. Jesteśmy wstrząśnięci tym złem. Według dotychczasowych informacji zginął ksiądz katolicki, a kilka innych osób zostało rannych. Składamy najgłębsze kondolencje rodzinie i bliskim… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 24, 2026 The attack took place on Thursday morning on the grounds of a Benedictine abbey in the town of Jarosław in southeast Poland. Local police reported that a 31-year-old Ukrainian man had stabbed four male victims and one female. Three were members of the clergy and two laypeople. Authorities later confirmed that one of the men, a priest, had died of his injuries in hospital and that two others were in serious condition. The cathedral in the nearby city of Rzeszów named the deceased as Stanisław Zbojnowicz. The superior of the Benedictine Sisters Monastery, Barbara Dendor, told news website Interia that Zbojnowicz had been in a confessional when the attack began. He had rushed out to attempt to close the gates and protect other people, but was stabbed by the assailant before he could do so. In its initial social media post announcing Zbojnowicz’s death, the cathedral also said that a second priest, Marek Pieńkowski, had died. However, a few minutes later it deleted that claim, blaming the “enormous information chaos surrounding today’s tragic event”. One person was killed and four were injured in a knife attack at a Catholic convent in Poland this morning, with clergy among the victims. Police have detained a 31-year-old Ukrainian man on suspicion of carrying out the attack. The motive remains unknown https://t.co/93nbqpwnIA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Thursday afternoon, prosecutors revealed that the suspect, who has not been named, had entered Poland from Germany in the early hours of Thursday and “was heading to the border crossing [with Ukraine] in Korczowa”, which is around 30km (18.6 miles) from Jarosław. However, he ultimately did not cross the border and, for unknown reasons, ended up in Jarosław, where he entered the grounds of the abbey and began his attack, using a knife taken from the kitchen. Prosecutors said that doctors would assess the suspect’s condition before he was interrogated. Blood samples were also taken to be tested for the presence of narcotics and alcohol. The motive for the attack remains unknown. Dendor told news website Wirtualna Polska that the perpetrator was unknown to them. “He looked like a madman, in shorts and a T-shirt, even though it was cold today,” she said. Wirtualna Polska reports, based on the accounts of unnamed witnesses, that the Ukrainian man had earlier in the day knocked on the gates of the abbey and asked for financial assistance. However, he was turned away due to the suspicion that he was drunk or under the influence of drugs and was asked to come back later. That is standard practice for places that offer aid, reports the news service. The man “flew into a rage when he didn’t get help and allegedly threatened priests”, said one of the unnamed sources. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk expressed his sympathy for the loved ones of the victims of the attack and pledged that the perpetrator “will be punished with the full severity of Polish law”. President Karol Nawrocki likewise expressed his condolences and called on the authorities to “quickly and thoroughly clarify all the circumstances of this tragedy”. Later on Thursday afternoon, Zelensky also extended his condolences in a social media post published in Polish. “We are shocked by this evil,” he wrote. “The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the applicable law.” Morderca z Jarosławia jest w rękach Polskiej Policji. Trwają czynności. Sprawca to obywatel Ukrainy. Będzie ukarany z całą surowością polskiego prawa. Łączę się w bólu z bliskimi ofiar tego brutalnego ataku. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 24, 2026 Earlier, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw had “condemned the brutal attack” in Jarosław. However, it also appealed for people “not to allow pain to turn into hatred or further violence”, saying that “accountability for the crime must be based solely on the law”. Polish-Ukrainian relations have been tense in recent months, amid rising anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland and anger at Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. There has been a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland this year. Marcin Piotrowski, a board member of the Folkowisko Foundation, which provides aid to Ukrainian refugees, told newspaper Rzeczpospolita today that the tragedy in Jarosław was already being exploited on social media. He expressed fear that “we are almost on the verge of lynchings”. 🔴Jesteśmy na granicy nastrojów linczowych. Obawiam się, że czyn pojedynczej osoby odbije się echem na milionach Ukraińców – mówi Marcin Piotrowski, socjolog i członek Rady Fundacji Humanitarnej Folkowisko, działającej na pograniczu polsko-ukraińskim.https://t.co/p048Fgg1Ct — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) September 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish constitutional court officials charged with preventing entry of new judges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further, after prosecutors charged two senior TK officials over their role in preventing new judges from taking up their positions on the court. Those judges were chosen by the government’s majority in parliament but rejected by President Karol Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, both of whom are aligned with the right-wing opposition. Following news of the charges, Święczkowski announced that he has initiated proceedings of his own against three other new judges who were admitted to the court this year after being chosen by the ruling coalition. That could result in them being expelled from their positions. Zarzuty w śledztwie dotyczącym niedopuszczenia sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego do orzekania: ⬇️https://t.co/MPiKCEqGBs — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 23, 2026 After coming to power in December 2023, the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk refused to recognise the TK, which was stacked with judges appointed by the former Law and Justice administration. It argued that, because some of those judges were unlawfully appointed, the TK itself was illegitimate. Earlier this year, Tusk’s majority in parliament finally began the process of appointing new judges to the TK to fill the growing number of vacancies. Normally, 15 judges sit on the tribunal, but many seats were empty after incumbents’ nine-year terms had expired and the government had previously refused to fill them. However, under Polish law, new TK judges must take an oath “before the president” in order to take up their position. Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS, has refused to swear in four of the six judges chosen by parliament in March. Nawrocki argues that there were legal doubts surrounding their election. The government rejects this, as do the judges themselves, who organised their own swearing-in ceremony before a notary and then submitted the documents to the presidential chancellery. Afterwards, the four judges attempted to take up their positions at the TK. However, Święczkowski, who served in the PiS government before becoming a TK judge, refused to admit them, arguing that they had not taken the necessary oath before the president. The judges took their case to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which in May issued an interim order requiring that they be allowed to take up their positions. But Święczkowski has refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the competence to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 While Święczkowski himself is protected from prosecution by legal immunity, two senior TK officials have now been charged over their role in refusing entry to the four judges. One of the two suspects, who can be named only as Zofia H. under Polish privacy law, is the director of the TK’s chancellery; the other, Piotr P., is the commander of the TK’s security service. They have been charged with abuse of power by a public official, which is punishable by up to three years in prison, and “maliciously and persistently” violating the employment rights of the judges, an offence that carries a sentence of up to two years. Prosecutors say that the officials’ actions were “to the detriment of the private interests of judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and the public interest in the proper functioning of the judiciary in Poland”. Both of the accused have been questioned and pleaded not guilty. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The decision to bring charges was welcomed by Waldemar Żurek, who serves as justice minister in Tusk’s government as well as prosecutor general. “In a building that should stand guard over the constitution, unlawful blockades were organised, humiliating inspections were conducted, and malicious bullying was directed at legally elected judges,” he wrote on social media. “A state official has no right to place themselves above the law, and the gates of the tribunal are not the gates of a private fortress,” he continued. “Anyone who carries out unlawful political orders and destroys the foundations of the rule of law must reckon with criminal liability.” W budynku, który powinien stać na straży Konstytucji, urządzono bezprawne blokady, upokarzające kontrole i złośliwy mobbing wobec legalnie wybranych sędziów. Urzędnik państwowy nie ma prawa stawiać się ponad prawem, a bramy Trybunału nie są bramami prywatnej twierdzy.… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 23, 2026 The TK itself, however, condemned prosecutors’ actions, calling them “unlawful” and a “tool of personal pressure and a form of intimidation”. “The director of the chancellery and all other employees of the TK have performed and continue to perform their duties and official orders in accordance with the applicable law,” wrote the tribunal on its official X account. It argued that it would, in fact, have been a criminal abuse of power to have “allowed persons who have not taken the oath before the President to assume the office of a TK judge”. W dniu dzisiejszym @PK_GOV_PL przedstawiła Pani Dyrektor Kancelarii Trybunału Konstytucyjnego absurdalne zarzuty z art. 231 § 1 i 218 § 3 Kodeksu karnego, które od początku do końca są oparte na wymyślonych podstawach prawnych. Działanie to stanowi kolejną próbę wywarcia wpływu… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) September 23, 2026 On Thursday, the day after the charges were announced, the TK issued a further statement saying that Święczkowski had initiated proceedings against three new TK judges who were chosen by parliament this year and sworn in by Nawrocki (two in March, the other in June). The TK said that it was assessing complaints that two of those judges filed against tribunal employees, as well as their refusal to participate in sessions of the TK’s general assembly. Those three judges have shown solidarity with their four excluded colleagues by refusing to participate. “These proceedings may conclude with the most severe ruling of the disciplinary court in the form of removal from office of the aforementioned TK judges,” wrote the TK. Prezes @TK_GOV_PL Bogdan Święczkowski, działając na wniosek jednego z sędziów, wszczął dzisiaj postępowanie mogące się zakończyć zarzutami dyscyplinarnymi wobec trojga sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego: Magdaleny Bentkowskiej, Dariusza Szostka oraz Sławomira Patyry.… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) September 24, 2026 An eighth new TK judge chosen this year, Maciej Berek, who was elected by parliament earlier this month, has also not yet been sworn in by Nawrocki. Berek’s appointment has been particularly controversial, given that he served in the government until being nominated to the TK. Tusk described Berek as his “right-hand man”. Even some MPs from Tusk’s ruling coalition voted against Berek’s appointment, arguing that it contradicted the government’s own efforts to “depoliticise” the judiciary, including by banning recently serving politicians from sitting on the TK. The presidential chancellery has so far refused to swear in Berek based on a technicality, arguing that there is no evidence he has previously served for at least ten years as a legal counsel, which is a requirement to sit on the TK. Berek says that he has presented such evidence. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A fire last night at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was caused deliberately, says digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which relies heavily on Starlink connections. Although the fire is still being investigated, “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian”, says Gawkowski. 🔴 Gawkowski o pożarze stacji Starlink. "Element wojny hybrydowej" Wicepremier Krzysztof Gawkowski ocenił pożar stacji Starlink na Mazowszu jako celową próbę zakłócenia łączności. – Wiele wskazuje na to, że pożar stacji Starlinków na Mazowszu to kolejny element wojny hybrydowej… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 24, 2026 Firefighters were called out at around 9 p.m. on Wednesday to the facility, which is located in the village of Wola Krobowska, just south of the capital Warsaw. Due to suspicions that the fire had been caused deliberately, police and officers from the Internal Security Agency (ABW) were also later dispatched to the scene. “We’re dealing with an arson attack that was intended to impact critical telecommunications infrastructure that influences internet operation,” Gawkowski, who also serves as deputy prime minister, told broadcaster TVN on Thursday morning. In a separate interview with TVP, the minister said that the facility is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel and “provides internet transmission through Poland, and also to Ukraine”. He noted that other internet providers use Exatel’s facility, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which is the owner of Starlink. Starlink terminals have been vital in Ukraine during Russia’s war against the country. Gawkowski told TVN that “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian” and “is another element of the hybrid warfare we are facing”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe, including a series of arson attacks. “The Russians want to paralyse critical infrastructure, cut off water, gas and electricity, paralyse the internet,” said the minister. “All these processes have one goal: to incite panic and stir up emotions.” However, in his remarks to TVP, Gawkowski acknowledged that, for now, “it is impossible to say” for sure whether Russia was behind the attack. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 The spokesman for Poland’s security services, Jacek Dobrzyński, likewise told TVN that “at this stage it is still too early to talk about the causes or motives of this fire”. However, he confirmed that “everything points to arson”. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also told broadcaster RMF that “this could be an act of sabotage, and we are taking that into account, so nothing can be ruled out here, especially since these are sensitive elements that ensure satellite communications”. Polish news service Defence24 notes that ground stations are used by Starlink to connect its satellite constellation with terrestrial communications infrastructure. The facility in Poland, alongside one in Lithuania, serves the entire Central and Eastern Europe region, including Ukraine. Tu nieco więcej o roli stacji naziemnych w systemie Starlink. https://t.co/EYys481dSi — Mariusz Marszałkowski (@MJMarszalkowski) September 24, 2026 Earlier this month, a fire broke out at a drone plant in Poland belonging to WB Electronics, which supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that there was “no doubt” the fire was caused deliberately, and that Russia was likely behind it. The Polish government has in recent months warned that Russia is planning to escalate its hybrid actions against Poland and other countries in the region, including through acts of sabotage, disinformation, and potential airspace and border violations. In July, a Russian missile entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland. On Wednesday this week, the same day as the fire in Wola Krobowska broke out, a Russian helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace. World.title: Five Free Things to Do in Prague This October
World.content:
Prague will offer a range of free cultural events in October, from exhibitions and science films to family entertainment and hands-on craft workshops.

Several major institutions will also open their doors to the public on October 28, Czech Independence Day.



Here are five events where the main program is free, followed by a guide to some of the places that can be visited without charge on the October 28 public holiday.

Free admission at the National Gallery

October 3–4 and October 28, 10:00 AM–6:00 PM

The National Gallery Prague will offer free access to selected exhibitions on two occasions in October.

On October 3 and 4, visitors can see 1956–1989: Architecture for Everyone at the Trade Fair Palace (Veletržní palác) without paying an entrance fee. The offer forms part of Architecture Day, this year’s festival built around the theme “I Dwell, Therefore I Am.”

The Architecture Day program will also include free tours and workshops at several National Gallery sites, including the Trade Fair Palace, the Convent of St. Agnes of Bohemia and Schwarzenberg Palace. Some activities require advance registration.

Another opportunity comes on October 28, when the National Gallery will waive admission to its eight permanent exhibitions. The program includes medieval and Old Master collections as well as exhibitions covering the First Republic, the period from 1939 to 2021 and Asian art.

The free admission applies to the specified permanent collections and does not cover all temporary exhibitions. The gallery is also preparing additional activities for the public holiday.

Midnight Circus brings family entertainment to Prague 8

October 3, 10:00 AM–7:00 PM and October 4, 10:00 AM–12:00 PM – DDM Prague 8 – Spirála, Přemyšlenská 15

The Spirála Children and Youth Center in Kobylisy will become a temporary circus venue during the first weekend of October.

Midnight Circus will feature clowns, fortune tellers, a storyteller and a House of Horrors, alongside other attractions aimed at families. Visitors can also enter a themed bathhouse.

The daytime program is free and does not require advance registration. Instead of paying directly for individual attractions, visitors receive “Principálky” at the entrance, a special circus currency that can also be earned through activities during the event.

An evening show on Saturday will feature a UV light performance followed by a fire show. Unlike the daytime program, this performance requires a ticket costing CZK 50, payable in cash at the venue. It is not recommended for children younger than five.

Try traditional crafts at the New Town Hall

October 13–14, 8:00 AM–4:00 PM – New Town Hall, Karlovo náměstí 1/23, Prague 2

The New Town Hall will host the 13th edition of Crafts Live (Řemesla živě), an event designed to introduce visitors to traditional and practical trades and the schools where they can be studied.

Visitors will have the opportunity to try different crafts for themselves and speak directly with representatives of vocational schools about their courses and study programs.

Admission to the event is free, although some individual workshops may charge a fee.

Science documentaries come to Suchdol

October 19–22 – Czech University of Life Sciences Prague, Suchdol

The Prague Science Film Fest returns with a program of international science documentaries, including several Czech premieres.

The films explore subjects ranging from the way the human brain can mislead us to the role of fungi and the behavior of otters. Among the scheduled titles are How the Brain Tricks Us, My Otter Diary and The Kingdom of Fungi.

Film screenings will be accompanied by discussions with scientists, filmmakers and other experts, giving visitors an opportunity to explore the topics beyond the films themselves.

The festival will also include an outdoor screening of the Oscar-nominated documentary Fire of Love, an exhibition focused on antelope conservation in Africa and a filmmaking workshop.

Admission is free, and this year’s program does not require registration.

Where to go for free on October 28

October 28 is a public holiday in Czechia, marking the establishment of the independent Czechoslovak state in 1918. Several important Prague buildings traditionally open to visitors on the day.

Straka Academy

The seat of the Czech government will open its meeting rooms, press rooms and garden to the public. The exact visiting hours had not yet been announced at the time of publication.

Wallenstein Palace and Kolowrat Palace

The Czech Senate will open both buildings from 7:30 AM to 5:00 PM. Visitors will be able to see, among other areas, the Senate meeting hall.

Thun Palace

The Chamber of Deputies will open Thun Palace on Sněmovní Street from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM. Tours start at the main entrance at Sněmovní 4.

Municipal House

The representative rooms on the first floor, including Smetana Hall and the Mayor’s Hall, will be accessible free of charge from 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM. Guided commentary in Smetana Hall will be available every 15 minutes.

World.title: Czech Women Win Billie Jean King Cup Again After Eight Years
World.content:
Czech Republic eased past Ukraine to win the Billie Jean King Cup for the 12th time.

This year’s Wimbledon finalists Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova breezed past their opponents to secure a 2-0 victory and deny the Ukrainians a first title in the competition.



Muchova, the runner-up at Wimbledon, comfortably beat Anhelina Kalinina 6-2 6-3 in the opening singles match before Noskova’s 6-3 ⁠7-6 (7-5) win over world number seven Elina Svitolina ‌secured the title.

It is the Czechs’ first win at the event since 2018, making them the second-most successful nation in its history after the United States, who have 18 titles.

In her first year as Czechia captain, Barbora Strycova has made history.

Former Grand Slam doubles champion Strycova is just the fourth woman to win the Billie Jean King Cup as both a player and a captain. Strycova joins a Hall of Fame cast of Margaret Court, Chrissie Evert and Billie Jean King in achieving that feat.

CZECHIA'S NEW ALL-STARS ARE WORLD CHAMPIONS 🇨🇿🏆#BJKCup pic.twitter.com/W8B2WucxI0 — Billie Jean King Cup (@BJKCup) September 27, 2026

She’s also the first player in event history to win the Billie Jean King Cup juniors title as a player and the Billie Jean King Cup title as a player and a captain. Strycova won the Billie Jean King Cup juniors title alongside Petra Cetkovska and Lucie Safarova in 2001.

The Czechs also knocked out Great Britain in the quarter-finals in Shenzhen, China, which led GB captain Anne Keothavong to describe them as “the strongest team here”.

World.title: Bolt and Lucid Plan 25,000 Autonomous Vehicles Across Europe
World.content:
Bolt and U.S. electric vehicle maker Lucid Group have announced a partnership to develop autonomous mobility services in Europe, with plans to deploy more than 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles across European cities over the coming years.

The vehicles will be based on Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform and use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference architecture and development platform for autonomous vehicles.



The companies plan to develop the vehicles for SAE Level 4 autonomous driving, which allows vehicles to operate without human control within defined conditions.

Bolt says the project is part of its wider ambition to have 100,000 autonomous vehicles operating on its platform by 2035.

The companies will work together from the early stages of vehicle development. Bolt will contribute traffic and mobility data, operational experience and knowledge of European markets, while Lucid will provide its software-defined vehicle platform and automotive technology.

Bolt will also define requirements covering the vehicle, software, safety and passenger experience. Its autonomous driving division will oversee the partnership and develop the infrastructure needed to operate the fleet.

This will include vehicle dispatch, charging, maintenance, remote assistance and customer support. Bolt also plans to own and operate the autonomous vehicles itself.

Rollout will depend on local regulations

The companies have not yet announced which European cities will receive the service first.

Bolt and Lucid said launches will take place city by city and depend on local regulations, official approvals and operational readiness. The companies also plan to work with autonomous driving technology providers, European regulators and policymakers before introducing the service.

For the foreseeable future, autonomous vehicles on the Bolt platform will operate alongside vehicles driven by human drivers.

Lucid’s side of the project will be led by Lucid Technologies, a newly established division bringing together artificial intelligence, advanced driver-assistance systems, autonomous driving and other digital technologies.

Bolt currently operates in more than 850 cities across 50 countries and says its platform serves more than 200 million customers. Its services include ride-hailing, car-sharing, electric scooters and food and grocery delivery.

Lucid Group, listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker LCID, develops electric vehicles and related technologies. The company operates manufacturing facilities in Arizona and Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Prague Airport Works to Speed Up Border Checks for Non-EU Travellers
World.content:
Prague Airport and the Czech Ministry of the Interior are preparing additional measures to reduce waiting times for passengers arriving from non-Schengen countries following the introduction of the EU Entry/Exit System (EES).

The new system has made border checks more complex, particularly for travellers from outside the EU. Prague Airport says it has already introduced several measures aimed at keeping passenger flows moving during busy periods.



Airport staff, known as the Red Team, are assisting passengers in the terminal, directing them through the new procedures and providing information where needed. The airport has also adjusted passenger flow corridors based on data collected since the system was introduced.

One of the main issues identified so far is the self-service registration process. According to the airport, a significant number of passengers do not complete their registration at the kiosks, which can lead to additional delays at passport control.

Prague Airport is therefore examining the entire journey from the registration kiosks to passport control and looking at ways to make the process easier, particularly for families and older passengers.

“Data has shown us that the most common delays occur when people interrupt the registration process at the terminals,” said Radomír Lašák, Chairman of the Board of Prague Airport. “Together with the Police of the Czech Republic, we are not merely putting together temporary stopgaps but are redesigning the entire process so that it remains resilient even during peak periods.”

Further measures are also being prepared at the European level, including the possibility of allowing passengers to complete parts of the EES registration before departure. Airlines could also provide passengers with information about the process during flights.

The Czech Ministry of the Interior and the Immigration Police are working with Prague Airport on the next steps and have committed additional resources to help manage the new system.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the authorities’ priority was to maintain security standards while limiting the impact of the new procedures on passengers.

The airport said it will continue monitoring passenger flows and adjusting its procedures based on actual operations, particularly during peak travel periods.

World.title: Czech Statehood Day 2026: What Is Open and What to Do in Prague
World.content:
September 28 is a public holiday in the Czech Republic, marking Czech Statehood Day and the feast of St. Wenceslas. This year, the holiday falls on a Monday, giving many people a three-day weekend.

For anyone planning to spend the day in Prague, however, there are two practical questions: which shops will be open, and what can you do around the city?



Where you can shop on September 28

Under Czech legislation regulating retail opening hours, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square meters must close on September 28.

The restriction applies throughout the day and covers large supermarkets, hypermarkets and home improvement stores.

Smaller shops with sales areas of up to 200 square meters are exempt and can open at their owners’ discretion. Petrol stations and pharmacies can also operate.

Other exceptions include shops located at airports, railway stations and bus terminals, as well as retail outlets inside healthcare facilities.

Why September 28 is Czech Statehood Day

The holiday commemorates Prince Wenceslas, a member of the Přemyslid dynasty who became one of the central figures in Czech history.

Wenceslas was killed by his brother Boleslav I on September 28, 935, in Stará Boleslav. His death later became the foundation of a cult that developed around him from the late 10th century onward.

His remains were transferred to Prague in 938 on Boleslav’s orders and buried in the Rotunda of St. Vitus. The reasons behind the transfer are not known with certainty, but the move helped strengthen Wenceslas’s status as a religious figure while also reinforcing Prague’s position as the center of the emerging Czech state.

Over the following centuries, Wenceslas became the patron saint of the Czech lands and an important symbol of Czech statehood.

The connection between Wenceslas and Czech political tradition was further strengthened under Charles IV, who commissioned the Crown of Saint Wenceslas. The crown became one of the principal symbols of the Czech monarchy and remains part of the Czech Crown Jewels.

See the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle

September 28 is also the final day of this year’s exhibition of the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle.

The jewels are being displayed in Vladislav Hall as part of the exhibition Habsburgs 500. Admission is free, and the display also includes a coronation robe dating from 1653 and other historical objects.

The exhibition closes at the end of the day on September 28.

Government buildings open to visitors

Several normally restricted buildings will also be accessible to the public.

Straka Academy, the official seat of the Czech government, will open its doors on September 28. Visitors can see the government meeting room, ceremonial areas and the building’s garden.

The program also includes an interactive exhibition called Journey of the Republic. Tours are free and begin at 10 a.m., with the final group scheduled to leave at 5 p.m.

The Ministry of Finance on Letenská Street will also welcome visitors. Tours start at 9:30 a.m. and include the ministry’s historic premises and the former monastery.

Museums and other attractions

The National Technical Museum in Letná will remain open on September 28, giving visitors access to its permanent exhibitions.

The Postal Museum will also be open.

For those looking for a more traditional Prague attraction, September 28 will be the final chance this year to ride the historic Letná Carousel.

Another option is the National Museum, where the Přemyslids exhibition examines the history of the dynasty that ruled the Czech lands during the country’s early medieval period.

The exhibition runs until October 15, 2026, making the public holiday particularly relevant for visitors interested in the history behind Czech Statehood Day.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation: The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy: A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance: The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

(Source material and reporting courtesy of Thailand NOW)

World.title: Hotline for Foreigners in Czechia: Tips to Save Time and Frustration
World.content:
Reaching the Client Centre for residence-related questions in Czechia requires patience.

More than 2,000 calls are received every day, so some waiting time is unavoidable.

However, you can significantly reduce your waiting time by calling during less busy hours, which are published through the authority’s official channels.



It is also worth having your identification document number ready before calling. This can speed up the process, particularly if you are calling to book an appointment.

Those who do not want to wait on the phone can use other ways to get in touch. Answers to many common questions are available in the Frequently Asked Questions section of the Information Portal for Foreigners (ipc.gov.cz).

If your matter is not urgent or your question is more complicated, you can also contact the centre by email at [email protected].

The current status of your application can be checked online using the dedicated service on the same portal.

When it comes to appointments, most bookings can be made through your personal account on the Information Portal for Foreigners.

You only need to book by phone in three cases: to provide biometric data, to inspect your case file, or to collect a residence card as an EU citizen.

World.title: Czech President Warns NATO Allies May Need to Shoot Down Russian Aircraft
World.content:
Czech President Petr Pavel has warned that NATO may eventually need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones that deliberately violate the alliance’s airspace.

Speaking to Fox News Digital in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, Pavel said Russia was testing NATO’s readiness and could interpret continued restraint as a sign of weakness.

“There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness,” Pavel said.



Pavel said the alliance needs to distinguish between accidental airspace violations and deliberate incursions in which an aircraft ignores warnings to leave.

“If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on,” he said.

His comments came after a series of incidents involving Russian aircraft and drones near NATO territory.

On Wednesday, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace after crossing from the Kaliningrad region. According to Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, the helicopter travelled around 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds.

On Thursday, Romania also scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after an unidentified aerial target entered its airspace from the direction of Ukraine. The object later crashed near the country’s border with Ukraine, with no casualties reported.

Pavel said Russia’s actions reminded him of incidents during his time at NATO, when Russian aircraft repeatedly tested the responses of allied forces.

“They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be,” he said.

In a speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, Pavel said Russia’s “aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security” and warned that the risks were increasing.

The Czech president also questioned whether Russia was genuinely prepared to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine. He said Moscow would need to agree to a ceasefire before entering meaningful negotiations without conditions.

World.title: Breaking: Hungarian parliament suspends PM Magyar’s immunity over alleged phone theft
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament has suspended Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s parliamentary immunity, clearing the way for a criminal investigation into an alleged phone theft dating back to 2024.

The decision was passed with 139 votes in favour, with no votes against and no abstentions at an extraordinary parliamentary sitting on Monday. The Fidesz and KDNP parliamentary groups did not take part in the session, according to Telex.

The case concerns an incident at the Ötkert nightclub in Budapest in June 2024, shortly after the European Parliament election.

Phone allegedly thrown into the Danube

According to the prosecution’s account, Magyar became involved in an argument with a man who was filming him at the nightclub on 21 June 2024. Magyar allegedly took the man’s phone and later threw it into the Danube.

The phone was subsequently recovered from the river with the help of divers. Prosecutors said at the time that the circumstances could constitute the criminal offence of theft.

The case was initially complicated by Magyar’s immunity as a Member of the European Parliament. In September 2024, the Hungarian prosecution requested that the European Parliament suspend his immunity, but the request was not granted. The investigation was consequently closed.

Photo: MTI

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

After Magyar moved from the European Parliament to Hungary’s National Assembly in May 2026, the investigation could be resumed, and prosecutors again requested the suspension of his immunity – this time from the Hungarian parliament.

The suspension does not mean that Magyar has been found guilty. It removes the legal protection that currently prevents investigative measures directly targeting him and allows the criminal proceedings to move forward.

Magyar asked MPs to suspend his immunity

Magyar himself had called on his fellow Tisza MPs to vote in favour of suspending his immunity. Speaking about the issue, the prime minister said that everyone should take responsibility before the law and that he had nothing to hide. He has denied committing a crime and said he would act in the same way again in the circumstances.

Magyar also argued that the prosecution was attempting to put his case alongside what he described as much more serious corruption cases. He criticised what he called members of the former Orbán-era prosecution establishment and accused the authorities of trying to divert attention from alleged corruption during the previous government.

The prosecution has rejected Magyar’s criticism, saying that the authorities’ role is to conduct proceedings lawfully and fairly.

Parliament also lifts immunity in two other cases

Magyar was not the only politician whose immunity was suspended at Monday’s extraordinary sitting.

Parliament also voted 139–0, with no abstentions, to suspend the immunity of former Fidesz minister Balázs Hankó and KDNP MP Miklós Seszták. Their cases concern separate investigations into alleged offences linked to the National Cultural Fund and the Volánbusz company, respectively.

Former minister Balázs Hankó. Photo: MTI

The votes came despite the parliamentary Immunity Committee failing to reach a majority in favour of lifting the protections. The plenary session nevertheless approved all three suspensions.

Read more about the case: Hungarian immunity rights: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

For Magyar, the decision now removes the parliamentary obstacle to investigative measures in the long-running phone case. It remains for the authorities to determine whether the evidence justifies further proceedings against him.

World.title: Shocking numbers: Here’s how much raising children really costs in Hungary
World.content:
Raising children in Hungary can represent a substantial financial commitment for an average-income family, even after taking state benefits and tax allowances into account. A new model calculation estimates what extra financial burden — however inappropriately it sounds — having a first child creates over the course of their upbringing and the mother’s working life.

Let’s imagine a fictional family earning the Hungarian average

The calculation assumes a young couple in which both partners earn a monthly gross salary of HUF 754,700, the average wage reported by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (Központi Statisztikai Hivatal, KSH) for June 2026. Without tax allowances, each would take home roughly HUF 502,000 a month. The model assumes that the mother has her first child at the age of 30 and that subsequent children arrive three years apart.

The children are financially supported until the age of 19. For the first four children, the hypothetical mother eventually returns to work, but after the birth of a fifth child, she is assumed to remain permanently outside the labour market from the child’s third birthday. The calculation is based on 2026 values without discounting future amounts, meaning that money received or lost at different points in the future is simply added together rather than adjusted for its timing.

Ugly question, but what does raising a child cost?

The model divides the financial cost of having children into three main categories. The first is the additional household income required to maintain the family’s standard of living, then the mother’s lost earnings, and finally, the resulting reduction in her future pension. The calculation does not attempt to put a monetary value on the time parents spend caring for children.

According to the same model, each of the second, third and fourth children adds a further HUF 66 million in financial costs. State benefits and tax allowances cover very different proportions of these costs: around 19 per cent for the first child, 97 per cent for the second, 54 per cent for the third and 43 per cent for the fourth.

For a family with three children, the model estimates a total financial burden of around HUF 232 million, of which the state covers approximately HUF 119 million. That leaves roughly HUF 113 million for the family to absorb. The figures are not intended to represent every Hungarian family. Rather, they are based on a hypothetical life course for a couple earning around the national average and are designed to illustrate the economic consequences of having children.

The additional cost of maintaining living standards

To estimate the direct financial burden of children, the model calculates how much additional household income is needed to maintain the family’s previous standard of living. It uses the modified OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) equivalence scale, under which the first adult in a household has a weighting of 1.0, the second adult 0.5, a child under 14 0.3 and an older child 0.5.

Starting from a combined net household income of around HUF 1 million a month, the model estimates that one child increases the family’s income requirement by approximately HUF 201,000 per month during childhood. From the age of 14, this rises to around HUF 335,000 a month. Over 19 years, that produces an estimated additional financial requirement of around HUF 53.8 million per child. The model does not take inflation into account, and assigns the same additional requirement to each subsequent child.

The mothers’ lost earnings

According to Portfolio’s analysis, the second major component is not a direct household expenditure, but an opportunity cost: income the mother would have earned had she not had children. The model assumes that, following childbirth, the mother earns no wages during the first year. In the second year, she earns 25 per cent of the reference income for a woman without children, rising to 50 per cent in the third year. Between the fourth and tenth years, her earnings are assumed to reach 80 per cent of the childless reference income, followed by 90 per cent until retirement.

These percentages are modelling assumptions designed to represent the persistent earnings penalty associated with motherhood found in a Hungarian research. Each subsequent birth is assumed to restart the earnings trajectory. Under these assumptions, the first child results in approximately HUF 37 million in lost earnings. The second, third and fourth children each add a further HUF 11.7 million or so in lost income.

The fifth child produces a substantially different result because the model assumes that the mother leaves employment permanently from the child’s third birthday, at the age of 45. Compared with the working trajectory assumed for a mother of four children, this results in an additional estimated HUF 115.9 million in lost employment income.

The impact on future pensions

Reduced earnings can also translate into lower pension income. The precise effect depends on factors including years of service and how periods spent caring for children are treated for pension purposes. For the purposes of the model, 20 years of retirement and 14 monthly pension payments per year are assumed. The estimated monthly pension for a woman without children is HUF 398,000, compared with HUF 363,000 for a mother of one child. Over the assumed retirement period, that represents a pension disadvantage of approximately HUF 9.9 million.

The second, third and fourth children are assumed to increase this disadvantage only marginally. For the mother of five who permanently leaves employment, the model assumes a monthly pension of HUF 300,000. Compared with the four-child working trajectory, this represents a further estimated HUF 17.4 million in lost pension income. These pension figures are model estimates rather than predictions of what individual mothers will actually receive.

How much does the Hungarian state cover?

Hungary’s family support system combines several forms of assistance, including cash benefits, tax and contribution allowances, and subsidised loans. The model includes CSED and GYED as household income because, from the family’s perspective, these benefits represent additional money available during the child-rearing period. It assumes that the family meets the relevant eligibility requirements for each benefit and tax allowance. Smaller or conditional forms of support are excluded, including certain home-renovation subsidies and benefits unrelated to the number of children. Subsidised loans are considered separately.

The first child would be about one-fifth covered: For the first child, the model estimates the combined value of CSED, GYED, GYES and the one-off maternity benefit at approximately HUF 12.05 million over the relevant period. The model also includes around HUF 2.78 million in family allowance and HUF 4.68 million in family tax allowance. Together, these forms of support amount to approximately HUF 19.5 million. Against a calculated additional financial burden of HUF 100.7 million, the state therefore covers around 19 per cent of the cost associated with the first child.

The second would be the “problem child”: The second child brings a further increase in family allowance and family tax benefits, while the mother also becomes eligible for personal income tax exemption under the assumptions used in the model. Over her entire earnings trajectory, this exemption is estimated to be worth approximately HUF 35.5 million. Including the recurring childcare benefits and other allowances, the additional state support associated with the second child is estimated at HUF 63.4 million. Against an estimated additional financial burden of HUF 65.6 million, that represents approximately 97 per cent.

The third child as the “golden goose”: The family tax allowance increases again with the third child, with its lifetime value rising by approximately HUF 22 million in the model. At the same time, the value of the mother’s income tax exemption falls by around HUF 2.65 million because her earnings are lower as a result of the additional period away from work. Once childcare benefits and the increase in family allowance are included, the additional support is estimated at HUF 35.7 million. That corresponds to around 54 per cent of the HUF 65.6 million additional financial burden.

The coverage falls further with the fourth child: For a fourth child, the per-child level of family allowance and family tax allowance no longer increases. The new child nevertheless generates additional benefits, while the mother’s repeated earnings interruption reduces the value of her income tax exemption. The model estimates net additional state support of approximately HUF 28.5 million, covering around 43 per cent of the HUF 65.6 million additional financial burden. The calculation assumes that both parents can fully use the available family tax allowance through their combined tax position.

What happens with a fifth child?

The fifth child produces a particularly different result because of the model’s assumption that the mother permanently leaves the labour market after the child reaches the age of three. Childcare benefits, family allowance and the family tax allowance continue to provide support, while the model also includes GYET, a benefit for families raising three or more children. However, the mother’s permanent withdrawal from employment substantially reduces the value of income tax exemptions. The model estimates that this reduces the lifetime value of her tax exemption by HUF 26.15 million.

The family also cannot fully use the available family tax allowance in years when it exceeds the tax and contribution liability of the sole working parent. As a result, the level of support improves by only around HUF 1.8 million compared with the four-child scenario in which the mother remains employed. For the five-child family as a whole, the model estimates a total financial burden of approximately HUF 486.9 million. The state covers around HUF 149 million, or roughly 31 per cent, leaving the family with an estimated HUF 337.9 million in financial costs and losses.

Subsidised loans can significantly alter the picture

The calculations above do not include the full effect of Hungary’s subsidised family loans. The Babaváró scheme provides a freely usable loan of up to HUF 11 million. Subject to the relevant conditions, it is interest-free, while the remaining debt can be written off when the third child is born. The CSOK Plusz is a housing loan, with the amount available to a family expecting three children potentially reaching HUF 50 million.

Under the scheme, HUF 10 million of outstanding debt is cancelled after each of the second and third children born following the loan. In the model’s three-child example, a HUF 50 million CSOK Plusz loan would result in total repayments of approximately HUF 44.9 million over 25 years. A market-rate loan of the same size at a constant 6.4 per cent interest rate would result in total repayments of around HUF 100.3 million.

The difference — approximately HUF 55.4 million — represents the combined advantage of the interest subsidy and debt cancellations in this particular calculation. The figure is not added to the earlier family-support totals because the payments occur at different points in time and the comparison simply adds the undiscounted repayments. The take-up of CSOK Plusz also appears limited compared with the number of births, although the two figures are not directly comparable. In 2024, around 11,300 CSOK Plusz contracts were signed, while almost 78,000 children were born in Hungary.

Both subsidised programmes come with conditions linked to family formation. Failure to meet those conditions can result in repayment obligations. For some young people, the child-related obligations attached to these programmes may also make Otthon Start, which does not require a child commitment, an alternative route to consider.

The tax exemption for mothers of two children

The model also raises questions about the economic incentives created by the personal income tax exemption for mothers of two children. From the perspective of having a first child, the measure provides a substantial financial benefit to women who subsequently become eligible for it. After the second child, however, the model points to a more complicated effect. Holding other factors constant, the exemption can increase the financial incentive to remain in employment, because having another child and taking additional time away from work reduces the earnings against which the exemption can be used.

The overall effect on birth incentives therefore depends in part on how strongly the measure affects decisions surrounding the first child compared with subsequent children. The modelling suggests that if policymakers retain the measure, additional forms of support may be needed to ensure that financial incentives do not diminish for families considering a third or subsequent child.

In case you missed it: Hungarian conservative CitizenGO falsely accuses British same-sex couple of abusing their daughter

What the numbers tell us — and what they do not

The figures should not be interpreted as a universal price tag for raising a child in Hungary. The model necessarily relies on numerous assumptions about wages, employment, family size, the timing of births, benefit eligibility, tax liabilities and future pension income. A family earning more than the assumed average would generally face higher income and opportunity costs, while many state benefits are fixed or subject to limits.

As a result, government support would account for a smaller proportion of the overall financial burden. For a lower-income family, support could represent a larger proportion of the cost, provided the household has sufficient taxable income and contributions to make full use of the relevant allowances. The model also does not capture every aspect of parenthood. The time parents spend caring for children, for example, is explicitly excluded.

This also might interest you: PM Magyar promises major family allowance hike and new constitution: here are the deadlines

The wider demographic question

The financial calculation sits within Hungary’s broader debate over family policy and population trends. A replacement-level fertility rate is generally associated with approximately 2.1 children per woman. From that perspective, every additional birth contributes to the demographic picture, while the transition from no children to one child and decisions about larger families have different financial implications.

The model therefore highlights two distinct challenges for family policy: reducing the financial barriers faced by couples considering their first child, while also addressing the particularly large economic costs associated with raising three, four or more children. The calculations suggest that families with a mother who remains outside the labour market for an extended period can lose not only employment income but also access to income-linked tax benefits.

For policymakers, the question is therefore not simply how much money is spent on family support, but how the design of that support interacts with employment, earnings and the number of children a family has. Ultimately, the model describes one hypothetical family rather than the experience of Hungarian households as a whole. Its main finding is that the financial effect of having a child changes considerably depending on birth order, maternal employment and the extent to which the family can use Hungary’s various benefits and tax allowances.

World.title: Northern Ireland vs Hungary: Rossi expects tough game but wants all three points
World.content:
Hungary head coach Marco Rossi expects a difficult Nations League clash in Belfast on Monday, but says his team will be aiming for all three points against Northern Ireland after Friday’s 1–0 defeat to Ukraine.

Speaking at Sunday’s press conference at Windsor Park, Rossi said Hungary had already turned its attention away from the loss to Ukraine and were preparing for a very different type of opponent, MTI reported.

Northern Ireland are expected to pose a more physical challenge, with particular danger coming from set pieces, crosses and long throws. Rossi also highlighted the hosts’ defensive discipline and the experience of players competing in England’s Championship.

“From the first minute to the last, we have to stay focused,” Rossi said, adding that Hungary cannot allow Northern Ireland to build sustained pressure inside the penalty area.

Rossi expects few goals

The Hungary coach said he does not expect an open, high-scoring encounter.

Northern Ireland traditionally place strong emphasis on organisation and defensive stability, and Rossi suggested Monday’s match could follow a similar pattern to previous meetings between the two sides.

He nevertheless made clear that Hungary’s objective remains victory.

Hungary likely to make some changes

Rossi confirmed that the tight schedule means some changes to the starting line-up are unavoidable, although he does not plan a major overhaul from the team that faced Ukraine.

The Hungarian Football Federation said Rajmund Tóth and József Szalai did not travel to Belfast and will therefore miss the game.

Preparation time has also been limited, with less than 48 hours between the Ukraine match and Sunday’s training session. Rossi said video analysis has therefore played an especially important role in preparing for Northern Ireland.

If you missed it: VIDEO: Szoboszlai sends strong message to journalists – but can a national team captain do this?

Injuries remain a concern

Hungary are still without several important attacking players.

Barnabás Varga and Roland Sallai remain unavailable because of injury, while Damir Redzic was also forced out after Friday’s match. Rossi said he would not use the absences as an excuse and insisted Hungary still have enough quality to compete.

“Without them, we will still be competitive,” he said.

Player expects a physical battle

Hungary forward Donát Bárány also spoke before the match and said the team had moved on from the disappointment of the Ukraine defeat. He described Northern Ireland as a much more physical side than Ukraine, with a strong focus on corners, long throws and direct play.

Bárány, who plays for ADO Den Haag, also said he is still rebuilding his fitness after injury and is not yet at 100%.

Hungary will face Northern Ireland at Windsor Park on Monday evening, with kick-off scheduled for 20:45 CET. After losing their opening Nations League match to Ukraine, Rossi’s side will be aiming to get points on the board in Belfast.

World.title: New four-lane road link between Hungary and Romania set for 2029
World.content:
Hungary will continue construction of the M49 expressway all the way to the Romanian border, Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced on Sunday. The project is expected to create a continuous four-lane road connection between the M3 motorway and Satu Mare by mid-2029.

According to Vitézy, the government has secured the financial framework needed to continue the project, which is expected to cost around HUF 190 billion gross.

The first section of the M49, running from the M3 motorway towards Ököritófülpös, is already under construction. Official project data show that this section is around 28.2 kilometres long and is being built as a 2×2-lane expressway, with several grade-separated junctions, bridges and rest areas.

Direct expressway link towards Satu Mare and new border crossing

The next section will extend the road from Ököritófülpös to the Romanian border near Csenger. According to the minister’s announcement, the roughly 45-kilometre continuation is scheduled to be completed by 30 June 2029.

Once finished, the M49 will provide a direct high-capacity road connection from the M3 motorway towards Romania. Hungary’s long-term road network plans designate the M49 as the route linking the M3 with the Romanian border in the Csenger area.

The development will also include a new border crossing. On the Romanian side, a corresponding expressway link towards Satu Mare is also planned, meaning the two projects together are intended to improve road access between north-eastern Hungary and northern Transylvania.

If you missed it: Construction projects in Hungary could be halted for six months over environmental violations

First section nearing completion

Construction of the first M49 section has been under way for several years. The official project covers the M3–Ököritófülpös stretch and includes 28.2 kilometres of new dual carriageway, four grade-separated junctions, five roundabouts and 22 engineering structures, and the contractor is Duna Aszfalt Építő Zrt.

The ministry’s current project database lists the road opening for traffic by the end of 2026.

The M49 is expected to become one of Hungary’s key new cross-border road links towards Romania, alongside existing motorway connections farther south.

Financing had remained uncertain

Vitézy said the continuation had previously faced uncertainty over state funding, even though a construction contract had already been signed.

He also stressed that inherited infrastructure projects will continue to place a heavy burden on Hungary’s central budget over the next two to three years. Large-scale developments such as the M49 and the Mohács bridge naturally span several government terms, but this also means that hundreds of billions of forints in road investment are already built into the 2027 budget even without launching new projects.

The ministry is therefore trying to find room within these constraints to finance long-delayed renovations across the national road network.

World.title: PM Magyar: Parliament to hand over two corrupt politicians to investigators on Monday
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Sunday evening that Hungary’s newly created National Asset Recovery and Protection Office will begin investigating several high-profile corruption cases on Monday, while parliament is expected to vote on lifting the immunity of two former ministers.

In a Facebook post published on Sunday evening, Magyar said the government’s “Operation Purgatory” would move into a new phase on Monday.

“On Monday, the landing begins as part of Operation Purgatory. The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office will begin investigating several high-profile corruption cases. Parliament will also hand over two corrupt politicians to investigators,” Magyar wrote.

The “two corrupt politicians” reference appears to concern former ministers Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták, whose immunity is due to be considered by parliament on Monday. Both face criminal allegations, but neither has been convicted, and both have denied wrongdoing. Parliament is also expected to consider the immunity of Prime Minister Péter Magyar and MP Mária Gurzó in separate cases.

What is the asset recovery office?

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) was established in 2026 as an independent state institution tasked with tracing, protecting and recovering public assets believed to have been unlawfully removed from public ownership.

Under the law establishing the body, it can examine transactions involving public procurement, state subsidies, concessions, EU funds, state-owned companies and other forms of public property. It also has investigative powers and can represent the public prosecution in court in cases falling within its remit.

The office was one of the central elements of Magyar’s “Operation Purgatory”, which he first announced in parliament in June as part of a broader anti-corruption and institutional reform programme.

For more on Monday’s high-profile immunity votes, see our earlier report: Hungarian immunity rights: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

Several corruption cases already in focus

Magyar did not specify in his Sunday post which cases the NVVH would formally open first. He has, however, repeatedly pointed to several high-profile cases involving public funds, state contracts and institutions linked to the former government.

Prosecutors are seeking to suspend Balázs Hankó’s immunity in connection with an investigation into the National Cultural Fund, while Miklós Seszták faces a separate corruption case linked to Volánbusz.

Monday’s extraordinary parliamentary session will add further political weight to the launch of the new office, with lawmakers expected to vote on several immunity cases involving senior politicians.

At the same time, the NVVH is expected to begin turning the government’s anti-corruption campaign into actual investigations and asset-recovery proceedings. That will make Monday an early test of how far the new authority is prepared to go — and which cases it chooses to prioritise first.
