World.title: Hungary moves to cut hospital waiting times with weekend operations and extra pay
World.content:
Hungary is launching a new programme aimed at cutting hospital waiting times by expanding surgery into afternoons and weekends, while offering extra financial incentives to medical teams. The move comes as patients in some hospitals still face waits of several months for planned procedures.

Hospital waiting lists are one of the most visible pressure points in Hungary’s healthcare system.

According to the National Health Insurance Fund’s current waiting-list database, average waiting times for cataract surgery exceed 200 days at several hospitals. At the Markhot Ferenc Hospital in Heves County, the average waiting time over the previous six months stood at 310 days, while patients at the Nagykanizsa hospital waited an average of 246 days. In Zala County, the figure was 188 days.

Against this backdrop, Health Minister Zsolt Hegedűs announced on Sunday that the government is launching a new waiting-list reduction programme previously promised by Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

“There is a strong commitment from the medical profession. Our task now is to bring together the additional funding, professional expertise, the right incentives and the available capacity in a way that allows patients to feel the benefits as soon as possible,” Hegedűs Zsolt wrote.

In his announcement, the minister said the aim is not simply to perform more operations, but to make better use of existing surgical capacity and give healthcare workers a direct financial incentive to take on additional work.

More surgeries after normal hours

The programme will primarily expand operations into the afternoon hours after regular shifts, while hospitals with sufficient staffing and professional capacity will also be able to perform additional surgery at weekends. A new financing incentive will be introduced to support this extra workload.

Hegedűs said a significant share of the additional funding would go directly to the teams that make the extra procedures possible, including doctors, nurses and other hospital staff.

Part of the new funding would be linked to quality indicators, patient-reported outcomes and patient satisfaction. The model is intended to move closer to what Hegedűs described as a “best practice tariff” approach, in which financing rewards both efficiency and measurable clinical outcomes.

Hospitals to be assessed individually

Each hospital will receive its own “problem map” identifying the main bottlenecks limiting surgical capacity. These may include staff shortages, inefficient operating-room management, competition from private healthcare providers and limited personal incentives for additional work.

The ministry also plans to monitor operating-room utilisation, actual surgical time, the time needed to change patients between procedures and the efficiency of the entire process.

Hegedűs argued that operating theatres are among the most expensive parts of hospital infrastructure and that unused capacity represents a significant loss.

If you missed it: Construction projects in Hungary could be halted for six months over environmental violations

Semmelweis and Pécs expanding capacity

Semmelweis University and the University of Pécs are already working on expanding surgical capacity under the programme.

Foreign specialists experienced in ERAS, or Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocols, are also expected to participate. These protocols are designed to shorten hospital stays where medically appropriate, speed up patient recovery and allow hospitals to admit the next patients sooner.

The programme will also include a review and “clean-up” of waiting lists, with the aim of identifying which patients are still genuinely waiting for surgery and removing outdated or inactive cases.

BMI rule also set to change

Another important change concerns orthopaedic surgery. A protocol introduced in April 2025 automatically placed temporary restrictions on certain patients with a BMI above 35. Hegedűs said this rule is now being reviewed.

Instead of an automatic threshold, future decisions would be based on individual patient risk, professional assessment and the judgment of the treating team.

Patients may also receive more comparable information about hospital performance, quality and outcomes, allowing them to make more informed choices about where to seek treatment.

World.title: Construction projects in Hungary could be halted for six months over environmental violations
World.content:
Hungary has tightened its construction rules, allowing authorities to suspend permitting procedures and block new construction or facility permits for at least six months if a project breaches environmental or nature protection requirements.

Hungary’s parliament has approved amendments to the country’s construction rules that significantly strengthen the consequences of environmental violations at major development projects.

Under the new framework, if authorities establish a breach of environmental or nature protection requirements, the relevant construction permitting procedure must be suspended. In addition, new construction or facility permits may be withheld until the unlawful situation is remedied — and for a minimum period of six months, according to Kormány.hu.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar presented the measure as a response to earlier cases in which major projects continued despite environmental concerns.

“We have seen the consequences in recent years when nothing happened after environmental rules were violated during a priority investment. We are putting an end to that now,” Magyar said in a video announcing the change.

The changes also affect major housing developments linked to the Otthon Start programme, where some priority projects may face temporary permitting restrictions while the government reshapes its wider housing construction policy.

Otthon Start projects also face new restrictions

The amendment specifically covers certain large-scale housing projects connected to the government’s fixed 3% Otthon Start housing loan programme.

Under the scheme, large housing projects can receive priority investment status if they meet specific conditions.

According to the government’s Otthon Start Programme Office, qualifying developments generally need to include at least 250 homes, with at least 70% of the units meeting the programme’s eligibility criteria. Priority status can significantly speed up administrative and permitting procedures.

The latest changes, however, introduce the possibility of temporarily halting permits even for projects that have already received priority status.

The government says this is necessary because some previously planned large-scale Otthon Start developments now need to be coordinated with a broader housing construction programme that is still being prepared. The amendment allows the government to set, by decree, a period during which authorities may not issue new permits for certain already-prioritised Otthon Start developments.

If you missed it: Budapest streets could change dramatically under new pedestrian plan

This is potentially significant for developers because priority status was originally designed to speed up these projects. In practice, the new framework means that a fast-track development could still face a pause if environmental rules are breached or if the project needs to be brought into line with the government’s revised housing policy.

New rules for construction material exports

The parliamentary package also removes an earlier restriction on exports of construction materials.

Since 2021, companies planning to export certain building materials have been required to notify the Hungarian state in advance. The state also had a pre-emption right over the products concerned.

That system will now be abolished. Exporters will no longer have to file the same notification, and the state will lose its right to intervene in those transactions or purchase the materials before they are exported.

The change follows a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, which found that the Hungarian mechanism restricted the free movement of goods and therefore conflicted with EU law. The European Commission subsequently launched infringement proceedings after the measure remained in force.

World.title: Cold mornings, warm afternoons: Hungary braces for huge temperature swings next week
World.content:
Hungary is heading into a mostly sunny and dry week, with afternoon temperatures climbing to around 25°C in many areas. The catch: mornings will be sharply colder.

A stretch of settled early autumn weather is expected across Hungary next week, with plenty of sunshine and little to no rain.

According to HungaroMet’s latest forecast, daytime highs will generally remain between 21 and 26°C, keeping conditions pleasantly warm for the end of September and start of October. At the same time, nights and early mornings will feel considerably colder, with minimum temperatures falling as low as 1–2°C in some areas.

The sharp contrast will be one of the defining features of the week.

Weather portal Időkép says daily temperature swings could exceed 20°C in places, particularly where clear skies and light winds allow temperatures to drop quickly overnight before sunshine drives rapid warming during the day.

In practical terms, that means a jacket or cardigan may be essential when leaving home in the morning, while a T-shirt could be enough by the afternoon.

Sunshine dominates the week

Monday is expected to bring largely uninterrupted sunshine across the country, with dry conditions and afternoon temperatures of around 22–26°C.

Tuesday is forecast to remain similarly bright and dry. Morning temperatures could fall to between 1 and 11°C, followed by highs of 22–26°C later in the day.

Wednesday will also be mostly sunny, although some high cloud may reach northern Hungary later in the day. Temperatures are expected to range from around 1–11°C at dawn to 22–25°C in the afternoon.

The dry pattern is then set to continue into Thursday and Friday, with filtered or uninterrupted sunshine and daytime highs mostly between 21 and 25°C.

Despite the warm afternoons, the colder nights mean autumn is becoming increasingly noticeable. Időkép notes that temperatures could fall close to 5°C in many places, while ground frost may still occur in some of the country’s more frost-prone locations.

If you missed it: Budapest streets could change dramatically under new pedestrian plan

Little sign of rain

HungaroMet expects mostly dry conditions throughout the working week, with sunshine dominating and only limited cloud cover at times. Winds should generally remain light or moderate, although stronger gusts may develop locally, particularly around Sopron and parts of eastern Hungary.

The result will be a classic early autumn pattern: cold starts, warm afternoons and large temperature swings throughout the day.

For anyone heading out early, layering will likely be the safest option — because what feels like jacket weather before breakfast may feel almost summery just a few hours later.

World.title: Finance Minister: Moldova Mustn’t Waste EU Funds Intended for Reforms
World.content:
Moldova is preparing draconian but necessary economic and financial reforms designed to align the country with EU standards, says Finance Minister Victoria Belous, and turn the post-Soviet republic into a European one.

However, turning EU financing into better public services is not simple, Belous told BIRN in an interview. Administrative delays are holding up investment, even as the government seeks to finance higher public-sector salaries and prepares tax changes for 2027, she explains.

“The problem for public investment projects is not lack of money but the capacity and efficiency of certain processes which, unfortunately, delay implementation,” Belous said.

This distinction runs through the government’s reform plans generally: spending commitments require dependable income, while investment requires institutions capable of putting projects into practice.

World.title: Hostile Reactions to Kosovo Wartime Leaders’ Verdict Miss Key Point: the Victims’ Ordeal
World.content:
The first-instance verdict in the trial of Hashim Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers was received in Belgrade and Pristina in a predictable manner: as yet another event interpreted through national political narratives.

Belgrade believes the sentences were not severe enough, that the court protected the interests of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, and that it failed to sufficiently take into account the crimes committed against Serbs.

In Pristina, politicians deemed the verdict unjust, and thousands of people took to the streets to express support for the convicted former KLA leaders.

There is nothing new in such reactions. We have witnessed similar responses regarding the verdicts of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY.

World.title: Failings of Bosnia’s ‘Trojka’ Offer Unreformed SDA a Path Back
World.content:
For months, the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s main Bosniak opposition party, the Party of Democratic Action, SDA, has carefully nurtured a singular political narrative: their return to power is not just an ambition, but a mathematical certainty.

After being pushed into the opposition benches in 2022 by a diverse coalition of civic and multi-ethnic parties known as the ‘Trojka’ [The Trio], the SDA under Bakir Izetbegovic has used the campaign for next month’s elections to frame the current administration as a failed foreign-imposed experiment.

However, beneath the confident rhetoric and aggressive campaign videos, independent analysts say the SDA’s triumphant comeback might be more of an internal propaganda illusion than a reality reflected in public sentiment.

Instead of a structural resurgence, the political landscape reveals a deeper, more systemic stagnation where voters feel trapped between an uninspired opposition and a ruling coalition that has rapidly absorbed the very governing vices it once promised to dismantle.

World.title: Bosnia Court Blocks Republika Srpska From Funding Secessionist Lobbying
World.content:
Bosnian lawmaker Denis Zvizdic, who initiated teh legal challenge. Photo: EPA/FELIPE TRUEBA.

Bosnia’s Constitutional Court on Friday declared that budgetary funds used by Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity to pay foreign consulting firms to lobby for independence violate the state’s constitutional architecture.

The ruling targets a consulting agreement signed between the Republika Srpska Representative Office in Vienna and a Montreal-based firm, Dickens & Madson Canada Inc., which listed “the independence of Republika Srpska” as a core political objective.

The legal challenge was initiated in April by a state-level lawmaker, Denis Zvizdic, who argued that using taxpayers’ funds to lobby against Bosnia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity was unconstitutional.

A 2008 ruling allowed the entity to engage foreign firms for general economic promotion. However, the court has now established that funding campaigns explicitly promoting secession represents an assault on the constitutional order.

“The Constitutional Court hereby prohibits all payments from the budget of Republika Srpska regarding the consulting services contract concluded with Dickens & Madson Canada Inc.,” the court said. “Financing lobbying services for goals that run counter to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is strictly incompatible with the constitutional order.”

The applicant, Zvizdic, welcomed the announcement, saying the entity had weaponised massive public funds for anti-state campaigns.

“Public money cannot be used to finance lobbying aimed against the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its territorial integrity, sovereignty and its institutions,” Zvizdic stated.

“This binding decision establishes a clear legal standard: citizens’ money must serve development and investment, not the undermining of the state,” he added.

Under Bosnia’s state-level laws, entities possess no constitutional right to unilateral secession. Furthermore, ignoring or violating a binding order of the Constitutional Court carries severe penalties.

The court said the full text of the judicial decision will be delivered to all parties and published on its official website within the month.

World.title: Week in Review: Spyware, AI and Arrests
World.content:
Montenegro’s parliament failed to debate a motion to dismiss Andrija Mandic of the right-wing New Serbian Democracy party as speaker because there was no quorum to hold the session. The motion came after Mandic sent a message of condolence to the son of the former Bosnian Serb military commander and genocide convict Ratko Mladic following his recent death.

This episode has renewed questions about how much Mandic’s politics have changed. The one-time opponent of Montenegro’s independence and NATO membership has become a speaker of parliament who now regularly speaks about Montenegro’s European future and works with European officials.

World.title: Serbia Sees First TV Debate Between Ruling Party and Student List
World.content:
Serbia’s first election debate ahead of October 25 polls aired on TV on Thursday night, pitting former prime minister and current speaker Ana Brnabic – third on the government’s “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” list – against Mirjana Nikolic, Rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade and a candidate on the rival “Student List – Students Win”.

The debate on the N1 TV channel was supposed to focus on education but quickly expanded into a wider confrontation over the anti-government student movement, the media, universities and the overall political situation.

Nikolic said she was initially apprehensive about debating a senior ruling-party official but welcomed the chance to present the Student List’s programme.

She said her previous meetings with Brnabic at parliament’s Education Committee had been marked by confrontation, adding that the televised debate offered a chance for both sides to present their programmes.

The appearance was notable because ruling SNS officials have largely avoided N1 during previous election campaigns and Brnabic last appeared in 2017.

“To be honest, I was not particularly happy to come to N1 this time either, given the way your television station has, over the past ten years, engaged in what I see as the dehumanisation of my President and my friend,” Brnabic said.

She accused N1 of having spread false information but said she had agreed to appear after Vucic encouraged her to give the television station “a chance”, following its change of management.

The debate quickly became heated, including an exchange over Nikolic’s alleged refusal to shake Brnabic’s hand.

The candidates also clashed over the student-led university blockades. Brnabic said students had been discriminated against “thanks to the Student List and the blockades”, while Nikolic accused her of promoting a misleading narrative about the protests and about how universities functioned.

On education, Brnabic defended the SNS record in government, pointing to higher teachers’ salaries, increased education spending and investment in science and technology infrastructure.

Nikolic challenged the figures, arguing that nominal salary increases did not necessarily mean education workers were better off, and questioned delays to university infrastructure projects.

She also criticised Brnabic’s understanding of Serbia’s education system, telling her: “As a professor, I have to tell you – Ana, you failed, you failed the exam.”

Nikolic said the Student List advocated free education, equal opportunities for students and teachers and the modernisation of the education system.

The debate was the first in a series of thematic election debates announced by N1 ahead of the October 25 parliamentary election.

World.title: Croatia Has Highest Number of Overnight Stays Relative to Number of Inhabitants
World.content:
September the 28th, 2026 – Croatia has the highest number of overnight stays relative to the number of inhabitants according to the latest Eurostat data.

Croatia has officially taken first place on the ranking of countries with the highest number of tourist overnight stays relative to the number of inhabitants. According to the latest Eurostat data, for every 1,000 inhabitants of Croatia, as many as 24,465 overnight stays in tourist accommodation are recorded annually. Index reports that this indicator does not refer to the total number of tourists, but compares the number of overnight stays with the number of inhabitants, so smaller countries that attract a large number of visitors during the year often end up at the top.

croatia steams ahead of malta and cyprus

According to data for 2025, Croatia is in first place ahead of Malta, which has 20,091 overnight stays per 1,000 inhabitants, and Cyprus with 18,533 overnight stays. Among the top ten are also Greece with 14,741 overnight stays, Austria with 14,619, Spain with 10,390, Italy with 9,084, Slovenia with 8,366, Montenegro with 8,339 and Portugal with 8,319 overnight stays per 1,000 inhabitants. Also on the list are the Netherlands with 8,102 and Ireland with 7,788 overnight stays per 1,000 inhabitants.

significant growth for croatia

Croatia reached the top of this ranking after strong tourism growth over the past decade. While Cyprus and Malta previously led according to this indicator, Croatia overtook them in 2016. Growing interest in Croatia was further boosted by the increasing popularity of Adriatic destinations, better connections with European markets, and the global recognition of certain locations. Among the factors that contributed to Croatia’s greater visibility is the popularity of the places where the series “Game of Thrones” was filmed.

By 2025, Croatia had reached 24,465 overnight stays per 1,000 inhabitants, which is about 1.22 times more than Malta, which is in second place.

small european countries attract plenty of attention

The ranking shows that the countries with the highest intensity of tourism are mostly smaller European states that receive a large number of visitors during the year relative to their population. For Croatia, this means that during the tourist season the number of people in individual coastal towns and places multiplies compared to the number of permanent residents.

World.title: Croatia Remains in a Favourable Position With Gas Reserves
World.content:
September the 28th, 2026 – Croatia continues to be in a very favourable position when it comes to gas reserves as autumn and then winter approach.

The Croatian Government has ordered the mandatory acceleration of gas stock filling so that the Okoli underground storage facility reaches the target level of at least 85 percent of capacity by October. Zrinka Gabelica Toplek reports for Poslovni that Croatia ended the summer with an enviable 73 percent gas storage fill level, placing it well above the EU average. While the rest of Europe is intensively preparing for the upcoming heating season, the situation across the continent varies considerably from country to country.

Nevertheless, joint European efforts are yielding results, as the EU average gas storage fill level stands at a solid 65 percent. At the very top of the ranking are Poland and Portugal, which already reached an excellent 93 percent of their capacity by the end of August. Neighbouring Italy also stands out with a high stock level of 83 percent. Croatia shares a high fourth place with Spain, as both countries have secured 73 percent of their stocks. Immediately behind them is France with 71 percent, while neighbouring Hungary records 69 percent and Austria 67 percent fill levels.

On the other hand, several key European economies are still lagging behind the average: Germany recorded only 53 percent storage fill at the end of summer, while Sweden and Slovakia secured exactly half of their capacity – just 50 percent. At the very bottom of the listed countries are the Netherlands with 47 percent and Latvia with 45 percent gas stocks.

This latest data suggest that Croatia is in a favourable position ahead of autumn and winter, but the overall picture at Union level shows that individual countries will have to accelerate the filling of gas storage in the coming weeks in order to achieve full energy security before the first serious cold spells. Although the current 73 percent fill level provides energy stability, the Croatian Government has ordered the mandatory acceleration of gas stock filling so that the Okoli underground storage facility reaches the target level of at least 85 percent of capacity by October, ahead of the official start of the heating season.

World.title: Croatian Agriculture Suffers Tremendously Due to Drought
World.content:
September the 28th, 2026 – Croatian agriculture as a sector has suffered tremendously as a result of long periods of drought this year, with arable land being the most vulnerable of all.

This year’s extreme and long periods of drought has significantly affected the arable production of Podravka Agri, and its final impact on revenues will only be known after all harvesting work is completed. The company told Hina that such a drought in eastern Croatia has not been recorded in the last 20 years. “Since the harvesting of individual crops is still under way, and the lifting of sugar beet has yet to begin, the impact of the drought on total arable revenues will be known only after all work is finished,” they said.

Ana Blaskovic reports for Poslovni that the prolonged lack of rainfall and extremely high temperatures particularly affected spring crops, including maize, soybeans and sugar beet, while sunflower performed somewhat better. An additional problem was the lack of irrigation possibilities due to historically low water levels of the Danube and Drava rivers during the summer months. Unlike the spring crops, winter wheat and barley did not suffer significantly because they finish their vegetation earlier, and their harvest was completed in the first half of July.

Climate extremes are becoming an increasingly important factor in planning agricultural production. At Podravka Agri, headed by Davor Doko, they note that in recent years they have been adapting production technologies and selecting more resistant hybrids and varieties in order to mitigate the consequences of climate change, preserve soil fertility and ensure the continuity of domestic food production.

On the other hand, the long period of dry weather this year also brought one positive consequence: it enabled the high-quality collection and storage of around 100,000 bales of straw, a quantity that will meet the needs of all 19 of Podravka Agri’s cattle farms.

World.title: Strikes Looming: Collapse Awaits Zagreb Today
World.content:
September the 28th, 2026 – Strikes will likely see the City of Zagreb totally collapse today, as ZET, Zagreb Holding and unions are set to down tools.

The management boards of Zagreb Holding and Zagreb Electric Tram (ZET) announced recently that a meeting with the unions failed to produce an agreement that would avert the strike today. According to their statement, the meeting was convened in another attempt to bring the positions of the employers and the unions closer and to prevent the strike.

“Despite acting in good faith, the representatives of the representative unions presented expanded demands to the managements of both companies as a condition for avoiding the strike, compared with those put forward during the mediation procedures,” the managements of Holding and ZET claim. Index reports that as an example, they cite the demand by the unions in Zagreb Holding for an increase in the base salary.

According to the managements, during mediation the unions sought a 12 percent increase in the base, while at today’s meeting they demanded 13 percent. “The managements of Zagreb Holding and ZET could not accept such an offer from the representative unions, which was presented as a condition for the strike not to take place,” they stated.

what do the unions say?

That no agreement was reached and that the strike will go ahead today was confirmed formally by Mumin Hodžić, president of the Union of Communal Workers and Drivers of Čistoća. He said the unions had “reduced” the percentage of the base salary increase to 13 percent, as well as the demands related to night-work and second-shift allowances. “We’ve given up on many things and we don’t intend to give up on anything else, especially since the other side has no other proposal except the one it already put forward,” he said.

Asked whether talks would continue tomorrow, he replied that they would not. “We came on Saturday at noon, we responded to the meeting, we put forward our offer with the aim of preventing the strike, reaching an agreement and avoiding the collapse that will happen today. However, the other side, which has constantly accused the unions of irresponsibility and this and that, came to the meeting only to hear what we would offer, while they themselves made no offer whatsoever,” he said.

“we were surprised by the offer from union reps”

Ivan Novaković, president of the Management Board of Zagreb Holding, told reporters that they were “totally surprised by the offer from the union representatives” because, he said, “they demanded more than their final offer at the end of mediation, so the meeting ended unsuccessfully.” Marko Bogdanović, president of the Management Board of ZET, said he expects arbitration at the beginning of next week to “provide an answer to the question of which essential services must continue during the strike.” The unions of ZET and Zagreb Holding had earlier sought a 19 percent increase in workers’ material rights, i.e. salaries, and the conclusion of collective agreements for a longer period. The managements had offered a 4.5 percent increase in the base salary.

the strike is due to begin today at 15:30, and the city will be left practically with zero public transport

Unless a new agreement is reached in the meantime, the strike by workers of ZET and Zagreb Holding has begun. The unions had previously announced that Zagreb could in that case be left practically without public transport. Dražen Jović, president of the Union of Transport and Communal Services of Croatia, said there is a high probability that not a single ZET vehicle will run after that point today.

The unions also described the situation by saying that if the strike goes ahead on the announced scale, people “will not see a single one of our vehicles.” Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević also warned that it is very likely that not a single tram will leave the depot and that public transport could come to a near-complete standstill during the day. He called on citizens who do not have to travel to stay at home, and on those who must go to work to leave earlier and expect significantly heavier traffic. He urged employers, where possible, to allow work from home and more flexible working hours. Tomašević also said that the City of Zagreb does not intend to pay workers for the days they spend on strike.

waste collection will also grind to a halt

The strike later today wouldn’t affect only ZET. Workers of Zagreb Holding perform a range of communal services, including waste collection, road maintenance and upkeep of green areas. The unions have announced that essential services will still be carried out. These include waste collection from hospitals, kindergartens, health centres and homes for the elderly, as well as burials. Regular household waste collection could, however, be entirely suspended or at the very least significantly reduced.

It has still not been fully resolved how many workers will have to continue to perform their essential duties during the strike. The managements of ZET and Holding proposed that a portion of employees continue working during the strike, but the unions rejected that proposal, which is why the matter has gone to arbitration.

World.title: Nations League: Croatia celebrate in Prague, Slaven Bilić kicks off with a win
World.content:
Croatia began their new Nations League campaign with a win, beating the Czech Republic 2-1 (0-0) in Prague in the opening round of Group 3 of the elite League A.

It was also a winning start for Slaven Bilić, who returned to the role of Croatia head coach, succeeding the trophy-laden Zlatko Dalić.

After a goalless first half, Croatia took the lead in the 47th minute when Luka Modrić scored his 30th goal for the national team.

The Czechs equalized seven minutes later, with Adam Karabec on target for 1-1. Croatia’s winning goal was scored by Marco Pašalić in the 77th minute, following a fine assist from Ivan Perišić.

Match report

Croatia’s indestructible captain Luka Modrić started the match, while Martin Baturina missed the game due to a virus. New Croatian talent Luka Vušković was also in the starting eleven, with Igor Matanović leading the attack.

The start of the match was fairly cautious on both sides, especially from the hosts. Croatia were the first to establish some authority on the pitch, and the first notable moment for the Czechs came in the 10th minute. Kovačić broke through a Czech line and set up Ivanović, whose shot was blocked. Three consecutive Croatian corners followed, but without any real chances.

The first big opportunity came in the 23rd minute, again after Kovačić launched a Croatian attack. The ball eventually reached Luka Sučić, who aimed for the far corner, but his shot flew just wide of the post.

The Czech players were largely harmless in attack, and even when they reached dangerous areas near the Croatian goal, they struggled to convert their approach play into real threats. Play remained largely in Croatia’s attacking half for the rest of the first half, with the best chance falling to Petar Sučić in the 42nd minute. A brilliant feint freed him from his marker, but his shot was saved by Czech goalkeeper Horniček, securing a 0-0 scoreline at the break.

Matanović also went close in the 45th minute with a long-range effort that passed just wide of the Czech goal.

Croatia took the lead immediately at the start of the second half. In the 46th minute, Matanović slid in to intercept a pass in the Czech defence. Modrić collected the loose ball, advanced to around 14 meters and finished into the far corner to put Croatia ahead. The Czechs created their first real chance in the 54th minute, and it paid off instantly with an equalizer. Hložek played the ball back into the Croatian box, and Karabec finished precisely to make it 1-1.

The two goals ignited the match, with the Czechs in particular looking energized and pushing forward with more purpose. Several dangerous moments followed at both ends, prompting Croatia coach Bilić to make his first substitutions, along with a change in formation — shifting to a back three, with Perišić moving further forward from a wing-back role.

In the 71st minute, the Czechs had a golden chance to turn the match around. Radosta received the ball in front of the Croatian goal but, in a one-on-one with Livaković, shot wide of the target.

Modrić was withdrawn in the 76th minute, replaced by Mišić, and just a minute later Croatia retook the lead. Perišić broke down the left and curled a superb cross into the Czech box. Marco Pašalić rose to head it home for 2-1.

This time Croatia’s lead lasted even less. Just two minutes later, with plenty of gaps in the Croatian defence, Radosta found the net to make it 2-2 — but the goal was disallowed for offside. The Czechs pushed unsuccessfully for an equalizer until the final whistle, with Croatia repelling every attack to secure all three points on the opening matchday of the Nations League.

Croatia’s best late chance fell to Budimir, who fired a shot in the 93rd minute, but Czech goalkeeper Horniček denied Croatia’s third goal.

In the next round, Croatia travel to Seville on September 29 to face reigning world champions Spain.

Two home matches follow: against England at Rujevica on October 3, and against Spain at Poljud on October 6.

World.title: Millions Still Being Spent on Tito’s Dilapidated Galeb Ship
World.content:
September the 27th, 2026 – Millions are still being spent on Tito’s dilapidated Galeb ship, with deadlines broken and no museum in sight.

The (in)famous, rusty old vessel Galeb has a history stretching from its construction back in the 1930s, through sinking during WWII to the status of Tito’s ship and a symbol of the Non-Aligned Movement. It is still waiting for its final conversion into a museum. Index reports that in more recent years, its story has been reduced to moves between different shipyards, successive deadline overruns and constantly rising costs. Around €22 million has so far been invested in the renovation and conversion, partly from EU funds.

more repairs, more deadlines

Galeb is now going to the Viktor Lenac Shipyard for the repair of damage caused in February, when a Turkish cargo ship hit it. The cost of the repair will be covered by the insurance of the Turkish ship, and at the same time the regular annual overhaul will also be carried out. President of the Management Board of the Viktor Lenac Shipyard, Luka Hrboka, confirmed the price of the works. “The amount is €860 thousand including VAT. The whole ship was built in the riveted system and that could be a bit more demanding than on some standard ship,” Hrboka stated for RTL. The ship should return to the Rijeka Port in about one month.

Project burdened by postponements

The museum on Galeb was supposed to open its doors back in 2021. The last announced deadline was February of this year. Now the opening has been postponed to the end of the year. Rijeka Mayor Iva Rinčić believes that the project was problematic from the start.

“I think there was a series of, I will dare to say, wrong decisions, from the purchase itself to, of course, the costs that exceeded the deadlines and so on. Now we are in a situation that in talks and negotiations with the Central Agency for Financing and Contracting of EU Programmes and Projects we are trying to open the ship and bring the project to an end so that we avoid as many penalties as possible,” Rinčić said.

the museum display is ready

From the Museum of the City of Rijeka they say that around 90 percent of the permanent display is ready. The exhibition will, through original objects, cover the entire history of Galeb, and not only the period related to Josip Broz Tito.

“Tito recognised it as an interesting vessel. He observed a military exercise of the Yugoslav Navy and, when he saw that the ship was very interesting, it simultaneously became both a school ship and his residential yacht for travels around the world. Of course we document all those attractive moments on the ship,” explained the spokesperson of the Museum of the City of Rijeka, Velid Đekić. That Galeb as a museum will certainly attract visitors is also believed by Rijeka resident Slavko Vanino. “Enemies will also come and will spit on it there,” he joked and added that the ship will certainly attract attention. After a series of unforeseen problems and broken deadlines, hope remains that Galeb will finally be opened to the public by the end of the year.

World.title: Patients of One Croatian Hospital Will Need to Pay While Waiting for an Examination!
World.content:
September the 27th, 2026 – Patients of one Croatian hospital will have to pay while waiting for an examination. It’s safe to say the users of Pula Hospital are far from impressed with these latest rules.

The body that came up with these new rules would do well to remember that people generally do not come to hospital because they want to, but because they have to. As of the 1st of October, parking charges will begin in the grounds of Pula Hospital: the first hour is free, and every subsequent started hour costs two euros. Poslovni reports that that sounds simple until you sit in the waiting room and realise that you don’t actually know whether you will be called in ten minutes or in two hours.

People generally aren’t rocking up at a hospital because they fancy a break. They come sick, injured, worried, devastated, waiting for test results, sitting down anxiously awaiting examinations, or as concerned companions to someone who cannot manage alone. It isn’t a walk in the park, nor is it predictable. Then, in addition to worrying about their health or the health of their loved ones, they now also apparently need to make sure they find mental room think about the clock that is ticking outside in the car park. After three hours of stay, the bill will amount to four euros, regardless of whether you spent the time at an examination or waiting for an examination.

The hospital says that by charging it wants to free up spaces for patients and that is a goal that makes sense. However, in typical Croatian style, this idea lacks logic and hasn’t been properly thought through whatsoever. It is hard to ignore that the bill will also be paid by those who are there precisely as patients with more than enough going on. Free parking is, however, provided for people on dialysis during the procedure and for oncology patients for the duration of any active therapy. While that is of course a good thing, it leaves even more room for confusion.

World.title: Minister: Trump-Zelenskyy UN encounter did not bring peace any closer
World.content:
The meeting took place last Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly (UNGA), which Tsahkna attended.

The minister noted it focused more on practical issues, such as licensing the production of Patriot systems under license, intelligence and defending Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

On the other hand, it did not move things any close to peace, Tsahkna went on, talking to "Ukraina stuudio".

"We have not actually moved any closer to peace, and Zelenskyy was absolutely right when he said in his speech and comments that it seems all the world's leaders want peace, but the only person who does not is Putin. The fact that the meeting with President Trump took place on the sidelines of the UN was good news by itself. I also got the opportunity to meet the Ukrainian foreign minister immediately after he came out of the room. He said it had been more of a practical meeting," Tsahkna said.

"President Zelenskyy has clearly said that they are prepared, if Russia stops bombing their energy infrastructure, to also halt their deep strikes. But in reality, nothing like that happened. And perhaps an even more interesting meeting, about which we know less, was the meeting between [U.S. Special Envoys] Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and the Ukrainian negotiating team, which took place after the meeting between President Trump and Zelenskyy, where perhaps something more practical was discussed," Tsahkna went on.

The meeting between US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov bore little fruit, Tsahkna added.

"They were still talking about the same things: That President Trump wants peace and that further meetings would be arranged. And the only major step we know about publicly is that President Putin was invited to attend the G20 summit. /.../ Russian propaganda will certainly take advantage of this opportunity to show that world leaders want to meet him, that he is emerging from the pressure of isolation and that he is an equal among everyone else. And in some ways, that does nothing to help bring peace to Ukraine."

Tsahkna was also critical of the meeting between German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Lavrov.

"We understand that Wadephul raised the issue of the Leipzig attack, but if we look at Russian propaganda, the image presented was essentially one in which Wadephul was very eager to meet. It was a total Russian propaganda victory, I would say, or at least they exploited it to the maximum, and it came across more as a humiliation. Just consider the historical ties between Russia — the successor to the Soviet Union — and Germany. Russia is essentially attacking Germany militarily today, although it is not at the level of Article 5, and then this meeting takes place, after which Lavrov even says, so to speak, that they accommodated the Germans by agreeing to meet and hear them out. And then comes the full-blown propaganda," Tsahkna said.

Margus Tsahkna. Source: ERR

According to Tsahkna, Russia's top leaders have recently become increasingly amenable as diplomatic interlocutors as well.

"Unfortunately, they are increasingly being treated as acceptable interlocutors, with more and more meetings taking place. But I also had a longer meeting with the Indian foreign minister, who explained that India is currently working very actively to secure an agreement on the Black Sea, particularly on grain exports. And I would also remind you that the Russians sank or fired on ships carrying quite a few Indian sailors. This is something that greatly concerns India. So in that sense, the expansion of the war beyond Ukrainian territory, both into Europe and affecting other countries or citizens connected with other countries, is something that has made many people nervous, particularly the issue of food security and the closure of the Black Sea," Tsahkna continued.

Tsahkna said he had to explain to some colleagues the realities of hybrid warfare versus the credible threat of an actual attack from Russia.

"This is something people are very concerned about, and it also gives us an opportunity to explain that, first of all, we do not see Russia carrying out military maneuvers beyond our borders. However, Russia is using all kinds of hybrid methods, drone attacks, sabotage and terrorist attacks — no longer so much directly against the Baltic states as against Germany and some other large countries. And globally, nobody really likes that. An aggressive Russia is not something anyone likes, and this casts Putin in a bad light, in a new way," Tsahkna said.

"And if you look at the headlines, it seems as though Russia is preparing for war and is about to attack someone in this region. But if you read the intelligence reports or talk to our intelligence people, who have a very good view of what is happening in Russia, they continue to say that the likelihood of preparations for a military invasion or aggression remains extremely low," the minister went on.

"Many different things are being combined, and that only benefits Russia if it creates this atmosphere of fear, this fear of escalation. And that is very characteristic of the Western world: for God's sake, let's not escalate, let's not be the ones to escalate, because otherwise we might end up at war. And that is simply one method of pressure that Putin has been using very skilfully against Western democracies for years," Tsahkna said.

Zelenskyy said during Tuesday's meeting he urged Trump to press Beijing to marshal its influence over Moscow, in order to help bring the invasion to an end.

Washington meanwhile is seeking initial "technical" talks between U,S,, Ukrainian and Russian delegations, with the UAE suggested as a possible venue

Zelenskyy also said Trump had approved the process to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot air defense systems under license.

The Wadephul-Lavrov meeting on Saturday was the first such talks since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Russia began in February 2022, and was largely fruitless.

World.title: 7-year sentence handed down to Oleg Bessedin for anti-Estonia activities
World.content:
The first-tier Harju County Court on Monday found Oleg Bessedin guilty, and also convicted him of repeated violations of international sanctions, under a plea agreement made last week.

The court found that the plea agreement complied with the law and had been entered into voluntarily, and approved it. Under the ruling, the state will confiscate €77,104.32 worth of assets owned by Bessedin. Procedural costs totaling €3,195.80 will also be covered from these seized funds.

The ruling follows a plea bargain reached with the Office of the Prosecutor General on the first day of Bessedin's trial, last Tuesday, September 22. He was arrested in November 2025 and has been detained in custody since then.

Bessedin, 52, was charged with activities against Estonia's national security, including spreading pro-Kremlin propaganda and distributing sanctioned Russian content, dating back to May 2022 and in coordination with Russian state organs and individuals involved in influence operations.

Harju County Court hearing which confirmed Oleg Bessedin's 7-year prison sentence. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

The activities entailed producing and disseminating narratives justifying Russia's war of aggression, false claims and fear-mongering rhetoric, primarily via a YouTube channel, with the aim of dividing Estonian society, reducing trust in state institutions and undermining support for NATO and the EU.

Bessedin was also found guilty of repeatedly violating sanctions imposed under Council of the European Union Regulation No. 269/2014 by allowing the TV channel TVN, which he controlled, to broadcast a program from a sanctioned Russian media outlet; publishing content linked to a sanctioned media outlet on his social media platform; transferring the screening rights to three of his films to a sanctioned Russian state media agency; and helping to launch a television channel through which content from Russian television channels under EU sanctions was broadcast.

Initially, under the plea agreement, he was to forfeit more than €73,000 in assets and serve seven years in prison. The court's ruling on Monday approved this agreement. The Harju County Court ruling has not yet entered into force.

World.title: Almost all forms of heating to become more expensive for Estonians this winter
World.content:
Prices for nearly all types of heating will rise as the heating season gets underway. The increase will be particularly steep for those who heat with natural gas, as its price on the global market has more than doubled.

Most homes in Estonia are heated by central heating, but wood-burning stoves, gas heating and heat pumps are also used. Global fuel prices have risen because of ongoing crises and this could have an impact on the cost of heating homes this winter.

Merike Kaljula, a longtime music teacher in Türi, still heats the more than 100-year-old house where she was born with firewood. Although firewood became more expensive this year, she believes switching to another type of heating would cost even more.

"I've been offered electric heating, like the heat pumps and everything they have now, but I don't want it. I bought my firewood at the beginning of May and it was €80 per cubic meter, and I bought 15 cubic meters. It is more expensive, but since I'm happy with Toosikannu, I'm not complaining," Kaljula said.

Mart Liivak, head of firewood sellers Harju Puu, said the increase in firewood prices over the past year has nevertheless been small because raw material prices have remained stable. There is a significant price difference between wet and dry firewood.

"The price of dry firewood may rise by 5 to 10 percent at most. When producing kiln-dried firewood, wood chips — which we use to heat the drying chamber — are a fairly significant expense for us. Electricity costs are also considerably higher. The lowest cost is for fresh, loose firewood, which explains the large price difference," Liivak said.

Wood pellets, however, are reaching record-high prices. They did not see their usual summer price decline because Estonia's pellet exports to Poland have increased by half.

"They had this Clean Air program, which helped quite a large proportion of people replace their wood-fired boilers, coal-fired boilers and old heating systems with more modern ones," Liivak said.

Central heating can be used to heat a row house or several apartment buildings at once. More than half of Estonia's residents, however, use district heating, through which heat producers supply large heating areas.

"We have eight district heating areas, including Tallinn and Maardu. Unfortunately, prices are indeed rising in five of the eight, with an average increase of around 10 percent. We've seen a relatively large increase in fuel prices. As for Tallinn specifically, the Iru waste-to-energy unit supplies heat to Tallinn residents and it raised its price by 6 percent this spring. Wood chips have risen by around 20 percent, by our estimate," said Robert Kitt, head of Utilitas Estonia.

The main culprit behind the price increases, however, is natural gas, which district heating companies use to produce between one-third and one-half of their heat. Compared with the previous heating season, the market price of natural gas has risen two and a half times because of the Hormuz crisis. Elenger is trying to keep its price increases smaller.

"The average price during the previous heating season was €0.54 per cubic meter and today it is €0.96. That's not a doubling," said Elenger Commercial Director Armen Kasparov.

Elenger has 15,000 customers who heat their homes with gas. Most live in detached houses, while 25 percent are apartment associations with their own boilers. The size of their price increase depends on the gas plan they use.

"If you've been on a market-price plan, that's the fairest comparison. You can expect an increase of 35 to 40 percent compared with the previous heating season, while district heating providers will also see some percentage increase," Kasparov said.

Narva is in the worst situation because the city's district heating system depends predominantly on gas. In a city where heating was inexpensive until recently, heating prices have now risen to the highest level in Estonia.

"There is one municipality in Latvia where it is even more expensive. They're at €150, while we're at €137 per megawatt-hour. And what's the reason? The price of gas," Narva Mayor Jaan Toots said.

Natural gas is currently more expensive than shale oil. Narva is asking the state for a special permit to use shale oil for heating this winter, saying residents could otherwise become unable to pay their bills.

"Thirty percent are pensioners and 13 percent are unemployed and both figures are considerably higher than in Estonia as a whole. And that hurts. Worst of all, of course, we have Khrushchev-era apartment buildings that, partly because of the residents themselves, have not been insulated or weatherproofed and have old windows, so the costs are enormous. Heating now eats up half the money pensioners receive. So this is a very serious problem for me as mayor and we hope the Environmental Board grants the exemption," Toots said.

The Environmental Board will issue Narva a special heating permit next week. Utilitas is also considering applying for one.

"As a provider of an essential service, continuity is naturally one of the most important things for us and we are seriously considering applying for permission to use other reserve fuels, including shale oil, should the need arise," Kitt said.

Utilitas will be able to reduce its dependence on gas to below 10 percent during the next heating season as a large-scale wastewater and seawater heat pump plant in Paljassaare nears completion.

World.title: NATO aircrews training in Estonia again this week
World.content:
NATO air defense aircraft based in the Baltic states are conducting training flights in Estonian airspace this week, including low-level flights.

Some flights may reach supersonic speeds, producing a shock wave and a sonic boom that can sound like an explosion or artillery fire.

This is the second consecutive week that NATO aircrews have conducted training flights in Estonian airspace.

The flights take place from Monday, September 28 to Sunday, October 4, between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m.

Any low-level flights will be conducted at an altitude no lower than 152 metres (500 feet). Aircraft may pass near populated areas or individual farms, although populated areas will be avoided where possible.

Today, Monday, between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., the Spanish Air Force contingent currently based at Ämari will be conducting live-fire exercises over the sea between Saaremaa and Hiiumaa using their y F/A‑18 Hornets' onboard canon, rehearsing drone neutralization. The Estonian Navy patrol vessel EML Valve will be involved in safety checks of the maritime area, while the entire exercise will be monitored and coordinated by the Estonian Air Force's Air Operations Control Squadron.

Spanish Air Force F/A‑18 Hornets. Source: Mil.ee

Low-level flights are planned for Hiiumaa, Lääne and Harju counties on October 1 between noon and 3 p.m., with October 2 between 9 a.m. and noon designated as a reserve date.

The Air Force asks the public not to be alarmed by increased aircraft noise during the training period. All flight exercises will be conducted in accordance with Estonian law and held in coordination with the civilian Estonian Transport Administration and Estonian Air Navigation Services (EANS).

Under a NATO decision, allied member states' air forces provide air defense for Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, whose air forces currently do not have fast jets. The mission is based at Ämari Air Base in Estonia and at Šiauliai Air Base in Lithuania.

The NATO air mission was recently upgraded to a defense posture. The mission is a routine peacetime operation, with allied aircraft on standby to respond to airspace violations.

The mission is held on a rotating basis by the air forces of NATO member states who have fast jet capacity. Turkey's Air force, flying F-16 Fighting Falcons, was recently joined at Ämari the Spanish F-18s.

World.title: Estonia law change will allow domestic cellphone roaming during crises
World.content:
From Thursday, mobile customers in Estonia will be able switch to a rival operator's network if their own is damaged during a crisis situation.

This follows the adoption in summer of wide-ranging legislation on crisis situations, including the introduction of domestic roaming between the three major suppliers, Elisa, Tele2 and Telia, where needed.

Domestic roaming will apply nationwide and is reserved for the most severe emergencies such as those affecting national security, and not during, for instance, electricity outages that often follow autumn storms, officials said.

From October 1, if a customer's own operator's network has been damaged, they can switch to another operator's network whose mast is still standing.

"This will work across the entire territory of Estonia. Since we are so small, it does not make sense to do this on a county-by-county basis. People's phones will select whichever operator is working in that location if their home network is not working," Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs spokesperson Mart Laas said.

"It seems disproportionate to activate such a large mechanism because of storms. The aim is for situations where there is a war or a very serious state of emergency in which a telecommunications company's network has suffered significant damage, is out of service and will clearly take a long time to restore," Laas went on.

Tele2, for example, has around 1,500 telecommunications antennae across Estonia. Some are mounted on tall telecommunications masts, while others have been installed on the roofs of buildings.

Tele2 technology director Tanel Sarri said there are several scenarios and crises which the company has had to prepare for.

"We need to have redundant external connections, batteries must be ready, generators — these are things we have worked on over the years," he said.

According to Sarri, Tele2 is already crisis-resilient; power outages even in a storm are now accounted for.

"The most important nodes are backed up by generators, while smaller sites have battery backup in order to ensure nationwide coverage, primarily outdoors," Sarri added.

The Crisis Situation and National Defense Act, adopted by the Riigikogu in the summer and entering into force on October 1, combines three existing laws on national defense and crisis management into a single framework. It assigns specific crisis tasks to local governments and introduces a nationwide crisis plan, along with changes to how the Estonian Defense Forces commander is appointed. Among its provisions is the introduction of domestic roaming, allowing mobile customers to switch to a rival operator's network if their own is damaged in a crisis.

World.title: Rae child protection services strained by migrants claiming to be minors
World.content:
Child protection services in Rae Municipality, just outside Tallinn, are under pressure from the number of cases of migrants who are minors authorities are having to process.

A total of 60 migrants held at the municipality's detention center have claimed to be minors; investigations proved this was the case in only two instances however.

Mayor of Rae Gerli Lehe (Isamaa) says each claim takes about a day and a half to process; the municipality has asked for "significantly" more state support from the start of next month.

Since September 17, police have detained 46 foreign nationals who entered Estonia illegally via Latvia, having crossed the border from Belarus.

The trend is part of a broader wave since July that Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) has described as organized activity by another state.

Migrant minors are protected under EU law, which has led to some false age claims as well as genuine ones. Municipal officials, who must respond immediately when notified that unaccompanied minors have arrived, say all the claims have produced a flood of work.

Our child protection specialists have to respond immediately when we receive notification from the detention center that unaccompanied minors have arrived there. It takes about a day and a half to deal with one person, and as their guardian we have to be present for all procedures involving them," Mayor Lehe told "Aktuaalne kaamera".

Since September, the state Social Insurance Board (SKA) has taken on some of the workload.

"The law stipulates that in an emergency, the Social Insurance Board steps in to assist the local government. We fully understand Rae municipality's situation at the moment: it is difficult, a large number of people requiring representation have arrived at once, and this has created a need to reorganize work at short notice," said Kaja Rattas, head of SKA's substitute care unit.

The new detention centre in Rae Municipality, just outside of Tallinn. Source: ERR

Lehe acknowledged that SKA has been providing support to the municipality outside working hours and at weekends, but added that the overall migration crisis cannot be left for Rae to resolve alone.

"Within our crisis plan, we have provided that for up to three months, until October 1, we are prepared to support the state. After that, we expect resources and significantly greater assistance from the state," Lehe continued.

The municipality says the workload also prevents child specialists from dealing with children in need from the Rae municipality itself, adding it wants to solve this.

Another issue is providing education to minors residing at the detention center: So far it is not clear what form this education should take, including in what languages.

"We are working this out together. This really is a new situation for Estonia, with children — or alleged children — in Estonia who speak such uncommon languages," Rattas said.

There are insufficient municipal funds to provide the educational services in any case; Helen Meumers, who heads up the children and families department at the Ministry of Social Affairs, said the extent of state support to be provided to Rae municipality is up for negotiation.

"As for specific practical support, Rae municipality and the Social Insurance Board must of course primarily discuss that between themselves. But since the decision has already been made that the Social Insurance Board will support Rae municipality, I believe the extent of that support and the need for it are matters for negotiation," Meumers said.

Since July, police have detained 187 foreign nationals who entered Estonia illegally, 72 of whom been handed over to Taro said the entries come in organized waves from forest camps in Belarus; Estonia has expanded its border-guard rotation on the Latvia-Belarus border and appealed to Finland for assistance.

Since mid-September alone, the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) have detained 46 foreign nationals who entered Estonia illegally via Belarus and Latvia; a court ordered a 54-year-old Romanian citizen to be held in custody on suspicion of human trafficking.

World.title: Mass publication of data on deceased persons makes historians' work easier
World.content:
In September, the Ministry of the Interior began publishing, as open data, the names, birth and death dates, and personal identification codes of deceased persons. For historians and name researchers, machine‑readable data makes research easier.

Enel Pungas, head of the population operations department at the Ministry of the Interior, explained that publishing the data is important, for example, for institutions with which the deceased had contracts. "All institutions need this information that a person has died," she said.

Historian and name researcher Fred Puss said that in many countries data about deceased persons has been public for decades. According to Puss, the data is also important for historians, and searching for it across different registers has been difficult — especially concerning people who died between 1944 and 1957.

A name researcher can learn from this data, for example, when a particular surname in Estonia died out — meaning when the last bearer of that name passed away.

"Unfortunately, this happens constantly. Forty‑four percent of all Estonian surnames are represented by only one bearer, and when that one bearer dies, the name disappears from Estonia. A large part of those names are not of Estonian origin, but among them are also Estonian names," Puss said.

The Data Protection Inspectorate asked the Ministry of the Interior to assess, before publishing the names, whether making them public could cause discomfort to the relatives of the deceased.

"In the Estonian Personal Data Protection Act there is even a provision that allows certain personal data of deceased persons to be processed without consent, but if such data is processed more broadly as open data, then in fact an additional impact assessment should be carried out," said Geili Keppi, a lawyer at the Data Protection Inspectorate.

Pungas said that as a result of the impact assessment, the data of the deceased will not be published immediately, but seven days after death. The Statistics Office and the Estonian Institute for Health Development have also reviewed the level of detail in death‑cause statistics to ensure that no one can be identified by cause of death.

World.title: Survey: most employees handle personal matters during working hours
World.content:
A CV.ee survey shows that the strict line between working time and personal time has long blurred in many workplaces.

CV.ee job portal conducted a survey (link in Estonian) about how people use their working time. A little over a 1,000 people responded to the questionnaire.

The results showed that 76 percent of respondents deal with personal matters during working hours, said CV.ee's marketing and communications specialist Gertu Matikainen.

"For example, going to the doctor, taking a child to kindergarten, or handling some other unavoidable matter is not always possible to push outside working hours," Matikainen said. "And if an employee can arrange such obligations flexibly and work tasks are always completed, it may be a reasonable solution compared with strictly separating nine‑to‑five working time and the rest of life."

Company culture matters

Nearly three‑quarters of respondents use working time to visit a doctor or handle other health‑related errands. In addition, personal emails are sent and time is spent on social media, Matikainen noted.

The study shows that people themselves see this rather as situation‑based. 51 percent of respondents believe that handling personal matters during the workday should be approached according to the situation and also the company's culture.

Matikainen said that flexible work arrangements must have clear boundaries so that personal errands do not hinder the completion of work tasks. Such flexibility may in turn mean that people are willing to deal with work also in their free time. For example, slightly under half of respondents read work emails every day while on vacation.

For the employer, flexible work arrangements can be positive, because they give the employee the opportunity to organize their life better and may reduce daily stress. For example, an employee can go to the doctor or handle child‑related obligations without having to take a separate vacation day for each such matter.

What people are thinking

How much do you deal with personal matters during working hours at your job? Some answers by people on the streets of Tartu:

"Very minimally, working time is working time, in that sense I respect working time and I respect my company."

"For me there isn't really much difference between work and personal matters. My work is different, I don't go to work in the usual way."

"Sometimes there is time during work to handle some personal matters, for example to write an email or pay a bill."

Most common personal tasks done during working hours:

Going to the doctor or handling health‑related errands (74%)

Sending and/or reading personal emails (66%)

Spending time on social media (41%)

Planning trips or making bookings (28%)

Child‑related errands (e.g., taking to kindergarten/school etc.) (24%)

Going to the store (24%)

Household chores, such as cleaning or repairs (22%)

Shopping in online stores (22%)

Source: CV.ee survey
