World.title: Tajikistan launches new construction materials enterprise in Khorog city
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 28. Tajik President Emomali Rahmon inaugurated a new construction materials production enterprise in the industrial zone of Khorog city, Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Region of Tajikistan.

According to the press service of the President of Tajikistan, the enterprise produces plastic doors and windows, construction profiles and lightweight bricks.

"On September 27, President of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon inaugurated three new industrial enterprises in the industrial zone of Khorog city. The activities of the new facilities, equipped with modern technologies, are aimed at processing fruits and vegetables, producing furniture and construction materials," the statement said.

Production is carried out using four modern machines. The enterprise plans to install two more machines in the future and, depending on market demand, launch the production of construction nails and gloves.

The enterprise was built by entrepreneur Vohid Iskandar as part of the implementation of the country’s strategic goals and is aimed at expanding local production of construction materials.

Overall, 46 new industrial workshops and enterprises have been built in Khorog over the past five years as part of preparations for the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan’s state independence, creating 300 jobs. As a result, the total number of industrial enterprises in the city has reached 72.

Meanwhile, Tajikistan has been expanding domestic industrial production in recent years, with a focus on increasing the processing of local raw materials and developing manufacturing capacity. The construction materials sector is among the areas receiving attention as the country works to strengthen local production and meet growing demand from the construction industry.

World.title: Uzbekistan to host UN crime prevention congress in 2031
World.content:
Photo: the telegram channel of the Head of Presidential Administration Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 28. Uzbekistan will host the next United Nations Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in 2031, after all participating countries backed the country’s bid to hold the event.

This was reflected in the statement posted by the Head of the Presidential Administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva, on her social media account.

The decision was confirmed in the congress’s final declaration following the 15th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in Abu Dhabi, which brought together about 5,000 participants from around the world.

The congress addressed international efforts to combat transnational crime, terrorism, drug trafficking, corruption and environmental offenses, as well as child protection and the strengthening of the rule of law.

Mirziyoyeva also met with Monica Juma, UN Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). She noted that Uzbekistan is actively cooperating with UNODC and implementing joint projects.

For Uzbekistan, the decision to host the next congress marks the beginning of a five-year preparation period. The country is expected to welcome delegates from around the world in 2031 for the major UN forum on crime prevention and criminal justice.

“All participating countries supported Uzbekistan’s initiative to hold the next session in our country, which was confirmed in the final declaration,” Mirziyoyeva said.

She described the decision as an important sign of international confidence in Uzbekistan, including confidence in the country’s openness and readiness for dialogue and joint efforts.

World.title: 'No possibility' for Swedish leader to form government after narrow win
World.content:
Swedish Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson says she has failed to form a government with the three other parties in the left-wing bloc following the country's September 13 general election.

Sweden's left-wing bloc wins general election Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has led Sweden since 2022 with a three-party centre-right coalition.

The centre-left won a narrow majority of 176 seats to the incumbent right bloc's 173 seats, in a vote widely seen as a referendum on outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's promise to form a coalition with the far-right Sweden Democrats.

The Left Party, one of the three which form the left-wing bloc, said over the weekend it would back a candidate for parliament speaker from the rival Moderate party, which Ms Andersson says undercut her attempt to build a government.

"Of course, I take the Left Party's message seriously, and based on that and the conversations I have had, I can conclude that there is currently no possibility for me to form a government," she told a press conference on Monday.

Right-wing bloc would also struggle to form government

The speaker of parliament is expected to task another party leader, likely Mr Kristersson, with trying to form a new government.

Ulf Kristersson attended the Moderate Party election watch night. (Reuters: Christine Olsson/TT News Agency)

Mr Kristersson currently leads a caretaker government.

His right-wing bloc, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats will struggle to find a majority in parliament.

He said following the loss that he was ready to explore options to find a majority among "non-socialist" parties.

He is seen as wanting to woo the Centre Party, which is now part of the left-wing bloc but used to belong to the right-wing, although it is staunchly opposed to a government which includes the extreme-right Sweden Democrats.

Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has refused to be a part of or support any government that gives influence to the parties on the far left or far right.

Reuters

World.title: Controversial Sydney data centre project pulled amid community anger
World.content:
A controversial proposed data centre has been withdrawn by its developer after it became a flashpoint amid growing opposition to the AI infrastructure development across the country.

Goodman Group confirmed on Monday it had told the NSW Department of Planning it would no longer proceed with its $1.2 billion Project Mars in Sydney's north shore, citing "changes in regulatory environment".

The Project Mars development is among a new generation of data centres forcing the federal government to walk a tightrope between enticing investment from AI companies and quelling community concerns about their environmental impacts.

New data centres set to escape rules Dozens of approved but yet-to-be-built AI data centre projects are expected to escape the federal government's proposed restrictions around energy and water use.

While not as large as some other proposed projects, the three-storey project situated in Lane Cove attracted controversy as it sought planning approval from the state.

The project was approximately 20 metres from the nearest house and 160 metres from Lane Cove West Public School.

In a statement, developer Goodman said the decision to shelve the project came after hearing from the local community and in response to changes in regulation.

"During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said.

"Goodman has carefully considered these changes together with feedback received through the planning process, including the views of the local community."

The Sydney suburb at risk of becoming a 'data centre wasteland' Sydney is in the middle of a data centre boom fuelled by the global AI race. In Lane Cove West and Ryde, residents and councils say they are the ones paying the price.

Goodman's decision comes after NSW introduced a new fast-track program for data centres that met certain requirements, and in anticipation of new federal rules for data centres that the Prime Minister now says will be introduced into Parliament by the start of this year.

Local community groups fiercely opposed the project, taking umbrage with its expected impacts.

These groups appeared before the first hearing of the federal senate inquiry into data centres and artificial intelligence last week, along with Goodman's general manager of developments Ben McGilp.

Liberal senator Sarah Henderson repeatedly pressured Mr McGilp to withdraw the proposal on the spot.

Henderson said the project was a "wholly unreasonable proposal… that shows contempt for local residents".

Sweltering Cities senior campaigner Sanaa Shah, who spoke before the committee, told the ABC she was glad to see the project shelved.

Know more about this story? Email Cam Wilson on wilson.cameron@abc.net.au or his secure email cmwlsn@protonmail.com

"It's a clear testament to the large scale community resistance that's forming to data centres. It's something we're observing across the country," she said

Last month, consultancy CT group told its clients that local opposition to data centres had become a risk to their development.

Advocacy group Data Centre Australia recently warned Australia risked losing data centre developments to neighbouring countries.

"Some of that is the approval processes, some of that is supply chain issues, some of that is physically getting in there or social licence issues," CEO Belinda Dennett said.

World.title: Inquest told man died after lying unconscious in police cell for hours
World.content:
Victoria Police has admitted failures and apologised after a man died from a brain injury following hours spent unconscious in a suburban holding cell.

Mistakes by officers and staff from Triple Zero Victoria were outlined today during an inquest into the death of John Makai, 58.

Barrister Andrew Imrie, representing the chief commissioner of police, said the care in custody offered to Mr Makai "fell short" of standards required under Victoria Police policy.

"On behalf of Victoria Police, my client offers his sincere condolences to John's family, friends and loved ones," he told the Coroners Court of Victoria.

Mr Makai, who had 10 children and a stepchild, was fondly described by one of his sons as "kind and loving".

However, it was an out-of-character act of violence that brought him to police attention on September 9, 2023.

Mr Makai struck another adult son, Terewa, over the head with a mug after becoming angry about a drink being spilled inside an Uber earlier in the night.

Terewa retaliated and punched Mr Makai in the head, the court heard.

Footage from police body-worn cameras, played to the court, showed officers arriving at the Sunbury home where the fight took place.

Mr Makai and Terewa were bleeding and being questioned by the officers when Mr Makai lost his balance and fell backwards, crashing into a wooden bookshelf.

The Coroners Court heard John Makai spent hours unconscious in a holding cell at Broadmeadows Police Station in 2023. (ABC News)

Officers were told an ambulance was not available and took a groggy Mr Makai to the Broadmeadows Police Station for observation.

During the ride, Mr Makai lost consciousness and slumped forward, falling off his seat.

On arrival, security cameras captured officers carrying a limp Mr Makai to a holding cell, where he was left on a bed.

For more than four hours, he was motionless, and nobody entered the cell to check on him, counsel assisting the inquiry Rachel Ellyard told the court.

Ms Ellyard said officers believed Mr Makai was drunk when, in fact, it was likely he was suffering the effects of a traumatic brain injury.

Two staff reported that they had checked on Mr Makai through a cell trap door and observed him moving. However, footage played to the court suggested otherwise.

A sergeant made repeated requests to Triple Zero Victoria for an ambulance to be sent to the station, but was told paramedics were too busy.

Later, a Triple Zero Victoria staffer made an "inadvertent error" and cancelled the ambulance to the police station, thinking it was no longer needed.

Eventually the sergeant rang Triple Zero and made an emergency request for help.

"This guy's breathing but we can't raise any verbals from him … we were expecting the ambulance here five hours ago," he said.

"I've never known anyone not to stir like this."

An ambulance arrived within minutes and took Mr Makai to hospital. A CT scan revealed evidence of oxygen deprivation to the brain, and Mr Makai was diagnosed with a "non-survivable" injury, the court heard.

His life support was switched off days later.

Ms Ellyard said there had been a "significant departure" from Victoria Police policy by officers who failed to actively check on Mr Makai.

Mr Imrie, the police barrister, said disciplinary action had been taken against some employees.

The coronial inquest will examine why an ambulance was not called sooner in 2023 for the unresponsive John Makai at the Broadmeadows Police Station. (ABC News)

The inquest will probe whether treatment delays contributed to Mr Makai's death, how police responded and why an ambulance was not called sooner to the police station.

This afternoon, Triple Zero Victoria operations support director Ryan Goon said ambulance cancellation errors were "extremely rare".

The staff member who accidentally cancelled the ambulance to the police station received extra training after Mr Makai's death, Mr Goon said.

Updated software was also being designed to reduce confusion for dispatchers, he said.

The inquest continues.

World.title: Bombers poach former Swans premiership coach John Longmire
World.content:
Essendon have poached former Sydney premiership coach John Longmire as their new general manager of performance in a huge recruiting coup.

Longmire departs Sydney after 25 years in various roles to reunite with his former assistant, new Bombers coach Mark McVeigh, in a new role.

"I'm really excited to be joining the Essendon Football Club," Longmire said in a statement.

"I've known Mark for a long time and have worked with him as well. He is passionate about the Bombers and has a clear vision for the team.

"I look forward to supporting both him and the staff as the club looks to take the necessary steps back towards being a consistent team who challenge the opposition every week."

The Bombers have effectively split the football boss role in two, with Longmire to oversee game strategy, player development, leadership, the coaching group, performance analytics and strength and conditioning.

The 55-year-old, most recently Sydney's executive director of club performance, will start this week ahead of the trade period.

John Longmire won the 2012 AFL premiership with the Swans in a 14-season spell as head coach. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Landing Longmire, who did not pursue any vacant head coach roles, is a huge result for the battling Bombers, who finished last on the ladder and needed to put support around first-year coach McVeigh.

"John's football experience and leadership are exactly what we have been looking for in this role," Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said in a statement.

"We have made no secret of our ambition to build a football program capable of delivering sustained success, and bringing in someone of John's calibre is a significant investment in that goal.

"Over 14 seasons as senior coach of the Sydney Swans, John built a program that consistently competed at the pointy end, including the 2012 premiership and four further grand final appearances.

"He knows what a winning program looks like from the inside and how to sustain it year after year.

"Just as importantly, John will be an enormous asset to Mark McVeigh.

"Very few people understand the demands of the senior coach role like John does and having someone of his experience alongside Mark to provide support, guidance and a sounding board will allow Mark to focus on coaching and developing our players."

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham hailed Longmire as a "much-loved and respected figure" and "legend".

Longmire joined Sydney as an assistant coach in 2002 and was involved in the drought-breaking 2005 premiership, later succeeding Paul Roos.

Across 333 games, Longmire, the Swans' longest-serving coach had a 63 per cent winning record, won the 2012 premiership and led Sydney to five grand finals and 12 finals campaigns.

He stepped down after the 2024 grand final loss to Brisbane.

"Having arrived at the Swans 25 years ago this club has meant so much to me and my family," Longmire said in a Swans statement.

"I will look back with extreme fondness of my time in Sydney and always be proud of what we achieved as a football club."

AAP

World.title: 'I'll be back': Cleary vows to return after surgery
World.content:
Penrith Panthers star Nathan Cleary has vowed to return after his 2026 season was brutally cut short on Sunday, thanking fans for their support from his hospital bed.

The 28-year-old suffered a horrific compound fracture of his left ankle in the Panthers' NRL preliminary final defeat against Newcastle, ruling him out of the Kangaroos' World Cup campaign.

The Panthers, who led 14-6 at half-time, ultimately fell apart to lose to the 12-man Knights, 22-14.

On Monday, the star halfback posted a photo from hospital, with his left leg bandaged following surgery.

"Surgery done," he wrote on Instagram, with a photo of him smiling and giving thumbs up to the camera.

"Thank you so much to everyone that has reached out, the support has been unbelievable.

"Yesterday sucked but it's all part of the journey and it's made me even more grateful for the people I have around me.

"I'll be back."

Nathan Cleary was taken from the field in agony. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The gruesome injury cast a pall over the Sydney Olympic Stadium, with Panthers players visibly distressed on field while their star was being treated by medical staff.

"He's one of my best mates," Panthers captain Isaah Yeo said post-match.

"He's your brother out there. You don't like seeing anyone like that. You just want to be there for him.

"It's a lonely little place out there when you've got something like that going on."

Cleary's father, coach Ivan Cleary, also revealed that seeing his son in such a state at half-time was "emotional".

It was later revealed that Cleary, who started the game from the bench, was already playing with a broken bone in his right foot as the Panthers hoped to manage his involvement in the prelim with half an eye looking forward to next weekend's grand final against the Sydney Roosters.

Cleary came onto the field 25 minutes into the first half, but only lasted 10 minutes before Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland fell onto his ankle in a tackle.

Crossland was sent off for a hip drop and was sent straight to the NRL judiciary by the match review committee, where a lengthy suspension could not only rule him out of Newcastle's first NRL grand final in 25 years, but also impact the Kiwi's World Cup campaign.

Slater calls for change

Phoenix Crossland is unlikely to play in the grand final. (Getty Images)

Crossland is likely to face a lengthy ban, but has been given support from former Maroons coach Billy Slater.

Speaking on The Billy Slater Podcast, Slater said the current rules were leaving players unsure as to how to tackle players effectively without giving away a penalty.

"It has to come down to the responsibility of the tackler," Slater said.

"[But] I honestly feel the game has a little bit of a responsibility in this as well. When you change interpretations and change rules, you always have a flow-on effect.

"If you think about the protection of kickers and ball players and not being able to tackle them even fractionally after they pass the ball … 10 years ago this wouldn't have happened. Fifteen years ago that tackle would not have happened because Phoenix Crossland would've had more speed and force going into that tackle.

"But because he was worried about tackling Nathan after he passed the ball he was actually in a passive position.

"He was on his inside, which is normally when you put pressure on the ball player and you go out and you make tackles on that ball player, even after they pass the ball slightly.

"Phoenix wasn't in that mindset. He was in a passive mindset thinking Nathan was going to pass, then all of a sudden Nathan threw a dummy and he had to make a tackle and he didn't have that force behind him.

"I've got no doubt that has contributed to why Phoenix Crossland is in this grabbing and sitting down position, because he doesn't have that momentum and force and mindset of making a tackle."

The NRL judiciary will sit on Tuesday, with Crossland needing to argue his case to have any chance of playing in the 2026 grand final.

World.title: Homes invaded by 'millions' of migrating bogong moths
World.content:
Reina Hill is playing the reluctant host to some unexpected visitors in her Batemans Bay home.

Since Friday, her house has been swarmed by bogong moths.

"I walked out my door and was hit in the face by thousands of them," she said.

"I swear there was millions of them layered on various areas under my deck, under my eaves and all around the windows."

Bogong moths covering on a house at Malua Bay. (Supplied: Sue McHutchison)

Ms Hill was not alone in noticing the sudden influx of the endangered insects.

About 800 moth sightings have been logged on the citizen science platform iNaturalist since Friday, with more than 200 logged in the past 24 hours.

Every year, the peanut-sized moths migrate to the NSW Alps to escape the summer heat before returning to their inland breeding grounds in autumn.

But the insect's population has fallen steadily since the 1980s due to drought and warming temperatures.

In 2017, numbers crashed by as much as 99.5 per cent, and in 2021 they were listed as endangered.

'Just trying to migrate'

Western Sydney University Entomologist Eleanor Drinkwater told 702 ABC Sydney it was pleasing to see the moths in such significant numbers.

"The last few years we haven't seen so many bogong moths," she said.

Dr Drinkwater said the moths were on their way to the high country around Mount Kosciuszko as the weather warmed up.

"They're not trying to get into your house, they're just trying to migrate," she said.

" For some of these little individuals that people might see, they're going to be travelling hundreds, if not thousands, of kilometres. "

Eleanor Drinkwater said the large numbers were a sign that something was going right. (Supplied: Eleanor Drinkwater)

Bogong Watch Project manager at Invertebrates Australia Linnea Emneby said many people had forgotten what a migration looks like.

"We have seen a decline in bogong moths this decade, which has changed people's perception of what a migration looks like," she said.

" It's just incredibly encouraging to see them actually bouncing back. "

According to Ms Emneby, there were several theories that might explain the phenomenon.

Linnea Emneby manages the Bogong Watch Project at Inverterbrates Australia. (Supplied: Linnea Emneby)

One is that increased rainfall in northern parts of the state has produced an abundance of food for larvae.

Another theory is that warmer weather has caused the flowers that attract the moths to bloom earlier than normal, luring them south.

But Ms Emneby said the small creatures had likely used recent north-westerly winds to travel to the alps.

"Bogong moths are known to kind of hitch a ride on winds," she said.

"They're very small creatures and they travel vast distances.

"If there is wind going the way of the migration, they'll fly at that level in the same way you descend or ascend in a hot air balloon."

Increase in numbers the 'norm'

The moths may have hitched a ride on recent north-westerly winds. (Supplied: Marina Pitsonis)

University of Sydney biologist Dieter Hochuli said the moths would be found hiding in crevices in the day to avoid predation by birds.

"There's a lot of birds and mammals and everything that's going to want to eat them.," Mr Hochuli told 702 ABC Sydney.

"So, basically, they're just finding a good spot to spend the day."

One 702 ABC Sydney listener said their boot was lined with moths in Penrith in Sydney's west. (Supplied)

The moths are a food source for many birds and pygmy possums.

Mr Hochuli said while the moth was listed as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), they were not listed as endangered in NSW or federally.

"The reason there are concerns is that they have these massive population fluctuations and cycles," Mr Hochuli said.

"They're a complicated animal for an endangered animal because there could be billions of them.

" Those of us that are old enough to remember the Sydney Olympics or the opening of Parliament House will remember we had similar kinds of events, just massive numbers. "

A bogong moth at Charlotte Pass, NSW. (Supplied: Associate Professor Kate Umbers)

Dr Drinkwater encouraged capturing and releasing the moths if they were stuck inside, or turning outside lights on and turning indoor lights off to draw them out of homes.

She also called for submissions of photos to iNaturalist and the Moth Tracker website to help researchers understand their migration.

“This is a brilliant opportunity for us to learn more about what they're doing," Dr Drinkwater said.

World.title: Inquest hears Qld mum felt 'dismissed' by doctors after asking for C-section
World.content:
An inquest into the death of a newborn at a central Queensland hospital has heard his mother felt she was "dismissed" by doctors when she requested a caesarean.

Alby Spreadborough died at Emerald Hospital on February 6, 2023, after an obstructed labour, a condition that occurs when the baby cannot move through the birth canal.

Today, the second coronial inquest into his death heard from his parents, Tim and Rebecca Spreadborough, and doctors.

Rebecca and Tim Spreadborough in the nursery they had prepared for their son. (ABC Capricornia: Rachel McGhee)

The court heard that while in "excruciating pain" during labour, Ms Spreadborough asked her midwife, "Can they cut it out of me?", but was advised by her doctor to continue the vaginal birth for another hour.

"I was a vulnerable mother in labour in excruciating pain," Ms Spreadborough said.

" I had trust in my care team, so I trusted they were making the right decisions for me. "

She said she felt there was "pushback" from her doctor regarding having a caesarean section after her initial request.

"I felt there was lots of pressure and encouragement to continue birthing vaginally," she said.

Assisting counsel Geoffrey Diehm asked Ms Spreadborough if the doctors may have been waiting to ensure she was sure she wanted to proceed with having a caesarean.

Ms Spreadborough said discussions were not balanced and were weighted towards the vaginal birth.

Bec Spreadborough's son died in 2023 following an obstructed labour. (ABC Capricornia: Jasmine Hines)

She said she later "firmly requested" a caesarean section and was taken into the operating theatre.

"I was already at a point where I couldn't bear any more pain … I reaffirmed my request for a caesarean section," she said.

Ms Spreadborough told the court that during the caesarean operation she realised something had gone wrong and that doctors were attempting to revive her baby.

"No-one came to me to communicate to me what had happened, but I could hear in the room what was happening," she said.

Both Ms Spreadborough and her husband told the court they did not recall any discussions with doctors about abnormalities in scans.

"The only thing I recall is them saying baby is really happy on the CTG [cardiotocograph]," Ms Spreadborough said.

A rare phenomenon

The court heard Emerald Hospital did not have a dedicated paediatrician at the time.

Rural generalist Brooke Davies, who was the doctor during the birth, told the inquest Ms Spreadborough had developed a rare medical phenomenon called a Bandl's ring, which is a ring of muscle that constricts between the upper and lower sections of the uterus.

Alby Spreadborough died at Emerald Hospital. (ABC Capricornia: Jasmine Hines)

She said it was the first time she had seen the ring in a patient and that she cut through the ring, but it remained tight.

"[It was] like I had cut through a steel ring rather than a rubber band," Dr Davies said.

She said initial scans of Alby and Ms Spreadborough did not indicate highly concerning abnormalities.

The road to an inquest

In February 2025, two years after Alby died, an initial central coroner's report found that the death was not preventable and was due to the formation of a Bandl's ring.

But the Spreadboroughs advocated for an inquiry due to concerns the report did not focus on the care surrounding the complication.

Alby Spreadborough's parents gave evidence during the inquest into their son's death. (ABC Capricornia: Rachel McGhee)

State Attorney-General Deb Frecklington ordered the inquest after meeting with the parents.

The inquest, before Deputy State Coroner Stephanie Gallagher in Townsville, will consider whether a caesarean section should have been performed earlier and if it had, whether Alby would have died.

The inquest will also investigate if the "manner and performance" of this operation contributed to the baby's death.

Evidence about medical procedures and decisions throughout the birth will also be examined.

The four-day inquest continues.

World.title: Weapons seized in SA shopping centres since new police powers a year ago
World.content:
Expanded police powers to search people in South Australian shopping centres will continue after dozens of weapons were seized over the past year, but the state's children guardian says "more transparent" data is needed.

At least 80 weapons have been seized since police were granted additional powers one year ago, from 10,000 wand searches across 18 shopping centres.

The laws enable police to stop and search anyone inside a declared shopping precinct and turn them away for 24 hours.

Speaking at Burnside Village today, Attorney-General Kyam Maher said the number of weapons found — amounting to just under 1 per cent of all searches — showed "by and large South Australians are doing the right thing".

"That doesn't mean we should be complacent … to make sure we don't see ourselves in position the eastern states have found themselves in with knife crime," he said.

Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland have similar search and move-on powers.

In June 2024, a group of teenagers allegedly wielding weapons during a brawl sparked a lockdown at Westfield Marion shopping centre.

A bladed weapon seized by SA Police at a shopping centre. (Supplied: SA Police)

Acting Assistant Police Commissioner David O'Donovan said he was "not aware of any pushback" from shoppers "about being the subject of a wand search".

"When you look at the ultimate outcome of us being able to make public spaces much safer, we will continue to use the legislation as long as it is available," he said.

"The information I have is that [the public] fully support our activities, and that we're operating in public places trying to make it much safer for them to be present."

He said over the past year, there have been incidents where "children have been in possession of weapons", but SA Police was unable to provide specific figures.

One of the numerous weapons seized by SA Police in the past 12 months. (Supplied: SA Police)

Laws won't tackle root causes: Children's guardian

Acting SA Guardian for Children and Young People Sue Macdonald said the numbers "do not tell us enough about the extent or nature of the problem", including "whether the weapons were carried by adults or children and young people".

"A more transparent discussion of the data would help the community assess the effectiveness of this policing approach," she said.

"While expanded policing powers may play a role in responding to immediate safety risks, they are not a long-term solution to youth offending or violence.

"To achieve lasting change, we need to better understand and address the factors that contribute to these behaviours, including experiences of abuse and neglect, family and domestic violence, social disadvantage, disengagement from education and substance misuse."

Traders and shoppers weigh in

Burnside Village butcher George Schofield was supportive of police searches using metal detector wands.

"I think this shopping centre is pretty good with security, so I don't think anyone has felt too worried here," he said.

"It's just that extra confidence knowing police are out there."

George Schofield says the additional police presence was reassuring. (ABC News)

Shopper Claire Langsford questioned if the patrols were a good use of public resources.

"I would suspect if the corporations that own shopping centres invested more resources in protecting staff … that might work out better for everybody," she said.

The maximum penalty for carrying an offensive weapon in public, which includes most knives, is six months in jail or a $2,500 fine.

The more serious charge of possessing a prohibited weapon, which includes machetes and swords, is two years' imprisonment or a $20,000 fine.

World.title: I’ve met some cold-hearted killers, but most crooks are ordinary and often quite pathetic
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCrime Opinion I’ve met some cold-hearted killers, but most crooks are ordinary and often quite pathetic Jason Doyle Contributor September 28, 2026 — 7:00pm

September 28, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In about AD 175, Roman emperor and philosopher Marcus Aurelius wrote of his day ahead: “I will encounter busybodies, ingrates, egomaniacs, liars, the jealous and cranks.” He could have been a police officer. Marcus was a keen observer of life, and as a police officer myself, I always sought to be the same. If there’s one thing I learnt, there is always a lot more going on under the surface than first appears. Oh, and that people can do remarkable things: good, bad and stupid. I’ve dealt with plenty of criminals. Mostly the bad ones because they’re easier to catch. People might be surprised how common criminality is; many crooks actually have regular day jobs to pay the bills. I had to laugh at the burglar brought into the station one night who pleaded to be let out in the morning, as he was expected on the worksite to resume his career as a tradie. Admirable dedication, I guess. Of course many crooks are engaged in white-collar crime, hiding behind their computers. It’s sobering to realise that criminals walk among us. It’s just that most don’t recognise them. Criminals walk among us, but they are rarely masterminds. iStock There are cold-hearted killers out there, and I’ve met some of them, but most crooks are decidedly ordinary and often quite pathetic. One serious offender came into the cells yelling abuse and issuing commands to his underlings to “tell the dogs nothin’” when interviewed. After five minutes of being alone in a cell, he was crying and asking to call his mother. Yep, a real tough guy. No doubt he would have lied about that to his cronies because when caught, most people lie. I snagged a burglar literally half in and half out of the hole he’d made in a front door, but like the Shaggy song he said, “It wasn’t me,” even with the stolen jewellery in his pockets. Similarly, after seeing a young offender commit a crime and flee, I was soon speaking to him and his mother at the front door of his home. He nervously denied everything, and his mum, who knew full well that her little angel had only just arrived home, declared he had been with her all morning. Two liars for the price of one. Having just used his mother to cover for his illicit activities, this young bloke, now emboldened, began to say the most disgusting things about my own dear mother, while standing behind his.



As well as wannabe criminal masterminds, police deal frequently with regular people. There is often a lot going on underneath a happy veneer, but sometimes the secrets burst into the open. After a physical fight between a successful (based on the car parked outside) businessman and a female victim, it soon became clear that the man didn’t live there and was married to someone else. He begged us to keep his affair quiet, but after the case made its way to court, I’m sure I wasn’t the only one surprised when the man’s wife arrived to give a character reference for her wayward spouse. Evidently, he had fessed up at some point. Related Article Opinion

Real life As a police officer, I made life and death decisions daily. They never leave you Jason Doyle Contributor The lives of other families are torn apart by violence, poor mental health, gambling debts or substance abuse problems. Why? Because life is complex, and often not easy to navigate. I learned that quickly. Sometimes despair leads to suicide or attempts. I’ve twice rescued people from suicide attempts in what might have been their final moments. What makes a person that desperate? I got an answer once when I sat with a young person after an attempt, and they opened up about why – they wanted to change sex, and their parents refused to accept this complexity of their child’s life. I wonder if some of the belligerent commentators on “woke” ideology and gender issues have ever had a conversation like this? Money and fame are no barrier to this scourge. I’ve attended the house of a celebrity who had made an attempt on their life, and I encountered an AFL footballer whose depression was so obvious that I had to intervene. This was back when sportspeople didn’t take time off to address their personal demons. That this is widely accepted now has to be a step forward. Police themselves are particularly susceptible to deteriorating mental health, due at least in part to the trauma they are regularly exposed to. Between 2000 and 2020, more than 100 serving Australian police officers took their own lives. Plenty more have done it after retiring. Our brains can only take so much. I encourage readers to check on their family and mates, police or not, as uncomfortable as these conversations may be.



Related Article Analysis

Naked City ‘You’re gunna get it’: How police stared down a double-murderer and prevented further carnage No matter how long you work the streets, human behaviour can still surprise. Once, when a truck hit a bridge in Flemington, I had to shut down the train station on top of the bridge because the truck had snared power lines and the whole place was potentially “live”. The scene was lit up with emergency vehicles, flashing lights, cones and tape. A jogger ignored all of that and ran right into the danger zone. I’m not sure how our species has accomplished so much when we can be so individually stupid. But some behaviours never seem to change. Despite modern innovations such as 3D-printed guns, and machetes as first-choice weapons, the people using these tools are the same. Even after we have flying cars and package holidays to the moon, we will still be calling police to pick up the pieces when it all goes wrong. Jason Doyle is a retired police officer. Support is available from Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Essendon land Longmire for head of performance role, Kangas zero in on their new coach
World.content:
In today’s AFL briefing, your wrap of footy news: John Longmire’s responsibilities at Essendon will include but not be limited to game strategy, player development, leadership, the coaching group.

Daniel Giansiracusa is among the key candidates for North Melbourne’s vacant coaching position as the Roos ramp up their search.

Jack Viney will fly to Perth to tour West Coast’s facilities as he plots a move away from the Demons. Essendon have pulled off a huge coup landing Sydney premiership coach John Longmire as their new head of performance. Longmire will oversee football operations and work alongside first time coach Mark McVeigh who was an assistant coach for Longmire at Sydney. His responsibilities will include game strategy, player development, leadership, the coaching group, performance analytics and strength and conditioning. His appointment is a massive coup for club president Andrew Welsh and CEO Tim Roberts as they look to rebuild the football department and attract players and coaches. John Longmire will head to Essendon. Getty



Longmire coached the Swans in five grand finals including the 2012 premiership after a stellar playing career with the Kangaroos. He stepped down as Sydney coach to make way for his successor Dean Cox at the end of 2024 and worked in a club performance role for the past two seasons. He was a candidate to coach the Tassie Devils before Ken Hinkley was appointed coach but decided not to put himself in the race to become North Melbourne coach after Alastair Clarkson was sacked. Longmire, 55, said he was excited to join the Bombers in a new role supporting the football department. “I’ve known Mark [McVeigh] for a long time and have worked with him as well. He is passionate about the Bombers and has a clear vision for the team,” he said. “I look forward to supporting both he and the staff as the club looks to take the necessary steps back towards being a consistent team who challenge the opposition every week.”



Longmire was prominent at the Swans as he supported key leaders at the club as they dealt with the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal where five players missed finals due to their behaviour after a round 23 match against the Bombers. Giansiracusa among Kangaroos’ coaching candidates Hawthorn development coach Daniel Giansiracusa is among the key candidates for North Melbourne’s vacant coaching position as the Kangaroos zero in on a new coach to replace Alastair Clarkson. Giansiracusa has a strong coaching resume. He was at the Western Bulldogs when they won their drought breaking flag in 2016 and won the assistant coach of the year in 2020. He then coached at Essendon in several line roles for five seasons before joining the Hawks as a development coach in 2026 as Hawthorn went within a minute of reaching the 2026 grand final.



Highly rated Hawthorn assistant Daniel Giansiracusa. Getty Images Giansiracusa presented strongly for the Kangaroos job at the end of 2020 and is considered to combine a great football brain with an ability to form relationships. He has worked under Luke Beveridge, Brad Scott and Sam Mitchell since his 256-match career finished in 2014. Geelong assistant and former Magpies coach Nathan Buckley impressed in his initial discussions with the Kangaroos and confirmed on grand final day he is going through the selection process while Dockers’ assistant Jaymie Graham is also in the mix. The club also met recently with Cats’ premiership player Corey Enright who recently accepted an assistant coaching role back at Geelong after five seasons at St Kilda. The Cats are aware of his ambitions to be a senior coach. North Melbourne are keen for Graham to present with club officials asking football people about the Fremantle assistant over grand final weekend. Graham was high on Carlton’s list before Josh Fraser earned the job with a strong presentation combined with a startling run as interim coach.



However the race is expected to be wide open for the gig. Club leaders met recently with Kangaroos premiership player and Eagles’ premiership coach Adam Simpson before he withdrew his candidacy after being left at that meeting with the sense he was not the direction they wanted to take. Buckley, who coached Collingwood into a 10th season before departing midway through 2021, interviewed for Melbourne’s job at the end of last season before joining Geelong as an assistant coach in 2026. He was a candidate for the Tasmanian Devils coaching job before they opted to appoint Ken Hinkley. Viney to head west as Eagles circle



Melbourne veteran Jack Viney will fly to Perth on Tuesday to tour West Coast’s facilities as he plots a move away from the Demons. Having been told opportunities might dry up for him in the midfield next year as the Demons favour younger players, Viney is looking at moving. Jack Viney’s only AFL game this year was the wildcard final against Carlton. Getty Images He met with West Coast officials in Melbourne in the past week and was impressed with the pitch from coaches. Essendon have also met with Viney. The Bombers would consider the 32-year-old a ready-made strong-bodied midfield replacement for Zach Merrett, who his likely to move to Hawthorn. Essendon is also attracted to Viney’s leadership, character and training standards to support their young playing group.



Their interest in Viney might now be redoubled after they missed out on securing Adelaide midfielder Luke Pedlar, who has requested a trade to cross-town rivals Port Adelaide. Tough midfielder-forward Luke Pedlar is crossing from the Crows to the Power. Getty Images The Bombers were in the hunt for the 24-year-old, who has not been able to cement a place in the Crows’ line-up, playing just 49 matches since being picked at No.11 in the 2020 national draft and battling a seriess of injury issues. But Pedlar decided to remain in his home state and join the Power, who have lost star free agent Zak Butters to the Western Bulldogs.



The Bombers have several trade targets as new coach Mark McVeigh settles in the role. Essendon are also interested in Lions’ premiership midfielder Sam Marshall and Geelong midfielder Jack Bowes as they look to recast their midfield with Merrett’s likely exit. The Bombers could also lose contracted defender Jordan Ridley, who has gained interest from Geelong and the Kangaroos. Ridley has played just 26 AFL matches in the past three seasons. Melbourne midfielder Trent Rivers is also looking to move with one year left on his contract. He has been interested in joining the Brisbane Lions, given his partner is from Brisbane, but he has also had some interest from West Coast. The trade period does not officially begin until next Monday, but talks have been underway for several months about possible trades and free agency moves. The free agency window opens this Friday, with the Giants’ Toby Greene, Gold Coast’s Ben King, the Lions’ Lachie Neale and Port Adelaide’s Butters all looking to move as free agents.

World.title: CCTV captures police car travelling at high speed before crash that killed Mia Lay
World.content:
CCTV footage has captured the moments before the patrol car carrying Constable Mia Lay smashed into a tree in Sydney’s inner-south, instantly killing the 20-year-old police officer and hospitalising the car’s driver, Constable Brandon Torrisi. Lay was killed when the marked police car in which she was a passenger crashed in Redfern during an urgent response to a reported vehicle theft in nearby Glebe about 1.30am on Friday. Security camera footage from a nail salon less than 200 metres from the crash site shows the Volkswagen Tiguan patrol car bursting down Gibbons Street, sirens and lights blaring, before the fatal accident. Mia’s father, Clem Lay, told the Herald that after his initial anger, he was relieved that Torrisi, his daughter’s fellow officer, had survived the crash.



“I want [Mia] to be remembered by as many as possible for as long as possible,” he said. “Everyone that she touched in her life has paid tribute.”



Clem told Nine News he hoped there was “no one at fault” for the crash that killed his daughter, saying that the immense loss his family is experiencing still hadn’t hit home. Clem Lay has said he was relieved there was a survivor in the crash that killed his daughter. Nine News Mourners have filled the site of the crash with flowers and tributes to Lay. Former colleagues and schoolmates of Lay were among those who left written tributes to the officer. One mourner tied the NSW Police badge to the tree with a scarf bearing the colours of the police uniform, while others brought shirts bearing the insignia of APIA Leichhardt, Lay’s former football club. Mourners laid flowers in tribute to Lay. Wolter Peeters



A NSW Police badge is tied to the tree at Gibbons Street. Wolter Peeters Police Minister Yasmin Catley didn’t weigh in on speculation Monday that Torrisi, 24, may have reached speeds surpassing 150km/h when the crash occurred, saying officers were entrusted with determining how quick they travel when they’re attending an urgent call. “Police make those decisions, but the investigation will determine if that’s the case,” she said. The NSW Law Enforcement Conduct Commission is overseeing the police investigation of the crash as it determines the circumstances leading to Lay’s death. The police watchdog can independently investigate the incident only once the police probe is complete.



Mia Lay at her attestation ceremony in 2025. Raphael Grzebieta, a road safety expert and professor emeritus at the University of NSW, said the nature of the collision – a “narrow offset” crash – meant the driver was further from the impact point. Mia Lay, who was a passenger in the police car, died instantly upon impact. NSW Police “A road where the speed limit is set at 50km/h indicates a high risk of serious injury or fatality if a vehicle travels at any speed above that value,” Grzebieta said. “What was the urgent danger that required them to travel at that speed? What was the urgent situation that required them to have those lights and sirens on?”



Jake Olivier, a professor of statistics at UNSW, said a car travelling above 50km/h – the speed limit on the stretch of Gibbons Street where Lay was killed – increased the risk of serious injury or death. “In normal driving conditions, I do not see this road really being a problem because the posted speed is set at 50km/h but travelling greater than that does pose a risk,” said Olivier, deputy director of the university’s Transport and Road Safety Research Centre. Olivier said hazards on the roadside, including trees, increased the likelihood of a fatal crash. Investigators are trying to piece together the circumstances around the crash. Sam Mooy “That’s one of the reasons speed limits are set as they are,” he said.



Olivier, who has driven the route Lay took on Friday morning, said the right-hand curve in the road where the 20-year-old’s vehicle collided with the tree “comes out of nowhere”. “It seems like it should be straight,” he said. “Psychologically, you kind of feel like you’re going straight.” Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Police thought John was in a deep drunken sleep. Instead, he lay dying
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCoroners Court of Victoria Police thought John was in a deep drunken sleep. Instead, he lay dying Lachlan Abbott September 28, 2026 — 6:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victoria Police has apologised for the death of a man who spent hours unresponsive with a brain injury in a Broadmeadows cell as he waited for paramedics. CCTV footage played in the Coroner’s Court on Monday showed three officers carrying John Makai’s limp body into a holding cell about 1.15am on September 10, 2023. An inquest is being held into the death of John Makai in September 2023. Facebook Police had arrived at Makai’s Sunbury home about an hour earlier, following a report the 58-year-old had fought with his adult son after both consumed alcohol. Opening the inquest into the death on Monday, Rachel Ellyard, counsel assisting the coroner, told the court Makai struck his son, Terewa, in the head with a mug and continued to approach him, despite warnings not to.



Makai was then punched twice and fell to the floor, Ellyard said. In a phone call played in court, a friend could be heard contacting Triple Zero to ask for an ambulance before changing his mind as others in the background told him to hang up. A dispatcher then created a police job instead. The Broadmeadows police station, as photographed in 2010. John Woudstra Body-worn camera footage showed officers arrived at a Timins Street house at 12.11am to find Makai and his son injured. Although both declined treatment, police requested paramedics attend. “They were advised there would be delays because of workload pressures that night on Ambulance Victoria,” Ellyard said.



She described Makai as “argumentative” in the body-worn camera footage, which captured him standing up, losing his balance, and falling back into a bookcase, where he hit his head. “He just blacked out, hey,” a man could be heard saying. The body-cam footage then showed Makai’s former partner tending to him and saying he was fine. Makai’s son told police: “This has never happened before.” Ellyard told the court police then designated Makai as having breached family violence laws, so he could be taken to Broadmeadows police station as paramedics weren’t immediately available.



He was carried from his home to the police divisional van. Makai was basically motionless for four hours, the court heard. “With the benefit of medical evidence, it appears … a developing brain injury was impeding his ability to walk,” Ellyard said. Video from inside the van shows Makai’s head was bumped again as he was dragged out by the ankles on arrival at Broadmeadows police station. “That vision shows John has experienced a serious decline in his consciousness and capacity to walk since he was put in that van,” Ellyard said.



Members of Makai’s family shook their heads in court on Monday as CCTV footage showed him being carried in a prone position onto a cell bed. Custody officers reported Makai was snoring, but Ellyard told the court there were no signs of voluntary movement. “What was perceived as a deep drunken sleep may have actually been a traumatic injury and bleeding into the brain,” she said. Custody Sergeant Neil Gregory called a police dispatcher at 1.25am to check on ambulance availability, but the court heard he was told crews were still busy. Another call was made at 2.18am, but the dispatcher said Ambulance Victoria was still dealing with 40 to 50 pending jobs. A dispatcher’s error then led to the ambulance being cancelled about 3am, the court heard. Gregory asked police subordinates to check on Makai every 15 minutes, but the court heard this did not occur as frequently as required.



Ellyard said cell footage showed Makai remained basically motionless from about 2am to 6am. “Apart from a very small movement to shield his eyes from glare ... no movement was recorded at all,” she said. Editor's pick Victorian election Level crossings on hold as Labor vows to fix Melbourne’s most unreliable train line No police entered the cell during this four-hour period. When a new watchhouse sergeant arrived after 6am and realised Makai was unable to be roused, officers entered his cell and tried to wake him by rubbing his sternum and pinching his arm. Gregory called Triple Zero after learning the earlier ambulance had been cancelled. “We were all expecting the ambulance here five hours ago,” Gregory said in a phone call aired in court. “I’ve never known anyone not to stir like this.”



Paramedics arrived at 6.29am and discovered Makai had a traumatic brain injury. He was taken to hospital, where he recorded a blood alcohol level of .13, and was later found to have suffered unsurvivable trauma. He died on September 12. Barrister Andrew Imrie, representing the police chief commissioner, said custody officers failed to complete a medical checklist and risk assessment at the Broadmeadows police station. “It’s a situation which we work tirelessly to avoid,” Imrie said. “In this case, however, my client acknowledges at the outset of this inquest that the standards of care in custody fell short of expected standards. “As the evidence currently stands, its unclear whether these shortcomings would have made a difference to the tragedy in this case … but [the chief commissioner] apologises.” The inquest continues. World.title: United Nations was a grand idea, but its time has passed
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nicholas Kristof rightly praises the UN’s aid efforts, but ignores its ultimate failure (“The UN is terrible – but right now, we need it desperately,” September 28). Formed after World War II to prevent global conflict, the UN’s core mission was crippled from the start by giving veto power to five nations. Today, it remains toothless against modern warfare. Nothing illustrates this futility better than Donald Trump using the UN forum to effectively declare war on Iran. We still need unified humanitarian systems but as a peacekeeper, the UN is an anachronism. It’s time for a global rethink on stopping war – one shaped by humanity, not politicians. Chris Rivers, Port Macquarie UK PM Andy Burnham meets US President Donald Trump during the United Nations General Assembly this month. Julia Demaree Nikhinson In the past week, the leaders of the United States and Israel used speeches at the United Nations to do exactly what the world organisation was created to avoid; they glorified the destruction of their enemies and threatened to go even further if their demands weren’t met. President Donald Trump’s contempt for the UN is well known. Under his leadership, the wealthiest country in the world refuses to pay its dues and he intends to replace it with his own “Peace Board”, which would be a puppet of his twisted view of world government. When Trump’s presidency thankfully comes to an end, we must wonder whether sanity will return to US foreign policy, or if he will be replaced by one of his disciples. Ian Adair, Hunters Hill Nicholas Kristof reminds us that despite the United Nations being reduced to a crumbling pillar of the geopolitical order that was created after World War II, it is needed now more than ever before. On January 24, 1946, just five months after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the first resolution adopted by the UN General Assembly was dedicated to the peaceful use of atomic energy and the elimination of weapons of mass destruction. With the temperature of the fireball created at Hiroshima reaching 7700C, this resolution was meant to shine a light on humanity’s darkest hour. But today’s nuclear arms race between the US, China and Russia places us all equally at the mercy of this newfound means of mass incineration. So if the UN is to have any relevance, it too must again remind us that such enslavement to the power of the atom is no match to the moral power inherent in human dignity. Rev Vincent Zankin, Rivett (ACT) Power couple Whatever your view on Australia’s energy policy and the way our electricity grid is changing, you have to admire what was achieved at Hornsdale (“Two billionaires, one online bet and a turning point for Australian energy”, September 27). A world-first grid-scale battery was built and operational in just 63 days. This goes well beyond energy. Australia has become used to major infrastructure projects taking years because of planning rules, environmental approvals and procurement processes. Hornsdale showed that when there is a clear goal, the money is available and governments and business are prepared to move quickly, things can happen much faster. We should be asking why the same approach cannot be used in other areas such as water, transport, telecommunications and urban development. Too often we seem to accept that big projects must be slow and expensive. Hornsdale showed that they don’t have to be. If governments and business can work together with a sense of urgency, Australia can get important infrastructure built much faster. This is not about policy or ideology – it’s about a can-do attitude and getting on with the job. John Kempler, Rose Bay It’s an impressive story, how we were the first country in the world to install a 100 megawatt big battery, back in 2017. But what’s happened since is even more impressive. Australia now has the third-highest level of battery storage in the world, behind only China and the United States. And we have the highest level of home battery storage – more than 12 gigawatts at last count. When you consider the figure was only 3.6GW a little over a year ago, the transformation is truly impressive. The challenge now is to keep this going so we transition our grid from near total dependence on fossil fuels to near 100 per cent renewable energy. Then we really will have something to boast about. Ken Enderby, Concord



The Hornsdale Power Reservation, where Tesla has installed a huge battery. Neoen Rather than blaming the 2016 storm that tore down 20 transmission towers, Josh Frydenberg and Barnaby Joyce falsely blamed over-reliance on renewables in South Australia for the statewide blackouts. With global warming we can expect many more such weather events. The Coalition and One Nation continue to aggressively fight renewables to this day, which just proves they are still unfit for office. Tony Simons, Balmain Brexit barriers I am an Australian and a European citizen, resident in Rome for more than 40 years. Britain may seek to re-enter the European Union, but the people of Europe will not welcome a return of the perfidious Albion to Brussels (“As three countries move to quit UK, a Brexit reversal might be its only hope”, September 28). It may work as an “associate”, which is basically a modified free trade agreement, but many Europeans think that a re-entry of the UK should be on the same terms as the entry of recent new members, which among other requirements would include the adoption of the Euro. The decision, if it comes, will depend on those few European countries that will refer the matter to the people by a referendum. It will not be easy. Alan Randell, Rome (Italy) I really don’t know what George Brandis expects from UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham by way of fixing the economic mess caused by Brexit. With all the past-glory revelling and Rule Britannia types such as Nigel Farage still in abundance, healing the UK’s self-inflicted wounds will be neither simple nor quick. And taking cheap shots at an ideological foe “just 10 weeks into the job” is typical of the attitude of some that will likely stymie any attempts to fix the problems. Brandis should aim his darts at those who caused the mess in the first place and acknowledge that you can’t just shout “clean-up in aisle four” and expect it to magically happen. Adrian Connelly, Springwood



RBA off target Shane Wright’s article on the dilemma faced by the RBA governor Michele Bullock makes for dispiriting reading (“Bullock’s reign as RBA governor has been defined by uncertainty”, September 28). As many correspondents have pointed out, the RBA has been left with just one arrow in its quiver, leaving it like William Tell with just one critical strike. Unfortunately, its recent strikes have been ineffective, so why does it think another will be any better? The trouble with this lack of options means that, among others, young people striving to pay off their homes are cruelly targeted, as was Tell’s son. It is manifestly unfair, especially when many aspiring homeowners were seduced by the government into taking mortgages for 95 per cent of their home’s value but who now find because of the RBA’s policies that they are in a position of negative equity. It is wrong and the government and the RBA must find another means of controlling inflation without harming the innocents. Lance Dover, Pretty Beach It seems wrong to curb inflation by only reducing the spending power of homebuyers through higher interest rates. The government could be fairer and more proactive by temporarily increasing taxpayers’ contribution to their superannuation as a form of deferred income. Conversely, during recessions these extra superannuation contributions could be returned to stimulate demand. John Woodward, Ashfield Great brain robbery Peter Hartcher is right to say we can’t afford to miss the AI wave, but he misses a critical point (“Why Australia simply cannot afford to miss this AI wave”, September 28). The “ore” in the AI economy isn’t data centres, it’s the vast volume of human-created content that has been harvested by the world’s largest technology companies without permission or payment to its creators. Globally, more than 145 copyright lawsuits are currently under way because AI companies have refused to negotiate licensing arrangements. Their goal is clear: change the law, minimise payment for content and set a global precedent. We keep hearing that copyright is the great obstacle to AI development, yet these same companies have no difficulty navigating and paying for every other essential input: land, power, water, chips and lobbying. The irony is striking. Earlier this year, both Anthropic and OpenAI accused Chinese AI firms of industrial-scale intellectual property theft. We understand their concern, but copyright is not the problem. The problem is that AI platforms have shown no interest in seeking permission and paying for the content that makes their systems valuable. Human creativity is not a peripheral input to AI. It’s the foundation. Australia should embrace the AI wave, but we must insist on permission and payment for creators. Helen Lear, Ultimo Photo: Megan Herbert



Medicare fading fast Badiucao’s cartoon of a Medicare card being eaten away by worms sums up today’s situation brilliantly (Letters, September 28). The disappearance of hospital specialist outpatient clinics with years-long wait lists; the long public surgical wait lists that drive people to the private system; the unaffordable private specialist fees that make essential medical management simply unavailable; the inadequate rebates that price many GPs out of patients’ reach – all these make me wonder how much of Medicare is really left. Dr Jennifer Briggs, Kilaben Bay Care in crisis Mental health problems are on the rise and the facilities are ill-equipped to cope (“Alarm as courts send mentally ill to EDs”, September 28). Patients fortunate enough to make it into the system are generally well cared for, especially if they are recipients of the NDIS. Those receiving proper care are now outnumbered by those denied the support needed. The Richmond Report was followed by the Mental Health Act of 1983, which resulted in the deinstitutionalisation of mentally ill people, despite the concerns of health professionals at the time. The promised community infrastructure was never fully funded or adequately built to meet the needs. Since then, successive governments have failed to address the parlous state of mental health care. Consequently, hospitals and the families of these patients are overwhelmed by the burden of providing the support required. It seems to be another case of government cost-saving without due consideration of the consequences. Graham Lum, North Rocks Unsung ICAC heroes Bevan Shields has done a stellar job with his awards for the current ICAC Operation Rosny hearings and its key figures (“Biggest idiot, grubbiest behaviour, best phone tap: The Operation Rosny Awards”, September 27). There does, however, seem to be one group of unsung heroes that has gone unmentioned: the diligent professional investigators and commission staff. They have clearly assembled a vast catalogue of documents and text messages, and listened to hundreds of hours of phone calls. Piecing together the apparent web of lies and deceit is no small task. While technology and AI have surely made these tasks easier, there’s no denying that the good public servants of NSW have worked hard for us, the people of NSW. Cathryn Callaghan, Croydon
