World.title: I’ve met some cold-hearted killers, but most crooks are ordinary and often quite pathetic
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCrime Opinion I’ve met some cold-hearted killers, but most crooks are ordinary and often quite pathetic Jason Doyle Contributor September 28, 2026 — 7:00pm

September 28, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In about AD 175, Roman emperor and philosopher Marcus Aurelius wrote of his day ahead: “I will encounter busybodies, ingrates, egomaniacs, liars, the jealous and cranks.” He could have been a police officer. Marcus was a keen observer of life, and as a police officer myself, I always sought to be the same. If there’s one thing I learnt, there is always a lot more going on under the surface than first appears. Oh, and that people can do remarkable things: good, bad and stupid. I’ve dealt with plenty of criminals. Mostly the bad ones because they’re easier to catch. People might be surprised how common criminality is; many crooks actually have regular day jobs to pay the bills. I had to laugh at the burglar brought into the station one night who pleaded to be let out in the morning, as he was expected on the worksite to resume his career as a tradie. Admirable dedication, I guess. Of course many crooks are engaged in white-collar crime, hiding behind their computers. It’s sobering to realise that criminals walk among us. It’s just that most don’t recognise them. Criminals walk among us, but they are rarely masterminds. iStock There are cold-hearted killers out there, and I’ve met some of them, but most crooks are decidedly ordinary and often quite pathetic. One serious offender came into the cells yelling abuse and issuing commands to his underlings to “tell the dogs nothin’” when interviewed. After five minutes of being alone in a cell, he was crying and asking to call his mother. Yep, a real tough guy. No doubt he would have lied about that to his cronies because when caught, most people lie. I snagged a burglar literally half in and half out of the hole he’d made in a front door, but like the Shaggy song he said, “It wasn’t me,” even with the stolen jewellery in his pockets. Similarly, after seeing a young offender commit a crime and flee, I was soon speaking to him and his mother at the front door of his home. He nervously denied everything, and his mum, who knew full well that her little angel had only just arrived home, declared he had been with her all morning. Two liars for the price of one. Having just used his mother to cover for his illicit activities, this young bloke, now emboldened, began to say the most disgusting things about my own dear mother, while standing behind his.



As well as wannabe criminal masterminds, police deal frequently with regular people. There is often a lot going on underneath a happy veneer, but sometimes the secrets burst into the open. After a physical fight between a successful (based on the car parked outside) businessman and a female victim, it soon became clear that the man didn’t live there and was married to someone else. He begged us to keep his affair quiet, but after the case made its way to court, I’m sure I wasn’t the only one surprised when the man’s wife arrived to give a character reference for her wayward spouse. Evidently, he had fessed up at some point. Related Article Opinion

Real life As a police officer, I made life and death decisions daily. They never leave you Jason Doyle Contributor The lives of other families are torn apart by violence, poor mental health, gambling debts or substance abuse problems. Why? Because life is complex, and often not easy to navigate. I learned that quickly. Sometimes despair leads to suicide or attempts. I’ve twice rescued people from suicide attempts in what might have been their final moments. What makes a person that desperate? I got an answer once when I sat with a young person after an attempt, and they opened up about why – they wanted to change sex, and their parents refused to accept this complexity of their child’s life. I wonder if some of the belligerent commentators on “woke” ideology and gender issues have ever had a conversation like this? Money and fame are no barrier to this scourge. I’ve attended the house of a celebrity who had made an attempt on their life, and I encountered an AFL footballer whose depression was so obvious that I had to intervene. This was back when sportspeople didn’t take time off to address their personal demons. That this is widely accepted now has to be a step forward. Police themselves are particularly susceptible to deteriorating mental health, due at least in part to the trauma they are regularly exposed to. Between 2000 and 2020, more than 100 serving Australian police officers took their own lives. Plenty more have done it after retiring. Our brains can only take so much. I encourage readers to check on their family and mates, police or not, as uncomfortable as these conversations may be.



Related Article Analysis

Naked City ‘You’re gunna get it’: How police stared down a double-murderer and prevented further carnage No matter how long you work the streets, human behaviour can still surprise. Once, when a truck hit a bridge in Flemington, I had to shut down the train station on top of the bridge because the truck had snared power lines and the whole place was potentially “live”. The scene was lit up with emergency vehicles, flashing lights, cones and tape. A jogger ignored all of that and ran right into the danger zone. I’m not sure how our species has accomplished so much when we can be so individually stupid. But some behaviours never seem to change. Despite modern innovations such as 3D-printed guns, and machetes as first-choice weapons, the people using these tools are the same. Even after we have flying cars and package holidays to the moon, we will still be calling police to pick up the pieces when it all goes wrong. Jason Doyle is a retired police officer. Support is available from Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Essendon land Longmire for head of performance role, Kangas zero in on their new coach
World.content:
In today’s AFL briefing, your wrap of footy news: John Longmire’s responsibilities at Essendon will include but not be limited to game strategy, player development, leadership, the coaching group.

Daniel Giansiracusa is among the key candidates for North Melbourne’s vacant coaching position as the Roos ramp up their search.

Jack Viney will fly to Perth to tour West Coast’s facilities as he plots a move away from the Demons. Essendon have pulled off a huge coup landing Sydney premiership coach John Longmire as their new head of performance. Longmire will oversee football operations and work alongside first time coach Mark McVeigh who was an assistant coach for Longmire at Sydney. His responsibilities will include game strategy, player development, leadership, the coaching group, performance analytics and strength and conditioning. His appointment is a massive coup for club president Andrew Welsh and CEO Tim Roberts as they look to rebuild the football department and attract players and coaches. John Longmire will head to Essendon. Getty



Longmire coached the Swans in five grand finals including the 2012 premiership after a stellar playing career with the Kangaroos. He stepped down as Sydney coach to make way for his successor Dean Cox at the end of 2024 and worked in a club performance role for the past two seasons. He was a candidate to coach the Tassie Devils before Ken Hinkley was appointed coach but decided not to put himself in the race to become North Melbourne coach after Alastair Clarkson was sacked. Longmire, 55, said he was excited to join the Bombers in a new role supporting the football department. “I’ve known Mark [McVeigh] for a long time and have worked with him as well. He is passionate about the Bombers and has a clear vision for the team,” he said. “I look forward to supporting both he and the staff as the club looks to take the necessary steps back towards being a consistent team who challenge the opposition every week.”



Longmire was prominent at the Swans as he supported key leaders at the club as they dealt with the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal where five players missed finals due to their behaviour after a round 23 match against the Bombers. Giansiracusa among Kangaroos’ coaching candidates Hawthorn development coach Daniel Giansiracusa is among the key candidates for North Melbourne’s vacant coaching position as the Kangaroos zero in on a new coach to replace Alastair Clarkson. Giansiracusa has a strong coaching resume. He was at the Western Bulldogs when they won their drought breaking flag in 2016 and won the assistant coach of the year in 2020. He then coached at Essendon in several line roles for five seasons before joining the Hawks as a development coach in 2026 as Hawthorn went within a minute of reaching the 2026 grand final.



Highly rated Hawthorn assistant Daniel Giansiracusa. Getty Images Giansiracusa presented strongly for the Kangaroos job at the end of 2020 and is considered to combine a great football brain with an ability to form relationships. He has worked under Luke Beveridge, Brad Scott and Sam Mitchell since his 256-match career finished in 2014. Geelong assistant and former Magpies coach Nathan Buckley impressed in his initial discussions with the Kangaroos and confirmed on grand final day he is going through the selection process while Dockers’ assistant Jaymie Graham is also in the mix. The club also met recently with Cats’ premiership player Corey Enright who recently accepted an assistant coaching role back at Geelong after five seasons at St Kilda. The Cats are aware of his ambitions to be a senior coach. North Melbourne are keen for Graham to present with club officials asking football people about the Fremantle assistant over grand final weekend. Graham was high on Carlton’s list before Josh Fraser earned the job with a strong presentation combined with a startling run as interim coach.



However the race is expected to be wide open for the gig. Club leaders met recently with Kangaroos premiership player and Eagles’ premiership coach Adam Simpson before he withdrew his candidacy after being left at that meeting with the sense he was not the direction they wanted to take. Buckley, who coached Collingwood into a 10th season before departing midway through 2021, interviewed for Melbourne’s job at the end of last season before joining Geelong as an assistant coach in 2026. He was a candidate for the Tasmanian Devils coaching job before they opted to appoint Ken Hinkley. Viney to head west as Eagles circle



Melbourne veteran Jack Viney will fly to Perth on Tuesday to tour West Coast’s facilities as he plots a move away from the Demons. Having been told opportunities might dry up for him in the midfield next year as the Demons favour younger players, Viney is looking at moving. Jack Viney’s only AFL game this year was the wildcard final against Carlton. Getty Images He met with West Coast officials in Melbourne in the past week and was impressed with the pitch from coaches. Essendon have also met with Viney. The Bombers would consider the 32-year-old a ready-made strong-bodied midfield replacement for Zach Merrett, who his likely to move to Hawthorn. Essendon is also attracted to Viney’s leadership, character and training standards to support their young playing group.



Their interest in Viney might now be redoubled after they missed out on securing Adelaide midfielder Luke Pedlar, who has requested a trade to cross-town rivals Port Adelaide. Tough midfielder-forward Luke Pedlar is crossing from the Crows to the Power. Getty Images The Bombers were in the hunt for the 24-year-old, who has not been able to cement a place in the Crows’ line-up, playing just 49 matches since being picked at No.11 in the 2020 national draft and battling a seriess of injury issues. But Pedlar decided to remain in his home state and join the Power, who have lost star free agent Zak Butters to the Western Bulldogs.



The Bombers have several trade targets as new coach Mark McVeigh settles in the role. Essendon are also interested in Lions’ premiership midfielder Sam Marshall and Geelong midfielder Jack Bowes as they look to recast their midfield with Merrett’s likely exit. The Bombers could also lose contracted defender Jordan Ridley, who has gained interest from Geelong and the Kangaroos. Ridley has played just 26 AFL matches in the past three seasons. Melbourne midfielder Trent Rivers is also looking to move with one year left on his contract. He has been interested in joining the Brisbane Lions, given his partner is from Brisbane, but he has also had some interest from West Coast. The trade period does not officially begin until next Monday, but talks have been underway for several months about possible trades and free agency moves. The free agency window opens this Friday, with the Giants’ Toby Greene, Gold Coast’s Ben King, the Lions’ Lachie Neale and Port Adelaide’s Butters all looking to move as free agents.

World.title: CCTV captures police car travelling at high speed before crash that killed Mia Lay
World.content:
CCTV footage has captured the moments before the patrol car carrying Constable Mia Lay smashed into a tree in Sydney’s inner-south, instantly killing the 20-year-old police officer and hospitalising the car’s driver, Constable Brandon Torrisi. Lay was killed when the marked police car in which she was a passenger crashed in Redfern during an urgent response to a reported vehicle theft in nearby Glebe about 1.30am on Friday. Security camera footage from a nail salon less than 200 metres from the crash site shows the Volkswagen Tiguan patrol car bursting down Gibbons Street, sirens and lights blaring, before the fatal accident. Mia’s father, Clem Lay, told the Herald that after his initial anger, he was relieved that Torrisi, his daughter’s fellow officer, had survived the crash.



“I want [Mia] to be remembered by as many as possible for as long as possible,” he said. “Everyone that she touched in her life has paid tribute.”



Clem told Nine News he hoped there was “no one at fault” for the crash that killed his daughter, saying that the immense loss his family is experiencing still hadn’t hit home. Clem Lay has said he was relieved there was a survivor in the crash that killed his daughter. Nine News Mourners have filled the site of the crash with flowers and tributes to Lay. Former colleagues and schoolmates of Lay were among those who left written tributes to the officer. One mourner tied the NSW Police badge to the tree with a scarf bearing the colours of the police uniform, while others brought shirts bearing the insignia of APIA Leichhardt, Lay’s former football club. Mourners laid flowers in tribute to Lay. Wolter Peeters



A NSW Police badge is tied to the tree at Gibbons Street. Wolter Peeters Police Minister Yasmin Catley didn’t weigh in on speculation Monday that Torrisi, 24, may have reached speeds surpassing 150km/h when the crash occurred, saying officers were entrusted with determining how quick they travel when they’re attending an urgent call. “Police make those decisions, but the investigation will determine if that’s the case,” she said. The NSW Law Enforcement Conduct Commission is overseeing the police investigation of the crash as it determines the circumstances leading to Lay’s death. The police watchdog can independently investigate the incident only once the police probe is complete.



Mia Lay at her attestation ceremony in 2025. Raphael Grzebieta, a road safety expert and professor emeritus at the University of NSW, said the nature of the collision – a “narrow offset” crash – meant the driver was further from the impact point. Mia Lay, who was a passenger in the police car, died instantly upon impact. NSW Police “A road where the speed limit is set at 50km/h indicates a high risk of serious injury or fatality if a vehicle travels at any speed above that value,” Grzebieta said. “What was the urgent danger that required them to travel at that speed? What was the urgent situation that required them to have those lights and sirens on?”



Jake Olivier, a professor of statistics at UNSW, said a car travelling above 50km/h – the speed limit on the stretch of Gibbons Street where Lay was killed – increased the risk of serious injury or death. “In normal driving conditions, I do not see this road really being a problem because the posted speed is set at 50km/h but travelling greater than that does pose a risk,” said Olivier, deputy director of the university’s Transport and Road Safety Research Centre. Olivier said hazards on the roadside, including trees, increased the likelihood of a fatal crash. Investigators are trying to piece together the circumstances around the crash. Sam Mooy “That’s one of the reasons speed limits are set as they are,” he said.



Olivier, who has driven the route Lay took on Friday morning, said the right-hand curve in the road where the 20-year-old’s vehicle collided with the tree “comes out of nowhere”. “It seems like it should be straight,” he said. “Psychologically, you kind of feel like you’re going straight.” Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Police thought John was in a deep drunken sleep. Instead, he lay dying
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCoroners Court of Victoria Police thought John was in a deep drunken sleep. Instead, he lay dying Lachlan Abbott September 28, 2026 — 6:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victoria Police has apologised for the death of a man who spent hours unresponsive with a brain injury in a Broadmeadows cell as he waited for paramedics. CCTV footage played in the Coroner’s Court on Monday showed three officers carrying John Makai’s limp body into a holding cell about 1.15am on September 10, 2023. An inquest is being held into the death of John Makai in September 2023. Facebook Police had arrived at Makai’s Sunbury home about an hour earlier, following a report the 58-year-old had fought with his adult son after both consumed alcohol. Opening the inquest into the death on Monday, Rachel Ellyard, counsel assisting the coroner, told the court Makai struck his son, Terewa, in the head with a mug and continued to approach him, despite warnings not to.



Makai was then punched twice and fell to the floor, Ellyard said. In a phone call played in court, a friend could be heard contacting Triple Zero to ask for an ambulance before changing his mind as others in the background told him to hang up. A dispatcher then created a police job instead. The Broadmeadows police station, as photographed in 2010. John Woudstra Body-worn camera footage showed officers arrived at a Timins Street house at 12.11am to find Makai and his son injured. Although both declined treatment, police requested paramedics attend. “They were advised there would be delays because of workload pressures that night on Ambulance Victoria,” Ellyard said.



She described Makai as “argumentative” in the body-worn camera footage, which captured him standing up, losing his balance, and falling back into a bookcase, where he hit his head. “He just blacked out, hey,” a man could be heard saying. The body-cam footage then showed Makai’s former partner tending to him and saying he was fine. Makai’s son told police: “This has never happened before.” Ellyard told the court police then designated Makai as having breached family violence laws, so he could be taken to Broadmeadows police station as paramedics weren’t immediately available.



He was carried from his home to the police divisional van. Makai was basically motionless for four hours, the court heard. “With the benefit of medical evidence, it appears … a developing brain injury was impeding his ability to walk,” Ellyard said. Video from inside the van shows Makai’s head was bumped again as he was dragged out by the ankles on arrival at Broadmeadows police station. “That vision shows John has experienced a serious decline in his consciousness and capacity to walk since he was put in that van,” Ellyard said.



Members of Makai’s family shook their heads in court on Monday as CCTV footage showed him being carried in a prone position onto a cell bed. Custody officers reported Makai was snoring, but Ellyard told the court there were no signs of voluntary movement. “What was perceived as a deep drunken sleep may have actually been a traumatic injury and bleeding into the brain,” she said. Custody Sergeant Neil Gregory called a police dispatcher at 1.25am to check on ambulance availability, but the court heard he was told crews were still busy. Another call was made at 2.18am, but the dispatcher said Ambulance Victoria was still dealing with 40 to 50 pending jobs. A dispatcher’s error then led to the ambulance being cancelled about 3am, the court heard. Gregory asked police subordinates to check on Makai every 15 minutes, but the court heard this did not occur as frequently as required.



Ellyard said cell footage showed Makai remained basically motionless from about 2am to 6am. “Apart from a very small movement to shield his eyes from glare ... no movement was recorded at all,” she said. Editor's pick Victorian election Level crossings on hold as Labor vows to fix Melbourne’s most unreliable train line No police entered the cell during this four-hour period. When a new watchhouse sergeant arrived after 6am and realised Makai was unable to be roused, officers entered his cell and tried to wake him by rubbing his sternum and pinching his arm. Gregory called Triple Zero after learning the earlier ambulance had been cancelled. “We were all expecting the ambulance here five hours ago,” Gregory said in a phone call aired in court. “I’ve never known anyone not to stir like this.”



Paramedics arrived at 6.29am and discovered Makai had a traumatic brain injury. He was taken to hospital, where he recorded a blood alcohol level of .13, and was later found to have suffered unsurvivable trauma. He died on September 12. Barrister Andrew Imrie, representing the police chief commissioner, said custody officers failed to complete a medical checklist and risk assessment at the Broadmeadows police station. “It’s a situation which we work tirelessly to avoid,” Imrie said. “In this case, however, my client acknowledges at the outset of this inquest that the standards of care in custody fell short of expected standards. “As the evidence currently stands, its unclear whether these shortcomings would have made a difference to the tragedy in this case … but [the chief commissioner] apologises.” The inquest continues. Fire crews have neutralised a 1000-litre chemical spill at a Gore company that triggered nearby buildings to be evacuated earlier on Monday.

Fire and Emergency shift manager Lyn Crosson said the crews had scaled down to clean up the spill at Mainfreight Transport on Oldham Street.

A container was pierced, causing the leak to spill 1000 litres of the chemical shortly after 2pm on Monday.

World.title: Left bloc may be able to form government latest poll suggests
World.content:
New polling from 1News-Verian shows a Green surge and the left bloc able to win government - presuming National refuses to work with the Opportunity Party.

The pollster modelled two possibilities based on how many electorates Te Pāti Māori (TPM) wins - either four Māori seats plus one for Mariameno Kapa-Kingi's Te Tai Tokerau party, or just one electorate seat for TPM - but in both scenarios Opportunity would hold the balance of power.

With National's leader Christopher Luxon having ruled out working with Opportunity, they would be expected to form a government with the left bloc.

National: 28 percent, down 1 (34 seats)

Labour: 28 percent, down 2 (34 seats)

Greens: 16 percent, up 4 (19 seats)

ACT: 11 percent, up 2 points (14 seats)

NZ First: 9 percent, up 1 (11 seats)

Opportunity 6 percent, down 2 (7 seats)

Te Pāti Māori: 1 percent, steady (4 seats)

Te Tai Tokerau party: (1 seat)

Some 13 percent did not know or refused to say who they would vote for.

On the preferred prime minister stakes Christopher Luxon, Chlöe Swarbrick and David Seymour all made two-point gains, while Chris Hipkins was down one-point, and Winston Peters remained steady.

Preferred prime minister:

Christopher Luxon: 19 percent - up 2 points

Chris Hipkins: 14 percent - down 1

Chlöe Swarbrick: 8 percent, up 2

David Seymour: 7 percent, up 2

Winston Peters: 7 percent, steady

The poll surveyed 1004 eligible voters and was weighted for demographics, with a margin of error of 3.4 percent at the 95 percent confidence interval. It was conducted between 23 and 27 September.

Party support percentages have been rounded up or down to whole numbers, except those less than 4.5 percent, which are reported to one decimal place. The data has been weighted to align with Stats NZ population counts for age, gender, region, ethnic identification and education level. The sample for mobile phones is selected by random dialling using probability sampling, and the online sample is collected using an online panel. Undecided voters, non-voters and those who refused to answer are excluded from the data on party support. The results are a snapshot in time of party support, and not a prediction.

World.title: Dannevirke hospital 'not capable of providing a safe and sustainable inpatient service'
World.content:
There are not enough clinicians at Dannevirke Community Hospital to ensure patients will receive safe care, an urgent audit has found.

Health New Zealand has put a temporary freeze on Tararua Health Group's hospital taking new patients while it finds more clinical staff, following a number of resignations.

They came after local doctors in the Tararua District raised concerns about referring patients there because of safety risks, and the health agency has carried out an audit of the hospital this week.

Health NZ central region director Geoff Gwyn told Checkpoint the findings of the audit were serious and those concerns were correct.

"[The audit] shows that they are not capable at the moment of providing a safe and sustainable inpatient service," he said.

"They don't have sufficient clinicians to actually deliver what we would consider a roster that is safe for patients who are admitted to the hospital."

Audio player for " Health NZ finishes review of Dannevirke Hospital " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1634305%2Fdannevirke-hospital-not-capable-of-providing-a-safe-and-sustainable-inpatient-service

Health NZ finishes review of Dannevirke Hospital Checkpoint Download MP3 10m

Five clinicians from Health NZ have been sent to work there to bolster staffing.

"It's insufficient and we have staff on site... we're working with them this week to get them back to a sustainable position in terms of their rostering."

Gwyn said the situation had deteriorated since a June audit found no critical concerns, but 23 low-to-medium level concerns.

"The fact that we are now intervening has significant contractual obligations for them or implications for them, which I can't discuss because they're commercially sensitive, but I don't think anyone would be surprised that I don't have a high level of confidence in the services they're currently providing."

He said Tararua Health Group had 30 days to fix the roster and recruit more clinical staff.

"No decision's been made about the contract. What we want now is for Tararua Health Group to fix the problems and prove to us that they can provide safe and sustainable care."

The hospital and a number of medical centres in the region are owned by the Tararua Health Group, which is owned by OmniHealth - a network of about 17 practices around the country.

Palmerston North Hospital is admitting patients, while Dannevirke Community Hospital has a freeze on admissions.

Tararua Health Group has been contacted for comment.

Pahīatua Medical Centre also audited

Health NZ also audited Pahīatua Medical Centre in the Tararua district, where six staff resigned last week amid concerns about extreme workload and patient safety.

Almost 5000 patients depend on the service.

Gwyn said the review was complete and would be shared with staff on Wednesday.

"What has changed since then is the PHO has put in a general practitioner and practice manager for the next three months. The GP has full daily bookings. There's some nurse practitioner support going in later this week and all of the overdue recalls have been reviewed, prioritised and have been actioned."

He said the GP has been hired full time for three months and he had confidence in the level of care with the extra staff brought in.

World.title: Ngā Manu Kōrero winners reflect on 'surreal' competition
World.content:
Two of New Zealand's up and coming speech-makers and kaikōrero have both made their mark on the famous speech competition Ngā Manu Kōrero.

The top secondary school orators in both English and Te Reo, senior and junior sections, were crowned last week in Kaikohe at the 61st Ngā Manu Kōrero 2026 competition.

Arihia Phillips from Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Kaikohe won the Tā Turi Kara (Sir Turi Carroll) Junior English section in front of her hometown crowd.

Phillips told Morning Report her topic was 'I'm from Kaikohe', expressing much she loved her hometown and the people in it, despite how it was often portrayed in the media.

Audio player for " 14yo wins bi-lingual speech competition in Kaikohe " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/te-ao-maori/1634475%2Fnga-manu-korero-winners-reflect-on-surreal-competition

14yo wins bi-lingual speech competition in Kaikohe Morning Report Download MP3 4m

"Some of the points was our local bakehouse, right in the middle of town, because, well, if you live in Kaikohe you get what I mean.

"Also my grandparents told me a lot about how before the Ngāwhā prison was built, Kaikohe was the humming hub of the north, but it is now known as the hub of youth crime and meth, so I got that point across."

Phillips could probably name all the people in the crowd during the speech and she saw plenty of tears.

"Unfortunately last year one of our rangatahi, a sister, she tragically lost her life in my hometown and I just thought it would be good to put it in there so that you get all sides of Kaikohe."

Phillips said one of the highlights from the competition was that the speaker who stood before her was her best friend.

"It was so beautiful to be able to listen to her stand and then for me to stand after her, it really meant a lot."

The winner of the senior English Korimako category was Kuramātakitaki Stevens, of John McGlashan College in Dunedin.

He told Māpuna the win feels surreal and still had not fully sunk in.

Audio player for " Ngā Manu Kōrero winner Kuramatakitaki Stevens " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/te-ao-maori/1634475%2Fnga-manu-korero-winners-reflect-on-surreal-competition

Ngā Manu Kōrero winner Kuramatakitaki Stevens Māpuna Download MP3 9m

Stevens has always had an interest in whaikōrero and oratory, his whānau have said that he was "born talking".

"Our household is certainly a loquacious one, at the dinner table it's always dominated by discussion and debate and there's usually a speaking queue.

"My two younger siblings, they probably don't talk anywhere near as much as me, but they are great public speakers and my brother's been succeeding in speech competitions in school and my sister actually placed second at regionals for the Junior Māori section at Manu Kōrero this year, she scored first equal but they had to go to another criteria to decide who they would take to nationals."

When ask who inspires him as an orator, Stevens said Tā Tipene O'Regan has had a big influence on him.

"He's clearly and excellent speaker and can command a room, and a whole iwi. It's only in the last year or two that I've really, closely been reading and analysing and appreciating the way that he speaks."

Stevens said it would be an honour to support his iwi of Ngāi Tahu through whaikōrero in the future.

World.title: Hundreds of homes given fast-track green light near Wānaka
World.content:
A 250-home development has been granted fast-track approval near Wānaka.

An application for the Mt Iron Junction Housing Scheme was lodged in February, including plans for a childcare centre and two recreational reserves on the Wānaka-Luggate Highway.

Thirteen of the new homes have been earmarked for the Queenstown Lakes Community Housing Trust for affordable housing.

Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop said it would provide a range of housing to help meet significant demand in the area.

"As well as providing much-needed additional housing, the project is predicted to contribute $86 million to the local economy, supporting jobs both during construction and once the development is complete," he said.

"The panel also accepted the applicant's proposal to limit visitor accommodation to 20 per cent of the development, with those properties able to be used for short-term stays for no more than 120 nights a year.

"This will help ensure these are primarily homes for people to live in, rather than holiday accommodation."

The houses were expected to be built over 10 years across five stages.

Locals had raised concerns about the wildfire risk in the area, including how close future residents might be to susceptible land, the ability to safely evacuate residents and the adequacy of firefighting water supply.

Plans for the Mt Iron Junction housing in Wanaka. Supplied / Mt Iron Junction Housing Scheme

In its decision, the fast-track panel acknowledged the concerns, but said it was satisfied the wildfire risk could be appropriately managed.

That was possible through the combination of subdivision design, access arrangements, defensible space, vegetation management, firefighting water supply, emergency response planning and imposed conditions, the panel said.

"While wildfire risk cannot be entirely eliminated, we are satisfied that the proposed mitigation measures appropriately reduce the risk to future residents and property and provide a suitable framework for ongoing management of that hazard."

Locals also flagged concerns about worsening traffic congestion at the roundabout of State Highway 6, State Highway 84, Riverbank Road and Junction Road.

The NZ Transport Agency flagged that the development would consume available capacity of the roundabout and would bring forward the need for future improvements.

The panel said the applicant volunteered a financial contribution to the agency towards the future costs, which the agency said it would be unable to receive.

During the decision process, the government flagged it was considering changes to the development contributions system to enable councils to recover more costs from fast-tracked developments.

But the panel said no commenter had raised any development contribution concerns, apart from the Transport Agency, so it did not consider the matter any further.

World.title: Jury selected for trial of men following deadly daylight Wairarapa shooting
World.content:
A High Court jury has been shown security camera footage and heard the 111 call from the people involved in a deadly daylight shooting in Wairarapa last year.

Doreion Peri Ropata Hard died after he was found in a vehicle with a gunshot wound in Carterton on 22 March, 2025.

Hard was discovered following reports of a red ute being shot at as it left a supermarket car park in nearby Featherston.

Pelikai Taukei'aho and Tauave Sue each pleaded not guilty to murder charges before the High Court at Wellington on Monday.

Counsel for the prosecution, Tim Bain told the court the incident in March was "a drug deal gone sideways".

He told the jury - ahead of proceedings - both men had entered guilty pleas for several charges relating to the possession and supply of cocaine in the months leading up to the shooting.

He said the accused had arranged - via communications app Signal - to sell several ounces of cocaine to Hard and each stood to make nearly $4000 profit from the deal.

However, he said Hard and four others had conspired to rob the pair and were armed with at least one firearm.

Tauave Sue has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in relation to the death of Doreion Hard. Mark Mitchell

The jury was shown communications between Hard as Sue drove with Taukei'aho down from Auckland - in a grey Holden - to conduct the deal.

Hard persuaded the pair to abandon a meeting point in Lower Hutt and travel over the Remutaka Hill to meet at the Fresh Choice carpark in Featherston.

Shortly before 4pm footage showed the accused as they arrived in the busy supermarket carpark.

Shoppers and several motorcyclist were moving about the space on the sunny afternoon - seemingly unaware of the events about to unfold.

Hard arrived in a red Mercedes followed by a red ute which boxed the grey Holden into its parking space.

Two men - including Hard - approached the Holden and - moments later - the red ute pulled away.

Footage showed Taukei'aho springing from the Holden and firing four shots at the rear of the ute.

Pelikai Taukei'aho has pleaded not guilty to the murder of Doreion Hard in Carterton on 22 March 2025. Mark Mitchell

Calls for help after drug deal gone wrong

The ute was driven to Greytown as the occupants sought medical assistance for Hard's injuries but found the medical centre closed.

The occupants then called emergency services as they sped towards Carterton.

"My mate's been injured real bad.

"He's in a bad way. Is there an ambulance in Carterton? We can meet them. I'm nearly in Carterton.

"He's been shot. He's unconscious. He's not breathing. Where are you?"

"He's f***ing dead man," the occupant said.

Accused looked frozen, afraid

A witness - who was using an EV charging station in the Featherston carpark - said he noticed the ute blocking the grey Holden and heard a "commotion".

"[The passenger] had his arms held up and looked, kind of, afraid or frozen. The person on the outside of the vehicle was opening the door and removing packages from the inside of the vehicle," he said.

He said one man appeared to put a firearm into his pants while another - on the passenger side of the vehicle - stashed the packages in the red ute.

The ute then pulled away and turned right out of the carpark towards Wellington and Taukei'aho and Sue climbed out of the car.

"One of the persons pulled out a firearm and started shooting multiple shots in the direction of the red ute," the witness said.

He said he tried to lower himself towards the ground as the shooter walked back to the vehicle with the gun at his side.

Crown prosecutor Tim Bain. Supplied

Counsel for Taukei'aho, Louise Szrayni asked the witness if he had seen a shot or projectile from the ute which may have caused the accused "to duck" after they left the grey Holden.

The witness said he was not aware of anything coming from the ute and described one of the men's purposeful pace has he strode towards the red ute before he opened fire while it drove away.

Sue and Taukei'aho fled the scene and their vehicle was spiked by police on the Upper Hutt side of the Remutaka Hill near Kaitoke in the hours following the shooting.

'No reason for self defence', prosecution

Prosecutor Tim Bain said police discovered firearms in the vehicle and nearly 50 rounds of live 9mm ammunition.

Bain told the jury the Crown would seek to prove that - in opening fire on the vehicle carrying Hard - Taukei'aho had either sought to harm the occupants or had, at least, acted recklessly in doing so.

He said that communications ahead of the deal would show the pair were prepared for the potential of a robbery and the decision to open fire on the vehicle carrying Hard was either an attempt to retrieve the cocaine or an act of revenge against the robbers.

"The robbery was complete. There was no threat, there was no reason for self defence," Bain said.

World.title: Socceroos expect Brazil backlash in Brisbane
World.content:
Ageless Socceroo Aziz Behich has no plans to pull the pin with the side on the rise, buoyed by a performance against Brazil they are keen to do better than in Brisbane.

Australia conceded a goal with the final play of their Townsville clash on Friday to walk away with a 1-1 draw that, tellingly, left them disappointed.

A Brazilian backlash is expected at Lang Park on Tuesday night, and the A-League's only player in the 26-man squad is primed to counter it.

"We've set the bar high for ourselves … it was good, but we need to be better," the 35-year-old said.

"How brave we were on the ball … we trusted each other and took the game on.

"When you do that against an opponent like that, you earn their respect and we need to do that again, that's for sure."

Incredibly Behich's 88th national appearance was his first game since the World Cup, but the veteran was able to display his trademark pace and work rate despite being in preseason mode with Melbourne City.

There is optimism the next generation of talent will take the Socceroos to new heights and, with the Asian Cup on the horizon in January, Behich plans to do more than stick around.

"I wouldn't call it hanging on … I'm still playing at a high level … it's exciting times," he said.

"I feel great. I'm a player that's always honest with myself. I know when I'm not at a level I should be. But I have a lot in the tank to give."

The Socceroos took the lead against Brazil, and deserved it as well. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Coach Tony Popovic echoed Behich's sentiment ahead of the Brisbane rematch.

"Being confident, being brave … we've clearly seen a difference in the players' demeanour since the World Cup," he said.

He said the challenge would be to back-up that performance on a short-turnaround.

"We don't have players playing regular Champions League, or in the top leagues, 60 games a year," he said.

"It's a great test."

The Brisbane fixture serves as a homecoming for rising defender Lucas Herrington.

The 19-year-old played his last game for the Roar in January this year, before using the World Cup to springboard from Colorado in the MLS to Hull in the Premier League.

"We've seen against Brazil a confident young man, defending against the very best," Popovic said.

"Now he's got the challenge of doing something he maybe hasn't done in a while, against that calibre, backing up three, four days later.

"Can the body do it and are you ready to play at that level once more?"

AAP

World.title: Matthews claims world championship silver after life-threatening crash
World.content:
Michael Matthews felt that his career was probably over at the start of the season.

Having missed a large portion of the 2025 season after a pulmonary embolism was discovered in his lung, a horrific collision with a fire truck while training in March could have cost him an awful lot more than just his career.

But less than eight months later the 36-year-old was standing on the world championship podium for the fourth time in his career, claiming second place in what was the greatest possible silver lining after two years of desperately bad luck.

"I'm pretty speechless I'm sitting here with a silver medal around my neck," Matthews said.

"Honestly, I wasn't sure exactly how today was going to go.

"The field was so strong. Leading into the race, I was quietly confident, but the world championships is always a bit of a lottery."

Michael Matthews felt he might not have been able to ride during the world championships after a horrific two seasons. (Supplied: AusCycling/Craig Render)

Matthews led the chasing pack home 13 seconds behind surprise American winner Brandon McNulty after a brutal 273.4-kilometre course in and around Montréal in Canada.

The Australian edged out former champion Mathieu van der Poel and Quinn Simmonds, who were both classified with the same time.

His silver medal will sit alongside the road race silver he won 11 years ago in Richmond, Virginia, as well ass road race bronze medals in 2017 (Bergen) and 2022 (Wollongong).

Matthews also has two gold medals and a bronze in the mixed team relay at world championships, and was the winner of the under 23 title in Geelong in 2010.

"I think this was probably my last opportunity to be a world champion. So, obviously, mixed feelings, but at the same time, I have to be proud of what the way I've bounced back," Matthews said.

"To be second around here on a circuit that many said was out of my reach, to show everyone that I'm still up there with the best in the world even after what I've been through, at the moment feels like a win."

Just getting to the start line would have been a victory of sorts for Matthews.

On March 5, the veteran Australian rider crashed head-on with a fire truck at a combined speed of 100km/h.

Michael Matthews was lucky to be able to continue after his horrific crash in March. (Supplied: Instagram/@Bling90)

Matthews suffered an open arm fracture, severed thumb tendons, broke both wrists and sustained a sinus fracture that required stitches to his face.

"I hit a fire truck at pretty much 100km/h, I was doing 50 and the truck was doing 50," Matthews told the Detour podcast prior to this year's Tour de France.

"With a crash like that, it could have ended my career, or even worse.

"I might not be here right now. I'm extremely blessed to be able to tell the story and how lucky I was."

Matthews said there were a couple of times over the past two years when he felt he would never be back at the pointy end of the professional peloton, crediting his family for always believing in him.

"What I've been through the last two years, with embolia in my lungs, thinking my career was done, to breaking both my arms at the start of this year, thinking my career was done. Now, bouncing back to being second in the Worlds road race — just speechless, honestly," he said.

"I said to my wife at the start of today, 'Let's just leave it all out there and be proud of the ride at the end of the day, make sure you finish with nothing.'

"It's exactly what happened today when I crossed the finish line. I put my head in my hands almost in disbelief.

"Honestly, it's just credit to my family, to the team, to all the support crew around me that didn't stop believing this could happen right now. So, I owe everything to them."

Michael Matthews was almost in disbelief at winning silver. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

The race itself was an absolute barnstormer of a contest from the very off.

Two-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar was absent from the race, recovering from a fractured neck and collarbone that he suffered in a crash that took him out of the Vuelta a España last month.

That left the race wide open, with a number of riders all believing they had a chance to claim the rainbow bands on a course that was hard enough to interest the climbers as much as the one-day specialist rouleurs.

The race exploded with 90km to go as Oscar Onley, van der Poel, Wout van Aert, Simmons and Primož Roglič built a lead, which was whittled down by the French team, led by Paul Seixas, and Isaac del Toro.

A flurry of frantic accelerations and regroupings at the front made for a frenetic, thrilling race, with the USA well placed with three of the leading 13 riders.

McNulty fired off the front with just over 30km to go and, despite brilliant surges from Ireland's Ben Healy and Britain's Tom Pidcock, the American soloed to victory.

Brandon McNulty is America's third male world road race champion after Lance Armstrong and Greg Lemond. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

The 28-year-old American, who rides with Pogačar at UAE Team Emirates-XRG, is just the third American to win the men's world road race title and the first since Lance Armstrong in Oslo in 1993.

"I'm really at a loss," McNulty said.

"Until the last hundred metres, I didn't believe it, I was so tired. I was just dying, but I kept pushing. We have said for weeks now that we had a super strong team. We talked about it, but I knew it would take a miracle. I guess miracles happen."

World.title: Hauser wins thrilling World Triathlon sprint, Parker breaks record
World.content:
Australian triathlete Matt Hauser showed he was up for the fight at the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Pontevedra, Spain overnight, beating Vasco Vilaça to the line in a thrilling sprint finish.

Defending series champion Hauser came into the series finale knowing he would be up against it to retain his title.

A number of crashes throughout the year meant Hauser needed to win and beat Vilaça by five places.

The Portuguese triathlete was in no mood to let the Australian get any sort of gap though, sticking with him through the swim and shadowing on the bike before the tremendous run stage.

"That's just ridiculous. I was just telling myself I can't lose this one, I can't lose this one," Hauser said.

"I've been so up and down this year and so inconsistent. I just really wanted it out there today.

"There is a lot to be thankful for and pleased for. I was really happy to get the win out there today and to execute when it really mattered.

"I'm not back-to-back world champion, but I can hang my head high. I achieved what I set out to achieve today and now looking onwards and upwards for next year."

Matt Hauser pushed the pace on the front during the run. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Hauser and Vilaça ran away from Olympic champion Alex Yee, whose stunning run leg bought him into contention in the closing stages.

The Briton could not stay with the leading pair though as they engaged in what turned into a furious battle for the line.

Hauser's 'world champion persona' Despite being Australia's first male triathlon world champion in 20 years, Matt Hauser is still building the blocks towards his aim of Olympic success in 2028.

Both men were credited with a time of 1:39:31, but the Australian's dip on the line ensured he would claim victory by 0.08 seconds.

"Credit to Vasco, what a champion," Hauser said.

"I mean we got a bit pushy, shovy in the end. Apologies to him. I gave him a bit of a bump on my way through to get to the line first.

"[But] you have to do these things to get the victory sometimes, to have that dog in you.

"I didn't want to lose the sprint finish to Vacsco. I haven't lost all year to him.

"I have this notch in my belt this year and will take the momentum into next year and to LA2028."

Lauren Parker breaks record

Lauren Parker now has a record six world para triathlon titles. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Lauren Parker also claimed victory in the PTWC race in Pontevedra, cementing her status as one of Australia's greatest-ever para triathletes.

PTWC events are for athletes who use a wheelchair in their daily life.

Racers in the PTWC category compete in a standard 750-metre open-water swim, but can use swim-exit handlers to help them out of the water. They then race a recumbent handcycle for the 20km cycling leg, before using a racing wheelchair for the 5km run leg.

The reigning Paralympic champion was never troubled in the race, leading from early on in the swim and thereafter, cruising to victory.

"I felt awesome out there in swim, bike and run," Parker said.

"I got a decent lead in the swim … I got on the bike and I felt so strong out there and I was pulling time into the girls, and extended my lead."

"And in the run, I was just holding them off."

The win secured the 37-year-old multi-sport star a sixth PTWC World Championship title.

It made Parker Australia's most successful ever Para triathlete, beating the legendary Bill Chaffey's previous benchmark of five world championship titles.

"It's just as special as my first title," Parker said.

"My first title was obviously [special because] it was my first. Number six means I've overtaken Bill Chaffey. It's awesome."

Parker won the PTWC class para-triathlon race at the Paris Olympics, having won silver in the same event in Tokyo in 2021.

She then backed up that performance to win para-cycling gold in the H1–4 road race and silver in the H1-3 time trial as well.

Not only that, but Parker can add four rainbow jerseys as a cycling world champion to her triathlon titles.

The Newcastle athlete also took to the snow in the past year, competing in both the biathlon and cross-country skiing at the Milano-Cortina Paralympic Winter Games in 2026.

Elsewhere, Anu Francis secured silver in the Women's PTS2 World Championship race.

The PTS2 classification is for non-wheelchair users for athletes who live with muscle power disorders or limb deficiencies.

World.title: Sandon Smith leads Newcastle out of an Immortal shadow
World.content:
It's rare that anybody in Newcastle shares an accolade with Andrew Johns, but Sandon Smith has managed it.

Fresh off his electric double in the Knights' 22-14 win over Penrith on Sunday, Smith will join Johns as the only men to play halfback for Newcastle in a grand final.

"It's pretty cool to hear. I don't think I'm anywhere near that [Johns]," Smith said.

"But it's an honour."

Talking about Johns is part of the deal when you play halfback for Newcastle but it's wrong to compare the two because it's wrong to compare anyone to Johns, who stands alone as the club and the city's ultimate legend and hero.

Johns was more than just a player to the Knights, even if he's the best player they have ever had or will ever know.

The 1997 and 2001 premierships made Johns a Newcastle folk hero and the personification of the Novocastrian dream, larger than life through his greatness and profoundly human at the same time, like if they found a demigod in the front bar of a Cessnock pub.

Every Newcastle halfback since his retirement in 2007 exists, to one extent or another, in his enormous shadow which has a gravitational pull from which some players never escaped.

Andrew Johns remains Newcastle's greatest ever player. (Getty Images via All Sports: Chris McGrath)

You'd have an easier time replacing Christ in Christianity, because at least then there's supposed to be a second coming.

The only way to do it is to opt out of that framing altogether, because it's a game that cannot be won and therefore shouldn't be played.

Smith doesn't need to be Andrew Johns for Newcastle to make a grand final, the prelim is proof that being himself is enough.

His first try was a clever effort backed by his speed but his second, a length of the field intercept in the dying seconds that sealed the club's first grand final berth in a quarter century, was something else entirely.

It brought Johns himself to tears and for the post-Johns generation, many of whom are seeing the Knights in a grand final for the first time, it was the greatest moment of their supporting lives.

"The first one I was just trying to stay in the game and I saw an opportunity. Those don't always come off, but it worked well," Smith said.

"The second one, I didn't know if I could make it. My little legs were hanging on for dear life. But I was happy to make it, I'm ecstatic.

"It's hard to put into words. There's so much emotion going on.

"I think there was a few tears coming out. I was happy, I was tired, I can't really explain it.

"When I came to the club, I heard a lot about the town and how our football affects the town.

"It's hard to put into words when you're a part of it, but it's so true and it's so special, to be a part of something like this that is bigger than ourselves."

One of those supporters was Johns himself, who wept openly and spoke with a voice clouded with emotion on Channel Nine commentary in the aftermath of Smith's last score.

It was a gift of a moment, a slice of heaven wrapped in red and blue, the kind that Johns gave his team and his town back in those olden days, but until Smith went all the way the Immortal had never received it himself.

That alone would be a high honour, but Smith stood up multiple times on his team's biggest game since the Johns age, creating the break that led to Dominic Young's try early in the second half and forcing a key error from Lindsay Smith late on.

It sets up a grand final berth against the Roosters, where Smith played from 2023 to 2025 before he travelled to Newcastle in an effort for more NRL starts after the Bondi club signed Daly Cherry-Evans.

He insists there's no bad blood with the Tricolours as he tries to pilot the Knights to a premiership at their expense.

"It won't change anything for me. I'll enjoy it, I'll embrace this whole week. I'll stay in the moment. It's just another team and it doesn't change anything for myself or the team," Smith said.

"If we win a grand final, I don't think it matters who it'd be against.

"They were transparent with me [around Cherry-Evans]. I've got no remorse, I loved the club and loved my time there, but I'm a Knight now."

Like many of his teammates, Smith's been trusted to do more than one job this season.

He's at halfback now, in relief of the injured Dylan Brown, but has also spent time at five-eighth and as the bench utility.

Sandon Smith joined Newcastle this year from the Roosters. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But he's played them all well and it's added up to the best season of his young career with Smith thriving under the coaching of Justin Holbrook, who he'd worked with as an assistant at the Roosters.

"Justo's been such a rock for me over the past few years, [especially] coming to the club with him when I was unsure about what this year would look like for me," Smith said.

"He constantly reassured me to keep my head down, keep enjoying myself and keep getting better.

"The NRL season is a long season and your moment will come. He kept saying you need to be ready when that moment comes."

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

All halfbacks wear pressure on their shoulders in grand finals and Smith does so with the added spectre of Johns's legacy.

But having already earned one opportunity that has eluded all other Knights halfbacks since Johns, Smith has a chance to win an even greater prize.

Newcastle's most glorious times are inextricably tied with Johns but now Smith and his teammates can write a new legend with victory on Sunday.

It is one which, for the first time in Knights history, can exist beyond Johns and his titanic legacy.

His shadow will always be longest, but now Smith and these Knights have stepped outside it they have the chance to cast one of their own.

World.title: Baird quits as CA chair as Big Bash sell-off fallout continues
World.content:
Mike Baird has sensationally quit as Cricket Australia chair, after his own state association refused to back its representative in the fallout over the privatisation of Big Bash League clubs.

The former NSW premier informed fellow board members on Monday he would not seek re-election at next month's annual general meeting, with David Boon to take over as interim chair.

The decision comes after Baird lost the support of Cricket NSW, with the country's most powerful state unhappy with the decision to allow private investment.

Baird had served as NSW's representative on the board, and approached it recently to confirm it would not support him in the current circumstances.

David Boon will step in as the interim chair. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

He did have the option of moving into an independent role, but AAP was told he did not wish to continue without the support of all states.

Cricket Australia (CA) officials maintain they continue to back the call for the privatisation of clubs, which was confirmed earlier this month.

"After much consideration I have decided to stand down as CA chair and director," Baird said in a statement.

"I am delighted that David Boon has agreed to undertake the interim chair role while we complete the formal chair process, and I will undertake a transition process with David over coming weeks."

Baird had been on the CA board for six years and had served as chair since February 2023.

Alongside Todd Greenberg, he formed one of the most powerful duos in Australian sport.

In a statement on Monday, he again referenced the privatisation of the BBL as a positive move for the sport.

"This year CA will report record revenue, profit, attendance and viewership, and most importantly a 40 per cent increase in participation over the past four years," Baird said.

"With recent decisions on the Big Bash I also believe the long-term sustainability is assured.

"I believe Australian cricket continues to be well lead by the CA board."

Baird's exit comes after Cricket NSW slammed the decision to allow privatisation earlier this month.

"This decision risks leaving cricket in NSW and Australia strategically and financially worse off, with direct consequences for our ability to invest in grassroots cricket," a Cricket NSW statement said.

World.title: Knights star sent to NRL judiciary for tackle that broke Cleary's leg
World.content:
Phoenix Crossland will have to argue his case at the NRL judiciary if he is to have any chance of playing in the grand final after he was cited for the hip drop that broke Nathan Cleary's leg.

The Newcastle hooker was sent off during the Knights' thrilling preliminary final win over the Penrith Panthers on Sunday and the match review committee referred him straight to the judiciary.

Crossland landed on Cleary's lower left leg as the Panthers superstar took on the line in the 36th minute at Stadium Australia and was wrapped up high by Knights back rower Francis Manuleleua.

The injury was immediately visible, and Manuleleua quickly signalled for medical attention.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

As Cleary was receiving medical attention, including painkillers via the famed green whistle, replays on the big screen prompted Penrith fans and players to urge referee Gerard Sutton to send Crossland off.

Sutton called out Crossland and explained the incident in detail to him and captain Kalyn Ponga.

"Initially he's up high, he makes a definite action to twist," Sutton said.

"[He] comes down on the leg with weight, there's extreme risk of serious injury. You're off."

Crossland will need a miracle to play in the grand final.

Crossland was dejected in the sheds before his team pulled off a stunning 22–14 comeback win to reach its first men's NRL grand final in 25 years, but was greeted on the field after the game, embraced by a number of his teammates.

He seems at long odds to take the field in the grand final against the Roosters on Sunday.

Dragons forward Ryan Couchman was referred straight to the judiciary in round three for a hip drop that ended the season of Parramatta's J'Maine Hopgood.

Couchman was suspended for four games for the tackle that left Hopgood with a torn ACL after a 90-minute hearing.

"Whilst the panel accepted that this did not incorporate any element of intention or recklessness, it took the view that the player's level of culpability was significant, a factor reflected in the serious injury sustained by the ball carrier," judiciary chair Geoff Bellew said.

But earlier this season, Broncos hooker Cory Paix was not penalised or charged for a tackle that left Manly prop Siosiua Taukeiaho with a visible leg injury similar to Cleary's, breaking both the fibular and tibia.

"It's a horrible injury and I'm sure I speak for all Manly fans in wishing Siua a speedy recovery," Manly chief executive Jason King said at the time.

The Sea Eagles reportedly queried the decision not to cite Paix with the NRL.

World.title: Ireland refuses handshake with Israel, wears black armbands for game
World.content:
There were no handshakes between Republic of Ireland and Israel players before their contentious Nations League match, with the Irish team wearing black armbands for its 3–0 victory.

The game faced bitter opposition in Ireland over Israel's actions in Gaza, with the players coming under huge pressure to boycott their two matches against Israel.

Reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazuno left the squad for both games on the eve of the first match because of what he said was his "personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong".

The Irish players looked down at the grass with their heads bowed and hands behind their backs during the playing of the Israeli national anthem.

And Irish captain Dara O'Shea approached the centre of the field for the pre-match talk with match officials and his opposite number with his hands still firmly clasped behind his back.

Republic of Ireland captain Dara O'Shea (left) shook officials' hands but not Israeli counterpart Manor Solomon. (Getty Images: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile)

O'Shea shook hands with the referee and his assistants, but there was no attempt to shake the hand of Israel captain Manor Solomon.

There was a small group of Israeli fans in the otherwise almost-empty stadium in Debrecen, Hungary, but an even smaller group of around 10 people without colours were celebrating when Troy Parrott broke the deadlock in the 13th minute.

There were not supposed to be any Irish fans present. Some Ireland supporters who managed to get tickets through the Israeli soccer federation told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that those had been cancelled before the game.

A smattering of Israeli fans heckled and abused Irish players. (Getty Images: Ben McShane/Sportsfile)

Adam Idah made it 2–0 three minutes after Parrott's opener and Jack Moylan got the third goal in the 25th.

Ireland needed goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher at his best to deny Israel after the break, and tempers became frayed around the hour mark after a clash between Idah and Raz Shlomo.

Both players were booked by German referee Harm Osmers.

Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was suspended for the game after his sending off following his goal celebration in Thursday's 3–1 loss to Austria.

Ireland and Israel meet again on October 4 in Ireland's "home" game in Backa Topola, Serbia.

World.title: Coach goes viral after smearing player's blood on own face
World.content:
Minnesota college football coach PJ Fleck's intensity was on full display after his team's win against Washington on the weekend.

"He's a crazy man," Golden Gophers linebacker Maverick Baranowski said of Fleck.

In the aftermath of the 27-24 win, Baranowski, who said he was hit by a boot on the last play of the game, was bleeding from his mouth. After the two embraced, Fleck grabbed the senior linebacker's head with two hands, then aggressively wiped the blood from Baranowski's mouth and brushed it on his own cheeks.

"Blood brother," said Fleck, who has coached Minnesota since 2017.

"Back in the day, I'm sure that's what they did — the frontiersmen out West. Little blood on there I guess."

Blood, sweat and tears helped the Gophers (3-1) get their first win on the road since a 24-7 victory at Wisconsin in November 2024.

"It's a great moment," Baranowski said.

"Winning's hard in the Big Ten, and when you get to win at a place like this, [it's] just so exciting, and [I] get to enjoy that with all my teammates and my head coach always having my back for the last five years. I love that guy more than anyone and [it was] an awesome opportunity to share that moment with him.

Receiver Javon Tracy, who had seven receptions for 41 yards and score, witnessed it firsthand.

"I would never do that, but PJ — he's different, man," Tracy said.

"Like, he's crazy. He's very energetic."

Fleck cleaned himself up, but had remnants of blood stains on his right white sleeve after the game.

Tech.title: Honor’s Magic 9 Pro Max has a big camera and a bigger battery
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Honor launches its new Magic 9 flagship phones in China today, and the 9 Pro Max features a design revamp, a capable camera, and a colossal battery.

This is Honor’s first flagship launch — Robot Phone aside — since it announced its collaboration with camera company Arri. The initial impact is twofold. The new camera island is Arri-inspired, drawing from the “three-lens turret” design first introduced in 1937’s Arriflex 35, complete with a knurled texture around the main lens.

Arri used variants of this three-lens turret design across most of its film cameras. Image: Honor

Arri has played a part in the camera itself, contributing the ability to shoot in Arri LogC3, together with 14 preset Arri Look LUTs, access to Arri’s wider library of official and third-party LUTs, and support for the APV 10-bit 4:2:2 codec. The cameras themselves include a 200-megapixel main lens using a 1/1.28-inch-type sensor, a 3.5x telephoto using the same resolution and a 1/1.4-inch sensor, and a 50-megapixel ultrawide — though this latter lens doesn’t support all the Arri Cinema Mode features. A “cinema-grade” directional microphone should help with video recording too. Less technically impressive, but just as useful, will be the square-format selfie camera, which like Apple’s Center Stage will be able to capture in either landscape or portrait.

Honor says that the wider camera island is more space-efficient, leaving extra space for a huge 8,800mAh battery, now up to 40 percent silicon content. The 9 Pro Max is powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. I asked Honor why it picked the Extreme version, given the 9 Pro Max doesn’t support the 8K60 or 4K240 video recording that chip enables, and was told it was “about delivering a complete and consistent flagship experience, rather than pursuing a single benchmark result.”

The Magic 9 Pro Max supports Honor’s G200 and G500 teleconverter lenses, plus a custom SmallRig video kit. Image: Honor

The Magic 9 series launches in China today. Honor has confirmed that an international launch is coming, but we’re still waiting to find out when.

Tech.title: Out of the Park Baseball lets me enjoy baseball even when the Mets suck
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

If you were to ask me what game or game series I’ve sunk the most time into, the answer would be easy: Out of the Park Baseball (OOTP). I have spent roughly 2,300 hours, according to Steam, playing various editions of the game. OOTP isn’t like MLB The Show or Super Mega Baseball. It’s not graphically impressive. It’s not a blast of simple arcade fun. It is basically a spreadsheet pretending to be a video game. It’s fantasy baseball, but without having to wait six months to see how disappointing that sleeper draft pick will be, because you can plow through an entire season in as little as a few hours.

You can play individual games and dig into play-by-play managing in OOTP if you want. But that becomes tedious. And frankly, it’s not where the game is the most fun. Instead, I think the game is at its best when you sit in the GM’s chair and maybe make some helpful “suggestions” about how to structure the lineup or bullpen.

The UI is complicated and dense. 90 percent of the time, you’re just looking at rows of stats and scouting reports. And the level of detail is deep. OOTP includes not just current MLB players, but historical MLB players, all minor league teams, Korea’s KBO League, and even the entire World Baseball Classic.

There’s something thrilling about digging through all this info and trying to find that diamond in the rough during a draft. Someone who might become the new franchise player for your favorite team in this alternate universe. Deciding whether to bet on that prospect developing into a superstar, or to trade them for an undeniable big-league All-Star is stressful. And you even have to worry about fans abandoning you if you fail to re-sign their favorite player.

On my Mets, Brandon Nimmo isn’t just a good player, he’s a damned superstar. Kodai Senga has won three Cy Young Awards. I signed Juan Soto, but also traded a raft of mid-tier prospects for Ronald Acuña Jr., made the playoffs four years in a row, and eventually won a World Series. (Look, as a Mets fan, I need this fantasy world, don’t harsh my vibe.)

Perhaps the best part of OOTP Baseball, though, is that it kinda lets you play however you want. It’s deeply customizable. You can manually play every game if you want. Or you can speed-simulate entire seasons in a couple of hours. Want an easier experience where players don’t get hurt? Turn down or off injuries. Don’t want to worry about budgets? Play in commissioner mode and tell the team owner where to stick it. And because it mostly just sits there, statically waiting for you, it’s easy to just leave it running in the background and dip in and out when you’ve got a few spare minutes.

OOTP Baseball is a cozy sim for a very particular brand of sports nerd. If you love fantasy baseball and wish you could play it year-round (and don’t want to deal with friends arguing about whether their bid for Alonso came in on time), or maybe you dig the idea of a cozy game like Tiny Bookshop, but wish they had a more Sabermetric bent, OOTP Baseball might be for you.

The current version, OOTP Baseball 27, is available now on Steam or directly from the developer.

Tech.title: Engram is a sampler that turns broken AI hallucinations into music
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Music startup Thoughtful Things has just launched the Kickstarter campaign for its first instrument, Engram. It’s a sampler and groovebox that uses AI to mangle incoming audio and even hallucinate completely new sounds. This isn’t Suno in a box, though. This isn’t a “push-button, get-song” device, aimed at creating something that sounds ready for top-40 radio. It’s about creating experimental, uncanny sounds and pushing AI audio models beyond their limits.

Engram isn’t connected to the internet. Instead, it runs a “tiny AI” locally. According to the Kickstarter listing, the model is designed in-house and custom-trained. The company says:

“We’ve trained our audio models on open datasets that only contain audio licensed for commercial use (CC-BY or similar). We have not trained and will never train our models on non-commercial, pirated, or otherwise stolen data.”

The company also plans to open up Engram’s firmware so that others can tweak it or load their own custom models. In the campaign video, founder Evan King uses his voice to ask for “piano,” and Engram spits out something glitchy and vaguely piano-like. He says to think of Engram as a “field recorder for latent space.” It’s about exploring the world of AI hallucinations and experimental sound design. It even draws inspiration from circuit bending, allowing you to tweak and even break its tiny AI models.

Thoughtful Things is launching with a limited run of Engrams for the Kickstarter campaign, starting at $675. The company hasn’t said what the retail price will be, though it’s likely to be between $850 and $900, as the $675 pledge is listed as a 30 percent discount.

Tech.title: OpenAI agents tried to ‘bruteforce’ a UN website
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to Howard-Jones, the agents were likely tasked with retrieving publicly available data related to the Productive Capacities Index (PCI) through the UNCTADstat API. However, the agents did not appear to have direct API access and were limited in their ability to pull data from UNCTADstat because of restrictions on their HTTP tools.

The agents eventually worked out a way to bypass their limitations and start pulling data from the site, but still encountered some errors. At this point, the AI went from creative to deceptive. Believing that the errors were due to its requests being caught by a nonexistent filter, it started to mask its behavior. It eventually realized it could hijack Google’s XSS game (a cross-site scripting learning tool) to accomplish its goals. The agents resorted to increasingly aggressive tactics to get access to UN data.

OpenAI and the UN did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Why OLPC’s $100 laptop never stood a chance
Tech.content:
The idea was big, exciting, and inspiring: What if we could get every kid in the world access to a computer? For a bunch of thinkers and executives in Silicon Valley, it felt like the way to fix everything. But the One Laptop Per Child initiative, and the XO-1 laptop designed to be given away, were both more complicated than anyone expected.

In the next episode of Version History, David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Adi Robertson and tech journalist David Imel to figure out why OLPC didn’t work, whether there’s anything to learn from the XO-1’s innovative design, and if this kind of computer giveaway could ever succeed.

I asked Brad to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:

The phone: Pixel 9 Pro XL

The wallpaper: My homescreen wallpaper is just an included Pixel wallpaper of plants in mellow green tones. My lockscreen is a fan-made Tekken Tag Tournament poster featuring Armor King and Modelo. It doesn’t have to make sense if the vibes are right.

The apps:

Right up top you’ll find two of my favorite mobile games. The first is Idle Obelisk Miner , an idle game I recently started playing that I’ve found compelling and generous given the genre’s normal conditions. My dark secret is that, if you swipe one page to the right, it’s all a disorganized mess of apps with no sorting or folders. If I’m looking for a specific app, I’ll swipe up and search for it.

I also asked Brad to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:

Ever since the final major Destiny 2 update, I’ve been chiseling away at some of the expansions I missed and finishing up old collections. With the recent announcement that old vaulted content would be coming back, I’m planning on continuing to sink time into one of my favorite games ever.

For music, I’ve been on a really chill kick lately, with Janelle Monáe’s The Age of Pleasure and Tom Misch’s Full Circle headlining a lot of my morning writing and deal-hunting sessions. I’ve been listening to a lot of vinyl recently, which I’ve found gives a nice rhythm and ritual to my day that just turning on Spotify and hitting shuffle doesn’t.
